questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Vector to a Plane Curve
questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy).$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡xy \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(0,\frac{\pi }{2})={f}_{y}(0,\frac{\pi }{2})i-{f}_{x}(0,\frac{\pi }{2})j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))\,j \\  & =(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))\,j \\ t(0,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0\operatorname{cos}⁡(0\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))j \\  & =-i+\frac{\pi }{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-i+\frac{\pi }{2}\,j.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Vector to a Plane Curve
questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $x+1={x}^{2}y.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={x}^{2}y \\ {x}^{2}y-x-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y-x-1$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,2)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,2)={f}_{y}(1,2)i-{f}_{x}(1,2)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-x-1)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-x-1)j \\  & ={x}^{2}\,i-(2xy-1)j \\ t(1,2) & =(1)^{2}\,i-(2(1)(2)-1)j \\  & =i-3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $i-3\,j.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Points on a Curve at which the Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to a Given Vector
questions.problem: At which points on the curve $2xy-3{x}^{2}=-y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy-3{x}^{2}=-y \\ 2xy-3{x}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2xy-3{x}^{2}+y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-3{x}^{2}+y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-3{x}^{2}+y)j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i-2(y-3x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j$, we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((2x+1)\,i-2(y-3x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -2(y-3x) & =0 \\ y & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=3x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy-3{x}^{2}+y & =0 \\ 2x(3x)-3{x}^{2}+3x & =0 \\ 6{x}^{2}-3{x}^{2}+3x & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}+3x & =0 \\ 3x(x+1) & =0 \\ x & =0\,\text{or}\,x=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=0$, we get $y=0$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=-3$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,-3).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Vector to a Plane Curve
questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $xy=3-{x}^{2}-{y}^{3}.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-1,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & =3-{x}^{2}-{y}^{3} \\ xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,-1)={f}_{y}(-1,-1)i-{f}_{x}(-1,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3})j \\  & =(x+3{y}^{2})i-(y+2x)j \\ t(-1,-1) & =(-1+3(-1)^{2})i-(-1+2(-1))j \\  & =2\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $2\,i+3\,j.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of Rank Greater Than One
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $B$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(4+\lambda )(\lambda -5)^{4}(\lambda +2)^{7},$ and for the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ there are exactly $4$ eigenvectors. If a basis of ${R}^{12}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $B$, how many of these generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2?$
questions.worked_solution:
The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is equal to the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda .$

In the characteristic polynomial

$$
p(\lambda )=(4+\lambda )(\lambda -5)^{4}(\lambda +2)^{7},
$$

we see that the root $\lambda =-2$ has multiplicity $7.$ So the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ is $7.$

However, there are only $4$ eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ so the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ is $4.$

Therefore, the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ corresponding to $\lambda =-2$ is $7-4=3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of a Given Rank Using Nullity
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $C$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(4+\lambda )(\lambda -3)^{4}(\lambda +6)^{17},$ the nullity of $(C+6I)^{3}$ equals $2,$ and the nullity of $(C+6I)^{4}$ equals $6.$ If a basis of ${R}^{22}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $C$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-6?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $C$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =-6,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(C+6I)^{4}v=0\,\text{and}\,(C+6I)^{3}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(C+6I)^{3}$ has dimension $2.$ This means that the solutions to $(C+6I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $2.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(C+6I)^{4}$ has dimension $6.$ This means that the solutions to $(C+6I)^{4}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $6.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(C+6I)^{3}$ is a subspace of dimension $2$ in $\text{Null}(C+6I)^{4}$, which is a subspace of dimension $6,$ our basis can contain only $4$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(C+6I)^{4}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(C+6I)^{3}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(C+6I)^{4}-\text{nullity}(C+6I)^{3}=6-2=4
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-6.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of a Given Rank
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $C$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(\lambda -\sqrt{3})^{18}(\lambda +3)^{7},$ the rank of $(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{6}$ equals $8,$ and the rank of $(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{5}$ equals $10.$ If a basis of ${R}^{25}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $C$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $6$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $C$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3},$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $6$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{6}v=0\,\text{and}\,(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{5}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice that $C$ must be a $25\times 25$ matrix.

- Since the rank of $(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{5}$ equals $10,$ then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{5}=25-10=15.
$$

So, the solutions to $(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{5}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{5}$ of dimension $15$ in ${R}^{25}.$

- Since the rank of $(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{6}$ equals $8,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{6}=25-8=17.
$$

So, the solutions to $(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{6}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{6}$ of dimension $17$ in ${R}^{25}.$

Since $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{5}$ is a subspace of dimension $15$ in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{6}$, which is a subspace of dimension $17,$ our basis can contain only $2$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{6}$ but do not lie in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{5}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{6}-\text{nullity}(C-\sqrt{3}I)^{5}=17-15=2
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $6$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3}.$

For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda = 9,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ is a vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that 

$$
(A - 9I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\quad \textrm{and} \quad
(A - 9I)^3 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.
$$

Notice that $A$ must be a $14 \times 14$ matrix.

- Since the rank of $(A-9I)^3$ equals $9,$ then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-9I)^3 = 14-9 = 5.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A - 9I)^3 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-9I)^3$ of dimension $5$ in $\mathbb{R}^{14}.$

- Since the rank of $(A-9I)^4$ equals $7,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-9I)^4 = 14-7 = 7.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A - 9I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-9I)^4$ of dimension $7$ in $\mathbb{R}^{14}.$

Since $\text{Null}(A-9I)^3$ is a subspace of dimension $5$ in $\text{Null}(A-9I)^4$, which is a subspace of dimension $7,$ our basis can contain only $2$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(A-9I)^4$ but not in $\text{Null}(A-9I)^3.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-9I)^4 - \text{nullity}(A-9I)^3 = 7-5=2
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=9.$

questions.problem:
A compact geological sensor of mass $6\,\text{kg}$ is launched vertically downward with an initial velocity of $1.8\,\text{m/s}.$ Let $v(t)$ be the sensor's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after release, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance acting on the sensor is negligible, and the only other force acting on it is its weight due to gravity.

What is the velocity of the sensor after $3$ seconds? Assume that acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

The velocity after $3$ seconds is
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a:$

$$
F=ma
$$

Since air resistance is negligible, the only force acting on the sensor is its weight due to gravity. The weight $w$ of the sensor is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =w \\  & =mg \\  & =6g.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\frac{dv}{dt}.$  Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the sensor, we get

$$
6g=6\,\frac{dv}{dt}.
$$

Simplifying and writing in standard form, we get

$$
\frac{dv}{dt}=g.
$$

Next, we integrate to solve for $v(t),$ as follows:

$$
\int \frac{dv}{dt}\,dt=g\int dt
$$

$$
v(t)=gt+C
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration. We're told that the initial velocity of the sensor is $1.8\,\text{m/s}.$ So, we apply the initial condition $v(0)=1.8$ and solve for $C:$

$$
v(0)=g\cdot 0+C
$$

$$
1.8=0+C
$$

$$
C=1.8
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the sensor $t$ seconds after release is

$$
v(t)=gt+1.8.
$$

Finally, the velocity after $3$ seconds is

$$
v(3)=9.8\cdot 3+1.8=31.2\,\text{m/s}.
$$

questions.problem:
A supply pod of mass $30\,\text{kg}$ free-falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the pod's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after the descent began, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the pod is proportional to its velocity with a constant of proportionality $k>0$ and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Which differential equation best models the velocity? Assume that the acceleration due to gravity is $g,$ and the only forces acting on the pod are the weight due to gravity and drag.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a:$

$$
F=ma
$$

In our case, there are two forces acting on the pod:

- The force due to gravity, given by the weight $w$ of the pod, which equals

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =mg \\  & =30g\end{aligned}
$$

- The force due to drag (air resistance) $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity of the pod (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D=-kv,
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Note that, since the drag, in $N=\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2},$ is the product of the constant $k$ and velocity, in $\text{m/s},$ the units of $k$ are

$$
\frac{\text{N}}{\text{m/s}}=\frac{\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2}}{\text{m/s}}=\text{kg/s}.
$$

Summing the forces, the resultant force acting on the pod is

$$
F=w+D=30g-kv.
$$

Also, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\frac{dv}{dt}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the pod, we have

$$
30g-kv=30\,\frac{dv}{dt}.
$$

Finally, simplifying and writing in standard form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}30\,\frac{dv}{dt}+kv & =30g \\ \frac{dv}{dt}+\frac{k}{30}v & =g.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A cargo sensor of mass $40\,\text{kg}$ is released from rest and falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the sensor's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after release, with downward taken as the positive direction. The air resistance on the sensor is proportional to its velocity and acts in the direction opposite to motion. At a particular moment during the fall, the sensor’s velocity is $10\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $8.3\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Find, rounded to one decimal place, the velocity of the cargo sensor after $5$ seconds. Assume that only gravity, $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ and drag act on the sensor.

The velocity of the cargo sensor after $5$ seconds is
{{field-1}}$\,\text{m/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that only two forces act on the sensor: the force due to gravity, given by the weight

$$
w=mg=40\cdot 9.8=392\,\text{N},
$$

and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity (and negative since it acts in the negative direction),

$$
D=-kv,
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Hence, the resultant force acting on the sensor is

$$
F=w+D=392-kv.
$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 392-kv & =40\,\frac{dv}{dt} \\ \frac{dv}{dt}+\frac{k}{40}v & =9.8\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that, at a particular moment, the sensor’s velocity is $10\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $8.3\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting these values into the ODE, we can solve for $k:$

$$
8.3+\frac{k}{40}\cdot 10=9.8\,⟹\,k=6\,\text{kg/s}
$$

Therefore, we have the following differential equation:

$$
\frac{dv}{dt}+\frac{3}{20}v=9.8
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${v}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{v}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{3}{20}{v}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{v}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-3t/20},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{v}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${v}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{v}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{3}{20}\alpha =9.8\,⟹\,\alpha =\frac{196}{3}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${v}_{p}(t)=\frac{196}{3}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
v(t)={v}_{c}(t)+{v}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-3t/20}+\frac{196}{3}.
$$

We're told that the sensor is released from rest. So, we can apply the initial condition $v(0)=0,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =A{e}^{-3(0)/20}+\frac{196}{3} \\ 0 & =A+\frac{196}{3} \\ A & =-\frac{196}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $v(t):$

$$
v(t)=-\frac{196}{3}{e}^{-3t/20}+\frac{196}{3}
$$

Finally, the velocity of the cargo sensor after $t=5$ seconds is

$$
v(5)=-\frac{196}{3}{e}^{-15/20}+\frac{196}{3}=34.472…≈34.5\,\text{m/s},
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.problem:
A body of mass $12\,\text{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v$ be its velocity, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the body is proportional to its velocity and acts in the opposite direction to the motion.
At a particular moment during the fall, the body’s velocity is $10\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $6.3\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

What is the terminal velocity ${v}_{\text{term}}$ of the body? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ and the only forces acting on the body are the weight due to gravity and drag.

${v}_{\text{term}}=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
Terminal velocity is the constant speed a falling object approaches as the upward resistive force (drag) grows to exactly balance the downward gravitational force.
That is, at terminal velocity (a constant), acceleration is zero, so by $F=ma,$ the resultant force is zero.

First, note that only two forces act on the body: the force due to gravity, given by the weight

$$
w=mg=12\cdot 9.8=117.6\,\text{N},
$$

and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity (and negative since it acts in the negative direction),

$$
D=-kv,
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Hence, the resultant force acting on the body is

$$
F=w+D=117.6-kv.
$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 117.6-kv & =12a\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that, at a particular moment, the body’s velocity is $10\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $6.3\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}117.6-10k & =12\cdot 6.3 \\ 117.6-10k & =75.6 \\ -10k & =-42 \\ k & =4.2\,\text{kg/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the resultant force acting on the body is

$$
F=117.6-4.2v.
$$

When the body reaches terminal velocity ${v}_{\text{term}},$ the resultant force is zero:

$$
117.6-4.2{v}_{\text{term}}=0\,⟹\,{v}_{\text{term}}=\frac{117.6}{4.2}=28
$$

Therefore, the terminal velocity of the body is ${v}_{\text{term}}=28\,\text{m/s}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
A cryogenic sample container of mass $31\,\textrm{kg}$ is launched vertically downward with an initial velocity of $2.9\,\textrm{m/s}.$ Let $v(t)$ be the container's velocity, in meters per second, $t \geq 0$ seconds after release, with downward taken as the positive direction.
 The air resistance acting on the container is negligible, and the only other force acting on it is its weight due to gravity. 

What is the velocity of the container after $7$ seconds? Assume that acceleration due to gravity is $g = 9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a{:}$

$$
F = ma
$$

Since air resistance is negligible, the only force acting on the body is its weight due to gravity. The weight $w$ of the body is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =w \\  & =mg \\  & =31g.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the container, we get

$$
31g = 31\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Simplifying and writing in standard form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dv}{dt} & =g.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate to solve for $v(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{dv}{dt}\,dt & =g\int dt \\ v(t) & =gt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.
We're told that the initial velocity of the container is $2.9\,\textrm{m/s}.$ So, we apply the initial condition $v(0) = 2.9,$ and solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0)=g\cdot 0+C \\ 2.9=0+C \\ C=2.9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the container $t$ seconds after release is

$$
v(t) = gt + 2.9.
$$

Finally, the velocity after $7$ seconds is

$$
v(7) = 9.8\cdot7 + 2.9 = 71.5 \,\textrm{m/s}.
$$

A geological sampler of mass $15\,\textrm{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the sampler's velocity, in meters per second, $t \geq 0$ seconds after the descent began, with downward taken as the positive direction.

At a particular moment during the fall, the sampler’s velocity is $9\,\textrm{m/s}$ and instantaneous acceleration is $7.4\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$

Find the constant of proportionality $k,$ and the differential equation that best models the velocity. Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g = 9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2,$ and the only forces acting on the sampler are weight due to gravity and drag.

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a{:}$

$$
F = ma
$$

In our case, there are two forces acting on the body:

- The force due to gravity, given by the weight $w$ of the body, which equals

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =mg \\  & =15g.\end{aligned}
$$

- The force due to drag (air resistance) $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity of the body (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D = -kv,
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Note that, since the drag, in $N=\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2,$ is the product of the constant $k$ and velocity, in $\text{m/s},$ the units of $k$ are

$$
\dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m/s}} = \dfrac{\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2}{\text{m/s}} = \text{kg/s}.
$$

Summing the forces, the resultant force acting on the body is

$$
F = w + D = 15g - kv.
$$

Also, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the body, we have

$$
15g - kv = 15\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Writing in standard form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}15\,\frac{dv}{dt}+kv & =15g \\ \frac{dv}{dt}+\frac{k}{15}v & =g.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we're given that, at a particular moment, the body's velocity is $9\,\textrm{m/s}$ and instantaneous acceleration is $7.4\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$
So, substituting $v=9, g = 9.8,$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = 7.4$ into our model, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}7.4+\frac{k}{15}\cdot 9 & =9.8 \\ 7.4+\frac{3k}{5} & =9.8 \\ \frac{3k}{5} & =2.4 \\ k & =4\,\text{kg/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the differential equation that models the velocity is

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac4{15}v = g.
$$

\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 313.6-kv & =32\,\frac{dv}{dt} \\ \frac{dv}{dt}+\frac{k}{32}v & =9.8\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that, at a particular moment, the body’s velocity is $8\,\textrm{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $7.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Substituting these values into the ODE, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
7.8 + \dfrac{k}{32}\cdot 8 = 9.8
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = 8\,\textrm{kg/s}
$$

Therefore, we have the following differential equation:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac14v = 9.8
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $v_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac14v_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
v_c(t) = Ae^{-t/4},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
v_p(t) = \alpha.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute $v_p=\alpha$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = (\alpha)' = 0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0 + \dfrac14\alpha = 9.8
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \alpha = \dfrac{196}{5}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is $v_p(t) = \dfrac{196}{5}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
v(t) = v_c(t) + v_p(t) = Ae^{-t/4} + \dfrac{196}{5}.
$$

We're told that the body is launched downward with an initial velocity of $7\,\textrm{m/s}.$ So, we can apply the initial condition $v(0) = 7,$ and solve for $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =A{e}^{-0/4}+\frac{196}{5} \\ 7 & =A+\frac{196}{5} \\ A & =-\frac{161}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $v(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =-\frac{161}{5}{e}^{-t/4}+\frac{196}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Terminal Velocity
canonical_examples.problem:
A sensor pod of mass $20\,\textrm{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v$ be its velocity, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the pod is proportional to its velocity and acts in the opposite direction to the motion.
At a particular moment during the fall, the pod’s velocity is $8\,\textrm{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $6.3\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$

What is the terminal velocity $v_\text{term}$ of the pod? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g = 9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2,$ and the only forces acting on the pod are the weight due to gravity and drag.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Terminal velocity is the constant speed a falling object approaches as the upward resistive force (drag) grows to exactly balance the downward gravitational force.
That is, at terminal velocity (a constant), acceleration is zero, so by $F=ma,$ the resultant force is zero.

First, note that only two forces act on the pod: the force due to gravity, given by the weight

$$
w = mg = 20\cdot9.8 = 196\,\textrm{N},
$$

and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity (and negative since it acts in the negative direction),

$$
D=-kv,
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Hence, the resultant force acting on the pod is

$$
F = w + D = 196 - kv.
$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 196-kv & =20a\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that, at a particular moment, the pod’s velocity is $8\,\textrm{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $6.3\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Substituting these values into the above, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}196-8k & =20\cdot 6.3 \\ 196-8k & =126 \\ -8k & =-70 \\ k & =8.75\,\text{kg/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the resultant force acting on the pod is

$$
F = 196 - 8.75v.
$$

When the pod reaches terminal velocity $v_\text{term},$ the resultant force is zero:

$$
196 - 8.75v_\text{term} = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
v_\text{term} = \dfrac{196}{8.75} = 22.4
$$

Therefore, the terminal velocity of the pod is $v_\text{term} = 22.4\,\textrm{m/s}.$

questions.problem:
| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ |

Compute $P(X=1\,|\,Y=6)$ given that the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above.
questions.worked_solution:
By the multiplication law for conditional probability, the required conditional probability is given by

$$
P(X=1\,|\,Y=6)=\frac{P(X=1,Y=6)}{P(Y=6)}=\frac{f(1,6)}{{f}_{Y}(6)},
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal distribution of $Y.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(6) & =f(1,6)+f(3,6) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8} \\  & =\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given table, we have that $f(1,6)=\frac{1}{4}.$ 

Finally, substituting ${f}_{Y}(6)=\frac{3}{8}$ and $f(1,6)=\frac{1}{4}$ in our formula above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=1\,|\,Y=6) & =\frac{f(1,6)}{{f}_{Y}(6)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{4})}{(\frac{3}{8})} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, we're required to compute the conditional probability

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(4\,|\,2)=P(X=4\,|\,Y=2).
$$

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(X=4\,|\,Y=2)=\frac{P(X=4,Y=2)}{P(Y=2)}=\frac{f(4,2)}{{f}_{Y}(2)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal distribution of $Y.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(2) & =f(2,2)+f(4,2) \\  & =0.4+0.15 \\  & =0.55.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals. Thus,

$$

$$

$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Parametric Form
questions.problem:
The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=3v-7u+7,\,y=v-2u+3.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax+by-2,\,v=-2x+7y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3v-7u+7 \\ v-2u+3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7u+3v \\ -2u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-7 & 3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1\cdot (-7)-3\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 2 & -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 2 & -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-7 \\ y-3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1\cdot (x-7)+3\cdot (y-3) \\ -2\cdot (x-7)+7\cdot (y-3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-x+3y-2 \\ -2x+7y-7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=(-1)x+3y-2,\,v=-2x+7y+(-7).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-1+3+(-7)=-5.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Type I Regions
questions.problem:
![](images/d1/d1c2f0e830c6d3beca27886e839816f46a00be322c9d7cff18248d118ed0e617.png)

Which of the following represents the shaded region above as a type I region in two-dimensional space?
questions.worked_solution:
A type I region can be written as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,a\le x\le b,\,g(x)\le y\le f(x)},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type I region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $x:$

$$
x=\sqrt{3-y}+1\,⟹\,y=3-(x-1)^{2}
$$

The function $y=0$ is already written as a function of $x.$

Notice that the region lies between the vertical lines $x=1$ and $x=2.$ So, we have $0\le x\le 1.$

We draw a vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower function $g(x)$ and the upper function $f(x).$ A vertical line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type I region.

![](images/be/be799df2140d3a437bb311427dcae0e297cb6bd3844f88932157eb6ace6e7e59.png)

The vertical line enters the region through the lower function $y=0$ and leaves through the upper function $y=3-(x-1)^{2}.$ So, we have $0\le y\le 3-(x-1)^{2}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3-(x-1)^{2}}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Center of Mass for a Collection of Masses Along the X-Axis
questions.problem: Consider the collection of point masses ${m}_{1}=4\,\text{kg},$ ${m}_{2}=6\,\text{kg},$ and ${m}_{3}=8\,\text{kg}$ located at ${x}_{1}=-3,$ ${x}_{2}=-1,$ and ${x}_{3}=3,$ respectively, along the $x$-axis, where the $x$-coordinates are measured in meters. What is the $x$-coordinate of the center of mass for this system?
questions.worked_solution:
The center of mass, denoted $\overset{―}{x},$ of a collection of point masses ${m}_{1},{m}_{2},…,{m}_{n}$ located at ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ along the $x$-axis is given by 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m},
$$

 

where 

- $m={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}$ is the total mass of the system,

- ${M}_{O}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{x}_{i}$ is the total moment of the system about the origin $O.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =4, & \,{m}_{2} & =6, & \,{m}_{3} & =8, \\ {x}_{1} & =-3, & \,{x}_{2} & =-1, & \,{x}_{3} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the total mass of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i} \\  & ={m}_{1}+{m}_{2}+{m}_{3} \\  & =4+6+8 \\  & =18\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

and the moment of the system about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & ={m}_{1}{x}_{1}+{m}_{2}{x}_{2}+{m}_{3}{x}_{3} \\  & =4\cdot (-3)+6\cdot (-1)+8\cdot 3 \\  & =-12-6+24 \\  & =6\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m}=\frac{6}{18}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Sum and Constant Multiple Rules
questions.worked_solution:
The sum and constant multiple rules for double summations state that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}+{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{b}_{ij}, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}k{a}_{ij} & =k{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying these rules to the given sum, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}2({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}) & =2{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}) \\  & =2{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}{a}_{ij}+2{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}{b}_{ij} \\  & =2\cdot 75+2\cdot 70 \\  & =150+140 \\  & =290.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Interior of a Set
questions.problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined by 

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,-1\le y<0}.
$$

The interior of $A$ is given by

$$
\text{int}\,A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<x<2,\,\,}.
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](images/fc/fc71859cb4d1e58ea3d15c2da66bce014898281fe237f2e0c2396f96c84c9e79.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.

![](images/ef/eff037b96b6a42120fdfa112a98d1e0749cdd56bd89acd647db448b08d7323ad.png)

So, in this case, the interior of $A$ is given by

$$
\text{int}\,A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<x<2,\,-1<y<0\,}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Function Is a Valid PDF
questions.problem:
![](images/8f/8f955ee719a4e69f0d09c678f0a74023f137efd7b5ae36d49b98706156384173.png)

Consider the function $f(x)$ whose graph is shown above.

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}x+\frac{1}{2},\, & 0<x<1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$
- ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$
- $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. From the graph, we see that $f(x)$ is nonnegative for all $x.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}]-[\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+\frac{0}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statements I and II are true, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the integral $\int 3x{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 3x{e}^{-x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=3 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-x}\, & ⟹\,v=-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3x\cdot {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & =3x\cdot (-{e}^{-x})-\int (-{e}^{-x})\cdot 3\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3x{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & =-3x{e}^{-x}+3\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3x{e}^{-x}-3{e}^{-x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}-\int (\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/4}x{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x & ={\frac{1}{4}x{e}^{4x}|}_{0}^{1/4}-\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1/4}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{4}x{e}^{4x}|}_{0}^{1/4}-{\frac{1}{16}{e}^{4x}|}_{0}^{1/4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4(1/4)}-0\cdot {e}^{4\cdot 0}]-\frac{1}{16}[{e}^{4(1/4)}-{e}^{4\cdot 0}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\frac{e}{4}-0]-\frac{1}{16}[e-1] \\  & =\frac{e}{16}-\frac{e}{16}+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Unions and Intersections of (Countably) Infinite Families of Indexed Sets
questions.worked_solution:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for at least one }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=1,$ we have ${X}_{1}={1}$

- if $i=2,$ we have ${X}_{2}={1,2}$

- if $i=3,$ we have ${X}_{3}={1,2,3}$

and so on. 

Notice that ${X}_{i}$ contain all the integers between $1$ and $i.$ So, every natural number $i$ belong to the sets ${X}_{i},\,{X}_{i+1},\,{X}_{i+2},…$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}=N.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Inverting a Permutation Matrix
questions.problem:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The given matrix can be obtained from the identity matrix by permuting its columns. Therefore, $A$ is a permutation matrix.

The inverse of a permutation matrix can be found as follows: 

$$
{P}^{-1}={P}^{T}
$$

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
questions.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $F(-5,-2,4)$ and $G(3,-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $F$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=f+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $f$ is the position vector of $F.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $F(-5,-2,4)$ and $G(3,-1,1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{FG} \\  & =⟨3,-1,1⟩-⟨-5,-2,4⟩ \\  & =⟨8,1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine
questions.problem:
![](images/fc/fc3c0c02be98834937150e6bee5a52ac14246bc128b189d3c095269f788d97a9.png)

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{x}^{2}+6,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{4},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{x}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rewrite the above formula as

$$
-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x=-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x).
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{x}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+{x}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+6x)\,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =[-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\frac{(\pi /4)^{3}}{3}+6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}]-[-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )+\frac{(-\pi /4)^{3}}{3}+6(-\frac{\pi }{4})] \\  & =(0+\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{192}+\frac{3\pi }{2})-(0-\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{192}-\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{96}+3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Singular Matrices
questions.problem:
Which of the matrices below does **not** have an inverse?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
- The matrix $A$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix. So, it is not invertible.

- For the matrix $B$, we have

$$
det(B)=4\cdot (-1)-(-2)\cdot 3=2.
$$

Because $det(B)\ne 0,$ we conclude that $B$ is invertible.

- For the matrix $C$, we have

$$
det(C)=4\cdot 9-3\cdot 12=0.
$$

Because $det(C)=0,$ we conclude that $C$ is not invertible.

Therefore, only $A$ and $C$ do not have an inverse.

questions.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression
questions.problem: $\int (2x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int (2x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x+3\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (2x+3)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =(2x+3)\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =-(2x+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+2\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(2x+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Reduced Row Echelon Form of a Singular 3x3 System With Two Pivots
questions.problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3x-3y+6z=9 \\ -x+4z=4 \\ x+y-2z=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
questions.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 6 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & 4 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Transforming $M$ into reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 6 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & 4 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 & -3 \\ -1 & 0 & 4 & 4 \\ -3 & -3 & 6 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -3 & -3 & 6 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the row echelon form above, we have only two pivots (in the $1$st and $2$nd columns). To transform the matrix to reduced row echelon form, we need to create zeros above the pivots only. This gives,

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -4 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-4z=-4 \\ y+2z=1 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final equation, we can remove this equation from the system. 

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4z-4 \\ y=1-2z \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4z-4 \\ 1-2z \\ z\end{aligned}],\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What surface is defined by the equation $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{12}$ in spherical polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We write the position of a point (vector) in spherical polar coordinates as $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ),$ where 

- $\rho \ge 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

- $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

With that in mind, let's examine our equation:

$$
\theta =\frac{5\pi }{12}
$$

This equation specifies that for any point on the surface, the angle that the corresponding vector makes with the positive $x$-axis must equal $\frac{5\pi }{12}.$ On the other hand, $\rho $ and $ϕ$ can vary arbitrarily in their respective domains. 

Therefore, since $\rho \ge 0,$ our surface is a half-plane.

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$

$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =4\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

- $\rho \in [0,4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ]$

- $\theta \in [0,\pi ]$

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$

Therefore, we have

$$
{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing Part of a Shifted Sphere in Spherical Coordinates
questions.problem:
![](images/9a/9ae8e3cb2b2554ec3bff9a4912cdca39d12acbfd7dcb93bf44248a35dccc3dfa.png)

The solid enclosed by the quarter-sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+2z=0$ for $x\ge 0$ and $y\ge 0,$ shown above, can be described in spherical polar coordinates as
questions.worked_solution:
We write the position of a point (vector) in spherical polar coordinates as $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ),$ where 

- $\rho \ge 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

- $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $(0,0,-1).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+2z=0$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+2z & =0 \\ {\rho }^{2}+2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & =0 \\ \rho (\rho +2\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/14/1499d492c526bad77e81aca1128b6160cc574a209ad7706e8d89b3012112e1df.png)

 

Notice that inside our region, the spherical polar coordinates vary within the following domains:

- $\rho \in [0,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]$

- $\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]$

- $ϕ\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]$

Therefore, we have

$$
{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le -2\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

$$

$$
questions.worked_solution:
The given matrix can be obtained from the identity matrix by permuting its columns. Therefore, $A$ is a permutation matrix.

$$
{P}^{-1}={P}^{T}

questions.problem:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we're given a Frobenius matrix:

- all entries on the main diagonal are ones

- the matrix has only one column (the $2$nd column) where some entries below the main diagonal are not zeros

- all the other entries outside the main diagonal are zeros

To find the inverse of a Frobenius matrix, we simply take the non-zero entries outside the main diagonal with opposite signs. 

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE With Polynomial Forcing
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+7y=14.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-7x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$y(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}+7{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-7x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\beta 
$$

where $\beta $ is a constant to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

To find the value of $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
0+7\beta =14
$$

Solving this equation gives $\beta =2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=2.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-7x}+2.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Classifying Recurrence Relations
questions.problem:
Which of the following recurrence relations are first-order?

- ${a}_{n}=4{a}_{n-1}+7$
- ${b}_{n}={b}_{n-1}+3{b}_{n-3}$
- ${c}_{n}=5{c}_{n-1}-2n$
questions.worked_solution:
The order of a recurrence relation is the largest index difference between ${a}_{n}$ and the preceding terms in the relation.

Let's examine each recurrence relation in turn.

- The largest index difference between ${a}_{n}$ and the preceding term ${a}_{n-1}$ in the relation is $1.$ So, this recurrence relation has order $1.$

- The largest index difference between ${b}_{n}$ and the preceding terms ${b}_{n-1}$ and ${b}_{n-3}$ in the relation is $3.$ So, this recurrence relation has order $3.$

- The largest index difference between ${c}_{n}$ and the preceding term ${c}_{n-1}$ in the relation is $1.$ So, this recurrence relation has order $1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\,{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{4}){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{4})-(-\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )}{4}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity 

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡t=\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying Differential Operators With Functions of X as Coefficients
questions.problem: Given that $D={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+3x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x},$ what is $D(y)$ for $y=\frac{1}{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The given operator is a third-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={f}_{3}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y.
$$

with ${f}_{3}={x}^{2},{f}_{2}=3x,{f}_{1}=-1,$ and ${f}_{0}=0.$

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D(y) & =D(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =({x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+3x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x})(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}(\frac{1}{x})+3x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(\frac{1}{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})+3x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})-(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})+3x(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{6}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{6}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using the Sign of the Slopes
questions.problem:
![](images/f9/f915caf118419deb78dc0b34f9bba0a977c01989c08a632fb2ae39b669f070e7.png)

The diagram shown above is the slope field for which of the following differential equations?
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/26/26137173c268215296020c7768cf43748b1c3fcdc06d73fe1f3ecfda7f515d58.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $y=-3$ and $y=1.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should equal zero on both of these lines.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(y+3)(1-y) \\ {y}^{′} & =-(y+3)(y-1)^{2} \\ {y}^{′} & =y(y+3)(y-1)\end{aligned}
$$

We can dismiss the equation ${y}^{′}=y(y+3)(y-1).$ Although the right-hand side evaluates to zero at $y=-3$ and $y=1,$ it also evaluates to zero when $y=0,$ which is behavior not exhibited by our slope field.

- Second, the lines $y=-3$ and $y=1$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<-3$ | $-3<y<1$ | $y>1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↘$ | $↗$ | $↘$ |
| Sign | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=(y+3)(1-y).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=(y+3)(1-y).$

questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)={x}^{3},$ $n=2,$ and $\lambda =5.$
Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first $2-1=1$ derivatives of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(5)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(5) & {f}^{′}(5) \\ 0 & f(5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{5}^{3} & 3\cdot {5}^{2} \\ 0 & {5}^{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}125 & 75 \\ 0 & 125\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Decomposition
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
E=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $E=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E).$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)$ and the given matrix $E,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi PJ{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi J)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $2$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).$ So, we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E)=[\begin{aligned}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi ) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi ) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 3-1\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}cos(\pi E) & =P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi J))\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

| ${({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(5))}^{2}=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} | $1$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $25$ | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-5}} |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(5))}^{2} & ={([\begin{aligned}{J}_{1}(3) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}(5)\end{aligned}])}^{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{({J}_{1}(3))}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {({J}_{3}(5))}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={({J}_{1}(3))}^{2}\,⊕\,{({J}_{3}(5))}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(3),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =3.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(3)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{3}(5),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{2} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(5)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(5) & {f}^{′}(5) & \frac{{f}^{″}(5)}{2} \\ 0 & f(5) & {f}^{′}(5) \\ 0 & 0 & f(5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{5}^{2} & 2\cdot 5 & 1 \\ 0 & {5}^{2} & 2\cdot 5 \\ 0 & 0 & {5}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 10 & 1 \\ 0 & 25 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 25\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(5)) & =({J}_{1}(3))\,⊕\,({J}_{3}(5)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 25 & 10 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 25 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 25\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Singular 3x3 System of Equations with One Pivot
questions.problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -4 & 3 \\ -3 & -6 & 12 & -9 \\ 2 & 4 & -8 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -4 & 3 \\ -3 & -6 & 12 & -9 \\ 2 & 4 & -8 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -4 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & -8 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -4 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+2y-4z=3 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove these equations from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
x+2y-4z=3
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables $y$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y,z.$ Doing this, we get

$$
x=3-2y+4z.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3-2y+4z \\ y=y \\ z=z\end{aligned}
$$

where $y,z$ (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3-2y+4z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Classify the recurrence relation

$$
{a}_{n}=4{a}_{n-2}+{a}_{n-1}+1,\,{a}_{1}=-1,\,{a}_{2}=3,\,n\ge 3.

questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following classifications of recurrence relations:

- The order of a relation ${a}_{n}$ is the largest index difference between ${a}_{n}$ and the preceding terms in the relation.

- A recurrence relation is *linear (with constant coefficients)* if it expresses ${a}_{n}$ as a sum of previous terms ${a}_{n-1},…,{a}_{n-k}$ with constant coefficients, together with possibly a final term that depends only on $n:$

$$
{a}_{n}={s}_{1}{a}_{n-1}+{s}_{2}{a}_{n-2}+…+{s}_{k}{a}_{n-k}+g(n)
$$

where ${s}_{1},{s}_{2},…,{s}_{k}$ are constants and $g(n)$ is a function, often called a *forcing function*, that does not involve ${a}_{n}$ or its preceding terms.

- A linear recurrence relation (with constant coefficients) is *homogeneous* if the forcing function is zero. Otherwise, it is *inhomogeneous.*

Let's classify the relation ${a}_{n}=4{a}_{n-2}+{a}_{n-1}+1.$

- The largest index difference between ${a}_{n}$ and the preceding terms ${a}_{n-1}$ and ${a}_{n-2}$ in the relation is $2.$ So, the relation has order $2.$

- The previous terms ${a}_{n-1}$ and ${a}_{n-2}$ occur only in the first power and their coefficients are constants. So, the relation is linear.

*The relation is linear, and the forcing function $g(n)=1$ is nonzero. So, the relation is inhomogeneous.

Therefore, the recurrence relation ${a}_{n}$ has order
$2,$
is
$\text{linear},$
and is
$\text{inhomogeneous}.$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true given that $T:{R}^{8}\to {R}^{8}$ is a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T,$ and $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})$ for some distinct vectors  ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}?$ 

- $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$
- $T$ is invertible
- $\text{rank}(T)<8$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{8}$ into ${R}^{8},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{8} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=8 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Since $T$ is a linear transformation, we have that

$$
T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})\,⟹\,T({v}_{1}-{v}_{2})=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since ${v}_{1}-{v}_{2}\in \text{Ker}(T)$ and ${v}_{1}\ne {v}_{2},$ we must have that $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement II is false. According to the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0},$ the transformation $T$ and the matrix $T$ are not invertible.

- Statement III is true. Since $T$ is not invertible, the invertible matrix theorem implies that $\text{rank}(T)\ne 8.$ In turn, this means that $\text{rank}(T)<8.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a function that is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where $a=⟨5,-3,2⟩$ and $b=⟨-4,6,-2⟩$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B,$ respectively. If $f(a)=9$ and $f(b)=3,$ then what is missing from the statement below?

The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(b)-f(a) & =∇f(c)\cdot (b-a) \\ 3-9 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c),{f}_{z}(c)⟩\cdot (⟨-4,6,-2⟩-⟨5,-3,2⟩) \\ -6 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c),{f}_{z}(c)⟩\cdot ⟨-9,9,-4⟩ \\ -6 & =-9{f}_{x}(c)+9{f}_{y}(c)-4{f}_{z}(c).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the complete sentence is as follows:

*The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $-9{f}_{x}(c)+9{f}_{y}(c)-4{f}_{z}(c)=-6.$ *

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,2⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,2⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ (2(2)^{3}-2)-(2(0)^{3}-1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨6{x}^{2},-1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨6{c}_{1}^{2},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =⟨6{c}_{1}^{2},-1⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =12{c}_{1}^{2}-1 \\ 16 & =12{c}_{1}^{2} \\ {c}_{1}^{2} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ {c}_{1} & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}<0<2,$ it's clear that $-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ corresponds to the $x$-coordinate of a point that does not lie on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ Therefore, we can ignore it. Thus, ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}$ to find ${c}_{2}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{2-1} & =\frac{x-0}{2-0} \\ y-1 & =\frac{x}{2} \\ y & =\frac{x}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},$ we obtain that ${c}_{2}=\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+1=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+1.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(6,5)-f(0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨6,5⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\ \sqrt{169-{5}^{2}}-\sqrt{169-{0}^{2}} & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨6,5⟩ \\ 12-13 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨6,5⟩ \\ -1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨6,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨0,-\frac{y}{\sqrt{169-{y}^{2}}}⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨0,\,-\frac{{c}_{2}}{\sqrt{169-{{c}_{2}}^{2}}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨6,5⟩ \\ -1 & =⟨0,\,-\frac{{c}_{2}}{\sqrt{169-{{c}_{2}}^{2}}}⟩\cdot ⟨6,5⟩ \\ -1 & =-\frac{5{c}_{2}}{\sqrt{169-{{c}_{2}}^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{169-{{c}_{2}}^{2}} & =5{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve this radical equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{169-{{c}_{2}}^{2}} & =5{c}_{2} \\ 169-{{c}_{2}}^{2} & =25{{c}_{2}}^{2} \\ 26{{c}_{2}}^{2} & =169 \\ {{c}_{2}}^{2} & =\frac{169}{26} \\ {{c}_{2}}^{2} & =\frac{13}{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{26}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the radical equation, we notice that ${c}_{2}=-\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2}$ does not satisfy the equation. Therefore, the only solution is ${c}_{2}=\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2}.$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}$ to find ${c}_{1}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-0}{5-0} & =\frac{x-0}{6-0} \\ \frac{y}{5} & =\frac{x}{6} \\ y & =\frac{5}{6}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{5}{6}{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{2}=\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2},$ we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2} & =\frac{5}{6}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{26}}{2} \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{3\sqrt{26}}{5}.\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:

$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)=3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨2,1,3⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,1,3)-f(0,0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,1,3⟩-⟨0,0,0⟩) \\ -7-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩ \\ -7 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨6x,\,-2y,\,-4z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨6{c}_{1},\,-2{c}_{2},\,-4{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-7 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩ \\ -7 & =⟨6{c}_{1},\,-2{c}_{2},\,-4{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩ \\ -7 & =12{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}-12{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-0}{3} \\ \frac{x}{2} & =y=\frac{z}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=2t,\,y=t,\,z=3t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=2t,\,{c}_{2}=t,\,{c}_{3}=3t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $12{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}-12{c}_{3}=-7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12(2t)-2t-12(3t) & =-7 \\ 24t-2t-36t & =-7 \\ -14t & =-7 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =2(\frac{1}{2})=1, \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{3} & =3(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}).$

Let $f(x,y)$ be a function that is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overline{AB},$ where $\mathbf a=\langle 5,3\rangle$ and $\mathbf b=\langle 4,2\rangle$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B,$ respectively. If $f(\mathbf a)= 5$ and $f(\mathbf b)=6,$ then according to the mean value theorem, which of the following must be true for some point $C\in \overline{AB}$ with position vector $\mathbf c?$

- $f_x(\mathbf c) + f_y(\mathbf c) = -1$

- $f_x(\mathbf c) + f_y(\mathbf c) = 1$

- $f_x(\mathbf c) +f_y(\mathbf c) = 2$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overline{AB},$ then there exists a point $C \in \overline{AB}$ with position vector $\mathbf c$ such that

$$
f (\mathbf b) − f (\mathbf a) = \nabla f (\mathbf c) · (\mathbf b − \mathbf a).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(b)-f(a) & =∇f(c)·(b-a) \\ 6-5 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot (⟨4,2⟩-⟨5,3⟩) \\ 1 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot ⟨-1,-1⟩ \\ 1 & =-{f}_{x}(c)-{f}_{y}(c)\end{aligned}
$$

which we can write as

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-2x,-2y⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-2{c}_{1},-2{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ -5 & =⟨-2{c}_{1},-2{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ -5 & =-4{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2} \\ 5 & =4{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overline{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-0}{1-0} & =\frac{x-0}{2-0} \\ y & =\frac{x}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf c = \langle c_1,c_2\rangle$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the equation $4c_1 + 2c_2 = 5,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{c}_{1}+2(\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}) & =5 \\ 4{c}_{1}+{c}_{1} & =5 \\ 5{c}_{1} & =5 \\ {c}_{1} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find $c_2 = \dfrac{c_1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $\left(1, \dfrac{1}{2} \right).$
