questions.problem: Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2y$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 3}.$ You are given that the function has a critical point at $(0,-1)\in D.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(0,-1)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+2(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡t+3{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ 2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives two solutions $t=\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain three candidate points:

$$
(\sqrt{3},0),\,(0,-\sqrt{3}),\,(0,\sqrt{3})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{3},0) & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{0}^{2}+2(0) \\  & =3+0+0 \\  & =3 \\ f(0,-\sqrt{3}) & =(0)^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+2(-\sqrt{3}) \\  & =0+3-2\sqrt{3} \\  & =3-2\sqrt{3} \\ f(0,\sqrt{3}) & ={0}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}+2(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =0+3+2\sqrt{3} \\  & =3+2\sqrt{3} \\ f(0,-1) & ={0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+2(-1) \\  & =0+1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-1$ at the point $(0,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $3+2\sqrt{3}$ at the point $(0,\sqrt{3}).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Global Maxima and Minima of a Function Whose Domain Is Piecewise Smooth
questions.problem:
![](images/87/876ae377e99bbd69205e8118c881568859f5de8154d087f2fbfa1c4c06626249.png)

Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+{x}^{2}-2x+1$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,x\le 0,\,y\ge 0,\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9},$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve  ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x-2,\,2y\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2x-2=0 \\ 2y=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(1,0).$ Since the point $(1,0)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(-3,0)$ and $(0,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (-3,0).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & ={0}^{2}+{t}^{2}-2t+1 \\  & ={t}^{2}-2t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-3,0),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{2}-2t+1)^{′} & =0 \\ 2t-2 & =0 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution, $t=1$ is not inside the interval $t\in (-3,0).$

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(0,3)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨0,t⟩,\,t\in (0,3).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(0,t) \\  & ={t}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2(0)+1 \\  & ={t}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,3),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{2}+1)^{′} & =0 \\ 2t & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution, $t=0$ is not inside the interval $t\in (0,3).$

- The quarter-circle connecting $(-3,0)$ and $(0,3)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,\sqrt{9-{t}^{2}}⟩,\,t\in (-3,0).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,\sqrt{9-{t}^{2}}) \\  & ={(\sqrt{9-{t}^{2}})}^{2}+{t}^{2}-2t+1 \\  & =9-{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}-2t+1 \\  & =10-2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points on the open interval $t\in (-3,0).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, we obtain three candidates on the boundary:

$$
(-3,0),\,(0,0),\,(0,3)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(-3,0)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(0,3)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $16$ | $1$ | $10$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $1$ at the point $(0,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $16$ at the point $(-3,0).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Number of Pivot Columns of a Matrix
questions.problem:
Determine the number of pivot columns of the matrix $C,$ given by

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 4 & -5 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to convert $C$ to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 4 & -5 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{4} & :={R}_{4}+(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 4 & -5 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the row echelon form, we see that $C$ has $4$ pivots, and therefore the number of pivot columns is $4.$

questions.problem:
The row echelon form matrix $R$ is given below. What are its **non**-pivot columns?

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the pivots of a matrix in row echelon form are the first non-zero entries in each row of the matrix.

We can see that $R$ has $3$ pivots in the $1$st, $2$nd and $4$th columns:

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the only non-pivot column is the $3$rd columns.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Polynomials
questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(1)y(1)+x(2)y(2)+x(3)y(3).
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $p(t)=10-2{t}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $p(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $p(t)=10-2{t}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
p(1)=8,\,p(2)=2,\,p(3)=-8.
$$

Computing $‖p(t)‖$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{p(1)p(1)+p(2)p(2)+p(3)p(3)} \\  & =\sqrt{[p(1)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2}+[p(3)]^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(8)^{2}+(2)^{2}+(-8)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64+4+64} \\  & =\sqrt{132} \\  & =2\sqrt{33}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(\pi -\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi }{2})-(0-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identities

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-1,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-1,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)={t}^{2}+1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({t}^{2}+1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+t)|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{3}+1)-(-\frac{1}{5}-\frac{2}{3}-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{3}+2 \\  & =\frac{56}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{\frac{56}{15}}=2\sqrt{\frac{14}{15}}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(1)y(1)+x(2)y(2)+x(3)y(3).\end{aligned}
$$

Normalize the  vector  $p(t)={t}^{2}-3t+4.$
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $p(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.
$$

Since $p(t)={t}^{2}-3t+4,$ we obtain

$$
p(1)=2,\,p(2)=2,\,p(3)=4
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),p(t)⟩ & =[p(1)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2}+[p(3)]^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2} \\  & =4+4+16 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $p(t)$, we divide $p(t)$ by its norm $‖p(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{p(t)}{‖p(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}-3t+4}{2\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{12}({t}^{2}-3t+4)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+3{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector  $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =2\cdot 2+3\cdot 1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =4+3+1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations
questions.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=5\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{2} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{25} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{6}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{6}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{\sqrt{6}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{6})^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{6} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{6}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{6} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The parametric equations of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1

are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{b}{a} & =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{5} \\ \frac{b}{5} & =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{5} \\ b & =\sqrt{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=5\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{7}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Expression for a Least-Squares Solution in Terms of the Matrices Q and R
questions.problem:
$$
\,x={Q}^{T}\,
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ \,R\,\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,\,\,b\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $R$ and $b.$

$$

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ \sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}20 \\ -4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=20 \\ 2\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-(-2) & =20 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =9.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of the Plane Perpendicular To a Given Line
questions.problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(1,1,0)$ and is perpendicular to the line 
$r=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨1,1,0⟩.$ From the vectorial equation, we find that the line is parallel to the vector $⟨-2,-3,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of the plane is 

$$
n=⟨-2,-3,1⟩.
$$

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-2,-3,1⟩ & =⟨1,1,0⟩\cdot ⟨-2,-3,1⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-2,-3,1⟩ & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above. Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-2,-3,1⟩ & =-5 \\ -2x-3y+z & =-5 \\ -2x-3y+z+5 & =0 \\ 2x+3y-z-5 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the Cartesian equation $3x+5y+15=0$ of the plane $Π$, find an equation of $Π$ in the form $(r-p)\cdot n=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, from the equation of the plane we get that the normal vector of $Π$ is $n=⟨3,5,0⟩.$

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of $Π$ for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+5y+15 & =0 \\ 5y & =-3x-15 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{5}x-3.\end{aligned}
$$

If we put, say, $x=0$, we get $y=-3.$ Hence, the point $P(0,-3,0)$ lies on $Π.$ Note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨0,-3,0⟩.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ (r-⟨0,-3,0⟩)\cdot ⟨3,5,0⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of the Plane Parallel To Two Vectors
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A,P$ and $Q$ are $a=⟨2,-2,1⟩,\,p=⟨5,0,3⟩,$ and $q=⟨1,1,-1⟩.$

First, using the $3$ points we build $2$ vectors parallel to the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & =\overset{\to }{AP} \\  & =⟨5,0,3⟩-⟨2,-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,2,2⟩ \\ {v}_{2} & =\overset{\to }{AQ} \\  & =⟨1,1,-1⟩-⟨2,-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,3,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now,  we need to find the normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & ={v}_{1}\times {v}_{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\times [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-10i+4j+11k \\  & =⟨-10,4,11⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-10,4,11⟩ & =⟨5,0,3⟩\cdot ⟨-10,4,11⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-10,4,11⟩ & =-17\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-10,4,11⟩ & =-17 \\ -10x+4y+11z & =-17 \\ 10x-4y-11z & =17 \\ 10x-4y-11z-17 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using the Sign of the Slopes and Factoring
questions.problem:
![](images/bb/bba667daa6bfd40eeb5450cc86066184819b903ace2641bc58c6b5c83869a4b6.png)

Which of the following equations could have generated the slope field shown above?

- ${y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2y$
- ${y}^{′}={y}^{2}-4y+4$
- ${y}^{′}=2y-{y}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/72/72801ec62e5e23173097ef674169b26c85fab65cbf543af44b3582f0e14fd0c4.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slope field is zero along the lines $y=0$ and $y=2.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should evaluate to zero on both of these lines.

- Second, the lines $y=0$ and $y=2$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<0$ | $0<y<2$ | $y>2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↗$ | $↘$ | $↗$ |
| Sign | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- The equation 

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2y=y(y-2)
$$

gives the required behavior.

- The equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-4y+4=(y-2)^{2}
$$

does *not* give the required behavior. The right-hand side evaluates to zero at $y=2$ only.

- The equation 

$$
{y}^{′}=2y-{y}^{2}=y(2-y)
$$

does *not* give the required behavior. The right-hand side evaluates to zero at $y=0$ and $y=2,$ but the sign of the slopes in the required regions (summarized below) do not correspond to the given slope field.

| Region | $y<0$ | $0<y<2$ | $y>2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↘$ | $↗$ | $↘$ |
| Sign | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $y=-3$ and $y=1.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should equal zero on both of these lines.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(y+3)(y-1) \\ {y}^{′} & =(y+3)(y-1)^{2} \\ {y}^{′} & =(y+3)^{2}(y-1)\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the lines $y=-3$ and $y=1$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<-3$ | $-3<y<1$ | $y>1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↗$ | $↘$ | $↗$ |
| Sign | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=(y+3)(y-1).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=(y+3)(y-1).$

questions.problem:
![](images/2b/2b25629c102be82d96b7ca94d5ab5ce499d327837ed53c6b4adb69ee214db81d.png)

Which of the following equations could have generated the slope field shown above?

- ${y}^{′}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}$
- ${y}^{′}=-\frac{1}{y-1}$
- ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}-1}$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/1b/1bf59ce83d7a82899587095217c080a5942f28a9c36c6971ec07ae5e8988e7fc.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- The slopes of the slope field become vertical as $y\to \pm 1.$

- The slopes of the slope field become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The slopes of the slope field are positive for $y\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )$ and negative for $y\in (-1,1).$

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}$ does *not* give the required behavior. Notice that

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}=\frac{1}{(1-\frac{1}{y})}\to 1\,\text{as}\,y\to \pm \infty .
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for this differential equation do not become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{y-1}$ does *not* give the required behavior. The slopes of the slope field for this differential equation do not become vertical as $y\to -1.$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}-1}$ gives the required behavior. Notice that ${y}^{′}\to 0$ as $y\to \pm \infty ,$ and ${y}^{′}\to \infty $ as $y\to \pm 1.$ Also, the right-hand side of this equation is positive for $y\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )$ and negative for $y\in (-1,1).$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using the Sign of the Slopes
questions.problem:
![](images/f4/f43ffff0a3266e9d25073aa6b184da780b7fbfd74c4dbd1b55907dd3606e71f0.png)

The diagram shown above is the slope field for which of the following differential equations?
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/07/071b9aa71508200a513fad3b6d03a3b5ef8e18e74d5e1115ca130625420d01eb.png)

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $y=1$ and $y=3.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should equal zero on both of these lines.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(y-1)(y-3) \\ {y}^{′} & =(y-1)^{2}(y-3) \\ {y}^{′} & =(y-1)(3-y)\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the lines $y=1$ and $y=3$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<1$ | $1<y<3$ | $y>3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↗$ | $↘$ | $↗$ |
| Sign | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=(y-1)(y-3).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=(y-1)(y-3).$

Which of the following equations could have generated the slope field shown above?

- ${y}^{′}=\frac{2}{{y}^{2}}$
- ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{y+1}$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/9b/9b6c8c113f59cc006f26e336b85abde6337a3af2a9f5d6dccc001eee636991ac.png)

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- The slopes of the slope field become vertical as $y\to 0.$

- The slopes of the slope field become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The slopes of the slope field are positive for $y<0$ and negative for $y>0.$

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- The equation ${y}^{′}=-\frac{1}{y}$ gives the required behavior. Notice that ${y}^{′}\to 0$ as $y\to \pm \infty ,$ and ${y}^{′}\to \infty $ as $y\to 0.$ Also, the right-hand side of this equation is positive for $y<0$ and negative for $y>0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing an Upper Riemann Sum for a Function That’s Neither Strictly Increasing nor Decreasing
questions.problem:
Let $R=[-2,1]\times [-4,-1]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=2x-y+4.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}={{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}},\,{P}_{2}={{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to $P$ is given by

$$
U(f,P)={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\boxed{}\,Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}
$$

where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1},$
what is the missing expression in the double summation above?
questions.worked_solution:
The upper Riemann sum is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{M}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ is the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ 

We consider an arbitrary subregion ${R}_{ij}$ of the partition. This subregion lies between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$ over the $x$-axis and ${y}_{i-1}$ and ${y}_{i}$ over the $y$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/88/88ffe30ae5401e00502b35d851b216768aad69bf94236561617adf23e1ce058f.png)

Notice that:

- $f(x,y)=2x-y+4$ increases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=2x-y+4$ decreases as $y$ increases.

![](images/01/01b291ca7cd81b88cf6ed06fdcdb2ffcbb1f78255d0f57d496823d347c2fb0b3.png)

As a result, the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *smallest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *bottom right corner* of each subregion.

![](images/de/de36b521dea1f925754a9c630c3d4a2c405c087a191138f1eaaa5771becb8c21.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{ij} & =f({x}_{i},{y}_{j-1})=2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j-1}+4\end{aligned}
$$

for all $1\le i\le m$ and $1\le j\le n.$

Finally, the upper Riemann sum is 

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j-1}+4)Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j-1}+4.$

questions.knowledge_point: Classifying a System as Consistent Dependent, Consistent Independent, or Inconsistent
questions.problem:
Consider the following system of equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & 3x+2y=8 \\  & x+y=-2 \\  & x+\frac{1}{2}y=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- The system has no solution
- The system is consistent independent
- The system is consistent dependent
questions.worked_solution:
To classify the system, we first try to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 2 & 8 \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 14 \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 14 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 14 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since any numbers $x$ and $y$ are solutions to the third equation $0x+0y=0$, we can remove this equation from the system. So, the corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+y=-2 \\ -y=14.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $y=-14.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(-14)=-2\,⟹\,x=12.
$$

 
So,  we conclude that the system is consistent independent.   

As a result, only statement II is true.

questions.knowledge_point: Classifying a System as Consistent Dependent, Consistent Independent, or Inconsistent
questions.problem:
Consider the following system of equations.

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x-3y+z=2 \\  & -2x+7y+2z=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- The system is consistent dependent
- The system has no solution
- The system is consistent independent
questions.worked_solution:
To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 7 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 7 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we can find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ 

Therefore, since there are infinitely many solutions, we conclude that the system is *consistent dependent*. 

As a result, only statement I is true.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Value of a Constant for Which a Given Linear System Is Consistent or Inconsistent
questions.problem:
Determine the value of $k$ for which the following system of linear equations is consistent dependent:

$$
{\begin{aligned} & -2x+6y=-4 \\  & 5x+(k-6)y=10\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 6 & -4 \\ 5 & k-6 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 6 & -4 \\ 5 & k-6 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{5}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 6 & -4 \\ 0 & k+9 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The corresponding system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned} & -2x+6y=-4 \\  & (k+9)y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is consistent dependent if it has infinitely many solutions. For the system to have infinitely many solutions, it must have at least one free variable.

If $k=-9,$ then the second equation is $0=0,$ which is true for any value of $y.$ So, we can remove this equation from the system. As a result, the system will contain only one equation, $-2x+6y=-4.$  

Then, the basic variable will be $x,$ and we will have a free variable $y.$ That means the system will have infinitely many solutions.

Therefore, our system is consistent dependent when $k=-9.$

questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
questions.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 3D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -15\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
questions.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-15.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -15 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-15,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-15)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-(-15)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}12 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-15)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}u\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }v\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }w\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 \\ x\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }y\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Given the action of the matrices $A-2I$ and $A+3I$ on the nonzero vectors $u,v,w,x$ and $y$ as depicted above, which of the following statements are true?

- $w$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$
- $u$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$
- $y$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A$
questions.worked_solution:
A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since 

$$
w\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-2I$ maps $w$ to $0$ in $1$ step, 
the vector $w$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A.$

- Statement II is false. Since

$$
u\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }v\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }w\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-2I$ maps $u$ to $0$ in $3$ steps, 
the vector $u$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3,$ not $2.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since

$$
y\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A+3I$ maps $w$ to $0$ in $1$ step, 
the vector $y$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ (a.k.a. an eigenvector) corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\,∗\, & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \,∗\, & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \,∗\, & \frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second and third columns, and

- the norm of the first column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=8.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{9}{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Constructing a Falling Body Model With Quadratic Drag
questions.problem:
A brick of mass $3\,\text{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the brick's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after the descent began, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the brick is proportional to the square of its velocity with a constant of proportionality $k=\frac{1}{20}\,\text{kg/m}$ and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Which differential equation best models the velocity? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g,$ and the only forces acting on the brick are the weight due to gravity and drag.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a:$

$$
F=ma
$$

In our case, two forces are acting on the brick:

- The force due to gravity, given by the weight $w$ of the brick, which equals

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =mg \\  & =3g.\end{aligned}
$$

- The force due to drag (air resistance) $D,$ which is proportional to the square of the velocity of the brick (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D=-k{v}^{2}=-\frac{1}{20}{v}^{2}
$$

Summing the forces, the resultant force acting on the brick is

$$
F=w+D=3g-\frac{1}{20}{v}^{2}.
$$

Also, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\frac{dv}{dt}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the brick, we have

$$
3g-\frac{1}{20}{v}^{2}=3\,\frac{dv}{dt}\,⟹\,\frac{dv}{dt}=g-\frac{1}{60}{v}^{2}.
$$

Which differential equation best models the velocity? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, the acceleration due to gravity is $g,$ and the only forces acting on the package are the weight due to gravity and drag.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a:$

$$
F=ma
$$

In our case, two forces are acting on the package:

- The force due to gravity, given by the weight $w$ of the package, which equals

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =mg \\  & =45g.\end{aligned}
$$

- The force due to drag (air resistance) $D,$ which is proportional to the square of the velocity of the package (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D=-k{v}^{2},
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Note that, since drag, in $\text{N}=\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2},$ is the product of the constant $k$ and squared velocity, in $(\text{m/s})^{2}={\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ the units of $k$ are

$$
\frac{\text{N}}{{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}}=\frac{\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2}}{{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}}=\text{kg/m}.
$$

Summing the forces, the resultant force acting on the package is

$$
F=w+D=45g-k{v}^{2}.
$$

Also, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\frac{dv}{dt}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the package, we get

$$
45g-k{v}^{2}=45\,\frac{dv}{dt}\,⟹\,\frac{dv}{dt}=g-\frac{k}{45}{v}^{2}.
$$

$$

$$
D=-k{v}^{2}=-24.5{v}^{2}
$$

Hence, the resultant force acting on the tool is

$$
F=w+D=40g-24.5{v}^{2}.
$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain a separable first-order differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 40g-24.5{v}^{2} & =40\,\frac{dv}{dt} \\ \frac{dv}{dt} & =g-0.6125{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dv}{dt} & =g(1-0.0625{v}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{1-0.0625{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dv}{dt} & =g \\ \int \frac{1}{1-0.0625{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dv}{dt}\,dt & =g\int dt \\ \int \frac{1}{1-(0.25v)^{2}}\,dv & =g\int dt \\ \frac{1}{0.25}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(0.25v) & =gt+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{artanh}⁡(0.25v) & =\frac{1}{4}gt+C \\ 0.25v & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{1}{4}gt+C) \\ v(t) & =4\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{1}{4}gt+C),\end{aligned}

where $C=0.25{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

$$

$$
v(t)=4\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{1}{4}gt+0.733)
$$

questions.problem:
A body of mass $25\,\text{kg}$ is released from rest and falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the body's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after release, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the body is proportional to the square of its velocity and acts in the direction opposite to motion.
At a particular moment during the fall, the body’s velocity is $1.25\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $7.35\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Find the equation for the velocity $v(t).$
Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ and the only forces acting on the body are the weight due to gravity and drag.
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that only two forces act on the body: the force due to gravity, given by the weight

$$
w=mg=25g
$$

and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity squared (and negative since it acts in the negative direction),

$$
D=-k{v}^{2},
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Hence, the resultant force acting on the body is

$$
F=w+D=25g-k{v}^{2}.
$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain a separable first-order differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 25g-k{v}^{2} & =25\,\frac{dv}{dt} \\ \frac{dv}{dt} & =g-\frac{k}{25}{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that, at a particular moment, the body's velocity is $1.25\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $7.35\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting these values and $g=9.8$ into the ODE, we can solve for $k:$

$$
7.35=g-\frac{k}{25}\cdot {1.25}^{2}\,⟹\,k=39.2\,\text{kg/m}
$$

Therefore, we have the following differential equation:

$$
\frac{dv}{dt}=g-1.568{v}^{2}
$$

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dv}{dt} & =g(1-0.16{v}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{1-0.16{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dv}{dt} & =g \\ \int \frac{1}{1-0.16{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dv}{dt}\,dt & =g\int dt \\ \int \frac{1}{1-(0.4v)^{2}}\,dv & =g\int dt \\ \frac{1}{0.4}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(0.4v) & =gt+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{artanh}⁡(0.4v) & =\frac{2}{5}gt+C \\ 0.4v & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{2}{5}gt+C) \\ v(t) & =2.5\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{2}{5}gt+C)\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=0.4{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the body is released from rest. So, we can apply the initial condition $v(0)=0,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =2.5\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{2}{5}g\cdot 0+C) \\ 0 & =2.5\operatorname{tanh}⁡(C) \\ \operatorname{tanh}⁡(C) & =0 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $v(t):$

$$
v(t)=2.5\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{2}{5}gt).
$$

Finally, evaluating $\frac{2}{5}g,$ we have

$$
v(t)=2.5\operatorname{tanh}⁡(3.92t).
$$

questions.problem:
A bag of cement of mass $30\,\text{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v$ be its velocity, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the bag is proportional to the square of its velocity and acts in the opposite direction to the direction of motion.
At a particular moment during the fall, the bag's velocity is $10\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $\frac{49}{9}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

What is the terminal velocity ${v}_{\text{term}}$ of the bag? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ and the only forces acting on the body are the weight due to gravity and drag. 

${v}_{\text{term}}=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
Terminal velocity is the constant speed a falling object approaches as the upward resistive force (drag) grows to exactly balance the downward gravitational force.
That is, at terminal velocity (a constant), acceleration is zero, so by $F=ma,$ the resultant force is zero.

First, note that only two forces act on the bag: the force due to gravity, given by the weight

$$
w=mg=30\cdot 9.8=294\,\text{N},
$$

and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the square of the velocity (and negative since it acts in the negative direction),

$$
D=-k{v}^{2},
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Hence, the resultant force acting on the body is

$$
F=w+D=294-k{v}^{2}.
$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 294-k{v}^{2} & =30a\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that, at a particular moment, the bag's velocity is $10\,\text{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $\frac{49}{9}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}294-k\cdot {(10)}^{2} & =30\cdot \frac{49}{9} \\ 294-100k & =\frac{1470}{9} \\ -100k & =-\frac{390}{3} \\ k & =\frac{392}{300} \\ k & =\frac{98}{75}\,\text{kg/m}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the resultant force acting on the bag is

$$
F=294-\frac{98}{75}{v}^{2}.
$$

When the bag reaches terminal velocity ${v}_{\text{term}},$ the resultant force is zero:

$$
294-\frac{98}{75}({v}_{\text{term}})^{2}=0\,⟹\,{v}_{\text{term}}=\sqrt{225}=15
$$

Therefore, the terminal velocity of the bag is ${v}_{\text{term}}=15\,\text{m/s}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
A supply crate of mass $24\,\textrm{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the crate's velocity, in meters per second, $t \geq 0$ seconds after the descent began, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the crate is proportional to the square of its velocity with a constant of proportionality $k=\dfrac{4}{5}\,\textrm{kg/m}$ and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

What differential equation best models the velocity? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g,$ and the only forces acting on the crate are the weight due to gravity and drag.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a{:}$

$$
F = ma
$$

In our case, two forces are acting on the crate:

- The force due to gravity, given by the weight $w$ of the crate, which equals

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =mg \\  & =24g.\end{aligned}
$$

- The force due to drag (air resistance) $D,$ which is proportional to the square of the velocity of the crate (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D = -kv^2 = -\dfrac{4}{5}v^2
$$

Summing the forces, the resultant force acting on the crate is

$$
F = w + D = 24g - \dfrac{4}{5}v^2.
$$

Also, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the crate, we have

$$
24g - \dfrac{4}{5}v^2 =24\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = g - \dfrac{1}{30}v^2.
$$

$$

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
An air mattress of mass $5\,\textrm{kg}$ is released from rest and falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the mattress's velocity, in meters per second, $t \geq 0$ seconds after release, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the air mattress is proportional to the square of its velocity and acts in the direction opposite to motion.
At a particular moment during the fall, the air mattress’s velocity is $0.5\,\textrm{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $7.35\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$

Find the equation for the velocity $v(t).$
Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2,$ and the only forces acting on the air mattress are the weight due to gravity and drag.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, note that only two forces act on the air mattress: the force due to gravity, given by the weight

$$
w = mg = 5g
$$

and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity squared (and negative since it acts in the negative direction),

$$
D=-kv^2,
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Hence, the resultant force acting on the air mattress is

$$
F = w + D = 5g - kv^2.
$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain a separable first-order differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 5g-k{v}^{2} & =5\,\frac{dv}{dt} \\ \frac{dv}{dt} & =g-\frac{k}{5}{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that, at a particular moment, the air mattress's velocity is $0.5\,\textrm{m/s}$ and its instantaneous acceleration is $7.35\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Substituting these values and $g = 9.8$ into the ODE, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
7.35 = g - \dfrac{k}{5} \cdot (0.5)^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = 49\,\textrm{kg/m}
$$

Therefore, we have the following differential equation:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = g - 9.8v^2
$$

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

where $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the air mattress is released from rest. So, we can apply the initial condition $v(0) = 0,$ and solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡(g\cdot 0+C) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡(C) \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $v(t){:}$

$$
v(t) = \tanh\left(gt\right)
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Terminal Velocity
canonical_examples.problem:
A body of mass $80\,\textrm{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v$ be its velocity, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the body is proportional to the square of its velocity with a constant of proportionality $k=1\,\textrm{kg/m}$ and acts opposite to the direction of motion.

What is the terminal velocity $v_\text{term}$ of the body? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g = 9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2,$ and the only forces acting on the body are the weight due to gravity and drag.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Terminal velocity is the constant speed a falling object approaches as the upward resistive force (drag) grows to exactly balance the downward gravitational force.
That is, at terminal velocity (a constant), acceleration is zero, so by $F=ma,$ the resultant force is zero.

First, note that only two forces act on the body: the force due to gravity, given by the weight

$$
w = mg = 80 \cdot 9.8 = 784\,\textrm{N},
$$

and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the square of the velocity (and negative since it acts in the negative direction),

$$
D = -kv^2 = -v^2.
$$

Hence, the resultant force acting on the body is

$$
F = w + D =784  - v^2.
$$

When the body reaches terminal velocity $v_\text{term},$ the resultant force is zero:

$$
784 - (v_\text{term})^2 = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
v_\text{term} = \sqrt{784} =28
$$

Therefore, the terminal velocity of the body is $v_\text{term} =28\,\textrm{m/s}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Integral Given Another Integral With Reversed Limits of Integration
questions.problem:
Given that ${\int }_{3}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2,$ calculate
${\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)+3x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{3}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)+3x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{0}^{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2+3\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {x}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-2+\frac{3}{2}({3}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =-2+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 9 \\  & =-2+\frac{27}{2} \\  & =\frac{23}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that ${\int }_{0}^{4}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=2$, calculate
${\int }_{4}^{0}(2x-6f(x))\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{0}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{0}^{4}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factoring out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{0}(2x-6f(x))\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{4}^{0}x\,\text{d}x-6{\int }_{4}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={2\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}|}_{4}^{0}-6(-2) \\  & =({0}^{2}-{4}^{2})+12 \\  & =-16+12 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that ${\int }_{3}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-6,$ calculate
${\int }_{1}^{3}(8-f(x))\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{3}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}(8-f(x))\,\text{d}x & =8{\int }_{1}^{3}\text{d}x-{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\cdot x\,{|}_{1}^{3}-6 \\  & =8(3-1)-6 \\  & =8\cdot 2-6 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Plugging in the known information gives

$$
(-6)+8={\int }_{-1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x\,⇒\,{\int }_{-1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2.
$$

Finally, compute the desired integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{5}(2f(x)+1)\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{-1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{5}1\,\text{d}x \\  & =2(2)+x\,{|}_{-1}^{5} \\  & =4+(5-(-1)) \\  & =4+6 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{-2}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2$ then what is ${\int }_{-2}^{1}(5+4f(x))\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+2={\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{5}{2}={\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{1}(5+4f(x))\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{-2}^{1}\,\text{d}x+4{\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\cdot x\,{|}_{-2}^{1}+4(\frac{5}{2}) \\  & =5(1-(-2))+10 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-5$ and ${\int }_{4}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x=8$ then what is ${\int }_{0}^{7}(7+3f(x))\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{4}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-5)+8={\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 3={\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}(7+3f(x))\,\text{d}x & =7{\int }_{0}^{7}\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =7\cdot x{|}_{0}^{7}+3(3) \\  & =7(7-0)+9 \\  & =58.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=4$ and ${\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=6,$ then what is ${\int }_{-2}^{3}(f(x)-6)\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4+6 & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 10 & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{3}(f(x)-6)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x-6{\int }_{-2}^{3}\text{d}x \\  & =10-6\cdot x\,{|}_{-2}^{3} \\  & =10-6(3-(-2)) \\  & =10-6(5) \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Suppose that $f(x)$ is a function such that ${\int }_{5}^{3}4f(x)\,\text{d}x=-1$ and ${\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2.$ What is the value of ${\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{5}^{3}4f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ 4{\int }_{5}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ -4{\int }_{3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ {\int }_{3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =6+(-6) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f$ and $g$ be continuous functions such that ${\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x=18,{\int }_{0}^{7}\frac{1}{2}g(x)\,\text{d}x=5,$ and ${\int }_{3}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x=4.$ What is the value of ${\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}\frac{1}{2}\,g(x)\,\text{d}x & =5 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =5 \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the adjacent intervals rule and substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the sum rule for definite integrals and substituting the known values, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ 18-10 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ 4 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x=4.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that ${\displaystyle \int_{0}^{6} \, f(x) \; \textrm d x = -54 },$ what is the value of
${\displaystyle \int_{6}^{0} \bigg( \dfrac 1 3 f(x) + 1 \bigg) \; \textrm d x }?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{0}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{0}^{6}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=54\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{0}(\frac{1}{3}f(x)+1)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{6}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{6}^{0}1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 54+x\,{|}_{6}^{0} \\  & =18+(0-6) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: If $\displaystyle \int_7^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x = 18$ and $\displaystyle \int_0^{7}f(x)\,\textrm d x = -6$ then what is $\displaystyle \int_0^{10} \big( 2f(x)+1 \big) \,\textrm d x?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\int_0^{7}f(x)\,\textrm d x + \displaystyle \int_7^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x = \displaystyle \int_0^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x.
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6+18={\int }_{0}^{10}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 12={\int }_{0}^{10}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a  function such that ${\displaystyle \int_4^1 2 \, f(x) \, \textrm dx = -1}$ 
and ${\displaystyle \int_{1}^{-1} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2}.$  What is the value of ${\displaystyle \int_{-1}^4 f(x) \, \textrm dx}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the first given integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{1}2\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ 2{\int }_{4}^{1}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ -2{\int }_{1}^{4}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ {\int }_{1}^{4}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The second integral can be rewritten as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =2 \\ -{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =2 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{\sqrt{3}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{3} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{2} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{3}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: What are the parametric equations of the hyperbola $\dfrac{y^2}{9} - \dfrac{x^2}{25} = 1?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{y^2}{a^2} - \frac{x^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

are given by

$$
x = b\tan{t}, \quad y = a\sec{t}.
$$

In our case, $a = \sqrt{9} = 3$ and $b = \sqrt{25} = 5.$ Therefore, the parametric equations are

$$
x = 5\tan{t}, \quad y = 3\sec{t}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](images/ac/ac922b185c42645f703c13d4f5016941b4125d81e85fa5ff529aa5c8d4010ac8.png)

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are $y=\pm 3x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\dfrac{y^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\tan{t},\quad y=a\sec{t},
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(0, \pm a).$ From the graph, we have that $(0,9)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=9.$

The asymptotes of a vertical hyperbola are $y = \pm \dfrac{a}{b}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are $y = \pm 3 x,$ and so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{b} & =3 \\ \frac{9}{b} & =3 \\ b & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=3\tan{t},\quad y=9\sec{t}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations
canonical_examples.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x =2\tan{t}, \, y =3\sec{t}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the $\tan{t}$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\sec{t}$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity $\tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Orthogonal Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix
questions.problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$ for every matrix $A?$

- $\text{Col}(A)$
- $\text{Null}(A)$
- $\text{Col}({A}^{T})$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$ is the left null space of $A.$ This consists of vectors that, when pre-multiplied by ${A}^{T},$ result in the zero-vector $0.$

When pre-multiplying a vector by ${A}^{T},$ we actually multiply each row of ${A}^{T}$, that is, each column of $A$, by that vector. So, $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$ must be orthogonal to the column space of $A,$ which is $\text{Col}(A).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

**Note:** In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](images/de/de22dd5b352e1d5be48f4b6ed3b2a4657ae623c1bd288d3464559758ea334af7.png)

questions.problem: Let $A$ be a $4\times 6$ matrix. What is the image of ${R}^{4}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${A}^{T}$ is a $6\times 4$ matrix.

Pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{4}$ by ${A}^{T}$ gives a linear combination of the columns of ${A}^{T}:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {a}_{1}^{T} & {a}_{2}^{T} & {a}_{3}^{T} & {a}_{4}^{T} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{T}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{1}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{2}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{3}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{4}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{4}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}$ must be $\text{Col}({A}^{T}),$ the row space of $A.$

questions.problem: Let $B$ be a $m\times n$ matrix. What is the image of $\text{Col}({B}^{T})$ under the action of $B?$
questions.worked_solution:
Pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ by $B$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $B:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & ⋯ & {b}_{n} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{B}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {b}_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {b}_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}]+⋯+{x}_{n}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {b}_{n} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{n}$ under the action of $B$ must be $\text{Col}(B),$ the column space of $B.$

Furthermore, since $\text{Null}(B)$ is mapped to the zero vector $0$ by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement $\text{Col}({B}^{T})$ must be $\text{Col}(B).$
