questions.knowledge_point: Classifying Solutions of Inhomogeneous BVPs
questions.problem:
Consider the following boundary value problem (BVP).

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+3y=2x,\,y(0)=3,\,y(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1
$$

Let ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ be fundamental solutions of the form $y={e}^{mx}$ to the corresponding homogeneous differential equation, and suppose we define the matrix $A$ as 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(0) & {y}_{2}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

Fill in the correct options in the reasoning below **without calculating the solution** to this BVP.

$\,$ The **absolute value** of $det(A)$ is {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the corresponding homogeneous BVP {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, our inhomogeneous BVP {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y≡0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem has a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

Let ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ be a fundamental set of solutions to the corresponding homogeneous differential equation ${y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0.$ 

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}].
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Dirichlet boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=1,{\beta }_{i}=0,a=0,$ and $b=1,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(0) & {y}_{2}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-4m+3 & =0 \\ (m-1)(m-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=1$ and $m=3,$ and so the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ e & {e}^{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|1\cdot {e}^{3}-1\cdot e| \\  & =|{e}^{3}-e| \\  & =e({e}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\text{has the unique solution }y≡0.$

Therefore, since the corresponding homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0$, our inhomogeneous BVP $\text{has a unique solution}.$

choices.value: has infinitely many solutions or no solution

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$

To find the solution of an inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP):

- First, we find the general solution ${y}_{h}(x)$ of the corresponding homogeneous equation.

- Then, we find a particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the inhomogeneous equation.

- Finally, we apply the boundary conditions to determine the arbitrary constants.

However, in this particular case, we can integrate the equation directly. By doing so, we get the general solution

$$
y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+Ax+B.
$$

 

Note that the derivative ${y}^{′}$ is

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}+A.
$$

Applying the condition $y(0)=0$ gives

$$
B=0.
$$

So, we have 

$$
y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+Ax.
$$

 

Applying the condition $y(1)-{y}^{′}(1)=-\frac{2}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{3}+A)-(1+A) & =-\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}+A-1-A & =-\frac{2}{3} \\ A-A & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

which is automatically satisfied for any $A.$

Therefore, the solution to the boundary value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+Ax.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
f(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3},\,g(x)=x.
$$

$$
{y}^{″}=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)-{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1
$$

A{e}^{-1}=0\,⇒\,A=0.

y_1(x) = \cos 4x, \qquad y_2(x) = \sin 4x.

$$
y_1'(x) = -4\sin 4x, \qquad y_2'(x) = 4\cos 4x.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot 0) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \pi ) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\alpha_1 y(a) + \beta_1 y'(a) = \gamma_1, \qquad 
\alpha_2 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = \gamma_2
$$

where $P, Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ are real constants such that $(\alpha_i, \beta_i) \neq (0,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m = \pm 4\textrm i.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
y_1(x) = \cos 4x, \qquad y_2(x) = \sin 4x
$$

and the general solution to the homogeneous equation is

$$
y_h = A\cos 4x + B\sin 4x.
$$

Next, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(x) = Cx\cos 4x + Dx\sin 4x
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′}(x) & =C\operatorname{cos}⁡4x-4Cx\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+D\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+4Dx\operatorname{cos}⁡4x \\ {y}_{p}^{″}(x) & =-8C\operatorname{sin}⁡4x-16Cx\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+8D\operatorname{cos}⁡4x-16Dx\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we reach (after some cancellation)

$$
\begin{aligned}-8C\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+8D\operatorname{cos}⁡4x=\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives $C = -\dfrac18$ and $D = 0.$ Therefore, our general solution is

$$
y = A\cos 4x + B\sin 4x -\dfrac18x\cos4x.
$$

Applying the condition $y(0) = 0$ gives

$$
A\cos (4\cdot 0) + B\sin (4\cdot 0) - \dfrac18 \cdot 0 \cdot \cos (4\cdot 0) = 0
$$

$$
y = B\sin 4x -\dfrac18x\cos 4x.

$$
\begin{aligned}B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-\frac{\pi }{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )=-\frac{\pi }{8} \\ 0-\frac{\pi }{8}=-\frac{\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

which is true for all values of $B$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =-\frac{1}{8}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+B\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡4x.\end{aligned}
$$

where $B$ is arbitrary.

$$
f(x) = -\dfrac18 x\cos 4x, \qquad g(x) = \sin 4x.
$$

$$
y''  + 16y = 0,  \qquad y(0) = 0, \quad y(\pi) = 0,\quad 0\leq x \leq \pi
$$

has infinitely many solutions. Therefore, the inhomogeneous BVP has either infinitely many solutions or no solution. Since we have found a solution that contains an arbitrary constant and satisfies both boundary conditions, the BVP has infinitely many solutions.

\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-9 & =0 \\ (m-3)(m+3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m = 3$ and $m = -3.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
y_1(x) = e^{3x}, \qquad y_2(x) = e^{-3x}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the homogeneous equation is

$$
y_h = Ae^{3x} + Be^{-3x}.
$$

Now, we seek a particular solution $y_p$ of the form

$$
y_p = Cx + D.
$$

Substituting this into our inhomogeneous equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Cx+D)^{″}-9(Cx+D) & =-9x-3 \\ -9(Cx+D) & =-9x-3 \\ -9Cx-9D & =-9x-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients of $x$ and constants, respectively, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-9C=-9\, & ⇒\,C=1 \\ -9D=-3\, & ⇒\,D=\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p = x + \dfrac13
$$

and the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{h}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A{e}^{3x}+B{e}^{-3x}+x+\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the condition $y(1) =  \dfrac{4}{3}$ gives

$$
Ae^3 + Be^{-3} +\dfrac43 =  \dfrac{4}{3} \qquad \Rightarrow\qquad B = - Ae^6.
$$

So, we have 

$$
y = Ae^{3x} - Ae^{-3x+6} + x +\dfrac13.
$$

 

Applying the condition $y(2) = \dfrac{13}{3}$ gives

$$
Ae^6 - Ae^{0} +2 + \dfrac13 = \dfrac{13}{3} \qquad \Rightarrow\qquad Ae^6 - A  = 2.
$$

Solving for $A,$ we have

$$
A = \dfrac{2}{e^6-1}.
$$

Substituting back into the first equation and solving for $B,$ we have

$$
B = - Ae^6 = -\dfrac{2e^6}{e^6-1}.
$$

Finally, for the function $g(x),$ we have

$$
g(x) = y_p(x) = x + \dfrac13.
$$

**Note**: The associated homogeneous BVP

$$
y'' - 9y = 0,  \qquad y(1) = 0, \quad y(2) = 0,\quad 1\leq x \leq 2
$$

has only the trivial solution $y\equiv 0.$ Therefore, the inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution. Since we have found a solution satisfying both boundary conditions, the solution to this inhomogeneous BVP is unique.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
questions.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve  $r(t)=\sqrt{1+t}\,i+({t}^{2}-5)\,j+(3t-1)\,k$ at the point $P(2,4,8),$  valid for all real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,4,8)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

where ${t}_{0}$ corresponds to the value of $t$ at the point $P.$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+4\,j+8\,k \\ \sqrt{1+t}\,i+({t}^{2}-5)\,j+(3t-1)\,k & =2\,i+4\,j+8\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+t}=2 \\ {t}^{2}-5=4 \\ 3t-1=8\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the third equation, we get $t=3.$ This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,4,8)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(3).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1+t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-5)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+t}}\,i+2t\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(3) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+(3)}}\,i+2(3)\,j+3\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}\,i+2\cdot 3\,j+3\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,i+6\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(2,4,8)$ is

$$
R(u)=2i+4\,j+8\,k+u(\frac{1}{4}\,i+6\,j+3\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨1-4{t}^{2},5t+1⟩$ at the point where $t=-1,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=-1,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(-1)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(-1)+u{r}^{′}(-1),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨1-4(-1)^{2},5(-1)+1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-4{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-8t,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(-1) & =⟨-8(-1),5⟩ \\  & =⟨8,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
R(u)=⟨-3,-4⟩+u⟨8,5⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j,$ $t\in (0,\infty ),$ find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-3)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ \frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j & =c(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}i+2t\,j) \\ \frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j & =-\frac{c}{{t}^{2}}i+2ct\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{t}=-\frac{c}{{t}^{2}} \\ {t}^{2}-3=2ct\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation we obtain $-t=c.$ Substituting $c=-t$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-3 & =-2{t}^{2} \\ 3{t}^{2}-3 & =0 \\ 3(t+1)(t-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =\frac{1}{1}\,i+({1}^{2}-3)\,j \\  & =\,i-2\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,-2).$

questions.problem:
![](images/22/22328ca144ecfaf7c1d52abd77c59f03dbf3c0da36fff21a809ce4e456ed56a5.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $x={y}^{3}-9y$ that lies in the fourth quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}-9y & =0 \\ y({y}^{2}-9) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=-3$ to $y=0.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}-9y)=3{y}^{2}-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}({y}^{3}-9y)\sqrt{1+(3{y}^{2}-9)^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}({y}^{3}-9y)\sqrt{1+9({y}^{2}-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{y-3}$ that lies between the lines $y=3$ and $y=\frac{15}{4}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{y-3})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y-3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{1}{4(y-3)}.
$$

Then, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{y-3}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4(y-3)}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{y-3}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{4y-11}{4(y-3)}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{4y-11}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=4y-11.$ Then, $\text{d}y=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$y$** | $3$ | $\frac{15}{4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{4y-11}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\sqrt{{4}^{3}}-\sqrt{{1}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Finite and Infinite-Dimensional Vector Spaces
questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?

- $D(R),$ the vector space of all differentiable functions on $R$
- ${\text{M}}_{10\times 100}(R),$ the vector space of all $10\times 100$ matrices over $R$
- ${R}_{200}[t],$ the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $200$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our vector spaces.

- $D(R)$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following subset of $D(R)$ is linearly independent:

$$
{1,\,t,\,{t}^{2},\,…,{t}^{n}},\,n\in N.
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{t}^{i}=0
$$

for all $t\in R$ if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of $D(R)$  of size $n,$ which imples that $D(R)$ cannot have finite dimension.     .

- ${\text{M}}_{10\times 100}(R)$ and ${R}_{200}[t]$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{10\times 100}(R))=10\cdot 100=1\,000
$$

 
and

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{200}[t])=200+1=201,
$$

are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
The intersection of the planes $3x+6y+3z=0$ and $x-y+2z+3=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{2},0⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$
questions.worked_solution:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation gives  

$$
3x+6y+3(0)=0\,⟹\,x=-2y,
$$

and substituting $z=0$ and $x=-2y$ into the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y+2z+3 & =0 \\ -2y-y+2(0)+3 & =0 \\ -3y & =-3 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-2y=-2$ and $a=⟨-2,1,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $3x+6y+3z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨3,6,3⟩.$

- For the plane $x-y+2z+3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,-1,2⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨3,6,3⟩\times ⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =15i-3j-9k \\  & =⟨15,-3,-9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can pick any vector that is parallel to ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}$ as a direction vector of the line. So, let 

$$
b=\frac{1}{3}({n}_{1}\times {n}_{2})=⟨5,-1,-3⟩.
$$

The equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨-2,1,0⟩+t⟨5,-1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=-2+1=-1,$ and $b=⟨5,-1,-3⟩.$

questions.problem:
Given the two planes $x-2y+z=0$ and $x-y+1=0$, which of the following statements are true?

- The normal vectors of the planes are parallel.
- The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $0.$
- The planes intersect on a line.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that:

- For the plane $x-2y+z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,-2,1⟩.$

- For the plane $x-y+1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,-1,0⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statements I and II are false. Indeed, computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,-2,1⟩\times ⟨1,-1,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i+j+k \\  & =⟨1,1,1⟩\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}\ne 0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are not parallel.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, two non-parallel planes in $3$-dimensional space must intersect on a line.

Therefore, only statement III is true.

questions.problem:
Given the two planes $y-z=1$ and $2x+z=3$, which of the following statements are true?

- The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $⟨1,-2,-2⟩.$
- The normal vectors of the planes are parallel.
- The planes intersect on a line.

First, notice that:

- For the plane $y-z=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,-1⟩.$

- For the plane $2x+z=3,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨2,0,1⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statement I is true. Computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,-1⟩\times ⟨2,0,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i-2j-2k \\  & =⟨1,-2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}\ne 0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are not parallel.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, two non-parallel planes in $3$-dimensional space must intersect on a line.

Therefore, only statements I and  III are true.

questions.problem:
Given the two planes $2x-4y+6z+2=0$ and $-x+2y-3z=0$, which of the following statements are true?

- The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $0.$
- The planes intersect on a straight line.
- The planes are coincident.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that:

- For the plane $2x-4y+6z+2=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨2,-4,6⟩.$

- For the plane $-x+2y-3z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨-1,2,-3⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨2,-4,6⟩\times ⟨-1,2,-3⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -4 & 6 \\ -1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =0i+0j+0k \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}=0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are parallel. Hence, the corresponding planes are also parallel. So, the planes can't intersect on a line.

- Statement III is false. Indeed,  the second plane passes through the origin  $O(0,0,0)$ but the first plane doesn't: 

$$
2(0)-4(0)+6(0)+2=2\ne 0
$$

 So, the planes can't be coincident.

Therefore, only statement I is true.

questions.problem:
The intersection of the planes $x+3y-2z-8=0$ and $2x+y-3z-16=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},0,{a}_{3}⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{3},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$
questions.worked_solution:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $y=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation gives 

$$
x+0-2z-8=0\,⟹\,x=2z+8,
$$

and substituting $y=0$ and $x=2z+8$ into the first equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2z+8)+0-3z-16 & =0 \\ 4z+16-3z-16 & =0 \\ z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=2(0)+8=8$ and $a=⟨8,0,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $x+3y-2z-8=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,3,-2⟩.$

- For the plane $2x+y-3z-16=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨2,1,-3⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,3,-2⟩\times ⟨2,1,-3⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 3 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-7i-j-5k \\  & =⟨-7,-1,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨8,0,0⟩+t⟨-7,-1,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{3}=8+0=8,$ and $b=⟨-7,-1,-5⟩.$

questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem to a First-Order System
questions.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
12{y}^{″}+5{y}^{′}-2y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-2
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(1)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={x}_{1}(1)=1 \\ {y}^{′}(1) & ={x}_{2}(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-\frac{5}{12}{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{6}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=1 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=1,q=-2,f(t)=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(1-(-2))(\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}) \\  & =3(\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Homogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation
questions.problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}+3{e}^{2t}{y}^{′}-5y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-3{e}^{2t}{y}^{′}+5y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-3{e}^{2t}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=5{x}_{1}-3{e}^{2t}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -3{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -3{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
The third-order differential equation ${y}^{‴}+6t{y}^{″}+8{t}^{2}y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & a \\ 0 & 0 & b \\ -8{t}^{2} & 0 & c\end{aligned}],
$$

and for $y=y(t),$ we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}y={x}_{1}(t) \\ {y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t) \\ {y}^{″}={x}_{3}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-6t{y}^{″}-8{t}^{2}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-6t{x}_{3}-8{t}^{2}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-8{t}^{2}{x}_{1}-6t{x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -8{t}^{2} & 0 & -6t\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $a=0,b=1,c=-6t,$ and $a+b+c=1-6t.$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Swapping the Order of Integration
questions.problem:
![](images/48/48d76f34becfba9f58658c3c38ba2df0e76ad6ff20b83ffc836e213c4eea4565.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[6]{\pi }}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})dz\,dy\,dx.$ The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[6]{\pi }}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})dz\,dy\,dx={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[6]{\pi },\,\,{y}^{3}\le z\le \sqrt{\pi }}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](images/86/86af6e58f4f13e79bb9672cef329572f006e5f4875178ede7908bddbd0dec404.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](images/83/83041605fcd79db34f249664b12311a4e5d797c331bcaf1279f03b5b68891b23.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

- The right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
z={y}^{3}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt[3]{z}.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{z}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/b5/b5a3fc034b713ce5fca98fbd0cca3c454d18e42e0e73eecc7ec18c51a8e7ebb5.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane with the bottom curve given by $z=\sqrt[3]{0}=0.$

![](images/54/54fa3b1c3a15391e0a87c15017b07594c4f2cca7fb741cd7480909a64e3d39db.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[6]{\pi }}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})dz\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{z}}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,dy\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{z}}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2}){[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{z}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\frac{1}{3}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})]}_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[x]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](images/22/22058df7ac75e085e1dc352736d1abf289e80d68f340ee63687e69d18e9b23c2.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\,dx\,dy\,dz.$ The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\,dx\,dy\,dz={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le \pi ,\,\,0\le y\le \pi ,\,\,0\le x\le y}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](images/c5/c5eec166cdce2fa4be756aa144b6a802082def0374c2b6150794cb2f0f22f1a6.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](images/50/50a93024f817970869a3dcef831abc2515fe14efac5ec9dd778701d063b8351d.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
x=y\,⟹\,y=x.
$$

- The right boundary of the region is

$$
y=\pi .
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,x\le y\le \pi },
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/ec/ec3bc5a58b5521286388294b97e1449bb41548004477d6d4555c9b7b917f2bd7.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the right curve given by $x=\pi .$

![](images/20/205c88cdd0b8a2676bc8396760095fa238ae39acd3660ed5aba2df3726161410.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\,0\le z\le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\,dx\,dy\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{x}^{\pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\,dy\,dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}[{\int }_{x}^{\pi }\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}[y]_{x}^{\pi }\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\cdot (\pi -x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[-\operatorname{cos}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-(-1-1)\,\text{d}z \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\text{d}z \\  & =2[z]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{\sqrt{z}}^{\sqrt{3}}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.
$$

so that it is integrated first with respect to $z,$ then $y,$ and then $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to find limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{\sqrt{z}}^{\sqrt{3}}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,y)}^{{u}_{2}(x,y)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,\sqrt{z}\le y\le \sqrt{3}}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type III region, we first sketch the projection onto the $xz$-plane, given by

$$
E={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3}.
$$

as shown below.

![](images/37/3771c3587542c781136e1802cf2ad809aaa7aff701328963572fe9296c1eb856.png)

![](images/8e/8e2aeb803b0458864560f894c3ec8635c38ac4b9febeb172115f4b3216fc44a5.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type I region and its projection $D$ onto the $xy$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $z$-axis and in the direction of increasing $z,$ as shown below.

![](images/38/385eed97efeb951228a44009faf76dc676f565204885c8f0df2cee0afc1657a8.png)

The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary:

- The top boundary of the region, written in the form $z=z(x,y),$ is

$$
y=\sqrt{z}\,⟺\,z={y}^{2}.
$$

- The bottom boundary of the region is

$$
z=0.
$$

Therefore, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le {y}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/83/837b43fa43b6d160d0734a629f08bb415bd91f382b99dbd6a5c227dd46b98f29.png)

![](images/90/90dc40b39cd7a3fdfcff0469b1915dcd64811a16aad0dad452c8f57d4118546b.png)

Hence, we have that

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{3}}.

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $z,$ then $y,$ then $x,$ we obtain

questions.problem:
${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{z/x}^{x}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x=$

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,y),$ ${u}_{2}(x,y),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{z/x}^{x}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,y)}^{{u}_{2}(x,y)}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le {x}^{2},\,\,\frac{z}{x}\le y\le x}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type III region, we first sketch the projection onto the $xz$-plane, given by

$$
E={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le {x}^{2}}
$$

as shown below.

![](images/2b/2b4cc501b983d6786c2e27680955a7ffdba17ff139ad4d9bed4a268521d365d9.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $\frac{z}{x}\le y\le x.$

![](images/5c/5c02178f02f39fa2ce2b27c0c51f58f33d9f2e7e54621e079e5645730cb20e56.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type I region and its projection $D$ onto the $xy$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $z$-axis and in the direction of increasing $z,$ as shown below.

![](images/f4/f4c313659ca62d8d595fda91f53be9b10c6f7fa1105475b7e833d7f0a2e8acbe.png)

The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary:

- The bottom boundary of the region is

$$
z=0.
$$

- The top boundary of the region, written in the form $z=z(x,y),$ is

$$
y=\frac{z}{x}\,⟺\,z=xy.
$$

Therefore, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le xy},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/79/79c4044d76be693decc1125ec88b53c162a6f29b0e701e0125319955bbe02fa1.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xy$-plane with the top curve given by $y=x.$

![](images/e1/e123941fc02ba0ff653feffd0cc9b3f778fcd1c01ad2656b658e98fbcbae8b98.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le x}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{z/x}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}{\int }_{0}^{xy}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})[{\int }_{0}^{xy}\text{d}z]\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})[z]_{0}^{xy}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}8xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[4x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4}){\int }_{0}^{x}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4}){[{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{4})]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System
questions.problem:
Find the least-squares solution to the system of linear equations given below. You're given that the columns of the corresponding coefficient matrix are linearly independent.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-4 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{8}{7} \\ -\frac{17}{7}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Distance Between a Vector to a Subspace of Solutions of a Linear System
questions.problem:
Consider the system $Ax=b$, where the matrix $A$ and the vector $b$ are given below. Given that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, find the minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖.$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}} \\ Ax & =b\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}])}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖$ is attained when $x=\overset{^}{x},$ which is the least-squares solution of the system $Ax=b.$ In this case, $A\overset{^}{x}$ represents the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A,$ and $‖A\overset{^}{x}-b‖$ is the distance between the vector $b$ and the column space. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}A\overset{^}{x}-b & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -4 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
‖A\overset{^}{x}-b‖=\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=3\sqrt{3}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a Decoupled Linear System of Differential Equations
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying a Decoupled System of Linear ODEs
questions.problem:
Which of the following systems of linear ODEs are decoupled?

- ${x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)$
- ${x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]x(t)$
- ${x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)$
questions.worked_solution:
A *decoupled system* consists of equations depending on only one variable, such as

$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently.  

In matrix form, a linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ is decoupled if $A$ is a diagonal matrix.

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

- System II is decoupled since its corresponding matrix is diagonal.

- Systems I and III are *not* decoupled because their matrices are not diagonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{({x}^{2}-1)^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[({x}^{2}-1)^{2}-1]}^{′}}{{[{x}^{2}]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4x({x}^{2}-1)}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4{x}^{3}-4x}{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{({x}^{2}-1)^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4{x}^{3}-4x}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[4{x}^{3}-4x]^{′}}{[2x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{12{x}^{2}-4}{2} \\  & =\frac{12(0)^{2}-4}{2} \\  & =\frac{-4}{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt{x}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{ln}^{2}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\sqrt{x}]^{′}}{{[{ln}^{2}⁡x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}{(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\sqrt{x}]^{′}}{[4\operatorname{ln}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}{(\frac{4}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{8\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt{x} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $D$ given below?

- $det(D)=1$
- $D$ is a singular matrix
- $det(D)=0$

 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 1 & 7\end{aligned}|+3|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(28-30)-2(7-5)+3(6-4) \\  & =1\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 2+3\cdot 2 \\  & =-2-4+6 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $det(D)=0$, the matrix is singular. 

Therefore, only statements II and III are true.

questions.problem:
$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & -3 & 0 \\ 1 & -7 & 6 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $C$ given above. Which of the following statements are true?

- $\lambda =2$ is an eigenvalue of $C$
- $\lambda =5$ is an eigenvalue of $C$
- The eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,C-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
C-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & -3-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & -7 & 6 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(C-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Notice that we can expand the $4\times 4$ determinant across the $4$th column, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(C-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & -3-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & -7 & 6 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, expanding the $3\times 3$ determinant across the $2$nd row, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5-\lambda )\cdot (5-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 4 \\ -5 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )^{2}\cdot ((2-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )+20) & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)^{2}({\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +14) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $D<0$ for the polynomial ${\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +14$ we have that the only real eigenvalue is $\lambda =5$ (with algebraic multiplicity $2$). 

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation Whose Characteristic Equation Has Real Roots
questions.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
{y}^{″}-y=8x{e}^{x}
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{x}+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constants omitted):*

$$
\int x{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}(2x-1){e}^{2x}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)=8x{e}^{x}.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{x}.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{-x})({e}^{x})^{′}-({e}^{-x})^{′}({e}^{x}) \\  & =({e}^{-x})({e}^{x})-(-{e}^{-x})({e}^{x}) \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent.

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{8x{e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{x}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4\int x{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(2x-1){e}^{2x} \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{8x{e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{-x}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =-(2x-1){e}^{2x}\cdot {e}^{-x}+2{x}^{2}\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & =-(2x-1){e}^{x}+2{x}^{2}\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & =(2{x}^{2}-2x+1){e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{x}+(2{x}^{2}-2x+1){e}^{x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+(B+1){e}^{x}+(2{x}^{2}-2x){e}^{x}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{x}+{{(2{x}^{2}-2x){e}^{x}}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=(2{x}^{2}-2x){e}^{x}.
$$

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{x}.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{-x})({e}^{x})^{′}-({e}^{-x})^{′}({e}^{x}) \\  & =({e}^{-x})({e}^{x})-(-{e}^{-x})({e}^{x}) \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2\ne 0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{10{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot {e}^{x}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-5\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{10{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot {e}^{-x}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\text{ }\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+y=\frac{{e}^{x}}{x}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{x}.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{x})(x{e}^{x})^{′}-({e}^{x})^{′}(x{e}^{x}) \\  & =({e}^{x})({e}^{x}+x{e}^{x})-{e}^{x}(x{e}^{x}) \\  & ={e}^{2x}+x{e}^{2x}-x{e}^{2x} \\  & ={e}^{2x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent. 

Let's compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{{e}^{x}\cdot x{e}^{x}}{x\cdot {e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \text{d}x \\  & =-x \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{{e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{x}}{x\cdot {e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(-x){e}^{x}+(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|)(x{e}^{x}) \\  & =x{e}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-x{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}+x{e}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-x{e}^{x} \\  & =A{e}^{x}+(B-1)x{e}^{x}+x{e}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
B:=(B-1),
$$

our general solution becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}+{{x{e}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=x{e}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+y={sec}^{3}⁡x.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)={sec}^{3}⁡x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent. 

Let's compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x):$

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{{sec}^{3}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x{sec}^{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then, we have $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x,$ and our integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{sec}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{{sec}^{3}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x{sec}^{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{cos}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2}{sec}^{2}⁡x)(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2{cos}^{2}⁡x})\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{-1+2{sin}^{2}⁡x}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{sec}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{{\,-\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{sec}⁡x}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{sec}⁡x.
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$

$$

Applying the sum rule to the given double summation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{16}({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}-2) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{16}{a}_{ij}+{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{16}{b}_{ij}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{16}2 \\  & =300+250-(2{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{16}1) \\  & =550-2({\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{16}1).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the fact that

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}1=mn,

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}550-2({\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{16}1) & =550-2\cdot (15\cdot 16) \\  & =550-480 \\  & =70.\end{aligned}

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{16}({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}-2)=70.

The product rule for double summations states that

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{b}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{b}_{j}.
$$

So, using the product rule for double summations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{\sum }_{j=1}^{20}({a}_{i}-1)({b}_{j}+1) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{10}({a}_{i}-1){\sum }_{j=1}^{20}({b}_{j}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the rules for single summations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}({a}_{i}-1){\sum }_{j=1}^{20}({b}_{j}+1) & =({\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{a}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}1)\cdot ({\sum }_{j=1}^{20}{b}_{j}+{\sum }_{j=1}^{20}1) \\  & =(12-10)\cdot (5+20) \\  & =(2)\cdot (25) \\  & =50.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the value of the double sum

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{5} \sum_{j=1}^{8} (1+2a_{ij}-b_{ij})
$$

given that

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{5} \sum_{j=1}^{8}  a_{ij} = 8, \qquad\sum_{i=1}^{5} \sum_{j=1}^{8}  b_{ij} = 15.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The sum and constant multiple rules for double summations state that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}+{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{b}_{ij}, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}k{a}_{ij} & =k{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum rule to the given double summation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{8}(1+2{a}_{ij}-{b}_{ij}) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{8}1+{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{8}2{a}_{ij}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{8}{b}_{ij} \\  & =({\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{8}1)+2{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{8}{a}_{ij}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{8}{b}_{ij} \\  & =({\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{8}1)+2(8)-15 \\  & =({\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{8}1)+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the fact that

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n 1 = mn,
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{8}1)+1 & =5\cdot 8+1 \\  & =40+1 \\  & =41.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{5} \sum_{j=1}^{8} (1+2a_{ij}-b_{ij}) = 41.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Double Integral Using Lower and Upper Riemann Sums
questions.problem:
Let $R=[-5,-2]\times [-6,-1]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}={{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}},\,{P}_{2}={{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $f$ is a function such that ${m}_{ij}={M}_{ij}=3$ for all partitions $P$ of $R,$ and ${m}_{ij}$ and ${M}_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ respectively in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P),
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R,$ where the lower and upper sums respectively are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{M}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

and ${m}_{ij}$ and ${M}_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ 

Now, since ${m}_{ij}={M}_{ij}=3,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)=U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}3\,Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3({\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i})({\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}) \\  & =3(-2-(-5))(-1-(-6)) \\  & =3\cdot 3\cdot 5 \\  & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
L(f,P)=45\le {∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A\le 45=U(f,P)
$$

which implies that

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=45.
$$

questions.problem:
Let $R=[5,6]\times [1,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j}\le 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-3\cdot \frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1}
$$

which simplifies to

$$
2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j}\le ({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{3}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{3}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}-\frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P).
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({6}^{2}-{5}^{2})(3-1)=22 \\ \frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{3}{2}({3}^{2}-{1}^{2})(6-5)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 22-12\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 10\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=10.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Spectral Theorem
questions.problem:
Given that $A$ is a $4\times 4$ real symmetric matrix, which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ is not diagonalizable
- If $u$ and $v$ are two eigenvectors that correspond to different eigenvalues, then $u⊥v$
- $A$ must have $4$ real (not necessarily distinct) eigenvalues
questions.worked_solution:
Given that $A$ is an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix over $R$, the spectral theorem states the following:

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are all real.

- Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

- $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the theorem, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable, hence, is diagonalizable.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues must be orthogonal.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, a $4\times 4$ matrix has $4$ (not necessarily distinct) eigenvalues and the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are real.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are all real.

- Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

- $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. According to the theorem, eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues must be orthogonal. But two eigenvectors that correspond to the same eigenvalue will always be parallel if the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue is $1.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are real. Also, since the roots of the characteristic polynomial have (algebraic) multiplicity all equal to $1,$ the eigenvalues are all distinct.

- Statement III is false. According to the theorem, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable, but not necessarily orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

- If $u$ and $v$ are two eigenvectors, then $u$ is parallel to $v$
questions.worked_solution:
Given that $A$ is an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix over $R$, the spectral theorem states the following:

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are all real.

- Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

- $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable.

- Statement II is false. According to the spectral theorem, the eigenvalues are real but there are not $36$ of them. An $n\times n$ matrix has at most $n$ distinct eigenvalues.

- Statement III is false. According to the theorem, eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues must be orthogonal. So if the two eigenvalues correspond to different eigenvalues, they cannot be parallel.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

questions.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =8$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =8.$ Computing $A-8I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-8I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & 0 \\ -5 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
