questions.knowledge_point: Constructing a Radially Projected Model
questions.problem: Consider a spherical  planet with radius $(6.1\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=8.3\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet, where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
questions.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(6.1\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-8.3\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-8.3 & =-\frac{k}{(6.1\times {10}^{7})^{2}} \\ k & =8.3\cdot (6.1\times {10}^{7})^{2} \\  & =8.3\cdot (6.1)^{2}\times ({10}^{7})^{2} \\  & =308.843\times {10}^{14} \\  & =3.08843\times {10}^{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{3.08843\times {10}^{16}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{3.08843\times {10}^{16}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

questions.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(2\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=20\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(6\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(2\times {10}^{7}),$
$g=20,$ and
${v}_{0}=(6\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 20\cdot (2\times {10}^{7})^{2}}{r}+(6\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 20\cdot (2\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{160\times {10}^{14}}{r}+(36\times {10}^{8})-(80\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{1.6\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(3.6\times {10}^{9})-(0.8\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{1.6\times {10}^{16}}{r}+((3.6-0.8)\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{1.6\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(2.8\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
F_\text{in} = G\,\dfrac{mM}{r^2},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-F_\textrm{in}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\dfrac{k}{r^2},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM > 0.$

When at the surface, $r=(6.3\times10^6)\,\textrm{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-9.7\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-9.7 & =-\frac{k}{(6.3\times {10}^{6})^{2}} \\ k & =9.7\cdot (6.3\times {10}^{6})^{2} \\  & =9.7\cdot (6.3)^{2}\times ({10}^{6})^{2} \\  & =384.993\times {10}^{12} \\  & =3.84993\times {10}^{14}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a = -\dfrac{3.84993\times10^{14}}{r^2}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}r} = -\dfrac{3.84993\times10^{14}}{r^2}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(8\times10^5)\,\textrm{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g = 16\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(9\times10^{4})\,\textrm{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
F_\text{in} = G\,\dfrac{mM}{r^2},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-F_\textrm{in}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\dfrac{k}{r^2},
$$

 with constant of proportionality $k=GM > 0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
-g = -\dfrac{k}{R^2} 
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = gR^2
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}r} = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2C_1$ is a constant of integration.

Let $v_0$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R) = v_0,$ we can solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
v^2 = \dfrac{2gR^2}{r} + v_0^2 - 2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(8\times10^5),$
$g=16,$ and
$v_0=(9\times10^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 16\cdot (8\times {10}^{5})^{2}}{r}+(9\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 16\cdot (8\times {10}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{2048\times {10}^{10}}{r}+(81\times {10}^{8})-(256\times {10}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+(8.1\times {10}^{9})-(0.0256\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+((8.1-0.0256)\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+(8.0744\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Escape Velocity
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider a planet with radius $(1.2\times10^{8})\,\textrm{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g = 18.9\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$
What is the escape velocity of an object launched radially outward from the planet's surface? Assume only the force due to gravity acts on the object, 

Express your answer in scientific notation, rounding to **three significant figures** where appropriate.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed from a planet’s surface required to escape its gravity and reach infinity, neglecting all forces except gravity.

Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
F_\text{in} = G\,\dfrac{mM}{r^2},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, $M$ is the planet's mass, and $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-F_\textrm{in}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\dfrac{k}{r^2},
$$

 with constant of proportionality $k=GM > 0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
-g = -\dfrac{k}{R^2} 
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = gR^2
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}r} = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2C_1$ is a constant of integration.

Let $v_0$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R) = v_0,$ we can solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
v^2 = \dfrac{2gR^2}{r} + v_0^2 - 2gR.
$$

For the object to escape the planet's gravity, we require a positive initial velocity, and for the velocity to never equal zero.

Notice in our velocity equation that as $r \to \infty,$ the expression $\dfrac{2gR^2}{r}$ approaches zero. So, for the velocity to never vanish, we must have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR & \ge 0 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & \ge 2gR \\ {v}_{0} & \ge \sqrt{2gR}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum velocity of the object to escape the surface of the planet is

$$
v_e = \sqrt{2gR}.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values $R=(1.2\times10^{8})$ and $g=18.9,$ we conclude that the escape velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{e} & =\sqrt{2\cdot (1.2\times {10}^{8})\cdot 18.9} \\  & =\sqrt{(2\cdot 1.2\cdot 18.9)\times {10}^{8}} \\  & =\sqrt{45.36}\times \sqrt{{10}^{8}} \\  & ≈(6.73\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three significant figures.

questions.problem: Find the inverse of the orthogonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
The inverse of an orthogonal matrix is equal to its transpose.

Therefore, since $D$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{-1} & ={D}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Orthogonal Matrices
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the $n\times n$ orthogonal matrices $P$ and $Q?$

- $2PQ$ is always orthogonal
- $P-Q$ is always orthogonal
- $P$ is **not** invertible
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the product $(2PQ)\cdot (2PQ)^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(2PQ)\cdot (2PQ)^{T} & =2PQ\cdot 2{Q}^{T}{P}^{T} \\  & =4P(Q{Q}^{T}){P}^{T} \\  & =4P(I){P}^{T} \\  & =4I \\  & \ne I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the following subtraction of two orthogonal matrices:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The resulting matrix is not orthogonal since, for example, its first column is not normalized.

- Statement III is false. The inverse of an orthogonal matrix $P$ is given by ${P}^{-1}={P}^{T}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true".

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of a Product of Matrices
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{61}} & \frac{6}{\sqrt{61}} \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{61}} & \frac{5}{\sqrt{61}}\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{13} & 2 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

Find $|\text{det}(PQ)|$ given that $P$ is an orthogonal matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the following facts: 

- The determinant of a product is equal to the product of the determinants.

- The determinant of an orthogonal matrix $P$ is equal to $\pm 1.$

Applying these ideas, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\text{det}(PQ)| & =|\text{det}(P)\cdot \text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|(\pm 1)\cdot \text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|\pm 1|\cdot |\text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|\text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|\sqrt{13}\cdot \sqrt{5}-0\cdot 2| \\  & =\sqrt{65}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $Q(0,5,2)$ lies on the plane $Π:r\cdot ⟨-6,2,3⟩=16$, find the shortest distance from $P(1,-4,5)$ to $Π.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨0,5,2⟩-⟨1,-4,5⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,9,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the equation of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨-6,2,3⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot (-6)+9\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot 3|}{\sqrt{(-6)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|6+18-9|}{\sqrt{36+4+9}} \\  & =\frac{|15|}{\sqrt{49}} \\  & =\frac{15}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-2,4,1⟩ & =3 \\ -2x+4y+z & =3 \\ z & =3+2x-4y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $x=1$ and $y=1,$ we get 

$$
z=3+2(1)-4(1)=1.
$$

So, the point $Q(1,1,1)$ lies on the plane. 

Now, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,1,1⟩-⟨-3,-4,-8⟩ \\  & =⟨4,5,9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the equation of a plane, we get a normal vector $n=⟨-2,4,1⟩.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|4\cdot (-2)+5\cdot 4+9\cdot 1|}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-8+20+9|}{\sqrt{4+16+1}} \\  & =\frac{|21|}{\sqrt{21}} \\  & =\sqrt{21}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-3y+6z & =-18 \\ 6(1)-3(2)+6z & =-18 \\ 6z & =-18 \\ z & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,2,-3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,2,-3⟩-⟨5,4,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨-4,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨6,-3,6⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-4)\cdot 6+(-2)\cdot (-3)+1\cdot 6|}{\sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-24+6+6|}{\sqrt{36+9+36}} \\  & =\frac{|\,-12\,|}{\sqrt{81}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $a=⟨5,\sqrt{2},0⟩$ and $b=⟨-1,1,0⟩.$ Find $a\times b.$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 5 & \sqrt{2} & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}5 & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(\sqrt{2}\cdot 0-0\cdot 1)i-(5\cdot 0-0\cdot (-1))j+(5\cdot 1-\sqrt{2}\cdot (-1))k \\  & =0\cdot i-0\cdot j+(5+\sqrt{2})k \\  & =⟨0,0,5+\sqrt{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 4 & 2 & -1 \\ x & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ x & -1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ x & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(-2+2)i-(-4+x)j+(8-2x)k \\  & =⟨0,4-x,8-2x⟩.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t)+\overset{f(t)}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8\end{aligned}]}},\,Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.

| ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)=\,\,$ |  | $-10{e}^{-2t}$ |  | $\,,\,$ | ${x}_{p}(t)=\,\,$ |  | $2$ |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} |  |  | {{field-2}} |  |  |  |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{4t}-(-3{e}^{4t})\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-6t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -10{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -4{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}5t \\ 7t\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

| $x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+\,\,\frac{1}{4}$ |  | $8t-14$ |  | . |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} |  |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}5t \\ 7t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{2t}-2{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{-t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-t}}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5t \\ 7t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =3t{e}^{t}-3{e}^{t} \\  & =3{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=1\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t & =(t)\cdot (-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2})-\int (-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2})\cdot (1\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{t{e}^{-2t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{4} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{4}(2t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ -\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{4}(2t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}12(t-1)-2(2t+1) \\ 24(t-1)-(2t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}8t-14 \\ 22t-25\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

| $x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\,\,$ |  | $-2t-3$ |  | . |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} |  |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-(-{e}^{t})\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & {e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & {e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=\frac{4}{3}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4}{3}t\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}t{e}^{2t}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}t{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t}(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-\frac{8}{3}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =-\frac{8}{3}t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot (-\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}-\frac{8}{3}\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}+\frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t}(2t-1) \\ \frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}(2t-1)-8(t+1) \\ 2(2t-1)+8(t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2t-3 \\ 4t+2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Find the matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the map $T:V\to {R}^{2}$ relative to these bases if 

$$
T({b}_{1})=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,T({b}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,T({b}_{3})=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 9\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $[T]_{B|C}$ is the matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $C.$

First, we need to find the coordinates of $T({b}_{i})$ relative to the basis $C$ for each $i=1,2,3.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the following matrix:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) & T({b}_{3}) \\ | & | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 & 6 \\ -2 & 1 & -3 & -1 & 9\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 3 & 21\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}-{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the right-hand side gives the matrix of the linear transformation relative to the bases $B$ and $C:$

$$
[T]_{B|C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Exponential Eigenfunctions
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-20\lambda {y}^{′}+100{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y\,(\frac{1}{2})+{y}^{′}\,(\frac{1}{2})=0,\,0\le x\le \frac{1}{2},\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and $y\,(\frac{1}{2})+{y}^{′}\,(\frac{1}{2})=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-20\lambda m+100{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-10\lambda )(m-10\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=10\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{10\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{10\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{10\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{10\lambda x}.
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A+B\cdot 0=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=Bx{e}^{10\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=B{e}^{10\lambda x}+10B\lambda x{e}^{10\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y\,(\frac{1}{2})+{y}^{′}\,(\frac{1}{2})=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}B{e}^{5\lambda }+B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ \frac{3}{2}B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{5\lambda }+\frac{10}{3}B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{5\lambda }(1+\frac{10}{3}\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require $B\ne 0.$ Thus, since ${e}^{5\lambda }>0,$ we must have

$$
\lambda =-\frac{3}{10}.
$$

Therefore, the corresponding eigenfunction is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =Bx{e}^{10\lambda x} \\  & =Bx{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-10\lambda {y}^{′}+25{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-10\lambda m+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-5\lambda )(m-5\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=5\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{5\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{5\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{5\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{5\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda x}+B{e}^{5\lambda x}+5B\lambda x{e}^{5\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda }+B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ 5A\lambda +B+5B\lambda  & =0 \\ (5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{10\lambda }+2B{e}^{10\lambda }+2(5A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(5A\lambda +B+10B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+10A\lambda +2B+20B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+(4+20\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}5\lambda  & 1+5\lambda  \\ 1+10\lambda  & 4(1+5\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\lambda \cdot 4(1+5\lambda )-(1+5\lambda )(1+10\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -(1+10\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -1-10\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )(10\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(3)=0,\,0\le x\le 3,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(3)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ does not correspond to an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 6\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-6A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(6\lambda x)+6B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(6\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-6A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+6B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(3)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(18\lambda )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
18\lambda =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{2}
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{36}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing the Lower Riemann Sum for a Strictly Decreasing Function
questions.problem:
Let $R=[-4,-1]\times [1,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=7-2x-3y.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}={{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}},\,{P}_{2}={{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the lower Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to $P$ is given by

$$
L(f,P)={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\boxed{}\,Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}
$$

where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1},$ what is the missing expression in the double summation above?
questions.worked_solution:
The lower Riemann sum is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${m}_{ij}$ is the *minimum* value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ 

We consider an arbitrary subregion ${R}_{ij}$ of the partition. This subregion lies between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$ over the $x$-axis and ${y}_{i-1}$ and ${y}_{i}$ over the $y$-axis, as shown below. 

![](images/88/88ffe30ae5401e00502b35d851b216768aad69bf94236561617adf23e1ce058f.png)

Notice that:

- $f(x,y)=7-2x-3y$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=7-2x-3y$ decreases as $y$ increases.

![](images/ce/ce0d90127e1f14654f4b32a933f1eb6e76e054c03f19ca40c3f04116aa3c2c93.png)

As a result, the *minimum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *top right corner* of each subregion. 

![](images/4a/4a10c8332a5f346d393c37531c13db6aa69d4cecb241efd7c34d57f32d5a98b8.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{ij} & =f({x}_{i},{y}_{j})=7-2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

for all $1\le i\le m$ and $1\le j\le n.$

Finally, the lower Riemann sum is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(7-2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $7-2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j}.$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

$$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}].

Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L4}$ and substitution from lines {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ and substitution from line {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular, 

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that ${x}_{2}\text{ is a solution of the system}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ By definition, the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column,

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}^{′}(t) & {x}_{2}^{′}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Using ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$ from $\text{L3},$ we substitute each derivative into the matrix to get

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substitution from $\text{L2}\text{ and }\text{L3}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L6}$ we have

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Using the definition $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$ from $\text{L1},$ we substitute to obtain

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by substitution from $\text{L1}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=-4x-5.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-4x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$y(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}+4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\alpha +4(\alpha x+\beta )=-4x-5
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
4\alpha x+(\alpha +4\beta )=-4x-5
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4\alpha =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \alpha +4\beta =-5\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,\,\beta =-1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-x-1.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-4x}-x-1.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=-{x}^{2}+2x-3.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}+{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $, and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma ,$  we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
(2\alpha x+\beta )+(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=-{x}^{2}+2x-3
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
\alpha {x}^{2}+(2\alpha +\beta )x+(\beta +\gamma )=-{x}^{2}+2x-3
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\alpha =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 2\alpha +\beta =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \beta +\gamma =-3\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,\beta =4,\gamma =-7.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-{x}^{2}+4x-7.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}-{x}^{2}+4x-7.
$$

questions.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-9x-3y \\ -12x-4y\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 \\ -12 & -4\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 \\ -12 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=-\frac{1}{3}y.
$$

 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}y \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}]y,\,y\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

questions.problem: Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+2y \\ 4y+3x\end{aligned}],$ find  $2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot column. Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=0.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-1=2\cdot 0-1=-1.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}10x+6y \\ 25x+15y\end{aligned}]$ and the vector $\,u=[\begin{aligned}k \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ Find the value of $\,k\,$ such that $\,u\in \text{Ker}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

So, we need to solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(u) & =0 \\ [\begin{aligned}10\cdot k+6\cdot 5 \\ 25\cdot k+15\cdot 5\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}10k+30 \\ 25k+75\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}10k+30=0 \\ 25k+75=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to both of these equations is $k=-3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
questions.problem:
Given the linear transformation
 $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3y-x-4z \\ 2x+7z-6y \\ 16z+4x-12y\end{aligned}],$ find $\text{nullity}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 2 & -6 & 7 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 2 & -6 & 7 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot columns (the 2nd one).  Therefore, 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.
$$

![](images/05/05f940e247c6cd5d862d81fc3a34658353bef5513dfe862bbc67a120c0345838.png)

First, we have that $z$ is bounded below by $0$ and above by $3.$ So, the type I representation of $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,0\le z\le 3\,}.
$$

Now, that base curve in the $xy$-plane of the cylinder's surface is the circle $\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1$ centered at $(0,0).$ Therefore, the domain $D$ is given by the following disc:

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}\,\,\le \,\,1}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The position of a point in cylindrical polar coordinates is written as $(r,\theta ,z),$ where

* $r\ge 0$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ are the usual plane polar coordinates, and

* $z\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ is the usual Cartesian $z$-coordinate.

The heater is a circular cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis of symmetry is the $z$-axis.

We note the following:

* Since the distance from any point on the cylinder's surface to the $z$-axis equals $3,$ we must have $r=3$ for every point on the surface.

* On the other hand, $\theta $ can vary arbitrarily in its domain, and $z$ varies arbitrarily in the domain $z\in [0,3].$

Therefore, the equation of the surface in cylindrical polar coordinates is $r=3,$ where $(\theta ,z)\in [0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral When the Integrand Contains Only One Variable
questions.problem:
The cost, in dollars, to manufacture the mesh for a cylindrical heater $r=f(\theta ,z),$ where $(\theta ,z)\in C,$ is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(\frac{r}{3}+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A.
$$

How much did it cost to make the mesh for the cylindrical heater?

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        The total cost is $

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
.
questions.worked_solution:
We found that the surface of the heater can be described in cylindrical polar coordinates as

$$
r=3,\,(\theta ,z)\in C,
$$

where
$C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

Hence, the cost to manufacture its mesh is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A
$$

Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{C}\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A.
$$

The function under the first integral is constant, so we have

$$
{∬}_{C}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(C)=2\pi \cdot 3=6\pi .
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $z.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A & =\frac{(3-0)}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }\cdot {[{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }((2\pi )^{2}-0) \\  & =6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $\theta .$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A & =(2\pi -0){\int }_{0}^{3}2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =2\pi ({3}^{2}-0) \\  & =18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A=\frac{1}{2\pi }(6\pi +6\pi +18\pi )=15.
$$

Therefore, the cost to manufacture the mesh of the cylindrical heater is $$15.$

questions.knowledge_point: Parametrizing an Elliptic Cylinder
questions.problem:
A parametrization of the cylindrical heater is $f(\theta ,z)=⟨$

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,$ where $(\theta ,z)\in C.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the circle

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1
$$

in the $xy$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,y⟩=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ),
$$

since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =\frac{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}{9}+\frac{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}{9} \\  & =\frac{9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{9}+\frac{9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{9} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $(\theta ,z)\in C$ and $C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Outward-Pointing Unit Normal Vector for a Positively Oriented Curve
questions.problem:
A heating element $E$ lies on the intersection of the cylindrical heater and the plane $z=2.$ Use your answer to part 4 to find an outward-pointing unit normal vector $n(x,y)$ to $E$ that lies within this plane. Express your answer in terms of $x$ and $y.$

*Hint: The matrix ${R}_{z}(ϕ)$ representing a counterclockwise rotation of $ϕ$ radians about the $z$-axis is given by*

$$
{R}_{z}(ϕ)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & -\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & 0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $n(x,y)=\,$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$\,i+\,$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-2}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$\,j\,+$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-3}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$\,k$
questions.worked_solution:
We found that a parametrization of the cylinder is given by

$$
f(\theta ,z)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z⟩\,(\theta ,z)\in C.
$$

Restricting the parametrization of the cylinder to $z=2,$ we get a parametrization $r(\theta )$ for the heating element:

$$
r(\theta )=f(\theta ,2)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,2⟩
$$

For convenience, we express $r(\theta )$ in column vector column:

$$
r(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ z(\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 
Notice that this curve is traversed *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

To calculate the outward-pointing unit normal vector to this curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1:** We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(\theta ).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(\theta ),$ we get

$$
{r}^{′}(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) \\ {y}^{′}(\theta ) \\ {z}^{′}(\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2:** Since $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(\theta )$ by $\frac{\pi }{2}$ radians clockwise $(ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2})$ to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

Using the hint, the rotation matrix corresponding to a $ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise rotation about the $z$-axis is

$$
{R}_{z}(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(\theta )$ by $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
\overset{~}{n}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we normalize the vector found in Step 2:

$$
\begin{aligned}||\overset{~}{n}|| & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{||\overset{~}{n}||} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{x}{3}\,i+\frac{y}{3}\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression for Flux
questions.problem:
Water flows over the element $E$ according to the vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=6y\,i+x\,j.
$$

Since the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $E$ found in part 5 has zero $k$-component, it may be considered a two-dimensional vector defined in terms of $i$ and $j$ only. Use this to find an expression for the flux of $F$ across the element in terms of $x$ and $y.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        Flux = 
${∮}_{E}$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$\text{d}s.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $E$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $E$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{E}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit vector to $E.$

![](images/2c/2cd5e4c7ab86cdb999e239e986713a51c07b8decb629b1ee4a656077590f04bb.png)

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{E}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{E}(6y\,i+x\,j)\cdot (\frac{x}{3}\,i+\frac{y}{3}\,j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{E}2xy+\frac{1}{3}xy\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{E}\frac{7}{3}xy\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
questions.worked_solution:
We will evaluate the integral

$$
{∮}_{E}\frac{7}{3}xy\,\text{d}s
$$

found in step 6 using the formula

$$
{∮}_{E}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(\theta ))\,‖{r}^{′}(\theta )‖\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

with the parametrization of the curve $E$ given by

$$
r(\theta )=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi .
$$

As we found previously, ${r}^{′}(\theta )=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}^{′}(\theta )|| & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x,y)=\frac{7}{3}xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(\theta )) & =\frac{7}{3}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =21\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{E}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(\theta ))\,‖{r}^{′}(\theta )‖\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }21\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 3\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =63{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta . \\  & =\frac{63}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{63}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{63}{2}{[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{63}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{63}{4}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Time Intervals on which a Particle is Moving in a Particular Direction
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-6t-6)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-6t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(1)^{3}-3(1)^{2}-6(1)+C \\ 0 & =1-3-6+C \\ C & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the skateboarder at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-6t+8.$

To find the time interval in which the skateboarder is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-6t+8=(t-1)({t}^{2}-2t-8)<0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t)$, we get the following picture.

![](images/c8/c86cdd70316b0bdb620a9a3224823be70069328e0aac83d2c0add2b925323423.png)

From the graph, we see that $v<0$ whenever $1\,<\,t\,<\,4.$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the earliest time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
questions.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. 

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for $t>0,$ are

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4},…
$$

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-12\cdot 1 \\  & =-12<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\text{d}t \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+C & =1 \\ 0+C & =1\,⟹\,C=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(\frac{\pi }{4})=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}.
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

$$

$$

Since ${v}^{″}(3)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2-\frac{2}{3}t)\text{d}t \\  & =2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+4.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(3)=2(3)-\frac{1}{3}(3)^{2}+4=7\,\text{m}/\text{s}

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)={t}^{1/3}-1,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ({t}^{1/3}-1)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(8)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =\frac{3}{4}(8)^{4/3}-8+C \\ 4 & =12-8+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t & =0 \\ t(\frac{3}{4}{t}^{1/3}-1) & =0 \\ t & =0,\frac{64}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ we discard the solution $t=0.$ Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{64}{27}\,\text{s}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6t-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3t(2-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t> 0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t = 2\,\textrm s.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =6-6t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =6-6(2) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Since $v''(2) <      0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\textrm s.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(1)^{2}-(1)^{3}+C & =2 \\ 3-1+C & =2\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Which of the following equations define a non-empty set of points in the ${x}_{1}{x}_{2}$-plane?

- ${x}_{2}^{2}=-7$

- The equation ${x}_{1}^{2}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{5}=-1$ defines an empty set. Notice that the left-hand side is non-negative for all ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ while the right-hand side is negative.

- The equation ${x}_{2}^{2}=-7$ defines an empty set. Notice that the left-hand side is non-negative for all ${x}_{2},$ while the right-hand side is negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}=4.
$$

 

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $2{y}_{1}^{2}$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}+4\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}=4
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{x}_{1} & =4 \\ 2{y}_{1}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2}) & =4 \\ 2{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{1}-4{y}_{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{1}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{1}-4{y}_{2} & =4 \\ 2({y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1})-4{y}_{2} & =4 \\ 2({y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1}+1-1)-4{y}_{2} & =4 \\ 2({y}_{1}+1)^{2}-2\cdot 1-4{y}_{2} & =4 \\ 2({y}_{1}+1)^{2} & =4{y}_{2}+6 \\ 2({y}_{1}+1)^{2} & =4({y}_{2}+\frac{3}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}={y}_{1}+1, \\ {z}_{2}={y}_{2}+\frac{3}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2({y}_{1}+1)^{2} & =4({y}_{2}+\frac{3}{2}) \\ 2{z}_{1}^{2} & =4{z}_{2} \\ {z}_{1}^{2} & =2{z}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

This represents a parabola that opens in the direction of the positive ${z}_{2}$-axis.

Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation
