[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}+3\sqrt{10}{x}_{2}=40.
$$

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $15{y}_{1}^{2}+5{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}+\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}+3\sqrt{10}{x}_{2}=40
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly: 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}+3\sqrt{10}{x}_{2} & =40 \\ 15{y}_{1}^{2}+5{y}_{2}^{2}+\sqrt{10}(-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2})+3\sqrt{10}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2}) & =40 \\ 15{y}_{1}^{2}+5{y}_{2}^{2}+10{y}_{2} & =40 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{2} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{2} & =8 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}+({y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{2}+1) & =8+1 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}+{({y}_{2}+1)}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2}={y}_{2}+1,\end{aligned}
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}_{1}^{2}+{z}_{2}^{2} & =9 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{3}+\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}+\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This represents an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt{3}$ and $3.$

Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$

$$

 

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $3{y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{{x}_{1}^{2}-8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}-12\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+6\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}+12=0
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{2}-8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}-12\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+6\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}+12 & =0 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2}-12\sqrt{5}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2})+6\sqrt{5}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2})+12 & =0 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2}+30{y}_{1}+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2}+30{y}_{1}+12 & =0 \\ 3({y}_{1}^{2}+10{y}_{1})-7{y}_{2}^{2}+12 & =0 \\ 3({y}_{1}^{2}+10{y}_{1}+25-25)-7{y}_{2}^{2}+12 & =0 \\ 3({y}_{1}^{2}+10{y}_{1}+25)-75-7{y}_{2}^{2}+12 & =0 \\ 3({y}_{1}+5)^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2}-63 & =0 \\ 3({y}_{1}+5)^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2} & =63\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}={y}_{1}+5, \\ {z}_{2}={y}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}_{1}^{2}-7{z}_{2}^{2} & =63 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{21}-\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{21})^{2}}-\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

This represents a hyperbola with semiaxes  $\sqrt{21}$ and $3.$

$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}={x}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}, \\ {y}_{2}={x}_{2}+2,\end{aligned}
$$

we get the following:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2} & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}) & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2})+2 & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2})+(\sqrt{2})^{2} & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}-\sqrt{2})}^{2}+2 & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}-\sqrt{2})}^{2} & =5\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-18t+27)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+27t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(3)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(3)^{3}-9(3)^{2}+27(3)+C \\ 0 & =27-81+81+C \\ C & =-27.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+27t-27=(t-3)^{3}.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v>0.$ This gives

$$
(t-3)^{3}>0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](images/e3/e36c5ac354bfca5db21249d75862731c028e9f771da9070aa3382c033975e412.png)

From the graph, we see that $v>0$ whenever $t>3.$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=2t-4,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds.  The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity $v=12\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=6\,\text{s},$ determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the left.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-4)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(6)=12.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =(6)^{2}-4(6)+C \\ 12 & =12+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}-4t.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{2}-4t=t(t-4)<0.
$$

The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 5-\frac{1}{2}t & =0 \\ t & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=10\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme values using the second derivative test. The second derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-\frac{1}{2}t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(10)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=10\,\text{s}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (5-\frac{1}{2}t)\text{d}t \\  & =5t-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}5(4)-\frac{1}{4}(4)^{2}+C & =3 \\ 20-4+C & =3\,⟹\,C=-13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity is given by $v(t)=5t-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}-13.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(10)=5(10)-\frac{1}{4}(10)^{2}-13=12\,\text{m}/\text{s}.

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=(2t+1)^{3}$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t+1)^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(2t+1)^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{65}{8}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{65}{8} & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {[2(1)+1]}^{4}+C \\ \frac{65}{8} & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot (81)+C \\ C & =\frac{65}{8}-\frac{81}{8} \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{8}(2t+1)^{4}-2.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}(2t+1)^{4}-2 & =0 \\ (2t+1)^{4} & =16 \\ 2t+1 & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $t=-\frac{3}{2}\,,\frac{1}{2}.$

Since $t>0$, we discard solution $t=-\frac{3}{2}.$ 
Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{s}.$

\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-6)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-6t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) =4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =(1)^{2}-6(1)+C \\ 4 & =-5+C \\ C & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = t^2-6t + 9.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-6t+9 & =0 \\ (t-3)^{2} & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=3 \,\textrm s.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-3x{y}^{′}+5y=0,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-3x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+5{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-3\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+5{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +5] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +5 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +5 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+5 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =2\pm \text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2+\text{i}} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}={x}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)), \\ {x}^{2-\text{i}} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{-\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}={x}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{2+\text{i}}+B{x}^{2-\text{i}} \\  & =A{x}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B{x}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & =(A+B){x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B){x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={x}^{2}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

$$
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-9t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+41{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-9\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+41{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-9\lambda +41] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-9\lambda +41 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25)-25+41 & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda -5 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =5\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{5+4\text{i}} & ={t}^{5}{e}^{\text{i}4\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)), \\ {t}^{5-4\text{i}} & ={t}^{5}{e}^{-\text{i}4\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{5+4\text{i}}+B{t}^{5-4\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for $y(x)$ as follows:

$$
y(t)={t}^{5}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1.$ First, we substitute ${c}_{1}=1$ and  differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & ={t}^{4}((5{c}_{2}-4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+(4{c}_{2}+5)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =4{c}_{2}+5 \\ -4 & =4{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={t}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis in a Two-Dimensional Vector Space
questions.problem:
Let $B$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ be a linear transformation. Find $[\,T\,]_{B}$, given that

$\,$ $T({b}_{1})=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,$ $T({b}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,$ and $\,B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}.$ The $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $B.$

To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination. Then, on the right-hand side, we will obtain the $B$-matrix for $T:$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 3 & 8 \\ 2 & 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & -1 & -7 & -18\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 7 & 18\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}-3{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -18 & -46 \\ 0 & 1 & 7 & 18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-18 & -46 \\ 7 & 18\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis in a Three-Dimensional Vector Space
questions.problem:
The basis $B$ of ${R}^{3}$ and the matrix $[\,T\,]_{B}$ of the linear transformation $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ relative to $B$ are given by

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]},\,[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}a & 1 & 5 \\ -3 & b & -5 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} & c\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the value of $\,a+b+c,\,$ given that  

$$
T([\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}x+y+z \\ x-y \\ x-z\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}.$ The $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B.$

First, let's find the image of ${b}_{1},$ ${b}_{2},$ and ${b}_{3}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T({b}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 5\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) & T({b}_{3}) \\ | & | & | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination. Then, on the right-hand side, we will obtain the $B$-matrix for $T:$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 & 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -3 & -1 & -10\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 5 \\ -3 & -2 & -5 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=3,$ $b=-2,$ $c=-2$ and 

$$
a+b+c=3+(-2)+(-2)=-1.
$$

First, let's find the image of ${b}_{1},$ ${b}_{2},$ and ${b}_{3}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T({b}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ T({b}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 0 \\ -8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) & T({b}_{3}) \\ | & | & | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination. Then, on the right-hand side, we will obtain the $B$-matrix for $T:$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 & -2 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 8 & -2 & -2 & -8\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 8 & -2 & -2 & -8\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 & 2 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{8}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{4} & -\frac{1}{4} & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -4 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{4} & -\frac{1}{4} & 1\end{aligned}].

questions.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)=1-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}\,$ on the ellipse $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We must find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y=0.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=0
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨-2x,-6y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,2y-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-2x=4\lambda x \\ -6y=2\lambda (y-1)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}x(1+2\lambda )=0 \\ y(\lambda +3)=\lambda \end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y=0$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-2y & =0\,⇒\,y=0,2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,0),(0,2).$

- Assuming $\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-\frac{1}{2}+3)=-\frac{1}{2}\,⇒\,y=-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the constraint condition $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y=0$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}=-\frac{11}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a contradiction.

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,0),\,(0,2).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(0,2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $-11$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at the point $(0,0)$ and its maximum value is $1.$

∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=0
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨-2x,-2y,2z⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,-1,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2x=2\lambda x \\ -2y=-\lambda  \\ 2z=2\lambda z\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}(1+\lambda )x=0 \\ y=\frac{\lambda }{2} \\ (1-\lambda )z=0\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- First, assume that $\lambda \ne \pm 1.$ Then, by the first and third equations, we must have $x=z=0.$ Also, by the constraint $g(x,y,z)=0,$ we have

$$
y={0}^{2}+{0}^{2}\,⇒\,y=0.
$$

This gives the critical point $(0,0,0).$

- Next, assume that $\lambda =-1.$ Then, by the second and third equations, we must have $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $z=0,$ but this contradicts the constraint $g(x,y,z)=0.$

- Finally, assume that $\lambda =1.$ Then, by the first and second equations, we must have $x=0$ and $y=\frac{1}{2}.$ Also, by the constraint $g(x,y,z)=0,$ we have

$$
\frac{1}{2}={0}^{2}+{z}^{2}\,⇒\,z=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}).$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $\,(x,y,z)\,$ | $\,(0,0,0)\,$ | $\,(0,\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y,z)\,$ | $\,0\,$ | $\,\frac{1}{4}\,$ |

$$

$$

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at the points $(0,\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}),$ and its maximum value is $\frac{1}{4}.$

questions.problem:
Which of the following gives the unit tangent vector to the curve
 $r(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t},\,t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩$ at an arbitrary point where $t\in (0,\infty )?$
questions.worked_solution:
For a curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),\,y(t),\,z(t)⟩$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we find the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\sqrt{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,1,\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}+(1)^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}+1+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1+{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{(1+{t}^{2})^{2}}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{1+{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{1+{t}^{2}}⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,1,\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}⟨-1,\,{t}^{2},\,\sqrt{2}t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=⟨t+1,\,8\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,2{t}^{2}+3⟩$ at the point $P(2,0,5)?$
questions.worked_solution:
For a curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t),z(t)⟩$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(2,0,5)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2,0,5⟩ \\ ⟨t+1,\,8\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,2{t}^{2}+3⟩ & =⟨2,0,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives the system

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}t+1=2 \\ 8\operatorname{ln}⁡t=0 \\ 2{t}^{2}+3=5.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,0,5)$ is at the tip of $r(1).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,\frac{8}{t},\,4t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1,\,\frac{8}{1},\,4(1)⟩=⟨1,8,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{8}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+64+16} \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(1)$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the given curve at $P(2,0,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(1)}{‖{r}^{′}(1)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}⟨1,8,4⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{9},\frac{8}{9},\frac{4}{9}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=⟨8t,\,3{t}^{2},\,2{t}^{3}⟩$ at the point $P(16,12,16)?$
questions.worked_solution:
For a curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t),z(t)⟩$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(16,12,16)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨16,12,16⟩ \\ ⟨8t,\,3{t}^{2},\,2{t}^{3}⟩ & =⟨16,12,16⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives the system

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}8t=16 \\ 3{t}^{2}=12 \\ 2{t}^{3}=16.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=2.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(16,12,16)$ is at the tip of $r(2).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨8,\,6t,\,6{t}^{2}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(2) & =⟨8,\,6(2),\,6(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨8,12,24⟩ \\  & =4⟨2,3,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(2)‖ & =4\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\  & =4\sqrt{4+9+36} \\  & =4\sqrt{49} \\  & =28\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(2)$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the given curve at $P(16,12,16):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(2) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(2)}{‖{r}^{′}(2)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{28}\cdot 4⟨2,3,6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{7},\frac{3}{7},\frac{6}{7}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,p(t)$ at the point corresponding to $t=-\frac{\pi }{6}$, given that  $p(-\frac{\pi }{6})=\sqrt{3}\,i+\sqrt{3}\,k$ and $\,{p}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6})=-2\,i-8\,j+4\,k.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a curve $r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j+z(t)k$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=-\frac{\pi }{6}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,p(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\cdot p(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p(t)) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,p(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,{p}^{′}(t) \\ {r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6}) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3})p(-\frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3}){p}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\sqrt{3}\,i+\sqrt{3}\,k)+\frac{1}{2}(-2\,i-8\,j+4\,k) \\  & =(3\,i+3\,k)+(-\,i-4\,j+2\,k) \\  & =2\,i-4\,j+5\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6})‖ & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{45} \\  & =3\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6}):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}T(-\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6})}{‖{r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6})‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}\cdot (2\,i-4\,j+5\,k) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{15}\,i-\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{15}\,j+\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector to the curve at the point that corresponds to $t=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ is
 $T(-\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{15}\,i-\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{15}\,j+\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\,k.$

questions.problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\,p(t)$ at the point corresponding to $t=0$, given that  $p(0)=2\,i+j-k\,$ and $\,{p}^{′}(0)=i-2\,j-2\,k.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a curve $r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j+z(t)k$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\,p(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1})\cdot p(t)+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p(t)) \\  & =-\frac{2t}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\,p(t)+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\,{p}^{′}(t) \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{2(0)}{{({0}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\,p(0)+\frac{1}{{0}^{2}+1}\,{p}^{′}(0) \\  & =0(2\,i+j-k)+(\,i-2\,j-2k) \\  & =\,i-2\,j-2k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(0):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}‖r(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(0):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(0)}{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (i-2\,j-2\,k) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,i-\frac{2}{3}\,j-\frac{2}{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector to the curve at the point that corresponds to $t=0$ is  $T(0)=\frac{1}{3}\,i-\frac{2}{3}\,j-\frac{2}{3}\,k.$

questions.problem:
$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,B={[\begin{aligned}| \\ {v}_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}]\,,[\begin{aligned}| \\ {v}_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}]\,,[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Suppose that $V=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ Given that $B$ is an orthogonal basis for $V,$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We find an orthogonal basis $B$ of $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1.** We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2.** We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}$ using the usual formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{8}{8}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** We find the vector ${v}_{3}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ using the usual formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-\frac{6}{8}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{18}{9}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-\frac{3}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2} \\ 6 \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=-\frac{3}{2},$ $c=\frac{3}{2},$ and $\frac{a}{c}=\frac{(-\frac{3}{2})}{(\frac{3}{2})}=-1.$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 5 \\ -1 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c \\ d\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $V=\text{Col}(A)$ spanned by the columns ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ of the matrix $A$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ shown above. Given that ${a}_{1}⊥{a}_{2},$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

**Step 2**: We set ${v}_{2}={a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3**. Next, we find ${v}_{3}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{3}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-(0)[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{b}{c}=\frac{(-2)}{(2)}=-1.
$$

$$

Consider the subspace $V=\text{Col}(A)$ spanned by the columns ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ of the matrix $A,$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ shown above. Given that ${a}_{1}⊥{a}_{2},$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|\,c\,|?$

Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: We set ${v}_{2}={a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3**. Next, we find ${v}_{3}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{3}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 10 \\ 5 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-\frac{10}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{25}{5}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 10 \\ 5 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${v}_{3}$ dividing it by $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{10}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{3} & =\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ \frac{\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5} \\ \frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $|\,c\,|=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}.$

questions.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{2}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{(2+\frac{5k}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].$
questions.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=2.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{5}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{5}{n}=\frac{b-2}{n}\,⟹\,b=7.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=2+\frac{5k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})={x}_{k}^{2}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{2}^{7}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{(2+\frac{5k}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)={x}^{2}$ and $b=7.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={x}^{3}+{e}^{x}$ and the point $P(0,1)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{3}+{e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+{e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(0,1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(1,0)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={2}^{x}+1.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(5).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(5),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(5)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(5))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(5).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(5)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(5) & =x \\ f(x) & =5 \\ {2}^{x}+1 & =5 \\ {2}^{x} & =4 \\ {2}^{x} & ={2}^{2} \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(5)=2.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={2}^{x}+1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot {2}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot {2}^{2} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace
questions.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}12 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}24 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{12} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}24 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
questions.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,2]\times [0,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where

$$
f(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1 \\ {x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2\end{aligned}].
$$

Fill in the blanks in the matrix equation below that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting  at the point $[1,\,1]^{T}.$

| $[$ | $3$ | {{field-1}} | $]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})\,=[$ | $4$ | $].$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| {{field-2}} | $8$ | {{field-3}} |  |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2} & -12{y}^{2} \\ 2x & 8y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2} & -12{y}^{2} \\ 2x & 8y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{[\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1 \\ {x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2} & -12{y}^{2} \\ 2x & 8y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{[\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1 \\ {x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3(1)^{2} & -12(1)^{2} \\ 2(1) & 8(1)\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-[\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}-4(1)^{3}-1 \\ (1)^{2}+4(1)^{2}-2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -12 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where

$$
f(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-xy-4 \\ {x}^{4}-2xy+{y}^{2}-5\end{aligned}].
$$

Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process that starts at ${x}_{0}=[0,\,1]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[-1.5,\,1.5]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).

| ${x}_{2}\,≈[$ | $-1.198$ | $]$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| {{field-1}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-xy-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-xy-4) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-2xy+{y}^{2}-5) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-2xy+{y}^{2}-5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x-y & 3{y}^{2}-x \\ 4{x}^{3}-2y & -2x+2y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}2x-y & 3{y}^{2}-x \\ 4{x}^{3}-2y & -2x+2y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-xy-4 \\ {x}^{4}-2xy+{y}^{2}-5\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{[\begin{aligned}2x-y & 3{y}^{2}-x \\ 4{x}^{3}-2y & -2x+2y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-xy-4 \\ {x}^{4}-2xy+{y}^{2}-5\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1.5 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2(-1.5)-1.5 & 3(1.5)^{2}-(-1.5) \\ 4(-1.5)^{3}-2(1.5) & -2(-1.5)+2(1.5)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}(-1.5)^{2}+{1.5}^{3}-(-1.5)\cdot 1.5-4 \\ (-1.5)^{4}-2(-1.5)(1.5)+{1.5}^{2}-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1.5 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}-4.5 & 8.25 \\ -16.5 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}3.875 \\ 6.8125\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1.5 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{-4.5\cdot 6-8.25\cdot (-16.5)}[\begin{aligned}6 & -8.25 \\ 16.5 & -4.5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3.875 \\ 6.8125\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1.5 \\ 1.5\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{109.125}[\begin{aligned}-32.953\,125 \\ 33.281\,250\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}-1.198 \\ 1.195\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{″}+4x{y}^{′}-2y={x}^{2},\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1
$$

We wish to approximate the solution using Euler's method by introducing $z={y}^{′}$ and reducing the equation to a system of first-order ODEs. What entries should be placed in the columns for $Δy$ and $Δz$ in the table below if the step size is $Δx=1?$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ |  |  | {{field-1}} |  |  | {{field-2}} |

Therefore, $y(1)≈$
{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′}=f(x,y,z),\, & z(a)=d,\end{aligned}
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}+4x{y}^{′}-2y & ={x}^{2} \\ {y}^{″} & =-4x{y}^{′}+2y+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′}$ and ${z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=-4xz+2y+{x}^{2}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(0)={y}^{′}(0)=-1.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(0)=2, \\ {z}^{′}=-4xz+2y+{x}^{2},\, & z(0)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, because the initial conditions are $y(0)=2$ and $z(0)=-1,$ we place $y=2$ and $z=-1$ in the table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ |  |  | $-1$ |  |  |

Next, we compute both ${y}^{′}$ and ${z}^{′}$ according to the given rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=-1 \\ {z}^{′} & =-4xz+2y+{x}^{2} \\  & =-4\cdot 0\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 2+{0}^{2} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ | $-1$ |  | $-1$ | $4$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ and $Δz$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =-1 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $4$ | $4$ |

To get the new values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x,$ $Δy$ to $y,$ and $Δz$ to $z,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0+1=1 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=2+(-1)=1 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=-1+4=3\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these values to our table in a new row gives the following:

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $4$ | $4$ |
| $1$ | $1$ |  |  | $3$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(1)≈1.$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-4y{y}^{′}=6x,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0
$$

Use Euler's Method with one step to approximate $y(\frac{5}{4})$ and ${y}^{′}(\frac{5}{4}).$

$y(\frac{5}{4})≈$
{{field-1}},
$\,{y}^{′}(\frac{5}{4})≈$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′}=f(x,y,z)\, & z(a)=d,\end{aligned}
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-4y{y}^{′} & =6x \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =6x+4y{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{6x+4y{y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{6x+4yz}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is
$z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=0.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(1)=0, \\ {z}^{′}=\frac{6x+4yz}{{x}^{2}},\, & z(1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

Since we want to find the values of $y$ and ${y}^{′}=z$ at $x=\frac{5}{4},$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=\frac{5}{4}-1=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

First, we place the initial condition data in the table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ |  |  | $0$ |  |  |

Next, we compute both ${y}^{′}$ and ${z}^{′}$ according to the given rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=0 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{6x+4yz}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6\cdot 1+4\cdot 0\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ | $0$ |  | $0$ | $6$ |  |

Next, we compute $Δy$ and $Δz$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =0\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =0 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{6}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $6$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |

To get the new values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x,$ $Δy$ to $y,$ and $Δz$ to $z,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{5}{4} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0+0=0 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=0+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these values to our table in a new row gives the following:

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $6$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| $\frac{5}{4}$ | $0$ |  |  | $\frac{3}{2}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(\frac{5}{4})≈0$
and
${y}^{′}(\frac{5}{4})=z(\frac{5}{4})≈\frac{3}{2}.$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{y}^{″} & ={x}^{2}-2{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2{y}^{′}}{3}.\end{aligned}

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=0.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(1)=2, \\ {z}^{′}=\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3},\, & z(1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=3.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=3$ is $2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{3-1}{2}=1.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=2$ and $z(1)=0.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ |  |  | $0$ |  |  |

**Step 1**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=0 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3}=\frac{{1}^{2}-2\cdot 0}{3}=\frac{1}{3} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=0\cdot 1=0 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 1=\frac{1}{3} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=2+0=2 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=0+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- If $A$ is symmetric, then ${A}^{-1}$ is always symmetric (if it exists).
- The sum of *any* two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
- If $A$ is *any*  $n\times n$ matrix, then ${A}^{T}A$ is always symmetric.
questions.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any non-singular symmetric matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}({A}^{-1})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{-1} \\  & ={A}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}({A}^{T}A)^{T} & ={A}^{T}({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem:
Find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the equation 

$$
{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x-4,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
This Cauchy-Euler equation has non-polynomial forcing, but we are not given two fundamental solutions, so we cannot use variation of parameters.

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x={e}^{t},$ we note that

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}=x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & ={{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}_{⏟}}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{⏟}}_{\text{chain rule}}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+2y=t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and polynomial forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{t}+B{e}^{2t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta $ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation for $y(t):$

$$
0-3\alpha +2(\alpha t+\beta )=t-4
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
2\alpha t+(-3\alpha +2\beta )=t-4.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\alpha =1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of }t) \\ -3\alpha +2\beta =-4\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\alpha =\frac{1}{2}$ and $\beta =-\frac{5}{4},$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{2}t-\frac{5}{4}=\frac{2t-5}{4}.
$$

Now, returning to the variable $x,$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5}{4}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation 

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-12y=4{x}^{2},\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-12y=0.
$$

Let $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-12{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-12{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-12] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -12 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda +3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-3$ and $\lambda =4.$
Therefore, the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{4}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{{x}^{3}}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is proportional to ${x}^{2}.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}
$$

where $\alpha $ is the constant that is to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(2\alpha )-12(\alpha {x}^{2}) & =4{x}^{2} \\ (2\alpha -12\alpha ){x}^{2} & =4{x}^{2} \\ -10\alpha {x}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get $\alpha =-\frac{2}{5}.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{2{x}^{2}}{5}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & ={c}_{1}{x}^{4}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{2{x}^{2}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x={e}^{t},$ we note that

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}=x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & ={{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}_{⏟}}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{⏟}}_{\text{chain rule}}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}+3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-10y=5t.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and polynomial forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=\frac{A}{{e}^{5t}}+B{e}^{2t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation for $y(t):$

$$
0+3\alpha -10(\alpha t+\beta )=5t
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-10\alpha t-10\beta +3\alpha =t.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-10\alpha =5\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of }t) \\ -10\beta +3\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the constants}).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2}$ and $\beta =-\frac{3}{20},$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{t}{2}-\frac{3}{20}.
$$

Now, returning to the variable $x,$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2}-\frac{3}{20}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the standard matrices of three linear transformations shown below. Which of the transformations map ${R}^{2}$ onto a line?

$$
{T}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{T}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -4 & 6\end{aligned}],\,{T}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a linear transformation over ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T,$ we have the following:

- $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto ${R}^{2}$ if and only if $\text{rank}(T)=2,$ i.e., $T$ is nonsingular.

- $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line if and only if $\text{rank}(T)=1.$

- $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto $(0,0)$ if and only if $\text{rank}(T)=0,$ i.e., $T$ is the zero matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- ${T}_{1}$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto $(0,0)$ since ${T}_{1}$ is the zero matrix, i.e. $\text{rank}({T}_{1})=0.$

- ${T}_{2}$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line. Notice that the columns of ${T}_{2}$ are linearly dependent but it's not the zero matrix. So, $\text{rank}({T}_{2})=1.$

- ${T}_{3}$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line. Notice that the columns of ${T}_{3}$ are linearly dependent but it's not the zero matrix. So, $\text{rank}({T}_{3})=1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{2}$ and ${T}_{3}$ only."

questions.problem:
Consider a linear transformation $T$ that maps ${R}^{2}$ onto  ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $⟨-1,0⟩\in \text{Im}(T)$
- $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$
- $\text{nullity}(T)=2$, where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a linear transformation $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto  ${R}^{2}$ if and only if 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=2
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, The condition $\text{rank}(T)=2$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Im}(T)={R}^{2}.
$$

Hence, $T$ is surjective and so  $⟨-1,0⟩\in \text{Im}(T).$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the condition $\text{nullity}(T)=0$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)={0}.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have that 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=1,
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. The point $(2,1)$ does not satisfy the equation of the line $y=2x$ since $1\ne 2\cdot 2.$ Hence, 

$$
⟨2,1⟩\notin \text{Im}(T).
$$

- Statement II is true. Since $\text{nullity}(T)=1,$ we get 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have that 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $3{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-3{x}^{2}.
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{7}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{7})^{2} & =-2(1)^{3}+C \\ C & =14+2 \\ C & =16\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x\ge \frac{1}{2}.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$

questions.worked_solution:
![](images/cd/cdb88c0c679ca9325df42c5c8c4feaea6ce6c0cf02655410158860d7b03d54dc.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-(4x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-(4x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-4x+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=1\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =-2{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+2(\frac{1}{2})+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-1 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ 2x(1-x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x\ge \frac{1}{2}$ is $x=1\,m.$

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(k-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k-x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (k-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(0)-\frac{(0)^{2}}{2}+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+8.
$$

Finally, since $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(2)-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+8 \\ 12 & =2k+6 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/33/33b95a6985a53b76eb7f74771825c18f21d1e59b2245325e14690a365a2a8bb0.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(10-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=10-2x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10-2x & =0 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=5\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,5)$ | $5$ | $(5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $4$ |  | $6$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2>0$ | $0$ | $-2<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=5\,m.$

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=10-2x.
$$

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (10-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=10x-{x}^{2}+C.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x \geq 1.$  When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(2x-2) \, \rm{m/s}^2,$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $\sqrt2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1\,\rm{m},$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](images/0c/0c47a1e988a75e4813c92a76acbf3a821364995123f3eb394b07d4bfaa95f80d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(2x-2)\,\rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -(2x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -(2x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int (-2x+2) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x + C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{2}\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=1\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2})^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+2(1)+C \\ C & =1+1-2 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x \geq 1$ is $x=2\,\rm{m}.$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =\sqrt{3}\text{i},$ and

$$

$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-\sqrt{3}\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}].

questions.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-2\text{i} & 4 \\ -2 & -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-2\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+(-2-2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-2\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=-2\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector of ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(-2)(-2)}{(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})}=2.
$$
