questions.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 5 \\ -4 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 5 \\ -4 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2+4\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(5)(5)}{(-2+4\text{i})(-2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(E) & ={E}^{2}+4E-5I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4+8-5 & 0+0-0 \\ 3+4-0 & 1+4-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Finding an Orthonormal Basis of a Vector Space
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}],\,B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $\text{Col}(A)$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ where $A$ and $B$ are given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $\text{Col}(A)$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|a|+|b|+|c|?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A.$  

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{3\cdot 4+2\cdot 0+4\cdot 2}{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis.

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $a=-\frac{1}{3},$ $b=\frac{2}{3},$ $c=\frac{2}{3}$ and  

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|=|-\frac{1}{3}|+|\frac{2}{3}|+|\frac{2}{3}|=\frac{5}{3}.
$$

questions.problem:
$$
V=\text{Span}{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]},\,B={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $V$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $V,$ given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|a|+|b|+|c|?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-3)\cdot (-4)+2\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{(-4)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis:

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{11}}{11}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}\frac{-2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{\sqrt{11}}{11} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{11}}{11}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V.$

Finally, $a=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11},$ $b=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11},$ $c=\frac{3\sqrt{11}}{11}$ and  

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|=|\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11}|+|\frac{\sqrt{11}}{11}|+|\frac{3\sqrt{11}}{11}|=\frac{5\sqrt{11}}{11}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Particle Is at Instantaneous Rest
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $2x\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $4\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/4b/4b08d915d0adf8bf603070aa96bde1edf0cfb392d9be5f9bd4786897a6c943fa.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2x\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-2x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+C \\ C & =8+1 \\ C & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=9-{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =9-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =9-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-3{x}^{2}+C.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(10+kx)\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-(10+kx).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-(10+kx).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int -(10+kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=12\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(12)^{2} & =-10(0)-\frac{k(0)^{2}}{2}+C \\ C & =72\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=72-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=2\sqrt{15}\,m/s$ when $x=4\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =72-10x-\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{15})^{2} & =72-10(4)-\frac{k(4)^{2}}{2} \\ 30 & =72-40-8k \\ 8k & =2 \\ k & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the value of $k.$

![](images/6f/6f34d18ec0aed1f28e77a143c5be0b3d4eaf44ba08649d02517c6c6ea5bc0af4.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(k-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k-x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (k-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(0)-\frac{(0)^{2}}{2}+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+8.
$$

Finally, since $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(2)-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+8 \\ 12 & =2k+6 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m$ and the particle has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\pi \,m,$ find the value of $k.$

![](images/b3/b396b80995e34fe348b3d059737b1eec3d4ce5a9d2e9138a8e7d4ed5c0945dc0.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=\pi \,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\ 32 & =8+k \\ k & =24.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x \geq 1.$  When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(2x-2) \, \rm{m/s}^2,$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $\sqrt2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1\,\rm{m},$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](images/0c/0c47a1e988a75e4813c92a76acbf3a821364995123f3eb394b07d4bfaa95f80d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(2x-2)\,\rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -(2x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -(2x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int (-2x+2) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x + C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{2}\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=1\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2})^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+2(1)+C \\ C & =1+1-2 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x \geq 1$ is $x=2\,\rm{m}.$

Also, since $v = 2\sqrt{6} \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 1 \, \rm{m},$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(5x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(5(1)-\frac{1}{2}{(1)}^{2})+3 \\ 12 & =\frac{9k}{2}+3 \\ \frac{9k}{2} & =9 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2(5x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =10x-{x}^{2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =20x-2{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+20x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \sqrt{-2x^2 + 20x + 6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
v_{\max} = v(5) =\sqrt{-2(5)^2 + 20(5) + 6} = 2\sqrt{14}\,\rm{m/s}
$$

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ $\overset{\to }{OB}=b$, and $T$ divides $\overset{―}{AB}$ in the ratio $AT:TB=1:1.$ Find $\overset{\to }{OT}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OT}=\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AT}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{AT}.$

First, from $△OAB,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $AT:TB=1:1,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{AT}=\frac{1}{2}\overset{\to }{AB}=\frac{1}{2}(b-a).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OT} & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AT} \\  & =a+\frac{1}{2}(b-a) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}a+\frac{1}{2}b.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+2{\pi }^{2}=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{2}\pi \text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\pi x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{2}\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\pi x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(18-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =B\sqrt{2}\pi +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(18-{n}^{2})} \\ B\sqrt{2}\pi  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(18-{n}^{2})} \\ B & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(18-{n}^{2})} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{\sqrt{2}{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3\sqrt{2}(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\pi x)$, we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\pi x){\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3\sqrt{2}(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(18-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an even function and the differential operator contains no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits the symmetry and is also an even function consisting only of cosine terms. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+8=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{8}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{8}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{8}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Differentiating the total solution gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼-A\sqrt{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{8}x)+B\sqrt{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{8}x)-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{a}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

Using the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =-A\sqrt{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+B\sqrt{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{a}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\ 0 & =0+B\sqrt{8}-0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because the total solution is an even function, its derivative is an odd function, which must vanish at $x=0.$

Next, we use the condition $y(0)=-2.$ With $B=0,$ the total solution is

$$
y(x)∼A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{8}x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

Applying $y(0)=-2$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =A+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n} \\ A & =-2-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $A$ back into ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{8}x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{8}x)(-2-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n})+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form $y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)$ is given by $y = y_c + y_p,$ where $y_c$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution $y_p.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no $y'$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
y_p(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty 
\dfrac{16(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^3\left(28-n^2\right)} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation $\lambda^2 + 7\pi^2 = 0$ gives roots $\lambda = \pm \sqrt{7}\pi \textrm i.$ So, we have

$$
y_c = A\cos(\sqrt{7}\pi x) + B\sin(\sqrt{7}\pi x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $y_p(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition $y'(0)=0.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
y'(x) \sim B(\sqrt{7}\pi)\cos(\sqrt{7}\pi x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty 
\dfrac{8(-1)^n}{n\pi^2\left(28-n^2\right)} \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
$$

Applying $y'(0)=0$ and noting that $\cos(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =B(\sqrt{7}\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(28-{n}^{2})} \\ B(\sqrt{7}\pi ) & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(28-{n}^{2})} \\ B & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(28-{n}^{2})} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{\sqrt{7}n{\pi }^{3}(28-{n}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into $y_c = B\sin(\sqrt{7}\pi x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)\sim 
\bbox[4pt,border: 0.5px solid black]{-\sin(\sqrt{7}\pi x)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{8(-1)^n}{\sqrt{7}n\pi^3\left(28-n^2\right)}}
+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty 
\dfrac{16(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^3\left(28-n^2\right)} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
$$

questions.problem: The domain of the function $f(x)=\frac{x+3}{3x-2a}$ is $(-\infty ,2)\cup (2,\infty ).$ What is the value of $a?$
questions.worked_solution:
A reciprocal function is defined for all values of $x$ except for those that make the denominator zero. So, to find the domain, we must exclude all values that make the denominator zero.

Setting the denominator equal to zero and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-2a & =0 \\ 3x & =2a \\ x & =\frac{2a}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point that must be excluded from the domain is $x=\frac{2a}{3}.$ 

On the other hand, we can see that $x=2$ is excluded from the domain. Equating this to $\frac{2a}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2a}{3} & =2 \\ \frac{a}{3} & =1 \\ a & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

A transformed reciprocal function of the form

$$
f(x)=\frac{a}{bx+c}+d
$$

has the horizontal asymptote $y=d,$ and therefore, its range is

$$
f(x)\in (-\infty ,d)\cup (d,\infty ).
$$

In our case, $d=2.$ Therefore, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2,$ and the range of the function is

questions.problem: Consider a linear transformation $T:{R}^{10}\to {R}^{10}.$ If $\text{rank}(T)=6$ then $\text{nullity}(T)=$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $T:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n},$ then

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=n.
$$

For the given transformation, we have $n=10.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T) & =n \\ 6+\text{nullity}(T) & =10 \\ \text{nullity}(T) & =10-6 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find $\text{nullity}(T)$ given that $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ and 

$$
\text{Im}(T)={[x,y,z]^{T}\,:\,-x+z=0}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Solving $-x+z=0$ for $z,$ we get $z=x.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ x\end{aligned}]=x{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+y{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=2.$ 

Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Using the Rank-Nullity Theorem
questions.problem:
Let $T:{R}^{5}\to {R}^{5}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T,$ and let ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ be a set of linearly independent vectors in ${R}^{5}.$ Consider the following statement:

*If  $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$, then $\text{__________}.$ *

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?

- $\text{rank}(T)=1$
- $\text{nullity}(T)=2$
- $T$ is a bijection
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{5}$ into ${R}^{5},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=5 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=5.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ and the set ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, we get that $\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=3.$

- Statement II is true. According to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =5-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =5-3 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\text{rank}(T)\ne 5$ (or since $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0$), the linear transformation $T$ cannot be a bijection according to the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, the correct option is "II only."

questions.problem:
Let $T:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- If $\text{Ker}(T)={⟨x,y,z⟩\,|\,x+y=0}$ then $\text{rank}(T)+1=n$
- If there exists a vector $v\notin \text{Im}(T),$ then $|T|\ne 0$
- If ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is linearly independent and $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=0$ then $\text{nullity}(T)=1$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{n}$ into ${R}^{n},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=n \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Solving $x+y=0$ for $x,$ we get $x=-y.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-y \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=y{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+z{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=2.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T) & =n \\ \text{rank}(T)+2 & =n.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If $v\notin \text{Im}(T)$ then $\text{Im}(T)\ne {R}^{n}$, so, according to the invertible matrix theorem, $T$ is not a bijection. Thus, the matrix $T$ is not invertible, and, consequently, $|T|=0.$

- Statement III is false. Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=0$, then ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}\in \text{Ker}(T).$ But the vectors are linearly independent, therefore, the dimension of  $\text{Ker}(T)$ is at least $2.$

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=y{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+z{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=2.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Solving $y-2z=0$ for $y,$ we get $y=2z.$ Solving $x+z=0$ for $x,$ we get $x=-z.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 2z \\ z\end{aligned}]=z{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=1.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T) & =3-\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. If the columns of $T$ are such that ${v}_{3}={v}_{1}-{v}_{2},$ then the set of vectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly dependent and therefore $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T)\ne {R}^{3}.$ Now, according to the matrix invertible theorem, we obtain that $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T) & =3-\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\text{rank}(T)\ne 3$ (or since $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0$), the linear transformation $T$ cannot be a bijection according to the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, the correct option is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Using the Rank-Nullity Theorem
questions.problem:
Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- If $\text{rank}(T)=2,$ then $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$
- If $[-2,0,0]^{T}$ is a solution of $T(x)=0$ then $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0$
- If $T(x)=[1,0,0]^{T}$ has no solution then $\text{rank}(T)=3$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement II is true. Since $[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is a solution of $Tx=0$, we have that $[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\in \text{Ker}(T)$ and therefore $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0.$

- Statement III is false. Since $T(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has no solution, we have that $\text{Im}(T)\ne {R}^{3}.$ Hence, $\text{rank}(T)\ne 3.$

Therefore, the correct option is "II only."

choices.value: None of the statements are true

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Rank or Nullity of a Linear Transformation Using the Rank-Nullity Theorem
canonical_examples.problem: Consider a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3.$ If $\textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T})=1,$ then what is $\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T})?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n,$ then

$$
\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T}) + \textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T}) = n.
$$

For the given transformation, we have $n=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T) & =n \\ \text{rank}(T)+1 & =3 \\ \text{rank}(T) & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find $\text{nullity}(\mathbf{T})$ given that $\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T})=\{ [ x, y, z ]^T \, : \, x=y=z\}.$

Any vector from $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T})$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ x \\ x\end{aligned}]=x{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T})=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}.$ Therefore, $\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T})=1.$ 

Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Shape of a Level Curve
questions.problem:
The level curves of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2y}$ are given by $f(x,y)=c.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $c=0$ gives a circle
- $c=1$ gives a hyperbola
- $c=2$ gives a parabola
questions.worked_solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2y} & =c \\ {x}^{2}+2y & ={c}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=0$ then the level curve is $y=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ which is not a circle.

- If $c=1$ then the level curve is $y=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ which is not a hyperbola.

- If $c=2$ then the level curve is $y=2-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ which is a parabola.

So, only statement III is true.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of a Hyperbolic Paraboloid
questions.problem: Given the hyperbolic paraboloid $(x-6)^{2}-8(y+2)^{2}=z+4$, find its intercepts with the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the $y$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $x=0$ and $z=0$ in the equation of the paraboloid:

$$
\begin{aligned}(0-6)^{2}-8(y+2)^{2} & =0+4 \\ 36-8(y+2)^{2} & =4 \\ 32 & =8(y+2)^{2} \\ (y+2)^{2} & =4 \\ y+2 & =\pm 2 \\ y & =-2\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions $y=-4$ and $y=0.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $y$-axis are $(0,-4,0)$ and $(0,0,0).$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Whether an Affine Transformation is Orientation-Preserving
questions.problem:
Consider the affine transformation $T$ defined as

$$
x=3u-v+2,\,y=v-u.
$$

Let $A$ be the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]$
- $det(A)=-2$
- The transformation $T$ is orientation-preserving
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is false. Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u-v+2 \\ v-u\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u-v \\ -u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$

- Statement II is false. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-1)=2.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $det(A)>0,$ the affine transformation $T$ is orientation-preserving.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined by an Implicit Cartesian Equation
questions.problem:
$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,\text{_____}⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(u,v)$ parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as 
$x+y-\sqrt{z}=0$
for $z\ge 0.$ What is the third component of $r?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y-\sqrt{z} & =0 \\ \sqrt{z} & =x+y \\ z & =(x+y)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
r=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩=⟨x,\,y,\,(x+y)^{2}⟩.
$$

Finally, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,(u+v)^{2}⟩
$$

Therefore, the third component of $r$ is $(u+v)^{2}.$

**Note:** The parametrization is well-defined for $u$ and $v$ such that $u+v\ge 0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Double Summation
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write out the inner summation by summing over the index $i:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{2}^{i}{3}^{j} & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{2}^{i}{3}^{j}] \\  & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}({2}^{1}{3}^{j}+{2}^{2}{3}^{j}) \\  & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}(2\cdot {3}^{j}+4\cdot {3}^{j}) \\  & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}(6\cdot {3}^{j})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we sum over the index $j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{2}(6\cdot {3}^{j}) & =(6\cdot {3}^{1})+(6\cdot {3}^{2}) \\  & =18+54 \\  & =72\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Center of Mass for a Collection of Masses Along the X-Axis
questions.problem: Consider the collection of point masses ${m}_{1}=2\,\text{kg},$ ${m}_{2}=4\,\text{kg},$ and ${m}_{3}=1\,\text{kg}$ located at ${x}_{1}=2,$ ${x}_{2}=-1.5,$ and ${x}_{3}=3,$ respectively, along the $x$-axis, where the $x$-coordinates are measured in meters. What is the $x$-coordinate of the center of mass for this system?
questions.worked_solution:
The center of mass, denoted $\overset{―}{x},$ of a collection of point masses ${m}_{1},{m}_{2},…,{m}_{n}$ located at ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ along the $x$-axis is given by 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m},
$$

 

where 

- $m={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}$ is the total mass of the system,

- ${M}_{O}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{x}_{i}$ is the total moment of the system about the origin $O.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =2, & \,{m}_{2} & =4, & \,{m}_{3} & =1, \\ {x}_{1} & =2, & \,{x}_{2} & =-1.5, & \,{x}_{3} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the total mass of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i} \\  & ={m}_{1}+{m}_{2}+{m}_{3} \\  & =2+4+1 \\  & =7\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

and the moment of the system about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & ={m}_{1}{x}_{1}+{m}_{2}{x}_{2}+{m}_{3}{x}_{3} \\  & =2\cdot 2+4\cdot (-1.5)+1\cdot 3 \\  & =4-6+3 \\  & =1\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m}=\frac{1}{7}.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Center of Mass for a Collection of Masses Along the X-Axis

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Continuous Random Variables Given in Context
questions.problem:
Which of the following are continuous random variables?

- The quantity of fat, in grams per kilogram, in a sausage
- The number of points out of $50$ that a student gets in a math test
- The weight, measured  in kilograms, of a randomly selected seventeen-year-old student
questions.worked_solution:
A random variable is a variable whose value is determined by the outcome of a trial or experiment. A *continuous* random variable is a random variable whose possible values are represented by an interval of real numbers.

Common examples of continuous random variables are shown in the diagram below.

![](images/05/05e3d893f6c069dce5b51dc7d9fa5830b44bca58fa071009548fde20ebe92c19.png)

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given statements.

- Statement I describes a continuous random variable. Its value is determined by the result of an experiment, and its possible values correspond to the real interval $[0,1\,000].$

- Statement II does *not* describe a continuous random variable. Its value is determined by the result of an experiment, but its possible values are the integers $0,1,2,3,…,50,$ which do not correspond to an interval of real numbers.

- Statement III describes a  continuous random variable. Its value is determined by the result of an experiment, and its possible values correspond to the real interval $(0,\infty ).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

provenance.kp_title: Identifying Continuous Random Variables Given in Context

questions.knowledge_point: Further Translating Problems With Proportional Rates of Change Into Differential Equations
questions.problem: The number of people $N$ infected by a particular virus increases with time. The rate of change of the number of infected people is proportional to the square of the number of infected people. What differential equation describes the rate of change of the number of people infected by the virus at time $t?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **number of people infected** by a particular virus $N$ **increases** with time. The **rate** of change of the number of infected people is **proportional** to the **square of the number of people infected** by the virus.  *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *number of infected people* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}$ is *proportional to* the *number of infected people squared.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}∝{N}^{2}.
$$

Recall that $∝$ means "is proportional to."

- Finally, we want to replace the proportionality symbol with an equality symbol. Let $k$ be a positive constant. Since the number of infected people *increases* with time, our derivative should be *positive*. Therefore, we can rewrite our proportionality statement as

$$
\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}=k{N}^{2}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Wronskian Using Abel's Identity
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+5y=0.
$$

Suppose ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions and their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies $W(1)=2.$ What is $W(4)?$

$W(4)=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=-3.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=3W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =3W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =3\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int 3\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =3x+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}{e}^{3x} \\ W & =C{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(1)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(1) & =C{e}^{3\cdot 1} \\ 2 & =C{e}^{3} \\ C & =2{e}^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
W(x)=2{e}^{-3}{e}^{3x}.
$$

Finally, we compute $W(4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(4) & =2{e}^{-3}{e}^{3\cdot 4}=2{e}^{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Computing the Wronskian Using Abel's Identity

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Wronskian Using Abel's Identity
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{2}{x}{y}^{′}+y=0,\,x>0.
$$

Suppose ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions and their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies $W(1)=6.$ What is $W(3)?$

$W(3)=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=\frac{2}{x}.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-\frac{2}{x}W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =-\frac{2}{x}W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =-\frac{2}{x}\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int -\frac{2}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}{x}^{-2} \\ W & =\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(1)=6$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(1) & =\frac{C}{{1}^{2}} \\ 6 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
W(x)=\frac{6}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, we compute $W(3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(3) & =\frac{6}{{3}^{2}}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ be solutions to the second-order homogeneous differential equation above, where $Q(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ The Wronskian satisfies $W(1)=2.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies the following first-order differential equation:

$$
{W}^{′}(x)={{field-1}}W(x)
$$

Solving this equation, we get

$$
W={{field-2}}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Now, using the fact that $W(1)=2,$ we obtain 
{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=3.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-3W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =-3W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =-3\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int -3\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =-3x+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}{e}^{-3x} \\ W & =C{e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(1)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(1) & =C{e}^{-3\cdot 1} \\ 2 & =C{e}^{-3} \\ C & =2{e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have $W(x)=2{e}^{3}{e}^{-3x}$ and $W(x)\ne 0\text{ for all }x\in R.$

questions.problem:
A triangle $S$ has vertices at $(0,2),(-1,2),(-1,0).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of ${S}^{′},$ the image of $S$ under the counterclockwise rotation ${R}_{{90}^{∘}}$ by an angle of ${90}^{∘}$ about the origin?

- $(1,-1)$
- $(0,-2)$
- $(-2,-1)$
questions.worked_solution:
The counterclockwise rotation ${R}_{{90}^{∘}}$ by an angle of ${90}^{∘}$ is given by the matrix

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the image of $S$ under the action of ${R}_{{90}^{∘}},$ we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under ${R}_{{90}^{∘}}$ by calculating the matrix product $RX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}RX & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of ${S}^{′}$ are $(-2,0),(-2,-1),(0,-1).$

So, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding and Classifying All Critical Points Using the Second Partial Derivatives Test
questions.problem:
Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x & 2{y}^{2}-2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x & 2{y}^{2}-2\end{aligned}],$ we must have 

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{y}^{2}-2.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4x=0 \\ 2{y}^{2}=2\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $(0,1)$ and $(0,-1)$ are the stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x)=4\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{y}^{2}-2)=0 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{2}-2)=4y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,1)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,1),$ we get

$$
det(H(0,1))=4\cdot 4-{0}^{2}=16>0.
$$

Now, since $H(0,1)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(0,1)=({f}^{″}(0,1))_{11}=4>0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(0,1).$

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,-1)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $H(0,-1),$ we get

$$
det(H(-1,0))=4\cdot (-4)-{0}^{2}=-16<0
$$

Therefore, $f(0,-1)$ is saddle point.

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,-1)$ and a local minimum at $(0,1).$

choices.value: $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,-1)$ and a local minimum at $(0,1)$
$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0)$ and a saddle point at $(1,1)$
$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-1,0)$ and a local minimum at $(0,1)$
$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(1,-1)$

answer_fields.correct_value: $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,-1)$ and a local minimum at $(0,1)$

questions.problem:
The function 
$f(x,y)$
has the first derivative

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\frac{y}{x} & \frac{x}{y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}]
$$

and has a stationary point at $(e,e).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $H(e,e)>0$
- $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(e,e)>0$
- The point $(e,e)$ is a saddle point of $f$
questions.worked_solution:
The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\frac{y}{x} & \frac{x}{y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\frac{y}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\frac{y}{x})=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=\frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{x} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(e,e),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(e,e)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{e} & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{e}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(e,e),$ we get

$$
H(e,e)=det({f}^{″}(e,e))=\frac{1}{e}\cdot (-\frac{1}{e})-{0}^{2}=-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}<0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(e,e)=({f}^{″}(e,e))_{11}=\frac{1}{e}>0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(e,e)<0,$ the point $(e,e)$ is a saddle point by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4x+4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4x+4)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x-4 & 6y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x-4=0 \\ 6y=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $x,$ we get

$$
2x-4=0\,⟹\,x=2.
$$

Solving the second equation for $y,$ we get

$$
6y=0\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

Hence, $(2,0)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x-4)=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6y)=0 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-4)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6y)=6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(2,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(2,0)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(2,0),$ we get

$$
H(2,0)=det({f}^{″}(2,0))=2\cdot 6-{0}^{2}=12>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(2,0)=({f}^{″}(2,0))_{11}=2>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(2,0).$

questions.problem:
The second-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{e}^{t}{y}^{′}+2ty={t}^{2}
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-{e}^{t}{y}^{′}-2ty+{t}^{2}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-{e}^{t}{x}_{2}-2t{x}_{1}+{t}^{2}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-2t{x}_{1}-{e}^{t}{x}_{2}+{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
f(t)=-2t{x}_{1}-{e}^{t}{x}_{2}+{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Given Only One Eigenvalue
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 6 & -8\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda =-5+3\text{i},$ and that $A=PC{P}^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

Since we are given the eigenvalue $\lambda =-5+3\text{i},$ we can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-5+3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 6 & -8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-5+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -5+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3-3\text{i} & -3 \\ 6 & -3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(3-3\text{i}){x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}+(-3-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(1-\text{i}){x}_{1}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (1-\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 8\text{i}-5\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2-2\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=2+2\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} \\ -5-8\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -5 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$

$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2+4t \\ 5+5t \\ -1+6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 5t \\ 6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(2,5,-1)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,5,6⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-5}{5}=\frac{z-(-1)}{6}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-5}{5}=\frac{z+1}{6}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-1)}{0}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-0}{-1}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+1}{0}=\frac{y-1}{2}=-z,
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{x+1}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-1:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1+2t \\ -t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{x+1}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-1,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{y-1}{2}=-z,\,x=-1
$$

questions.problem:
![](images/30/30299b98c822a5b06b332860bafbed4f465a4567a7135dc3257c4c9e40e490fa.png)

Find a Cartesian equation of the line shown in the figure above.
questions.worked_solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(2,-3,4)$ and $Q(-1,-3,7).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ which is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-1,-3,7⟩-⟨2,-3,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,0,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point $P$ and the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{-3}=\frac{y-(-3)}{0}=\frac{z-4}{3}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-2}{-3}=\frac{y+3}{0}=\frac{z-4}{3}.
$$

But the above equation is problematic because $\frac{y+3}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=-3.$ For example, our two points $P(2,-3,4)$ and $Q(-1,-3,7)$ both have $y$-coordinates of $y=-3.$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{y+3}{0}$ part and instead write $y=-3,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x-2}{-3}=\frac{z-4}{3},\,y=-3.
$$

questions.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-y},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & ∗ \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2x+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y} \\ -{e}^{x-y} & {e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-1)+(-1)+(x-1)=2x-3.
$$

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z

$$

$$

$$

and

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =2, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(x)≈2+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y \\ z-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y \\ z-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y \\ z-1\end{aligned}]

$$
f(x)≈1+e+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+b+4c?$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ 4 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 & -1 \\ 4 & -4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

 From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=-3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(-3)+2{x}_{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-4-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4-2{x}_{3} \\ -3 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+4c=(-2)+(-3)+4\cdot 0=-5.
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]\,+\,{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a-4b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 6 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & -4 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(-\frac{3}{2})+2{x}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1-2{x}_{3} \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-4b+c=-2-4\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})+0=4.
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=3 \\ 6{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $-4a+\frac{b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}54 & -18 \\ -18 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}54 & -18 & -9 \\ -18 & 6 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}54 & -18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{9}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-4a+\frac{b}{c}=-4\cdot (-\frac{1}{6})+\frac{(\frac{1}{3})}{1}=1.
$$

{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=2 \\ -{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $5a+\frac{b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & 12 \\ 12 & 24\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 12 & 6 \\ 12 & 24 & 12\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & 12 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=1-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
5a+\frac{b}{c}=5\cdot 1+\frac{(-2)}{1}=3.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent to a Parametric Curve at a Given Point
questions.problem:
![](images/94/9434dda63c08fc1202d16ab5410fe7061050515876ffa473d8720db39079af3e.png)

For the parametric curve 

$$
x={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

shown above, calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+2t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2t}{3{t}^{2}+2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{3t+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2}{3(2)+2} \\  & =\frac{2}{6+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
