questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Hyperboloid of Two Sheets
questions.problem:
The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ),$ given by

$$
f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨6\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,\,\text{_____},\,5\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

parametrizes one sheet of the hyperboloid of two sheets defined in Cartesian coordinates as 

$$
-\frac{{x}^{2}}{36}+{y}^{2}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{25}=-1.
$$

 

By first considering the transformations

$$
x=6Z,\,y=Y,\,z=5X
$$

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the second component of $f.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that the hyperbola ${Z}^{2}-{r}^{2}={k}^{2}$ can be parametrized as $⟨Z,r⟩=⟨k\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,k\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩$* for $ϕ\in R.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, substituting the transformations

$$
x=6Z,\,y=Y,\,z=5X
$$

into our equation, we get

$$
{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}-{Z}^{2}=-1.
$$

If $(r,\theta ,Z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
X=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,Y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,Z=Z.
$$

Substituting this into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}-{Z}^{2} & =-1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-{Z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-{Z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {r}^{2}-{Z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {Z}^{2}-{r}^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the hyperbola ${Z}^{2}-{r}^{2}=1$ represents the intersection of our hyperboloid with the plane that passes through the $Z$-axis and makes the angle of $\theta $ with the positive $X$-axis. Using the hint, a parametrization of such hyperbola can be given as

$$
⟨Z,r⟩=⟨\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩,\,ϕ\in R.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨6Z,Y,5X⟩ \\  & =⟨6Z,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,5r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨6\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,(\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,5(\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨6\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,5\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ and $ϕ\in R.$

Therefore, the third component of $f$ is $\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

questions.problem:
The probability distribution of the random variable $X$ is given below. Given that $\text{E}[X]=-\frac{1}{2},$ calculate $\text{Var}[\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}X].$ 

| $x$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constant $a,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}X] & ={(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & =(-2)^{2}\cdot f(-2)+(-1)^{2}\cdot f(-1)+{1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2) \\  & =4(\frac{1}{2})+1(\frac{1}{8})+1(\frac{1}{8})+4(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{13}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{13}{4}-{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{13}{4}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}X] & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns
questions.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ ${a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 6 \\ -2 & -1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Given Set Is a Basis of a Span
questions.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ ${a}_{3},$ and ${a}_{4}$ are given below. Determine whether $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3},$ where ${a}_{4}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -9\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{4}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=2 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-4 \\ -9{x}_{1}-8{x}_{3}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$

questions.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ ${a}_{3},$ and ${a}_{4}$ are given below. Determine whether $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3},$ where ${a}_{4}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{4}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 15 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 15 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=6 \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=15 \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 15 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=1,$ ${x}_{2}=3,$ and ${x}_{3}=2,$ meaning that

$$
1\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+3\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+2\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 15 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=1+3+2=6.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Radius of Gyration of a Non-Uniform, Non-Rectangular Laminar
questions.problem: A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ bounded by the curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ the line $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=4My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}}.
$$

Hence, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{y}^{2}\cdot 4My\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =M{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{x} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{M}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A plate of mass $M$ occupies the part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9$ in the second quadrant. Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{2}{9\pi }M\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{2}{9\pi }Mr.$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{9\pi }M{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{9\pi }M({\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{2}{9\pi }M\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{0}^{3}\cdot \theta {|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2M}{9\pi }\cdot \frac{243}{5}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{27M}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{0} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{27M}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =3\sqrt{\frac{3}{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ bounded by the curve $y={x}^{2}$ and the line $y=x.$ Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=15My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le x}.
$$

Hence, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 15My\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =15M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x}{x}^{2}y+{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =15M{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =15M{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})-(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{8})\text{d}x \\  & =15M{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{4}{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{6}-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & =15M{[\frac{3}{20}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{14}{x}^{7}-\frac{1}{36}{x}^{9}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =15M(\frac{3}{20}-\frac{1}{14}-\frac{1}{36}) \\  & =15M\cdot \frac{16}{315} \\  & =\frac{16M}{21}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{0} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{16M}{21}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{16}{21}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{16}}{\sqrt{21}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{21}}{21}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Hence, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}{x}^{2}\cdot 5Mx\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =5M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =5M{\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{3}y]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5M{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5M{[\frac{1}{7}{x}^{7}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =5M\cdot \frac{1}{7} \\  & =\frac{5M}{7}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=2.1x(1-0.025x)-1.1xy \\ {y}^{′}=-5.5y+2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the modified Lotka-Volterra model, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators.

The maximum carrying capacity is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity is given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

In our case, the equation describing the dynamics of the prey is given by

$$
{x}^{′}=2.1x(1-0.025x)-1.1xy
$$

where 

- the $2.1x(1-0.025x)$ term defines the growth, and

- the $-1.1xy$ term defines the decay due to interaction with predators.

In the case of the complete absence of predators, we have $y=0,$ and this equation becomes

$$
{x}^{′}=2.1x(1-0.025x).
$$

General solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2.1x(1-0.025x)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,40\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=40.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the maximum capacity.

Therefore, the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators is $40.$

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=3x(1-0.3x)-4xy \\ {y}^{′}=-y+xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\,0]^{T},$ we get

| $J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |

$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are 
{{field-5}}.

{{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=3x(1-0.3x)-4xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-y+xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x(1-0.3x)-4xy)=3-1.8x-4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x(1-0.3x)-4xy)=-4x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+xy)=-1+x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}3-1.8x-4y & -4x \\ y & -1+x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}3-1.8(0)-4(0) & -4(0) \\ 0 & -1+0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=x(1-x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x(1-x)-xy)=1-2x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x(1-x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+2xy)=-1+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}1-2x-y & -x \\ 2y & -1+2x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.5 \\ 0.5\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}1-2(0.5)-0.5 & -0.5 \\ 2(0.5) & -1+2(0.5)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.5 & -0.5 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-0.5-\lambda  & -0.5 \\ 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-0.5-\lambda )(-\lambda )-1(-0.5) & =0 \\ \lambda (0.5+\lambda )+0.5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5\lambda +0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-0.25\pm 0.25\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are complex with negative real parts, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=4x(1-2x)-3xy \\ {y}^{′}=-5y+4xy\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[0.5, \, 0]^T,$ and classify this equilibrium point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=4x(1-2x)-3xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-5y+4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-2x)-3xy)=4-16x-3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-2x)-3xy)=-3x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-5y+4xy)=4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-5y+4xy)=-5+4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/4d/4d0b2b480e0423052a4461a0cae9c8b1fa7bb61d3a1ca4d20ed84e4e5e7bc874.png)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/08/08337f194eb5fb80b86f88f62978e79bb1d1b4e87c0862458e1603b930cba6af.png) to get

![](images/15/1548452943d27f02cd2651cc8affb4800369e22e4685fc818fdd390d359bde18.png)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = -4$ and $\lambda_2=-3.$ Since the eigenvalues are real and both negative, our equilibrium is an asymptotically stable sink.

questions.problem:
The entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ k & 6 & 0\end{aligned}]$
equals $18.$ Find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ k & 6 & 0\end{aligned}| & =1|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ k & 0\end{aligned}|+3|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ k & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(0-24)-2(0-4k)+3(0-k) \\  & =8k-3k-24 \\  & =5k-24.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(0-18) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21} \\  & =\frac{1}{5k-24}\cdot 18 \\  & =\frac{18}{5k-24}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{13}^{′}=18$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{18}{5k-24} & =18 \\ \frac{1}{5k-24} & =1 \\ 1 & =5k-24 \\ 25 & =5k \\ k & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

questions.problem:
![](images/f5/f531f2467284ef84e0af0758a8e8554f1e5f72ea08d30d0b80c83076fbe5d7a3.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,0)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(0+t(1-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+t)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & =1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[t+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(0+\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}2y\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(-2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-12{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3x+2y,$ we obtain

$$

$$

questions.problem:
![](images/be/be3ad044a611d99e67c89d053d4878a2835be65828a4dc9300697bfd61822994.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the below-left quarter of the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(-1,0)$ to the point $(0,-2),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =4{\int }_{-1}^{0}{u}^{3}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{0}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{u}^{4}{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =-[(0)^{4}-(-1)^{4}] \\  & =-(-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{5}},\,s>0
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{5}}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{3!}{{s}^{3+1}}} \\  & ={t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{3}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-6}}\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ} & =L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace
questions.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 1+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace
questions.problem:
Find the distance between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 3 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 3 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 3 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}18 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2-(-1))^{2}+(2-(-1))^{2}+(5-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9+9} \\  & =\sqrt{27} \\  & =3\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace
questions.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 3+0\cdot (-1)}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{13}\sqrt{11}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{13}})≈{23.09}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto the Solution Space of a Linear System
questions.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Given the Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues of the Corresponding Matrix
questions.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $x(t),$ and that $x(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -7\end{aligned}],
$$

find the position of the particle at $t=3$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-5{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-5{c}_{1}=10 \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-7.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-5{c}_{1}=10\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=-2.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
-2+{c}_{2}=-7\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-5.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $x(3)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(3) & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3\cdot 3}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\cdot 3} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-9}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}]{e}^{6} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10{e}^{-9} \\ -2{e}^{-9}-5{e}^{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem for a Linear System of Differential Equations
questions.problem:
Find the solution to the following initial value problem.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}]
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=0\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=3.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=9 \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{c}_{1}=15\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${c}_{1}=5$ into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}5+{c}_{2}=6\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =5[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Given the General Solution
questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 8\end{aligned}]
$$

given that the general solution to our differential equation is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The solution to the initial value problem is

| $x(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $\,\,{e}^{2t}+\,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  | $\,\,{e}^{-t}.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} |  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
To find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=1 \\ 2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations, we get

$$
3{c}_{1}=9\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
3+{c}_{2}=1\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-2.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}\,+\,(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}\,+\,[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are

$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{{(1+{x}^{3})}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{4}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{{(1+{x}^{3})}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{4}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{u}^{-4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{u}^{-4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{3}{u}^{-3}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{{a}^{3}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}

- ${\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's work out each integral.

For the first integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-5}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{6}^{a}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[2\sqrt{x-5}]}_{6}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-5}-2\sqrt{6-5}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-5}-2) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3}\,{x}^{-2/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{x}^{1/3}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\sqrt[3]{a}-1) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1+\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

In conclusion, only integrals I and II are divergent.

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{1}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{3}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+1|]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+1|]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3a+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3a+1|) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\infty ) \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_2^\infty \dfrac { 8}{t^5}  \,\textrm{d}t.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{8}{{t}^{5}}\,\text{d}t & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{8}{{t}^{5}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}{t}^{-5}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{-4}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =-2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =-2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{{a}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{2}^{4}}) \\  & =-2(0-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit Using Substitution
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty \dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2} \,\textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=x+1.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}u =\textrm{d}x.
$$

Since $u \to \infty$ when $x \to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x+1$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\int_0^\infty \dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2} \,\textrm{d}x
=
\int_1^\infty \dfrac{1}{u^2} \,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{u}^{-2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{u}^{-2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-{u}^{-1}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{u}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-1\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{1}] \\  & =-1\cdot (0-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{0}    \dfrac{1}{(x-4)^2} \,\textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that, this time, it's the *lower* limit of integration that's unbounded.  

First, we substitute $u=x-4.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}u =\textrm{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty$ when $x\to -\infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x-4$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-4$ | $-\infty$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{0}    \dfrac{1}{(x-4)^2} \,\textrm{d}x
=\int_{-\infty}^{-4} \dfrac{1}{u^2}  \,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{1}{(x-4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{-4}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{-4}{u}^{-2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-4}{u}^{-2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-{u}^{-1}]}_{a}^{-4} \\  & =-1\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{u}]}_{a}^{-4} \\  & =-1\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\frac{1}{(-4)}-\frac{1}{a}] \\  & =-1\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =-1\cdot (-\frac{1}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Divergent Improper Integrals
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following improper integrals are divergent?

- $\displaystyle \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{x} }\,\textrm{d}x$

- $\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{-2} \frac{1}{(1+x)^2}\,\textrm{d}x$

- $\displaystyle \int_{1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{x^3} \,\textrm{d}x$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's work out each integral.

- For the first integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}{x}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{[2{x}^{1/2}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =2{lim}_{b\to \infty }{[\sqrt{x}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =2{lim}_{b\to \infty }[\sqrt{b}-1] \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

- For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-2}\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-2}\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{1+x}]}_{a}^{-2} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }[-\frac{1}{1-2}+\frac{1}{1+a}] \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\frac{1}{1+a}+1] \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent (not divergent).

- For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}{x}^{-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }[-\frac{1}{2{b}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2({1}^{2})}] \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{b}^{2}}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent (not divergent).

In conclusion, only integral I is divergent.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Circulation of a Vector Field Over a Region Containing Holes
questions.problem:
![](images/1f/1f308d1a3ecf3bd0090e22c4f70389311db4db3ff06f7038db0cf7770a8837c7.png)

Suppose that $F$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=5,\,{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-2,\,{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-9,
$$

where ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ are oriented clockwise and ${C}_{3}$ is oriented counterclockwise, calculate the value of ${∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](images/2b/2bed1b367cd101e0e90674c619ad87da8c90744df570eeea4d9b0333ccee0de1.png)

Notice that the positive orientations of the outer curve ${C}_{1}$ and the inner curve ${C}_{3}$ are opposite those stated in the question.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-5+(-2)-(-9) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying Green's Theorem to Regions With Holes
questions.problem:
![](images/0e/0e86380c457bc9d37d0180057d4ce8c035055986d32254d95fab3a69254531a5.png)

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}6y\,dx+9x\,dy,$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=6y$ and $Q(x,y)=9x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=6,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=9.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(9-6)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3\,\text{Area}(D) \\  & =3\cdot (\pi \cdot {3}^{2}-\pi \cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 5\pi  \\  & =15\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({sin}^{2}⁡y)-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})\,dy,$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({sin}^{2}⁡y)-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}={y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-{x}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({sin}^{2}⁡y)-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}-((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}-{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}-{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{2}^{4}-{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-2\pi \cdot {\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot ({4}^{4}-{2}^{4}) \\  & =-120\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4xy.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})\,dx+(2{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy-2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as ${Δ}_{1}∖{Δ}_{2},$ where

- ${Δ}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,-1\le y\le 2}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${Δ}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{Δ}_{1}}2xy\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{{Δ}_{2}}2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-1}^{2}y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-1}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={x}^{2}\,{|}_{-2}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{2}-{x}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{1}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(4-4)\cdot (2-\frac{1}{2})-(1-1)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =0\cdot \frac{3}{2}-0\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](images/16/16026d4ac7deeb30c1abb3a066df23a06a544116463b364b0a1e9e0bac0608c8.png)

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
\oint\limits_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = 10, 
\qquad 
\oint\limits_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = -8, 
\qquad 
\oint\limits_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = 3,
$$

where $C_1$ and $C_3$ are oriented clockwise, and $C_2$ is oriented counterclockwise, calculate the value of $\displaystyle\oint\limits_{\partial D}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve $C_1$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse $C_1$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves $C_2$ and $C_3$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse $C_2$ and $C_3$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](images/11/11445c083440ee2fde1864d599a8bbd68146d522c61de11b3e90dc231e6eddf1.png)

Notice that the positive orientations of the outer curve $C_1$ and the inner curve $C_2$ are opposite those stated in the question.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-10-(-8)+3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate

\oint\limits_{\partial D} (2x^3y^2-x^5) \,\mathrm{d}x + (3x^4y+y^4) \,\mathrm{d}y,$
where $D$ is the region shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=2x^3y^2-x^5$ and $Q(x,y)= 3x^4y+y^4.$ Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 4x^3y, \qquad 
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 12x^3y.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-{x}^{5})\,dx+(3{x}^{4}y+{y}^{4})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}12{x}^{3}y-4{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as $\Delta_1\setminus\Delta_2,$ where

- $\Delta_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq x \leq 1, -1 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- $\Delta_2 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -1 \leq x \leq 0, 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

questions.problem:
Let $E$ be the set of all functions of the form $f(x)=a\,\text{ }{2}^{x},$ where $a\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- For any $f(x)\in E,$ we have $1\cdot f(x)=f(x).$
- For any $f(x)\in E$ and $\alpha ,\beta \in R$, we have $(\alpha +\beta )f(x)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(x).$
- For any $f(x),g(x)\in E$ and $\alpha \in R$, we have $\alpha (f(x)+g(x))=\alpha f(x)+\alpha g(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any $f(x)\in E$ and for any fixed $x\in R,$ the result of $f(x)$ is just a real number. Thus,

$$
(1\cdot f)(x)=1\cdot f(x)=f(x).
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any $f(x)\in E$ and for any fixed $x\in R,$ the result of $f(x)$ is just a real number. Thus, for any $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
(\alpha +\beta )f(x)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(x).
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any $f(x)\in E$ and for any fixed $x\in R,$ the results of $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are just real numbers. Thus, for any $\alpha \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
\alpha (f(x)+g(x))=\alpha f(x)+\alpha g(x).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem:
Let $F$ be the set of all $2\times 2$ matrices of the form $[\begin{aligned}a & a \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}],$ where $a\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- The identity matrix ${I}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$ belongs to $F.$
- For the zero matrix $O$ and any $A\in F,$ we have $A+O=A.$
- For any $A,B\in F,$ we have $A+B=B+A.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, every element $A$ in $F$ satisfies ${a}_{12}={a}_{11}={a}_{22},$ however, for the identity matrix ${I}_{2}$ we have ${i}_{12}=0\ne {i}_{11}.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, as for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ with real entries, we have

$$
A+O=A.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, For any matrices $A,B\in F$ we obtain that 

$$
A+B=B+A
$$

since matrix addition is commutative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
Let $S$ be the set of all $2\times 2$ matrices with real entries and determinant different from $0.$ Which of the following statements are true?  

- The  matrix $[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ belongs to $S.$
- For any $A\in S,$ we can find the corresponding negative matrix $-A\in S$ such that $A+(-A)=O.$
- For any $A,B,C\in S,$ we have $A+(B-C)=(A+B)-C.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, we have

$$
|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 1-2\cdot 1=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with real entries,   there is a corresponding negative matrix $-A$ such that

$$
A+(-A)=A-A=O.
$$

Notice if $A\in S$ then 

$$
|-A|=|-1\cdot A|=(-1)^{2}\cdot |A|=1\cdot |A|=|A|\ne 0,
$$

hence $-A\in S.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any matrices $A,B\in S,$ we obtain that 

$$
A+(B-C)=A+(B+(-C))=(A+B)+(-C)=(A+B)-C
$$

since matrix addition is associative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
Let $P$ be the set of all $2\times 2$ real matrices $A=({a}_{ij})$ such that ${a}_{11}+{a}_{22}>0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- For any $A,B\in P$ and any $\alpha \in R,$ we have $\alpha (A-B)=\alpha A-\alpha B.$
- The scalar multiplication of matrices in $P$ is associative.
- For any $A\in P,$ we have $(-1)\cdot A\in P.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's verify the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ matrices $A=({a}_{ij})$ and $B=({b}_{ij})$ from $P,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, for any $\alpha \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
\alpha ({a}_{ij}-{b}_{ij})=\alpha {a}_{ij}-\alpha {b}_{ij},
$$

and hence,

$$
\alpha (A-B)=\alpha A-\alpha B.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A=({a}_{ij})$ from $P,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, for any $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
\alpha (\beta {a}_{ij})=(\alpha \beta ){a}_{ij},
$$

and hence,

$$
\alpha (\beta A)=(\alpha \beta )A.
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ from $P.$ Then,

$$
(-1)\cdot A=(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\notin P
$$

because $-1+0≯0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
$$
{y}^{‴}-2{y}^{″}-21{y}^{′}-18y=3+4{e}^{-x},\,{{y}_{1}={e}^{-3x},\,{y}_{2}={e}^{-x},\,{y}_{3}={e}^{6x}}
$$

Consider the differential equation and the set of fundamental solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation above. 
Using the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution of the equation can be written in the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){e}^{-3x}+{u}_{2}(x){e}^{-x}+{u}_{3}(x){e}^{6x}.
$$

What is the function ${u}_{1}(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}+{u}_{3}{y}_{3},\,{u}_{i}=(-1)^{3-i}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{i}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x,\,i=1,2,3,
$$

where $g(x)$ is the forcing term, $W(x)$ is the Wronskian of ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{1}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{2}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{3}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the forcing term is $g(x)=3+4{e}^{-x}.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{-3x},\,{y}_{2}={e}^{-x},\,{y}_{3}={e}^{6x}.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W(x) & =W({y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3}) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3x} & {e}^{-x} & {e}^{6x} \\ -3{e}^{-3x} & -{e}^{-x} & 6{e}^{6x} \\ 9{e}^{-3x} & {e}^{-x} & 36{e}^{6x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =({e}^{-3x}\cdot {e}^{-x}\cdot {e}^{6x})|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -3 & -1 & 6 \\ 9 & 1 & 36\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{2x}[1(-36-6)-1(-108-54)+1(-3+9)] \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-42+162+6) \\  & =126{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are linearly independent. 

Now, to find ${u}_{1},$ we compute the determinant

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{1}(x) & ={W}_{1}({y}_{2},{y}_{3}) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x} & {e}^{6x} \\ -{e}^{-x} & 6{e}^{6x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =6{e}^{5x}+{e}^{5x} \\  & =7{e}^{5x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =(-1)^{3-1}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{1}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{(3+4{e}^{-x})(7{e}^{5x})}{126{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{21{e}^{5x}+28{e}^{4x}}{126{e}^{2x}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{6}{e}^{3x}+\frac{2}{9}{e}^{2x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{18}{e}^{3x}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{2x} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}({e}^{3x}+2{e}^{2x}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}^{‴}-{y}^{″}+{y}^{′}-y=-2(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x),\,{{y}_{1}={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{3}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x}
$$

Consider the differential equation and the set of fundamental solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation above. 
Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{x}+B\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{1}(x){e}^{x}+{u}_{2}(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{u}_{3}(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

What is the function ${u}_{2}(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}+{u}_{3}{y}_{3},\,{u}_{i}=(-1)^{3-i}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{i}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x,\,i=1,2,3,
$$

where $g(x)$ is the forcing term, $W(x)$ is the Wronskian of ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{1}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{2}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{3}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the forcing term is $g(x)=-2(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x).$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{3}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W(x) & =W({y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3}) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & \operatorname{cos}⁡x & \operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {e}^{x} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {e}^{x} & -\operatorname{cos}⁡x & -\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡x & \operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 1 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ 1 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡x & -\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x}[1({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)-1(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+1({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)] \\  & ={e}^{x}[1(1)-1(0)+1(1)] \\  & =2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are linearly independent. 

Now, to find ${u}_{2},$ we compute the determinant ${W}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{2}(x) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & \operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {e}^{x} & \operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2}(x) & =(-1)^{3-2}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{2}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{-2(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot {e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{2{e}^{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x-{sin}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/ec/ec4af1357e75dcee6d7d5412467c2ee2ea9e54fa38fb6e83817b0ae909c529aa.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2+3{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2x-3{e}^{-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2(0)-3{e}^{-0}+C \\ 2 & =-3+C \\ C & =2+3 \\ C & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2x-3{e}^{-x}+5 \\ {v}^{2} & =4x-6{e}^{-x}+10 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4(3)-6{e}^{-3}+10} \\ v & =\sqrt{22-6{e}^{-3}} \\ v & ≈4.7\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is ${cos}^{2}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/76/768db6b8051d8f4bea528f6c5b5d386ffc0d6529517d2fe72641cb33f6e8ac10.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-{cos}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-{cos}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we obtain the differential equation

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-{cos}^{2}⁡x.
$$
