questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/32/3278eca2ae91f59c7c20d91f9190611291924dcc0cd6ffe74456552ba8400335.png)

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(-\sqrt{\pi })^{2} & =-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+C \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =-2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+C \\ C & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x \\ {v}^{2} & =2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v=-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡3)} \\  & ≈-1.1\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at $x=1\,m$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/f0/f08c9d1e8dce3c0ae7c37719cadc3fc60bf5de3030ce8c44ca7528a98f3abf7e.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -8{e}^{1-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8{e}^{0}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =16{e}^{1-x} \\ v & =\pm 4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4{e}^{(1-x)/2} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{(1-x)/2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=1$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{(x-1)/2}=2t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+1 \\ \frac{x-1}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x-1 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)+1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Jacobian Determinant
questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡v\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡u$ and $y(u,v)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot (-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-0\cdot 0 \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})}=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=3.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(1,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}+v \\ 2u-{v}^{3}\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 1 \\ 2 & -3{v}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-3{v}^{2})-1\cdot 2 \\  & =-6u{v}^{2}-2 \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,2)} & =(-6u{v}^{2}-2)\,{|}_{u=1\,v=2} \\  & =-6(1)(2)^{2}-2 \\  & =-26\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-26|\cdot \delta A \\  & =26\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(2,1)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u-v) \\ v-{u}^{2}\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{u-v} & -\frac{1}{u-v} \\ -2u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{u-v}\cdot 1-(-2u)\cdot (-\frac{1}{u-v}) \\  & =\frac{1-2u}{u-v} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(2,1)} & ={(\frac{1-2u}{u-v})\,|}_{u=2\,v=1} \\  & =\frac{1-2(2)}{2-1} \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-3|\cdot \delta A \\  & =3\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Given By a Polynomial
questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{ft}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=3{t}^{2}-2t-3$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=6\,\text{ft}/\text{s}$ when $t=3\,\text{s}$, find the velocity (in $\text{ft/s}$)  of the particle at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-2t-3)\text{d} \\  & ={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(3)=6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =(3)^{3}-(3)^{2}-3(3)+C \\ 6 & =27-9-9+C \\ C & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-3t-3.$

questions.problem:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in ${\text{m/s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6{t}^{2}-12{t}^{5}+4,$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. Find the speed of the particle at the moment $t=2\,\text{s}$ given that the particle has velocity $v=3\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s}.$

The speed at the moment $t=2\,\text{s}$ is
{{field-1}} $\text{m/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6{t}^{2}-12{t}^{5}+4)\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{3}-2{t}^{6}+4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =2({0}^{3})-2({0}^{6})+4(0)+C \\ 3 & =0+C \\ C & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2{t}^{3}-2{t}^{6}+4t+3.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=2\,\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =2({2}^{3})-2({2}^{6})+4(2)+3 \\  & =2(8)-2(64)+8+3 \\  & =16-128+8+3 \\  & =-101\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $101\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{ft}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=20t-12{t}^{2}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=8\,\text{ft}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=2\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (20t-12{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =10{t}^{2}-4{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=8.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =10(1)^{2}-4(1)^{3}+C \\ 8 & =6+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=10{t}^{2}-4{t}^{3}+2.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=2\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =10(2)^{2}-4(2)^{3}+2 \\  & =40-32+2 \\  & =10\,\text{ft}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)}{4}+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =-\frac{1}{4}+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}{4}+\frac{1}{2}.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s},$ and get

$$

$$

questions.problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to two-fifths of the rate of increase of the diameter. Determine the radius of the circle at that moment.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $D$ the diameter of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the diameter $D$ of the circle. Since $D=2r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $D$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{D}{2})}^{2}=\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}D}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2} \\ \frac{2}{5} & =\frac{\pi D}{2} \\ D & =\frac{4}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $D=2r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2r & =\frac{4}{5\pi } \\ r & =\frac{2}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/9a/9a864a350b6493794639ea031c7d40242717f5e7325eb326228f82a9cb1c10c9.png)

A graphic designer is animating a circle in such a way that the area of the circle increases at a rate of $7\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$ How fast is the radius of the circle increasing at the moment when the radius is $1\text{ cm}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=1,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=7\pi .$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=7\pi $ and $r=1,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}7\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi (1) \\ 7\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =3.5.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the radius is increasing at a rate of $3.5$ centimeters per second.

![](images/5d/5d502faeec99cbebf849c97ed701fae7eed470422754d84b4dd6d4cf798c175c.png)

A hot air balloon is descending in such a way that its shadow is a circle increasing at a constant rate. The radius of the shadow increases at a rate of $3\,\text{cm/min}.$ How fast is the area of the shadow increasing at the moment when the radius is $50\,\text{cm}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=50,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=3.$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=3$ and $r=50,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =3\cdot 2\pi (50) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =300\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area of the shadow is increasing at a rate of $300\pi {\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.$

questions.problem:
![](images/5b/5bf71c5c613c69263e15137bbd5aa56716a8c289a4457a95a9c7b1fddd8af03b.png)

A spherical balloon is inflated at the rate of $18{\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ If at a particular moment the balloon's radius is changing at the rate $\frac{1}{2\pi }\text{ cm/s},$ then what is the radius of the balloon at this moment? Do not round the answer.

$r=$
{{field-1}} $\text{cm}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=18{\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s},
$$

and we want to find $r$ when $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\text{ cm/s}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=18$ and $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{2\pi },$ and solve for $r.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}18 & =\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 18 & =2{r}^{2} \\ r & =\sqrt{9} \\ r & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius at that moment is $3\text{ cm}.$

questions.problem:
![](images/e1/e13f4de3d3d66ba1205b3da8cbe8abec300a94d2e53453af3c9c12667e1d7907.png)

A spherical soap bubble is expanding, causing its enclosed volume to increase at a rate of $24\pi \text{ }{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$ How fast is the radius increasing at the moment when the radius is $3\text{ }\text{cm}?$ Do not round the answer.

The radius of the bubble is increasing at a rate of 
{{field-1}} $\text{cm}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the bubble and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=24\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=3\,\text{cm}.$

To start, let's write down the formula for the volume of a sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=24\pi $ and $r=3,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}24\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (3)^{2} \\ 24\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 36\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when the radius is of the bubble is $3\,\text{cm},$ the radius is increasing at a rate of  $\frac{2}{3}$ $\text{ }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.$

questions.problem: A snowball is rolling down a snow-covered hillside. At a particular moment, the rate of increase in the volume of the sphere is numerically equal to three times the rate of increase in its surface area. What is the radius of the sphere at that moment?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the sphere, $V$ the volume of the sphere, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{(\frac{A}{4\pi })}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =12\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & ={(12\sqrt{\pi })}^{2} \\ A & =144\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =144\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =36 \\ r & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/2e/2ef2330edb3a3822e6edd8bd443238d027e45e1a8b12ceb8b6be53f9fa68fbd7.png)

A large latex balloon is inflated with helium so that its radius increases at a rate of $3\,\text{in/s}.$ How fast is the volume of the balloon increasing at the moment when the radius is $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{in}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=3\,\text{in/s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=\frac{3}{2}\,\text{in}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=3$ and $r=\frac{3}{2},$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3\cdot 4\pi {(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =27\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the balloon is increasing at a rate of $27\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/s}$
when the radius is $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{in}.$

canonical_examples.problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to half the rate of increase of the circumference. What is the radius of the circle at that moment?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $C$ the circumference of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\textrm d C}{\textrm d t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A = \pi r^2,$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A =  \pi r^2 =  \pi \left(\dfrac{C}{2\pi} \right)^2 = \dfrac{C^2}{4\pi}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\textrm d C}{\textrm d t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi } \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{C}{2\pi } \\ C & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $C = 2\pi r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi r & =\pi  \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
A circular oil spillage is being cleaned up by a team using specialized cleaning equipment. If the area of the circle is *decreasing* at a rate of $6\pi\,\text{m}^2/\text{h}$, what is the rate at which the radius is decreasing at the instant when the radius is $2\,\text{m}?$

![](images/d7/d769569ed7854f4d6eb085853b51eb0e5aab0e14cfc3bcdf1e5a480d996ccc9e.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d t}$ at the moment when $r=2,$ and we are also told that  $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = -6\pi.$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm dA}{\textrm dt} = -6\pi$ and $r=2,$ and solve for $\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi (2) \\ -6\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the radius is decreasing at a rate of $\dfrac{3}{2}$ meter per hour.

canonical_examples.problem:
Air is leaking from a spherical balloon at the rate of $500\pi\,\text{cm}^3/\text{s}.$ How fast is the radius of the balloon decreasing when the radius is $10\,\text{cm}?$

![](images/46/460fd4059be2c655e01b89db2738225a50578b5c76bbe048f83312f0bff655ec.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} = -500\pi\,\text{cm}^3/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt}$ when $r=10\,\text{cm}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} = -500\pi$ and $r=10,$ and solve for $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-500\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (10)^{2} \\ -500\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 400\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{5}{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-1.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the balloon is decreasing at a rate of $1.25\,\text{cm}/\text{s}$ when the radius is $10\,\text{cm}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Flux Integral as a Surface Integral
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,xz,\,z+{y}^{2}⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,xz,\,z+{y}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,xz,\,z+{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})+0-(z+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}-z}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{{x}^{2}-z}{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-z\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨3-x,\,x+y,\,z-2x⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=2x+2y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=3.$  Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x+2y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+2y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨3-x,\,x+y,\,z-2x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨3-x,\,x+y,\,2y⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2(3-x)+2(x+y)-2y) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(6-2x+2x+2y-2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 3 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,-3y,\,z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x-y+2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{3}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y+2$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=2,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-2.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y+2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,-3y,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x,\,-3y,\,x-y+2⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x+3y-(x-y+2)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(4y-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(4y-2)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(4y-2)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(4y-2)\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{3}}}(4y-2)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4y-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(4y-2)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}(4y-2)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[x]_{0}^{3}\cdot {[2{y}^{2}-2y]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 12 \\  & =36\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨y,\,z,\,2x-y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=3$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=3$ for  $1\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,z,\,2x-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨y,\,3,\,2x-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-(2x-y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-(2x-y))\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(2x-y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}(-(2x-y))\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}[({x}^{2}-xy){|}_{x=1}^{x=2}\,]\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}(3-y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[3y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 3,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$

$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,z,\,4xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-4xy)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}(-4xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}2y\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{[{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{3}\cdot {[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-36\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{y}^{3}) \\  & =3{y}^{2}+(-3{y}^{2}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}{{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Scalar curl of }F}\,\text{d}A.
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}{{(3x{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{P}\,dx+{{(-{y}^{3})}_{⏟}}_{Q}\,dy
$$

In part 2, we found that the scalar curl of $F$ is

$$

$$

Therefore, by applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A={∬}_{D}-6xy\,\text{d}A.

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}-3{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,dr\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }[{\int }_{0}^{2}-3{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,dr]d\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }{[-\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]}_{r=0}^{r=2}\,d\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }(-\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+0)\,d\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,d\theta \end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve
questions.problem:
![](images/cf/cfbc570ba4fc6bd4923edc2d0efae0e735e671f9b4350226159e591e0bdae6c7.png)     
                                
                            

   

                            The net $L$ is represented by the line segment shown in the diagram above. 
Calculate the flux of $F$ through $L,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${\int }_{L}^{}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s\,=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

* the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

* the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the line segment $L,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}t,\,y=-\sqrt{2}t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the line from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2}).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x{y}^{2} \\  & =3(\sqrt{2}t)(-\sqrt{2}t)^{2} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}{t}^{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =-{y}^{3} \\  & =-(-\sqrt{2}t)^{3} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}t)=\sqrt{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{2}t)=-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{L}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{L}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6\sqrt{2}{t}^{3})\cdot (-\sqrt{2})-(2\sqrt{2}{t}^{3})\cdot (\sqrt{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-12{t}^{3}-4{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-16{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4[{t}^{4}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4(1-0) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](images/83/8354a964dc235f1c9676754cf7d163cb4a54f05bd5899ff398acb11a4287861d.png)     
                                
                            

   

                            Let $∂R$ be the boundary of the region $R,$ shown above. Use Green's theorem to calculate the following integral:

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${∮}_{∂R}^{}F\cdot \text{d}r\,={∮}_{∂R}^{}3x{y}^{2}\,dx-{y}^{3}\,dy\,=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

As we saw earlier, we can use Green's theorem to write our line integral in polar coordinates as 

$$
{∮}_{∂R}3x{y}^{2}\,dx-{y}^{3}\,dy={∬}_{Δ}-3{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta .
$$

But this time, our region $R$ (in polar coordinates) is given by 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{Δ}-3{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-3{[\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2}]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{r=1}^{r=2}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(1-1)\cdot \frac{1}{4}({2}^{4}-{1}^{4}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\pm \text{i}.$*

| ${e}^{At}=\,\,$ |  | $\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)$ | {{field-1}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-2}} | $\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)$ |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & -{\alpha }_{1}t \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\text{i}t) & ={e}^{\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot \text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t & =-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & =\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $2,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $-t$ | $1-t$ |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

$$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(t)={e}^{t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(t)={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
t{e}^{t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}(1-t).

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 36\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=6$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=36,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-36I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 36\end{aligned}]-36[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-36 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-36I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 36\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-0I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]

{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10} \\ 2\sqrt{10} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{3}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

$$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

- For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=36,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-36I & =[\begin{aligned}26 & -10 \\ -10 & 26\end{aligned}]-36[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-10 & -10 \\ -10 & -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Equation of a Wide Ellipse
questions.problem:
![](images/e1/e1bfe4335b41f14dce0f3d614ca108a4d6d83c4aa65fc44f169431175c82f1b5.png)

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?

{{field-1}}$=1$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=8$ and the vertical radius has length $b=\frac{9}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{8}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(\frac{9}{2})}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{64}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\frac{81}{4})} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{64}+\frac{4{y}^{2}}{81} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=8$ and ${b}^{2}=24.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=8,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=24,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt{6}.$

Thus, the semi-major axis has length $b=2\sqrt{6},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=2\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 2\sqrt{6}=4\sqrt{6},$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot 2\sqrt{2}=4\sqrt{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Rational Function With Two Linear Factors as a Sum of Partial Fractions
questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
\frac{x-4}{(x-2)x}=\frac{A}{(x-2)}+\frac{B}{x},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are real constants, calculate $A+B.$
questions.worked_solution:
Our task is to find $A$ and $B$ such that

$$
\frac{x-4}{(x-2)x}=\frac{A}{(x-2)}+\frac{B}{x}.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $(x-2)x$ gives

$$
x-4=Ax+B(x-2).
$$

For $x=0$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}0-4 & =A(0)+B(0-2) \\ -4 & =-2B \\ B & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=2$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2-4 & =A(2)+B(2-2) \\ -2 & =2A \\ A & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{x-4}{(x-2)x}=-\frac{1}{(x-2)}+\frac{2}{x}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
A+B=-1+2=1.
$$

Given that

$$
\frac{-2x-9}{(x+3)x}=\frac{1}{(x+3)}+\frac{B}{x},
$$

what is the value of $B?$
questions.worked_solution:
Our task is to find $B$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-2x-9}{(x+3)x}=\frac{1}{(x+3)}+\frac{B}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides by $(x+3)x$ gives

$$
-2x-9=x+B(x+3).
$$

For $x=0$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2(0)-9 & =0+B(0+3) \\ -9 & =3B \\ B & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Rational Function With Two Linear Factors as a Sum of Partial Fractions
questions.worked_solution:
Our task is to find $A$ and $B$ such that

$$
\frac{3x+10}{(x+4)(x+5)}=\frac{A}{x+4}+\frac{B}{x+5}.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $(x+4)(x+5)$ gives

$$
3x+10=A(x+5)+B(x+4).
$$

For $x=-4$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3(-4)+10 & =A(-4+5)+B(-4+4) \\ -2 & =A \\ A & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=-5,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3(-5)+10 & =A(-5+5)+B(-5+4) \\ -5 & =-B \\ B & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{3x+10}{(x+4)(x+5)}=\frac{-2}{x+4}+\frac{5}{x+5}.
$$

questions.problem:
| $x$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** | **$5$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $3$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $-1$ |

The vector of coefficients of the curve $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{2}{x}^{2}$ that best fits the data above can be found using polynomial regression as 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{2}\end{aligned}]=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y,
$$

where $X$ is the corresponding design matrix and $y$ is the observation vector. Which of the following is the design matrix $X$ in this context?
questions.worked_solution:
| $x$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** | **$5$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $3$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $-1$ |

The coefficients of the curve 

$$
y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{2}{x}^{2}
$$

that best fits the data can be found as the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{\beta }$ to the system 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & {1}^{2} \\ 1 & {2}^{2} \\ 1 & {3}^{2} \\ 1 & {4}^{2} \\ 1 & {5}^{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

$$
{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{3}^{2},\,{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}=\boxed{} \\ {y}_{2}=\boxed{} \\ {y}_{3}={x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

From top to bottom, what is missing from the blank spaces?

questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Form to Canonical Form Using Lagrange's Method: 2D-Case
questions.problem:
Lagrange's method can be used to reduce the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}-8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ to the canonical form given below. 

$$
2{y}_{1}^{2}+\boxed{}\,{y}_{2}^{2},\,{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}=\boxed{} \\ {y}_{2}={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

From left to right, what is missing from the blank spaces?
questions.worked_solution:
We apply Lagrange's method as follows:

First, we group ${x}_{1}^{2}$-term with all cross-product terms that contain ${x}_{1}$ and factor out the coefficient of ${x}_{1}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}-8{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & =(2{x}_{1}^{2}-8{x}_{1}{x}_{2})+9{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2({x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2})+9{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we complete the square inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}2({x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2})+9{x}_{2}^{2} & =2([{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}]-4{x}_{2}^{2})+9{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2(({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})^{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2})+9{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we simplify the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})^{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2})+9{x}_{2}^{2} & =2({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})^{2}-8{x}_{2}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the canonical form is

$$
2{y}_{1}^{2}+1{y}_{2}^{2},\,{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}={x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}={x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, from left to right, the missing parts are as follows:

$\,$ $1\,$ and $\,{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}.$

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the general equation of an ellipse centered at $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the ellipse is centered at $(3,-1),$ the horizontal radius has length $a=5,$ and the vertical radius has length $b=2.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{(y-(-1))^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

- Since ${b}^{2}=4,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{4}=2.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 2=4,$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot \sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x)
$$

on $[-1,1]$, where $f$ is $2$-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $2$-periodic on $[-1,1]$, we have $L=1$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{1})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{1}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x),\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=4
$$

where $f(x)$ is $2$-periodic and even. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+5y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{y}_{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0$, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(0)={y}_{c}^{′}(0)\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(1)={y}_{c}^{′}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions. 

- Use ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{5}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{5}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).$

- Use ${y}^{′}(1)=4$ with $B=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ 4 & =-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+0 \\ A & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

We write the solution as $y=y_c+y_p$, where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation $y''+2y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sin(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
y'(x)=-A\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sqrt{2}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+y_p'(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since $y_p'(0)=0$ and $y_p'(1)=0$, we have

$$
y'(0)=y_c'(0)\qquad\text{and}\qquad y'(1)=y_c'(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y'(0)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{2}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{2}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x).$

- Use $y'(1)=-5$ with $B=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ -5 & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+0 \\ A & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)\sim \bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt gray]{\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2})}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)}
+\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(n\pi x).
$$

questions.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨2-{t}^{2},\,{t}^{2}+4,\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+4),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,\,2t,\,t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-2t)}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}+{(t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{t}^{2}} \\  & =3t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,4].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{4}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}3t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{2}({t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & ={e}^{t}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =|{e}^{t}|\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{2({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}

from $t=0$ to $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

find $L{u(t-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
questions.worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}={e}^{-as}\,L{g(t+a)},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L{u(t-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)}.
$$

Therefore, $a=2,$ and we have 

$$
L{u(t-2)\,g(t)}={e}^{-2s}\,L{g(t+2)},
$$

where $g(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t).$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+2) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi (t+2)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t+4\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t+2\cdot 2\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t+2)} & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-2)\,g(t)} & ={e}^{-2s}\,L{g(t+2)} \\  & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find $L{u(t-2)(t-2)^{2}},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
questions.worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0,$ then

$$
L{u(t-a)\,f(t-a)}={e}^{-as}F(s),
$$

where $F(s)=L{f(t)}.$

In our case, we wish to find the transform of

$$
u(t-2)(t-2)^{2}.
$$

By comparing this expression to the form in the theorem, we can identify the following:

- The shift is $a=2.$

- The shifted function is $f(t-2)=(t-2)^{2}.$

From the shifted function, we can deduce the original unshifted function $f(t)$ by simply replacing $(t-2)$ with $t:$

$$
f(t)={t}^{2}
$$

Now, we calculate the Laplace transform $F(s)$ of the unshifted function using the rule $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}:$

$$
F(s)=L{{t}^{2}}=\frac{2!}{{s}^{2+1}}=\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}
$$

Finally, we apply the shifting theorem formula $L{u(t-a)\,f(t-a)}={e}^{-as}F(s)$ by multiplying $F(s)$ by the exponential delay factor ${e}^{-2s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-2)(t-2)^{2}} & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot F(s) \\  & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w},$ where

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the acute angle between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${v,w}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${v,w}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}x+{\text{proj}}_{w}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{v}$ and $\text{Span}{w}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{3\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+0\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{3\cdot 2+3\cdot (-1)+0\cdot (-1)}{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}w=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{2}{3}{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+3\cdot 1+0\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{18}\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{9}{6\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2\cdot 1+2\cdot 1+(-4)\cdot 4}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}}{a}_{1}=(-\frac{2}{3})[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{2\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+(-4)\cdot (-1)}{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{4}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =(-\frac{2}{3})[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+\frac{4}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}([\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x$ coincides with the projection, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is zero $0.$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$

$$

$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{(-18)\cdot (-2)+(-16)\cdot 2+1\cdot 4}{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}v=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{(-18)\cdot (-3)+(-16)\cdot 3+1\cdot (-3)}{(-3)^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}w=\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 2}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{1}=2[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{2\cdot 3+3\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (-1)}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2-3)^{2}+(3-3)^{2}+(-5-(-3))^{2}+(2-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
