questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Find the acute angle between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal. Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{4\cdot 1+0\cdot 0+2\cdot (-1)}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{4\cdot 1+0\cdot 1+2\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ 

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}\,x}{‖x‖\,‖{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x‖} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3+0\cdot 2+2\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{14}{\sqrt{20}\sqrt{14}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{14}}{\sqrt{20}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{7}{10}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\sqrt{\frac{7}{10}})≈{33.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(1,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}+v \\ 2u-{v}^{3}\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 1 \\ 2 & -3{v}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-3{v}^{2})-1\cdot 2 \\  & =-6u{v}^{2}-2 \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,2)} & =(-6u{v}^{2}-2)\,{|}_{u=1\,v=2} \\  & =-6(1)(2)^{2}-2 \\  & =-26\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-26|\cdot \delta A \\  & =26\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at $x=1\,m$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/f0/f08c9d1e8dce3c0ae7c37719cadc3fc60bf5de3030ce8c44ca7528a98f3abf7e.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -8{e}^{1-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8{e}^{0}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =16{e}^{1-x} \\ v & =\pm 4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4{e}^{(1-x)/2} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{(1-x)/2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=1$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{(x-1)/2}=2t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+1 \\ \frac{x-1}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x-1 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)+1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined by an Implicit Cartesian Equation
questions.problem:
$$
r(u,v)=u\,i+v\,j+\text{_____}\,k
$$

The vector-valued function $r(u,v)$ parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as 
$\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡z=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$
 What is the third component of $r?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}{2}) \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
r=x\,i+y\,j+z\,k=x\,i+y\,j+\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}{2}\,k.
$$

 

Finally, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
r(u,v)=u\,i+v\,j+\frac{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}{2}\,k
$$

Therefore, the third component of $r$ is $\frac{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}{2}.$

questions.worked_solution:
We write the position of a point (vector) in spherical polar coordinates as $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ),$ where

- $\rho \in [0,5]$

- $\theta \in [0,\pi ]$

$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Type II Regions
questions.problem:
![](images/76/768046952484d181a404486547db84882424d98da4f677254484e1083580a39b.png)

Which of the following represents the shaded region above as a type II region in two-dimensional space?
questions.worked_solution:
A type II region can be written as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,a\le y\le b,\,g(y)\le x\le f(y)},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type II region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $y:$

$$
y={x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y}
$$

The function $x=y$ is already written as a function of $y.$

Notice that the region lies between the horizontal lines $y=0$ and $y=1.$ So, we have $0\le y\le 1.$

We draw a horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left function $g(y)$ and the right function $f(y).$ A horizontal line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type II region.

![](images/d5/d55cb7ea67d9865368c744577bb4a4b22a3635e8e62869ee65e945612d6c0e98.png)

The horizontal line enters the region through the lower function $x=y$ and leaves through the upper function $x=\sqrt{y}.$ So, we have $y\le x\le \sqrt{y}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le \sqrt{y}}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Proving the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution: Homogeneous Systems
questions.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ 

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$ 

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the 
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by 
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by substitution from lines {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix, every solution of the system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c\,\text{for some constant vector }c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Evaluating the identity $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ at $t=0$ gives 

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Substituting ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ from $\text{L1}$ and $c=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$ into $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c,$ we obtain

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0).
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ and substitution from $\text{L1}\text{ and }\text{L5}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-6y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

| $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-2}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\, \\ \,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, any solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2}$ we have

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Evaluating this identity at $t=0$ gives

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is precisely line $\text{L3}.$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we know

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Replacing ${Φ}_{0}(0)$ with ${I}_{n}$ in the equation $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is line $\text{L5}.$ Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{replacing }{Φ}_{0}(0)\text{ with }{I}_{n}\text{ in }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$

questions.problem:
The level curves of the function $f(x,y)=9x+3y-4$ are given by $f(x,y)=c.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $c=0$ gives an ellipse
- $c=-4$ gives a line
- $c=5$ gives a hyperbola
questions.worked_solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}9x+3y-4 & =c \\ 3y & =-9x+c+4 \\ y & =-3x+\frac{c+4}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=0$ then the level curve is $y=-3x+\frac{4}{9},$ which is not an ellipse.

- If $c=-4$ then the level curve is $y=-3x,$ which is a line.

- If $c=5$ then the level curve is $y=-3x+3,$ which is not a hyperbola.

So, only statement II is true.

The level curves of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x+y}{x}$ are given by $f(x,y)=c.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $c=-1$ gives the $x$-axis, excluding the origin
- $c=0$ gives the $y$-axis, excluding the origin
- $c=1$ gives the line $y=x,$ excluding the origin
questions.worked_solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+y}{x} & =c \\ x+y & =cx \\ y & =(c-1)x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=-1,$ the level curve is the line $y=-2x,$ excluding the origin. So, I is false.

- If $c=0,$ the level curve is the line $y=-x,$ excluding the origin. So, II is false.

- If $c=1,$ the level curve is $y=0,$ which is the $x$-axis (excluding the origin). So, III is false.

So, the correct answer is "None of the listed".

The level curves of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ are given by $f(x,y)=c.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $c=0$ gives the point $(0,0)$
- $c=1$ gives a circle of radius $1$
- $c=4$ gives a parabola
questions.worked_solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =c \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={c}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=0,$ the level curve is $x=y=0,$ which gives the point $(0,0).$ So, I is true.

- If $c=1,$ the level curve is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ which gives a circle of radius $1.$ So, II is true.

- If $c=4,$ the level curve is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ which gives a circle of radius $4.$ So, III is false.

So, the correct answer is "I and II only".

questions.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{3}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{3}x)
$$

Let $F(x)=4{x}^{2}-6x+3$ for $x\in [-3,3).$ The Fourier series of the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=3$ and $f(x)=4{x}^{2}-6x+3$ for $x\in [-3,3).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(4{x}^{2}-6x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+3x]}_{-3}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((\frac{4}{3}\cdot {3}^{3}-3\cdot {3}^{2}+3\cdot 3)-(\frac{4}{3}\cdot (-3)^{3}-3\cdot (-3)^{2}+3\cdot (-3))) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(18-(-72)) \\  & =30.\end{aligned}
$$

$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{4}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
![](images/eb/eb13301f8706ec829441c4a56b7c170e8d43e6ebfd0b8718dfab9aeb823a6b53.png)

Find the differential equation governing the current $I$ (in amperes) at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $24\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.004\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $4\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=24\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=24I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.004}=250q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=4\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
8\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)=24I+250q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(24I+250q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 40\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & =24\,\frac{dI}{dt}+250\,\frac{dq}{dt}+4\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+62.5I=10\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

questions.problem:
![](images/0b/0b6e5f0ccf9a4f34ad60e82306db85fce99816de088bf66c90fcaf1a5bac10ed.png)

Find an equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit given in the diagram above, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{2}{3}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $1\,\text{A}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $3\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $5\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $\frac{1}{3}\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=5\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=5I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{\frac{1}{3}}=3q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
3=5I+3q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(3) & =\frac{d}{dt}(5I+3q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+3\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{3}{2}I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-3t/2}$ and $I={e}^{-t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-3t/2}+B{e}^{-t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{2}{3}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $1\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{2}I-\frac{3}{2}q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=1$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{2}I(0)-\frac{3}{2}q(0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{2}\cdot 1-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3} \\  & =-2,\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=1$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A{e}^{-3(0)/2}+B{e}^{-0} \\ 1 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-\frac{3}{2}A{e}^{-3t/2}-B{e}^{-t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-2$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =-\frac{3}{2}A{e}^{-3(0)/2}-B{e}^{-0} \\ -2 & =-\frac{3}{2}A-B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}1=A+B \\ -2=-\frac{3}{2}A-B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=2$ and $B=-1.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=2{e}^{-3t/2}-{e}^{-t}.
$$

questions.problem:
A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $10\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $13\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.2\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $6\,\text{H}.$ Find, in amperes, the amount of current in the circuit after $0.3$ seconds, given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{2}{5}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{A}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

![](images/7c/7c1973678326840251311631211043fc6fab84764e7123e0381b03380cbccd00.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=13\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=13I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.2}=5q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=6\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=6\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
10=13I+5q+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(10) & =\frac{d}{dt}(13I+5q+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =13\,\frac{dI}{dt}+5\,\frac{dq}{dt}+6\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+\frac{13}{6}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{5}{6}I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-5t/3}$ and $I={e}^{-t/2}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-5t/3}+B{e}^{-t/2}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{2}{5}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{5}{3}-\frac{13}{6}I-\frac{5}{6}q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\frac{3}{2}$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{5}{3}-\frac{13}{6}I(0)-\frac{5}{6}q(0) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}-\frac{13}{6}\cdot \frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{6}\cdot \frac{2}{5} \\  & =-\frac{23}{12},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\frac{3}{2}$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & =A{e}^{-5(0)/3}+B{e}^{-0/2} \\ \frac{3}{2} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-\frac{5}{3}A{e}^{-5t/3}-\frac{1}{2}B{e}^{-t/2}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-\frac{23}{12}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{23}{12} & =-\frac{5}{3}A{e}^{-5(0)/3}-\frac{1}{2}B{e}^{-0/2} \\ -\frac{23}{12} & =-\frac{5}{3}A-\frac{1}{2}B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}=A+B \\ -\frac{23}{12}=-\frac{5}{3}A-\frac{1}{2}B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=1$ and $B=\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)={e}^{-5t/3}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t/2}.
$$

questions.problem:
The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, and current $I(t),$ in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+5I+6q=12.
$$

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{9}{20}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $\frac{9}{10}\,\text{A}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dI}{dt}+5I+6q) & =\frac{d}{dt}(12) \\ \frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+6\,\frac{dq}{dt} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+6I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-3t}$ and $I={e}^{-2t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-3t}+B{e}^{-2t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{9}{20}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\frac{9}{10}\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the given relation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=12-5I-6q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\frac{9}{10}$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =12-5I(0)-6q(0) \\  & =12-5\cdot \frac{9}{10}-6\cdot \frac{9}{20} \\  & =\frac{24}{5},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\frac{9}{10}$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10} & =A{e}^{-3(0)}+B{e}^{-2(0)} \\ \frac{9}{10} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3t}-2B{e}^{-2t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=\frac{24}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{24}{5} & =-3A{e}^{-3(0)}-2B{e}^{-2(0)} \\ \frac{24}{5} & =-3A-2B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10}=A+B \\ \frac{24}{5}=-3A-2B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{33}{5}$ and $B=\frac{15}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{33}{5}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{15}{2}{e}^{-2t}.
$$

questions.problem:
A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $12\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $9\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.5\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $4\,\text{H}.$ Find, in amperes, the amount of current in the circuit after $0.4$ seconds, given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $1\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $2\,\text{A}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

![](images/ff/ff2c0f79fcacd14a8243aceac56beceee0d3c585a7c7e904d0d38dc1e6da62ce.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=9\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=9I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.5}=2q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=4\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
12=9I+2q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(12) & =\frac{d}{dt}(9I+2q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =9\,\frac{dI}{dt}+2\,\frac{dq}{dt}+4\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+\frac{9}{4}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{1}{2}I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-2t}$ and $I={e}^{-t/4}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-t/4}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $1\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $2\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=3-\frac{9}{4}I-\frac{1}{2}q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=2$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =3-\frac{9}{4}I(0)-\frac{1}{2}q(0) \\  & =3-\frac{9}{4}\cdot 2-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =-2,\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=2$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A{e}^{-2(0)}+B{e}^{-0/4} \\ 2 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-2A{e}^{-2t}-\frac{1}{4}B{e}^{-t/4}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-2$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =-2A{e}^{-2(0)}-\frac{1}{4}B{e}^{-0/4} \\ -2 & =-2A-\frac{1}{4}B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2=A+B \\ -2=-2A-\frac{1}{4}B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=\frac{6}{7}$ and $B=\frac{8}{7}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=\frac{6}{7}{e}^{-2t}+\frac{8}{7}{e}^{-t/4}.
$$

Finally, the current in the circuit after $0.4$ seconds, in amperes, is

$$
I(0.4)=\frac{6}{7}{e}^{-2(0.4)}+\frac{8}{7}{e}^{-(0.4)/4}≈1.419,
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=12\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=12I.

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{\frac{1}{8}}=8q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=4\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
24=12I+8q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(24) & =\frac{d}{dt}(12I+8q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =12\,\frac{dI}{dt}+8\,\frac{dq}{dt}+4\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+3\,\frac{dI}{dt}+2I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-t}$ and $I={e}^{-2t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $2\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=6-3I-2q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=2$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =6-3I(0)-2q(0) \\  & =6-3\cdot 2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=2$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A{e}^{-0}+B{e}^{-0} \\ 2 & =A+B.\end{aligned}

Consider the RCL circuit shown above. Given that the current $I(t)$ in the circuit at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-5t/2}+B{e}^{-t}+\frac{P}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{Q}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),
$$

where $A,$ $B,$ $P,$ and $Q$ are constants, find the value of $P+Q.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $14\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.1\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $4\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=14\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=14I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.1}=10q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=4\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=14I+10q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(14I+10q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =14\,\frac{dI}{dt}+10I+4\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+\frac{7}{2}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{5}{2}I=\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+\frac{7}{2}\cdot \frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{5}{2}{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-5t/2}+B{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+\frac{7}{2}(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\,\,\, \\ +\frac{5}{2}(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ (-\frac{3}{2}\alpha +7\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-7\alpha -\frac{3}{2}\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}\alpha +7\beta =\frac{5}{2}\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -7\alpha -\frac{3}{2}\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{3}{41}$ and $\beta =\frac{14}{41}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{14}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-5t/2}+B{e}^{-t}-\frac{3}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{14}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Therefore, we have $P=-3$ and $Q=14,$ and

$$
P+Q=-3+14=11.
$$

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+7I=10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+7{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)={e}^{-t}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\,t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\,t)),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+2(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ +7(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ (3\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-4\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3\alpha +4\beta =10\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -4\alpha +3\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

V_C=\dfrac{q}{C}=\dfrac{q}{0.002}=500q.

V_L = 5\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(30I+500q+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -24\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =30\,\frac{dI}{dt}+500\,\frac{dq}{dt}+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}

![](images/08/085fe02b43301629af58379289fc9d1c49c90e71a83e0dd33f491ecf4b21bfc8.png)

Find an equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit given in the diagram above, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\dfrac25\,\textrm{C}$ and the initial current is $\dfrac34\,\textrm{A}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The circuit is a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $9\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor of resistance $10\,\Omega,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\textrm{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $4\,\textrm{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=10\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 10I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C=\dfrac{q}{C}=\dfrac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence,

$$
V_L = 4\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
9=10I+4q+4\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(9) & =\frac{d}{dt}(10I+4q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =10\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4\,\frac{dq}{dt}+4\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t},$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+\dfrac52\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I=e^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I=e^{-2t}$ and $I=e^{-t/2}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=Ae^{-2t}+Be^{-t/2}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\dfrac25\,\textrm{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\dfrac34\,\textrm{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t},$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}=\dfrac94-\dfrac52I-q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\dfrac34$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{9}{4}-\frac{5}{2}I(0)-q(0) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{4}-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =-\frac{1}{40},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\dfrac34$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4} & =A{e}^{-2(0)}+B{e}^{-0/2} \\ \frac{3}{4} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
I'=-2Ae^{-2t}-\dfrac12Be^{-t/2}.
$$

Substituting in $I'(0)=-\dfrac1{40}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{40} & =-2A{e}^{-2(0)}-\frac{1}{2}B{e}^{-0/2} \\ -\frac{1}{40} & =-2A-\frac{1}{2}B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}=A+B \\ -\frac{1}{40}=-2A-\frac{1}{2}B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\dfrac{7}{30}$ and $B=\dfrac{59}{60}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\dfrac{7}{30}e^{-2t}+\dfrac{59}{60}e^{-t/2}.
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+2(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ +(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (-3\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-4\alpha -3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha +4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -4\alpha -3\beta =-3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha=\dfrac{12}{25}$ and $\beta=\dfrac{9}{25}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
I_p(t)=\dfrac{12}{25}\cos(2t)+\dfrac{9}{25}\sin(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t) = I_c(t) + I_p(t) = Ae^{-t} + Bte^{-t} + \dfrac{12}{25}\cos(2t) + \dfrac{9}{25}\sin(2t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $I_c(t) = Ae^{-t} + Bte^{-t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $I_p(t) = \dfrac{12}{25}\cos(2t) + \dfrac{9}{25}\sin(2t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$
I(t)\approx I_p(t) = \dfrac{12}{25}\cos(2t) + \dfrac{9}{25}\sin(2t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{12}{25}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{9}{25}\right)^2} = \dfrac35.
$$

questions.problem: Construct the vector field that has the stream function $ψ(x,y)={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+x.$
questions.worked_solution:
A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if the following equations hold:

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}
$$

Computing the partial derivatives of the function $ψ(x,y),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{∂ψ}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+x) \\  & =2y, \\ Q & =-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x} \\  & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+x) \\  & =2x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field with the stream function $ψ(x,y)={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y) & =P\,i+Q\,j \\  & =2y\,i+(2x-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following vector fields have a stream function?

- $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$
- $F(x,y)=xy\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$
- $F(x,y)=2x\,i-y\,j$
questions.worked_solution:
A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0+0=0
$$

- Vector field II doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=y+2y\ne 0.
$$

- Vector field III doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2+(-1)\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)=3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,i-6xy\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})$ and $Q(x,y)=-6xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=6x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=6x+(-6x)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=6xy.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)=3{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)=3{x}^{2}y+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=0,$ and $g(y)=-{y}^{3},$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)=3{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}.
$$

questions.problem: Determine the equation of the streamline that passes through the point $P(-1,-1)$ for the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i-2xy\,j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.
. 

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i-2xy\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-2xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+(-2x)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}={x}^{2},\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2xy.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y.
$$

Finally, we find the level curve of the stream function $ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ that passes through $P.$
First, we find the value of the stream function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(-1,-1) & =(-1)^{2}\cdot (-1) \\  & =1\cdot (-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,-1)$ is the $-1$-level curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}y & =-1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,-1)$ is $y=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.$
The vector field and the streamline through the point $P$ are shown below.

$$

$$

Note that $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

Finally, we find the level curve of the stream function $ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ that passes through $P.$
First, we find the value of the stream function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(0,\pi ) & ={e}^{(0)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Construct the vector field that has the stream function $\psi(x,y) = e^{x} \cos{y}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A function $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ if the following equations hold:

$$
P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y},\qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}
$$

Computing the partial derivatives of the function $\psi(x,y),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{∂ψ}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y, \\ Q & =-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x} \\  & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field with the stream function $\psi(x,y) = e^{x} \cos{y}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y) & =P\,i+Q\,j \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining Cases Where a Stream Function Exists
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following vector fields have a stream function?

- $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = x^4y\,\mathbf{i} - 2x^3y^2\,\mathbf{j}$

- $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \sin x \sin y\,\mathbf{i} + \cos x \cos y\,\mathbf{j}$

- $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = 4x^2y\,\mathbf{i} -4x^2y^2\,\mathbf{j}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A vector field $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4{x}^{3}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-4{x}^{3}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
= 4x^3y + (- 4x^3y)
= 0
$$

- Vector field II has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
= \cos x \sin y + (- \cos x \sin y)
= 0.
$$

- Vector field III doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=8xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-8{x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
= 8xy + (- 8x^2y)
\neq 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

canonical_examples.problem:
Find a stream function for the vector field $\mathbf F,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = 2y\,\mathbf{i} +2x\,\mathbf{j}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A vector field $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.
$$

Note that $\mathbf{F}(x,y) =  2y\,\mathbf{i} +2x\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D=\mathbb{R}^2,$ where $P(x,y) = 2y$ and $Q(x,y) =2x.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\mathbf F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0 + 0 = 0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ if 

$$
P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} = 2y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} = -2x.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
\psi(x,y) = y^2 + f(x), \qquad 
\psi(x,y) = -x^2+ g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f(x)=-x^2$ and $g(y)=y^2,$ we have

$$
\psi(x,y) = y^2-x^2.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Determine the equation of the streamline that passes through the point $P(-1,1)$ for the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (x^3-3xy^2)\,\mathbf{i} + (y^3-3x^2y)\,\mathbf{j}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.

A vector field $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.
$$

Note that $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (x^3-3xy^2)\,\mathbf{i} + (y^3-3x^2y)\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D=\mathbb{R}^2,$ where $P(x,y) = x^3-3xy^2$ and $Q(x,y) = y^3 - 3x^2y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =3{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\mathbf F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = (3x^2-3y^2) + (3y^2 - 3x^2) = 0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ if 

$$
P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} = x^3-3xy^2, \qquad \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} = -y^3+3x^2y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
\psi(x,y) = x^3y - xy^3 + f(x), \qquad 
\psi(x,y) = -xy^3 + x^3y + g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
\psi(x,y) = x^3y - xy^3.
$$

Finally, we find the level curve of the stream function $\psi(x,y) = x^3y - xy^3$ that passes through $P.$
First, we find the value of the stream function at $P{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(-1,1) & =(-1)^{3}(1)-(-1)(1)^{3} \\  & =-1-(-1) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,1)$ is the $0$-level curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3} & =0 \\ xy({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ xy(x+y)(x-y) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our possible streamlines are $x=0,$ $y=0,$ $y=-x,$ or $y=x.$ The streamline that passes through $P(-1,1)$ is $y=-x.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse
questions.problem: Calculate the point where the ellipse $\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y+6)^{2}}{36}=1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercept, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y+6)^{2}}{36} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(0+6)^{2}}{36} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{36}{36} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+1 & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4} & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =0 \\ x-2 & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at the point $(2,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+2x+24y+21 & =0 \\ {0}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+2\cdot 0+24y+21 & =0 \\ 4{y}^{2}+24y+21 & =0 \\ 4[{y}^{2}+6y]+21 & =0 \\ 4[(y+3)^{2}-9]+21 & =0 \\ 4(y+3)^{2}-36+21 & =0 \\ 4(y+3)^{2}-15 & =0 \\ 4(y+3)^{2} & =15 \\ (y+3)^{2} & =\frac{15}{4} \\ y+3 & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2} \\ y & =-3\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,-3-\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2})$ and $(0,-3+\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}).$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate the point where the ellipse $(x-2)^2 + \dfrac{(y-2)^2}{4} = 1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercept, we need to substitute $y = 0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2}+\frac{(0-2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2}+1 & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =0 \\ x-2 & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at the point $(2,0).$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate the point where the ellipse $\dfrac{(x-1)^2}{4}+\dfrac{(y-3)^2}{16}=1$ intercepts the $y$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the $y$-intercept, we need to substitute $x = 0$ in the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $y.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{(0-1)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{4}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{(y-3)^{2}}{16} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ (y-3)^{2} & =12 \\ y-3 & =\pm \sqrt{12} \\ y-3 & =2\sqrt{3} \\ y & =3\pm 2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at the points $(0,3 -2\sqrt{3})$ and $(0,3 +2\sqrt{3}).$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Cosine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula
questions.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-4x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{n}.$$\,{a}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}
for $n\ge 1$
questions.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-4x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{8}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{8}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{8}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{8}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{8}{n\pi }(0+\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{8(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions at a Given Time
questions.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨8{t}^{2},\,45⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8{t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(45)⟩ \\  & =⟨16t,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=3,$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨16(3),\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨48,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨\frac{{3}^{t-1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3},5t+1⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{3}^{t-1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{3}^{t-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3},5⟩ \\  & =⟨{3}^{t-1},5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=2,$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{3}^{2-1},5⟩=⟨3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=2$ we calculate the magnitude of $v(2),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(2)| & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+25} \\  & =\sqrt{34}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed when $t=2$ is $\sqrt{34}.$

$$

$$

The solution $t=2$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

questions.knowledge_point: Computing One Step Using the Trapezoidal Method
questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=-2x+y,\,y(1)=0
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with one step to approximate $y\,(\frac{3}{2}),$ rounded to two decimal places

$$
y\,(\frac{3}{2})≈{{field-1}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

First, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=\frac{3}{2},$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=\frac{3}{2}-1=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-2x+y+(-2{x}_{\text{new}}+{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-2x-2{x}_{\text{new}}+y+{y}_{\text{new}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-2x-2{x}_{\text{new}}+y)+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{4}(-2x-2{x}_{\text{new}}+y)+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}(-2x-2{x}_{\text{new}}+5y)+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}(-2x-2{x}_{\text{new}}+5y) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2{x}_{\text{new}}+5y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is ${x}_{\text{new}}=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}.$ Hence, the new $y$ value is

$$

First, note that we are given $y(-1)$ and asked to find $y(1).$ The distance from $x=-1$ to $x=1$ is $2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{1-(-1)}{2}=1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((2x+3y)+(2{x}_{\text{new}}+3{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+3y)+\frac{3}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+3y)+\frac{3}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+5y)+\frac{3}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+5y) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =-(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+5y)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x=-1,\,y=0.

$$

x=0,\,y=2.

questions.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\,i+(t-{t}^{3})\,j+(2{t}^{2}-2t)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+x\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y=t-{t}^{3},\,z=2{t}^{2}-2t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,k \\  & =(t-{t}^{3})\,i+({t}^{2}-t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-{t}^{3})\,j-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-2t)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(1-3{t}^{2})\,j+(4t-2)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-{t}^{3})\,i+({t}^{2}-t)\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(1-3{t}^{2})\,j+(4t-2)\,k) \\  & =(t-{t}^{3})\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (1-3{t}^{2})+({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =t-4{t}^{2}+5{t}^{3}-2{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-4{t}^{2}+5{t}^{3}-2{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{5{t}^{3}}{4}-\frac{2{t}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{4}{3}+\frac{5}{4}-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨y,\,2yz,\,-{z}^{2}+1⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=-3.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,2yz,\,-{z}^{2}+1⟩{|}_{z=-3} \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-6y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-8}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot 0-(-6y)\cdot 0-8)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-8\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ with radius $3$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-8\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}-8\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8[\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{r=0}^{r=3} \\  & =-8(2\pi -0)\cdot (\frac{9}{2}-0) \\  & =-72\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2+2x-y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2+2x-y)=-1\end{aligned}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =z\,i+3x\,j+2{y}^{2}\,k \\  & =\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+2{sin}^{2}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{3}{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\frac{3}{2}t+\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(1+\frac{3}{2}(2\pi )+0)-(1+\frac{3}{2}(0)+0) \\  & =3\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Surface Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
questions.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=(y-z)\,i+(z-x)\,j+(x-y)\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z=1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-z)\,i+(z-x)\,j+(x-y)\,k \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\,i+(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,i+(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,i+(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k) \\  & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-2{sin}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2{sin}^{2}⁡t-2{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2t]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(-1+0-2(2\pi ))-(-1+0-2(0)) \\  & =-4\pi \end{aligned}
$$
