questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Polar Curve
questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for the polar curve $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta }.$ 

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ 

Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
x=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ,\,y=1.
$$

Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }=0.
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(0)}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Quotient of Complex Numbers in Polar Form
questions.problem: Express $z=\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-1-\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1+\text{i})(-1-\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1)^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{1+1} \\  & =3(-1-\text{i}) \\  & =-3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=-3-3\text{i},$ the magnitude is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=-3$ and $y=-3$ are both negative, $z$ lies in the third quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-3}{-3}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡1 \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=3\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4}))
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Quotient of Complex Numbers in Polar Form
questions.problem: Express $z=-\frac{2}{3\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-3\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =-\frac{2}{3\text{i}} \\  & =-\frac{2(-3\text{i})}{(3\text{i})(-3\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6\text{i}}{-9{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6\text{i}}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{2}{3}\text{i}=0+\frac{2}{3}\text{i},$ the magnitude is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=0$  and $y=\frac{2}{3}$ is positive, $z$ lies on the positive direction of the $y$-axis. So,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=\frac{2}{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Left Riemann Sum With Irregular Step Size
questions.problem:
The following table shows some values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the interval $[2,12].$

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ | $10$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Use the left Riemann sum, with the four subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[2,12].$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Product Rule and Swap Rules
questions.worked_solution:
The product rule for double summations states that

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{b}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{b}_{j}.
$$

So, using the product rule for double summations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}3{a}_{i}(4-{b}_{j}) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{15}3{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}(4-{b}_{j}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the rules for single summations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}3{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}(4-{b}_{j}) & =(3{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{a}_{i})\cdot ({\sum }_{j=1}^{12}4-{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}{b}_{j}) \\  & =(3{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{a}_{i})\cdot (4{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}1-{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}{b}_{j}) \\  & =(3\cdot 30)\cdot (4\cdot 12-45) \\  & =(90)\cdot (48-45) \\  & =(90)\cdot (3) \\  & =270\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Simple Sums Over Partitions of the Real Line
questions.problem: Let $P={{z}_{0},{z}_{1},…,{z}_{q}}$ be a partition of the interval $[1,5].$ If $Δ{z}_{k}={z}_{k}-{z}_{k-1},$ calculate ${\sum }_{k=1}^{q}3Δ{z}_{k}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the factor $3$ outside the summation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}3Δ{z}_{k}=3{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}$ is just the length of the interval $[1,5],$ because

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k} & =({z}_{1}-{z}_{0})+({z}_{2}-{z}_{1})+({z}_{3}-{z}_{2})+⋯+({z}_{q}-{z}_{q-1}) \\  & =(\cancel{{z}_{1}}-{z}_{0})+(\cancel{{z}_{2}}-\cancel{{z}_{1}})+(\cancel{{z}_{3}}-\cancel{{z}_{2}})+⋯+({z}_{q}-\cancel{{z}_{q-1}}) \\  & =-{z}_{0}+{z}_{q} \\  & ={z}_{q}-{z}_{0} \\  & =5-1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
3{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}=3\cdot 4=12.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Source-Free Vector Fields
questions.problem:
Given the vector field $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j,$ which of the following statements must be true?

- $∇\cdot F=0$
- $F$ is a source-free vector field
- Given two arbitrary curves ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2},$ we have ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

Note that $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. This follows from statement I.

- Statement III is false. Since $F$ is source-free, the result ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ is guaranteed only for curves with the same start and endpoints.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,ds$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,ds={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,ds.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =0+0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $F$ is a source-free vector field. So, the flux of $F$ across any closed curve is zero.
Hence,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,ds=0.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = 4y(x^2+y^2)\,\mathbf{i} - 4x(x^2+y^2)\,\mathbf{j},$ which of the following statements must be true?

- $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F= 0$

- $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field

- For two arbitrary curves $C_1$ and $C_2,$ we have $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s \neq \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the following are equivalent:

- $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

- $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.$

- The flux $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1,C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ for $\mathbf{F}.$

Note that $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D=\mathbb{R}^2,$ where 

$$
P(x,y) = 4y(x^2+y^2),\qquad Q(x,y) = - 4x(x^2+y^2).
$$

Computing the partial derivatives, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=8xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-8xy.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
=
8xy + (-8xy) = 0.
$$

- Statement II is true. This follows from statement I.

- Statement III is false. Since $\mathbf F$ is source-free, we have that $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s$ for all curves *with the same start and endpoints*.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

$$

 through $C_1$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector  $\mathbf{n}_1,$ as shown above. 

*Hint: You're given that $\mathbf F$ is source-free.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the following are equivalent:

- $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

- $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.$

- The flux $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ for $\mathbf{F}.$

First, notice that

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{y^3}\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\right) = 0+0 = 0,
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $\mathbf{F}$ is source-free, we know the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s,
$$

where $C_2$ is the straight line from $A(5,3)$ to $B(1,3)$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](images/2a/2aeb26e58251923821d4058f886eada6a29b473ea70714b32e98c5338ddd0b28.png)

Notice that both $\mathbf n_1$ and $\mathbf n_2$ are $90^\circ$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C_2,$ we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_{C_2} P\,\textrm{d}y - Q\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t).$

Parametrizing $C_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\,i+3\,j+t\cdot [(i+3\,j)-(5\,i+3\,j)] \\  & =(5-4t)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=3\sqrt{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\sqrt{(5-x)^{3}}=\sqrt{(5-(5-4t))^{3}}=8\sqrt{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-4t)=-4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3\sqrt{3})\cdot (0)-(8\sqrt{{t}^{3}})\cdot (-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32{t}^{3/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{64{t}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{64(1)^{5/2}}{5})-(\frac{(64(0)^{5/2}}{5}) \\  & =\frac{64}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1\, \textrm{d}s = \dfrac{64}{5}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Moment of Inertia of a Lamina Given a Mass Density Function
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,1\le y\le 2}$
with mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=3(x+y).$ Find the moment of inertia of this plate about the line $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$

The distance between a point on $D$ and the line $x=1$ is given by

$$
r(x,y)=|x-1|.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{l} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}3(x+y)|x-1{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}3(x+y)(x-1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{3(x+y)^{2}}{2}(x-1)^{2}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3((x+2)^{2}-(x+1)^{2})}{2}(x-1)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+3)(x-1)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-4x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-2{x}^{2}+3x]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}((\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}-2+3)-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{7}{6}) \\  & =\frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](images/cb/cbb338df240f1dff7d946a584cc2499f0290cfde3938d7a36d7eae30acd08fb0.png)

A plate with mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the curves $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and $y=(x-1)^{2}$, as shown above. Given that the region has an area of $\frac{1}{3},$ find the moment of inertia of the plate about the line $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,(x-1)^{2}\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/de/de82c9b30dfb156dea8ace88e27f00887dcecf197e7a50493f34f6a08dfae161.png)

The distance between a point on $D$ and the line $x=1$ is given by

$$
r(x,y)=|x-1|.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=3M.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{(x-1)^{2}}^{1-{x}^{2}}|x-1{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{(x-1)^{2}}^{1-{x}^{2}}(x-1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3M{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-1)^{2}[y]_{y=(x-1)^{2}}^{y=1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3M{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-1)^{2}(1-{x}^{2}-(x-1)^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3M{\int }_{0}^{1}-2{x}^{4}+6{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3M{[\frac{-2{x}^{5}}{5}+\frac{3{x}^{4}}{2}-2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3M(-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{3}{2}-2+1-0) \\  & =\frac{3M}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:

A plate with mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the curves ${y}^{2}=2x$ and $y=x$, as shown above. Given that the region has an area of $\frac{2}{3},$ find the moment of inertia of the plate about the line $y=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\le x\le y},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/a3/a34ed2c8c25aa5c3c1e28e4458e11779f6b5948acbebdcb6e05b5bf1257689d4.png)

The distance between a point on $D$ and the line $y=2$ is given by

$$
r(x,y)=|y-2|.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{3M}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $y=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{y}^{2}/2}^{y}\frac{3M}{2}|y-2{|}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{y}^{2}/2}^{y}(y-2)^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(y-2)^{2}[x]_{x={y}^{2}/2}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(y-2)^{2}(y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3M}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}(-{y}^{4}+6{y}^{3}-12{y}^{2}+8y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3M}{4}{[-\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}+\frac{3{y}^{4}}{2}-4{y}^{3}+4{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3M}{4}(-\frac{32}{5}+24-32+16-0) \\  & =\frac{6M}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M$ occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,\,1\le y\le 2}.$
The mass density at each point is proportional to its $y$-coordinate. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the line $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$

First, the distance between a point and the line $x=1$ is given by

$$
r(x,y)=|x-1|.
$$

Next, the mass density can be written as $\lambda (x,y)=ky,$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find the value of $k$ by integrating the mass density function over the plate.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}ky\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =k({\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{1}^{2}y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =k\cdot {[x]}_{-1}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =k(1-(-1))(2-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =3k.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\lambda (x,y)=ky=\frac{M}{3}y.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{l} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{M}{3}y|x-1{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{M}{3}y(x-1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}({\int }_{-1}^{1}(x-1)^{2}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{1}^{2}y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\frac{M}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}(x-1)^{3}]}_{-1}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}(0-(-8))\cdot [\frac{1}{2}(4-1)] \\  & =\frac{M}{3}\cdot \frac{8}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](images/87/87bee8d151dd23793bbe9f11c3c2b81170401e86b7ffb2b1473f66b09c2e02f9.png)

A triangular plate with mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the parabolas $y=2-2{x}^{2}$ and $y=1-{x}^{2}.$
The mass density at each point is proportional to the square of its distance from the $y$-axis. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the line $x=-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,\,1-{x}^{2}\le y\le 2-2{x}^{2}},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/02/026b560b2e81899cb767930a5c63173e4a3489c6bc10b7148007127e132406c9.png)

Also, the distance between a point and the line $x=-1$ is given by

$$
r(x,y)=|x+1|.
$$

Next, the mass density can be written as $\lambda (x,y)=k{x}^{2},$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find the value of $k$ by integrating the mass density function over the plate.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}k{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[{x}^{2}y]}_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}(2-2{x}^{2}-1+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =k\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4k}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k{x}^{2}=\frac{15}{4}M{x}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{l} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}\frac{15}{4}M{x}^{2}|x+1{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}\frac{15}{4}M{x}^{2}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}({x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}){\int }_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2})[y]_{1-{x}^{2}}^{2-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2})(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-{x}^{6}-2{x}^{5}+2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M{[-\frac{1}{7}{x}^{7}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M(-\frac{2}{7}+0+0+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{15}{4}M\cdot \frac{8}{21} \\  & =\frac{10M}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
A circle of radius $k$ centered at the origin has the polar equation $r=k.$

$$
\begin{aligned}k & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-12)^{2}+{16}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{144+256} \\  & =\sqrt{400} \\  & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the circle is $r=20.$

![](images/c3/c3d18d92739af7c6ea7c2a8560ab54c4c08b8b20f9ee33ba52a254b16315d9bf.png)

Find the polar equation of the circle centered at the origin that passes through the point $A(9,12)$, as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
A circle of radius $k$ centered at the origin has the polar equation $r=k.$

We can compute the radius $k$ of our circle using the Pythagorean theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}k & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{9}^{2}+{12}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{225} \\  & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the circle is $r=15.$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point
questions.problem:
Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}=(x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3},\,\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}=6x{z}^{2}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3}) \\  & =(x{y}^{2}+2y)\cdot x{e}^{xy}+(2xy+2)\cdot {e}^{xy}+0 \\  & =({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4xy+2){e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(6x{z}^{2}) \\  & =12xz.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =(0+0+2){e}^{0}=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =12(1)(1)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =2+12=14.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point
questions.problem:
Evaluate ${f}_{xyy}(2,2,2)$ given that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{yx}(x,y,z)=2y\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyy}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{yxy}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{yx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}) \\  & =2\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{x}(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}}) \\  & =2\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}-\frac{3}{2}{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{{y}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point  $(2,2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyy}(2,2,2) & =2\sqrt{\frac{(2)^{3}}{(2)}}-\frac{3}{2}(2)^{3}\sqrt{\frac{(2)}{(2)^{3}}} \\  & =2\cdot 2-3\cdot 2 \\  & =4-6 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=6{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=6xy$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=15{x}^{2}-y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=8y+x$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=-3{y}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2})=6y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy)=6y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(15{x}^{2}-y)=-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8y+x)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2})=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=-2y{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}}$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-{y}^{2})$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-{y}^{2})$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\sqrt{x}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}})=-4y{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y{e}^{2x+{y}^{2}})=-4y{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-{y}^{2}))=4y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-{y}^{2}) \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-{y}^{2}))=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-{y}^{2})+4x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x})=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.knowledge_point: Modeling Inhibited Growth
questions.problem: A shipping company’s management noted that the growth of a ship’s speed is directly proportional to the difference between the ship’s maximum cruising speed and its current speed. Let $V(t)$ be the speed of the ship, measured in kilometers per hour, and let $t\ge 0$ be the time in hours. If the maximum cruising speed of the ship is $90$ $\text{km/h}$, which differential equation could be used to model the ship’s speed? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
questions.worked_solution:
The rate at which the speed $V(t)$ of the ship changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum cruising speed and the current speed. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=k(a-V),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum cruising speed of the ship, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=90\text{ km/h},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=k(90-V).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE With Sinusoidal Forcing
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-9y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{3x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$y(x)=A{e}^{3x}\,+\,($
{{field-1}}
$)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,+\,($
{{field-2}}
$)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
3\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}-9{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$ So, we assume the particular solution to be 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
3(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-9(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(6\beta -9\alpha )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(-6\alpha -9\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}6\beta -9\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ -6\alpha -9\beta =6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{4}{13},\beta =-\frac{6}{13}.$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{4}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{6}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x}+(-\frac{4}{13})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(-\frac{6}{13})\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a Bernoulli Differential Equation to First Order Linear
questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+y=-\frac{x}{y}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=1,\,q(x)=-x,\,n=-1.
$$

First, we multiply the differential equation by $y,$ and we get

$$
y\frac{dy}{dx}+{y}^{2}=-x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2z=-2x.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=-2x.$

questions.knowledge_point: Using the Chain Rule for Differentiation
questions.problem: If $f(u)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ {e}^{u}\end{aligned}]$ and $u(t)=4t-3,$ then $(f∘u)^{′}(t)=$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we can write

$$
(f∘u)^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(u(t)){u}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(u) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}\,(\operatorname{cos}⁡u) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({e}^{u})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ {e}^{u}\end{aligned}] \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-3)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘u)^{′}(t) & ={f}^{′}(u(t)){u}^{′}(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u(t)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u(t)) \\ {e}^{u(t)}\end{aligned}]\cdot {u}^{′}(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t-3) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t-3) \\ {e}^{4t-3}\end{aligned}]\cdot 4 \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t-3) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t-3) \\ 4{e}^{4t-3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Hermitian Inner Product
questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

- $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
- $⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C$
- $⟨a,a⟩>0$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry.

- Statement II is true. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument, we have 

$$
⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=\overset{―}{(\overset{―}{\alpha })}⟨a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that if $a=0$ then $⟨a,a⟩=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Second-Degree Taylor Polynomial of a Given Function About a Point
questions.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)={e}^{\pi x/2}$ about $x=0$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(0)(x-0)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{\pi x/2} & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\pi }{2}{e}^{\pi x/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{e}^{\pi x/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =1+(\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot x+(\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4})\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2} \\  & =1+\frac{\pi }{2}x+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x}$ about $x=5$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=5,$ we plug $a=5$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(5)+{f}^{′}(5)(x-5)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(5)(x-5)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(5),$ ${f}^{′}(5),$ and ${f}^{″}(5):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+1}{x} & ⟹ &  & f(5) & =\frac{6}{5} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(5) & =-\frac{1}{25} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{x}^{-3} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(5) & =\frac{2}{125}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(5),$ ${f}^{′}(5),$ and ${f}^{″}(5)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =(\frac{6}{5})+(-\frac{1}{25})\cdot (x-5)+(\frac{2}{125})\cdot \frac{1}{2}(x-5)^{2} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}-\frac{1}{25}(x-5)+\frac{1}{125}(x-5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}}$ about $x=0$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(0)(x-0)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}}=(1+x)^{-1/2} & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}(1+x)^{-3/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{3}{4}(1+x)^{-5/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying Properties of the Hermitian Inner Product
questions.problem:
Given that $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\,b-(1+3\text{i})c⟩$ if 

$\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=1+\text{i}\,$ and $\,⟨a,c⟩=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. 

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨a,\,b-(1+3\text{i})c⟩ & =⟨a,b⟩-⟨a,(1+3\text{i})c⟩ \\  & =⟨a,b⟩-(\overset{―}{1+3\text{i}})⟨a,c⟩ \\  & =⟨a,b⟩-(1-3\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨a,b⟩-(1-3\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}-(1-3\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}-(1-3\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =\overset{―}{1+\text{i}}-(1-3\text{i})\cdot 2 \\  & =1-\text{i}-2+6\text{i} \\  & =-1+5\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Hermitian Inner Product
questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

- $⟨ia,b⟩=i⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
- $⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=⟨\alpha a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C$
- $⟨ia,a⟩\in R$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true.  Indeed, the inner product in ${C}^{n}$ is linear in the first argument. So, a constant multiple from the first argument can be factored out.

- Statement II is true. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument and linearity in the first argument, we have 

$$
⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=\overset{―}{(\overset{―}{\alpha })}⟨a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩=⟨\alpha a,b⟩.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that $⟨a,a⟩\in R$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}.$ Therefore, if $a\ne 0,$ then

$$
⟨ia,a⟩=i⟨a,a⟩\notin R.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

$$
5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+10y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-2x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,+\,($
{{field-2}}
$)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
5\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}+10{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $7\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).$ So, we assume the particular solution to be 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
5(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))+10(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))=7\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(10\alpha +15\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+(-15\alpha +10\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)=7\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}10\alpha +15\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)) \\ -15\alpha +10\beta =7\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{21}{65},\beta =\frac{14}{65}.$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{21}{65}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\frac{14}{65}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+(-\frac{21}{65})\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+(\frac{14}{65})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{2x}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

Now, we can find the constant $A$ using the initial conditions.

Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{2\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 0)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0) & =2 \\ A-2-0 & =2 \\ A & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=4{e}^{2x}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Transformation That Maps a Rectangular Region Onto a Given One
questions.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ enclosed in the first quadrant of the $xy$-plane between the curves

$$
x=y,\,x=5y,\,x=\frac{2}{{y}^{2}},\,x=\frac{7}{{y}^{2}}.
$$

A transformation $T,$ where

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

maps a rectangular region $Δ$ with sides parallel to the $u$- and $v$-axes from the $uv$-plane onto $D$ in the $xy$-plane. Given that

$$
T:(u,v)\to (\sqrt[3]{{u}^{2}v},\,\,),
$$

what could be the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
We would like to find a rectangular region of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v)\,:\,a\le u\le b,\,\,c\le v\le d} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,a\le u(x,y)\le b,\,\,c\le v(x,y)\le d},\end{aligned}
$$

where the equations of the left, right, bottom, and top sides are

$$
u(x,y)=a,\,u(x,y)=b,\,v(x,y)=c,\,v(x,y)=d.
$$

With that in mind, let's analyze the boundary of our region $D.$ 

Rewriting the equations 

$$
x=y,\,x=5y,\,x=\frac{2}{{y}^{2}},\,x=\frac{7}{{y}^{2}}
$$

by moving both variables $x$ and $y$ to the left-hand side, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{y}=1,\,\frac{x}{y}=5,\,x{y}^{2}=2,\,x{y}^{2}=7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we put $u(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ and $v(x,y)=x{y}^{2},$ we can define the transformation ${T}^{-1}$ as

$$
{T}^{-1}:(x,y)\to (\,\frac{x}{y}\,,\,x{y}^{2}).
$$

To find $T,$ we should express $x$ and $y$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$ Recall that we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}u=\frac{x}{y} \\ v=x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, $x=uy.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get 

$$
v=u{y}^{3}\,⟹\,{y}^{3}=\frac{v}{u}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{v}{u}}.
$$

Finally, substituting $y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{v}{u}}$ back into $x=uy,$ we obtain

$$
x=u\sqrt[3]{\frac{v}{u}}=\sqrt[3]{{u}^{2}v}.
$$

Therefore, the transformation $T$ can be given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (\sqrt[3]{{u}^{2}v},\,\sqrt[3]{\frac{v}{u}}).
$$

questions.problem:
Let $D$ be the finite region bounded by the curve 
$(3x+{y}^{2})^{2}+y=5$ and the line $y=0.$ Consider the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where $u=3x+{y}^{2}$ and $v=y.$ Find the representation of ${T}^{-1}(D)$ in the $uv$-plane.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we are given that 

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x+{y}^{2} \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

Substituting $3x+{y}^{2}=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x+{y}^{2})^{2}+y=5\,⟹\,{u}^{2}+v=5\,⟹\,v=5-{u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\,⟹\,v=0.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v=5-{u}^{2} \\ v=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm \sqrt{5} \\ v=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{5},0).$

![](images/f6/f667b68a08f6897af0116778f5f21c5b8b0d1ce6aff09e315431dc445d6998bb.png)

As a result, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation 

$$
{T}^{-1}(D)={(u,v)\,:\,-\sqrt{5}\le u\le \sqrt{5},\,0\le v\le 5-{u}^{2}}.
$$

questions.problem:
Let $D$ be the finite region bounded by the curve 
$(x-y)^{2}+x+y=0$ and  the line $y=0.$ 
Consider the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where $u=x-y$ and $v=x+y.$ Find the representation of ${T}^{-1}(D)$ in the $uv$-plane.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we are given that 

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x-y \\ x+y\end{aligned}].
$$

Substituting $x-y=u$ and $x+y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-y)^{2}+x+y=0\,⟹\,(x-y)^{2}+(x+y)=0\,⟹\,v=-{u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Now, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}x-y=u \\ x+y=v\end{aligned}\,⟹\,y=\frac{v-u}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this value into the equation of the given line yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\, & ⟹\,\frac{v-u}{2}=0 & \,⟹\,v=u\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, to find the intersections of the resulting lines in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v=-{u}^{2} \\ v=u\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u(u+1)=0 \\ v=u.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1).$ 

![](images/05/05d7e65dca3c6d116d01be9e57fc83f3e3edcda4135a3f96fea82af8db4f2d1e.png)

As a result, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation 

$$
{T}^{-1}(D)={(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 0,\,u\le v\le -{u}^{2}}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the region $D,$ given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 2 \leq \sqrt{xy} \leq 4, \: 2x \leq y \leq 3x \big\}
$$

and the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where $u=\dfrac{y}{x}$ and $v=xy.$ Find the representation of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D)$ in the $uv$-plane.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that $\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D)$ is the image of $D$ under the action of the transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Let's find the image of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D)$ in the $uv$-plane. To do that, we write the region $D$ in terms of $u$ and $v,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(D) & ={(u,v)\,:\,2\le \sqrt{xy}\le 4,\,2x\le y\le 3x} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,{2}^{2}\le (\sqrt{xy})^{2}\le {4}^{2},\,2\le \frac{y}{x}\le 3} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,4\le xy\le 16,\,2\le \frac{y}{x}\le 3} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,4\le v\le 16,\,2\le u\le 3} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 3,\,4\le v\le 16}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $2 \leq \sqrt{xy}\leq 4,$ we must have $x \neq 0.$ Therefore, $u=\dfrac{y}{x}$ is well-defined.

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ enclosed in the first quadrant of the $xy$-plane between the curves

$$
y=x, \qquad
y=7x, \qquad
x=\dfrac{3}{y^2}, \qquad
x=\dfrac{5}{y^2}.
$$

A transformation $\mathbf{T},$ where

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

maps a rectangular region $\Delta$ with sides parallel to the $u$- and $v$-axes from the $uv$-plane onto $D$ in the $xy$-plane. Given that

$$
\mathbf{T} : (u,v) \to \Big(\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{v}{u^2}}, \: \bbox[5pt, white, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}} \, \Big),
$$

what could be the missing expression?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We would like to find a rectangular region of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v)\,:\,a\le u\le b,\,\,c\le v\le d} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,a\le u(x,y)\le b,\,\,c\le v(x,y)\le d},\end{aligned}
$$

where the equations of the left, right, bottom, and top sides are

$$
{\color{blue}u(x,y)} = a, \qquad 
{\color{blue}u(x,y)} = b, \qquad
{\color{red}v(x,y)} = c, \qquad 
{\color{red}v(x,y)} = d.
$$

With that in mind, let's analyze the boundary of our region $D.$ 

Rewriting the equations 

$$
y=x, \qquad
y=7x, \qquad
x=\dfrac{3}{y^2}, \qquad
x=\dfrac{5}{y^2}
$$

by moving both variables $x$ and $y$ to the left-hand side, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x}=1,\,\frac{y}{x}=7,\,x{y}^{2}=3,\,x{y}^{2}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we put $u(x,y)={\color{blue}\dfrac{y}{x}}$ and $v(x,y)={\color{red}xy^2},$ we can define the transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ as

$$
\mathbf{T}^{-1} : (x,y) \to \left( \, {\color{blue}\dfrac{y}{x}}\,, \: \bbox[2pt, white, border: 1pt solid black]{\color{red}xy^2} \right).
$$

To find $\mathbf{T},$ we should express $x$ and $y$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$ Recall that we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}u=\frac{y}{x} \\ v=x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, $y=ux.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get 

$$
v = u^2x^3
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x^3 = \dfrac{v}{u^2} 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{v}{u^2}}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{v}{u^2}}$ back into $y=ux,$ we obtain

$$
y =u\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{v}{u^2}} = \sqrt[3]{uv}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Transformation That Maps a Region Onto a Type I Region
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $D$ be the finite region bounded by the curve 
$(x+y)^2 + y = 3$ and the line $y=-1.$
Consider the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where $u=x+y$ and $v=y.$ Find the representation of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D)$ in the $uv$-plane.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we are given that  

![](images/61/61a3c6677ac0c20f5cccc6808fa7b078f91c3ad784d59167d11a9829cd0f86c3.png)

Substituting $x+y = u$ and $y = v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{2}+y=3\,⟹\,{u}^{2}+v=3\,⟹\,v=3-{u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y = v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=-1\,⟹\,v=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v=3-{u}^{2} \\ v=-1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 2 \\ v=-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2, -1).$

![](images/84/84c624aab456b9a090c9c4e6d23c82d8e1f69425050b6f3ee9d4afd18e3f0cec.png)

As a result, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation 

$$
\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D)  = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -2 \leq u \leq 2, \quad  -1 \leq v \leq 3-u^2 \big\}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The area scale factor of a linear transformation $T$ with standard matrix $T$ is equal to $|det(T)|.$ Therefore,

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Differentials to Approximate the Value of a Function
questions.problem: Estimate $\sqrt[3]{10}+\sqrt{150}$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{x}+\sqrt{y}$ at the point $(8,144).$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3{x}^{2/3}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(8,144),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\frac{1}{3\cdot {8}^{2/3}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{144}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{24}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(8+Δx,144+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈\frac{1}{12}\,Δx+\frac{1}{24}\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\sqrt[3]{10}+\sqrt{150}=f(10,150),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(10,150).$

Moving from $(8,144)$ to $(10,150),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =10-8=2, \\ Δy & =150-144=6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈\frac{1}{12}(2)+\frac{1}{24}(6) \\  & ≈\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & ≈\frac{5}{12} \\  & ≈0.417.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.417.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10,150) & ≈f(8,144)+0.417 \\ \sqrt[3]{10}+\sqrt{150} & ≈\sqrt[3]{8}+\sqrt{144}+0.417 \\  & ≈2+12+0.417 \\  & ≈14.417.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Differentials to Approximate the Change in a Multivariable Function
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz),$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(1,1,1)$ to $(2,3,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y+\frac{1}{z}\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(1,1,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(1,1,1) & =1\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y+1\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(1+Δx,1+Δy,1+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈Δx+Δy+Δz.
$$

Moving from $(1,1,1)$ to $(2,3,4),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =2-1=1, \\ Δy & =3-1=2 \\ Δz & =4-1=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈Δx+Δy+Δz \\  & ≈1+2+3 \\  & ≈6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ increases by approximately $6.$

questions.problem: Given a right triangular prism, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ if the height is $h=5$ and the base is a right triangle with legs $a=4$ and $b=6.$

The volume of a given right triangular prism is $V=\frac{abh}{2}.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{bh}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{ah}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{ab}{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=4,$ $b=6,$ and $h=5,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(4,6,5) & =\frac{6\cdot 5}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{4\cdot 5}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{4\cdot 6}{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =15\,\text{d}a+10\text{d}b+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/4a/4ae6f37660956d6d7015289c4a185c12ef4ab39f84e9cff394f534b14854c5cd.png)

The sides of a square are decreasing in length at a rate of $3\text{ m/min}.$ At what rate is the area of ​​the square decreasing when the side is $12\,\text{m}$ long?

The area is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{m}}^{2}/\text{min}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $3\,\text{m/min},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3.$ Also, when the sides are $12\,\text{m},$ we have $x=12.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-3\cdot 2(12)=-72{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square is decreasing at $72\,{\text{m}}^{2}/\text{min}.$

A manufacturing process gradually reduces the size of a square opening by shortening its diagonals at a rate of $2.2\text{ mm}\text{/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the opening decreasing when each diagonal measures $10\,\text{mm}?$

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of decrease is positive.

The area is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $h$ be the length of the diagonals and $A$ be the area of the square. Using the Pythagorean theorem, the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $h$ decreases at a rate of $2.2\,\text{mm/s},$ so

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-2.2.
$$

When the diagonal length is $h=10,$ substituting into the expression above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=(-2.2)(10)=-22{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.
$$

Therefore, the area of the square opening is decreasing at a rate of $22{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Each side of a square is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min}.$ How fast is the area of the square decreasing when the sides are $10\,\text{cm}?$

![](images/a0/a06eb0963dc6d01e45acb9349e5232ba70a11c98c99ee63c2ec0dae3d748f5ed.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} .
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A = x^2.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min},$ so we have $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} = -2.$ Also, when the sides are $10\,\text{cm},$ we have $x=10.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =(-2)\cdot 2(10)=-40{\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square decreases at a rate of $40\,\text{cm}^2/\text{min}.$

$$

canonical_examples.problem: The sides of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to twice the rate of increase of the diagonal. What is the area of the square at that moment?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A = \dfrac{h^2}{2}.
$$

Using implicit differentiation and the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 2\dfrac{\textrm d h}{\textrm d t}$, so replacing $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm dt}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 2\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 2 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have $h=2,$ and therefore the area of the square at that moment is

$$
A = \dfrac{2^2}{2} = 2.
$$

For any set $Y,$ we have $\left|\mathcal{P}(Y)\right| = 2^{\left| Y \right|}.$

$$

For any set $S,$ we have $\left|\mathcal{P}(S)\right| = 2^{\left| S \right|}.$ Also, $|S \times T| = |S| \cdot |T|.$

In our case, 

$$
\left| Y \right| = 1, \qquad
\left| Z \right| = 2.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}|P(Y\times Z)| & ={2}^{|Y\times Z|} \\  & ={2}^{|Y|\,\cdot \,|Z|} \\  & ={2}^{1\cdot 2} \\  & ={2}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|P(P(Y\times Z))| & ={2}^{|P(Y\times Z)|} \\  & ={2}^{4} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
questions.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)$ at the point $(1,-1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z$, then our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)k \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2x+y}\text{ }j-1\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }j-k \\  & =2\text{ }i+\,j-k \\  & =⟨2,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{1}=\frac{z-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}=1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,4).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})\,j \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}x\,i+\frac{1}{8}y\,j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =-\frac{2}{9}(0)\,i+\frac{1}{8}(4)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,j \\  & =⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,4)=⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-0)\frac{1}{2}-(y-4)0 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3$ at the point $(-1,-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x},$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(0,0,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,k \\  & =({e}^{y}+z{e}^{x})\,i+(x{e}^{y}+{e}^{z})\,j+(y{e}^{z}+{e}^{x})\,k \\ ∇f(0,0,1) & =({e}^{0}+(1){e}^{0})i+((0){e}^{0}+{e}^{1})j+((0){e}^{1}+{e}^{0})k \\  & =2\,i+e\,j+k\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Complex Number in Exponential Form
questions.problem: Write the complex number $z=-1+\text{i}$ in exponential form.
questions.worked_solution:
To write our complex number in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{(1)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $z$ lies in the second quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)| \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=\sqrt{2}$ and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get 

$$
z=\sqrt{2}\,{\text{e}}^{3\pi \text{i}/4}.
$$

Finally, substituting $r=\sqrt{13}$ and $\theta =0.588$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get 

$$
z=\sqrt{13}\,{\text{e}}^{0.588\,\text{i}}.
$$

The complex number shown in the Argand diagram can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x+\text{i}y \\  & =-3+3\text{i}.\end{aligned}

To write it in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)| \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=3\sqrt{2}$ and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=3\sqrt{2}\,{\text{e}}^{3\pi \text{i}/4}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩, \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,0,-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,0,-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡3t & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡3t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡3t & 0 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =⟨0-0,-(-{cos}^{2}⁡3t-{sin}^{2}⁡3t),0-0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{t},{e}^{t},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}},\,\frac{{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{5{e}^{2t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t},\,-5{e}^{2t}⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(2{e}^{t})^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}+{(-5{e}^{2t})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t}+25{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{1+5{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{5{e}^{2t}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t},\,-5{e}^{2t}⟩}{(\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{5{e}^{2t}+1})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2,\,1,\,-5{e}^{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{t},{e}^{t},1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2,\,1,\,-5{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & 1 \\ 1 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & 1 \\ 2 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}⟨-5{e}^{2t}-1,-(-10{e}^{2t}-2),2{e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}⟨-(5{e}^{2t}+1),\,2(5{e}^{2t}+1),\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-1,2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}})}=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩\times ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨0-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-(0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\sqrt{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+\sqrt{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$
