questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ -12\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}15 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set ${v,w}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{15\cdot 3+(-3)\cdot 6+(-3)\cdot (-12)}{{3}^{2}+{6}^{2}+(-12)^{2}}v=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ -12\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{15\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}w=4[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{3\cdot 1+2\cdot (-1)+5\cdot 1+1\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{a}_{1}=2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{3\cdot 2+2\cdot 4+5\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3-4)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(5-4)^{2}+(1-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ -9 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}},$ $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}},$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{3}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{3\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 4+(-9)\cdot 1+3\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=(-1)[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}], \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{3\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 0+(-9)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1}{(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{3\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot (-1)+(-9)\cdot 0+3\cdot 4}{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}}{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3-0)^{2}+(-3-(-5))^{2}+(-9-(-2))^{2}+(3-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{63} \\  & =3\sqrt{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Find the acute angle between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal. Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{4\cdot 1+0\cdot 0+2\cdot (-1)}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{4\cdot 1+0\cdot 1+2\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ 

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}\,x}{‖x‖\,‖{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x‖} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3+0\cdot 2+2\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{14}{\sqrt{20}\sqrt{14}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{14}}{\sqrt{20}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{7}{10}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\sqrt{\frac{7}{10}})≈{33.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Constant Term For the Fourier Series
questions.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{2}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{2}x)
$$

Let $F(x)=3{x}^{2}+2x$ for $x\in [-2,2).$ The Fourier series of the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and $f(x)=3{x}^{2}+2x$ for $x\in [-2,2).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(3{x}^{2}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}]}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(({2}^{3}+{2}^{2})-((-2)^{3}+(-2)^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(12-(-4)) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Mapping an Area to a Rectangular Region: Transformations Given
questions.problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{1}{xy},\,v={x}^{2}y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
y=\frac{1}{2x},\,y=\frac{1}{3x},\,y=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,y=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=\frac{1}{xy},\,v={x}^{2}y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=\frac{1}{xy}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{2x} & ⟹\, & \frac{1}{xy}=2 & ⟹\, & u=2 \\  & y=\frac{1}{3x} & ⟹\, & \frac{1}{xy}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v={x}^{2}y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹\, & {x}^{2}y=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹\, & {x}^{2}y=3 & ⟹\, & v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 3}
$$

![](images/05/05d2ca47db245b147cb52f95a474a60ece144931c8b6e1e40c6628a99b53d690.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y} & -\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}} \\ 2xy & \text{ }\text{ }{x}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=y=\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}=\frac{1}{{u}^{2}v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}v}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =(-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2})\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the lines

$$
y=3x-2,\,y=3x+2,\,y=1-2x,\,y=3-2x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=y-3x,\,v=y+2x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=y-3x$ into the equations of the first and second lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=3x-2 & ⟹\, & y-3x=-2 & ⟹\, & u=-2 \\  & y=3x+2 & ⟹\, & y-3x=2 & ⟹\, & u=2\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=y+2x$ into the equations of the third and fourth lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=1-2x & ⟹\, & y+2x=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=3-2x & ⟹\, & y+2x=3 & ⟹\, & v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 3}
$$

![](images/9c/9c17c81b4abc0d4ebd1eadfe951b0eb0c2674d9eb07b785e7fd972fd00e513ae.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $y+2x=u$ into the equation of the first line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2x=1\,⟹\,u=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y-2x=v$ into the equation of the second line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2x=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=y+2x$ and $v=y-2x$ into the equation of curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4{x}^{2}=4\,⟹\,(y+2x)(y-2x)=4,\,⟹\,uv=4.\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection point of the two lines in the $uv$-plane is $(1,1).$

To find the intersection of the curve with the first line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}uv=4 \\ u=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=1 \\ v=4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curve with the second line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}uv=4 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=4 \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(1,1),$ $(1,4)$ and $(4,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le \frac{4}{u}}.
$$

![](images/30/30fff9564451baadff3cae48dbfb91dc08fc8591e596e7cd2f65d8cfc6c9c5a6.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(4)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{4}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}[{\int }_{1}^{4/u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}[v]_{1}^{4/u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{4}{u}-1)du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[4\operatorname{ln}⁡u-u]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-4+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x-y,\,v=y+1,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x-y)^{2}+y=2$ and the line $y=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x-y,\,v=y+1
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x-y=u$ and $y=v+1$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-y)^{2}+y=2\,⟹\,(y+1)=3-(x-y)^{2}\,⟹\,v=3-{u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

 

while substituting $y=v-1$ into the equation of the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v=3-{u}^{2} \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm \sqrt{2} \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{2},1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-\sqrt{2}\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,1\le v\le 3-{u}^{2}.}.
$$

![](images/9c/9cec7ff29557aa14cd19309e9180482a44091e7ef215205285822674e7bc25b0.png)

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{3-{u}^{2}}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}[v]_{1}^{3-{u}^{2}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(3-{u}^{2}-1)\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(2-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & ={[2u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =(2\sqrt{2}-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3})-(-2\sqrt{2}+\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x+y)^{4}-x+y=0$ and  the line $y=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=u$ and $x-y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{4}-x+y=0\,⟹\,(x+y)^{4}-(x-y)=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

Now, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}x+y=u \\ x-y=v\end{aligned}\,⟹\,y=\frac{u-v}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this value into the equation of the given line yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\, & ⟹\,\frac{u-v}{2}=0\,⟹\,v=u\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{4} \\ v=u\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}(u-1)=0 \\ v=u.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{4}\le v\le u}.
$$

![](images/1e/1ed905e319e689d3fc7955a30f58e0f3ae2e7a751c27b80201d2b43f58b4206c.png)

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(-2)^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{u}^{4}}^{u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[v]_{{u}^{4}}^{u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(u-{u}^{4})du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{u}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3}{10}) \\  & =\frac{3}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]

$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3x)^{2}-x=3\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=3\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}-3,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2}-3 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 2 \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2,1).$

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,{u}^{2}-3\le v\le 1}.
$$

![](images/26/2687f0cc14eb0b476ea5f4ba7272e7f248bb7dcb276a0e2b0c39e551501b011d.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(-1)^{-1}=-1.

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-1|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}-3}^{1}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[v]_{{u}^{2}-3}^{1}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(1-({u}^{2}-3))\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & ={[4u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =16-\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u = \dfrac{y^2}{x}, \qquad v= xy,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
x = {y^2}, \qquad x=\dfrac{y^2}3, \qquad y=\dfrac2x, \qquad y=\dfrac4x.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](images/e4/e4acf61532998ca5b0768b7edde16be779298c1be15ef11b14472678ba43043a.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u = \dfrac{y^2}{x}, \qquad v= xy
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/37/3706f0373bb39ebd41d78dd453896548ec03638a656e1fe36604f2a43108ba8e.png)

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u= \dfrac{y^2}{x}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x={y}^{2} & ⟹\, & \frac{{y}^{2}}{x}=1 & ⟹\, & u=1 \\  & x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & ⟹\, & \frac{{y}^{2}}{x}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v = xy$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{2}{x} & ⟹\, & xy=2 & ⟹\, & v=2 \\  & y=\frac{4}{x} & ⟹\, & xy=4 & ⟹\, & v=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 1 \leq u \leq 3, \quad 2 \leq v \leq 4\big\}
$$

![](images/12/1207d8cdb8afd7c55d712caca043edfe9f0d0395343a6cbd329cf5861ec3bce7.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{2y}{x} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{3{y}^{2}}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = -\dfrac{x}{3y^2} = -\dfrac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (4-2) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the following curves.

$$
e^y = \dfrac{5}{e^x}, \qquad e^y=\dfrac{10}{e^x}, \qquad e^x=e^y, \qquad e^x=2e^y
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](images/f4/f47c1b7ce7e9073a10c2665821a4fc0d5b38ce6ad6c0f79a75a5b203962112cd.png)

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v,
$$

  

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
e^{x+y} = 5, \qquad e^{x+y}=10, \qquad e^{x-y} = 1, \qquad e^{x-y} = 2
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u = e^{x+y}, \qquad v = e^{x-y}
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/88/88c92ebc206481c3ef86661ee413358bb060cb85f642148c609de0bf1a9da2d1.png)

**Step 2**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=e^{x+y}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x+y}=5\,⟹\,u=5 \\  & {e}^{x+y}=10\,⟹\,u=10\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v =e^{x-y}$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x-y}=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & {e}^{x-y}=2\,⟹\,v=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 5 \leq u \leq 10, \quad 1 \leq v \leq 2\big\}
$$

![](images/10/105745a82e8f67b086f526b0166e3b442d3eaf02e4df69314ed9d3ffd5fca071.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+y} & {e}^{x+y} \\ {e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =-{e}^{2x}-{e}^{2x} \\  & =-2{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} =  -\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-2x}=-\dfrac{1}{2uv}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)}\neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{2uv}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{uv}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{5}^{10}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡5)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region
canonical_examples.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u =3x-2y, \quad v=x+y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(3x-2y)^2 - y - x = 0$ and the line $x+y=4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](images/87/87b44aa661a51ee39011c33c2eb000edcebb127508d45d5819339cf532258f3e.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u = 3x-2y, \qquad v=x+y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/88/88c92ebc206481c3ef86661ee413358bb060cb85f642148c609de0bf1a9da2d1.png)

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $3x-2y = u$ and $x+y = v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-2y)^{2}-y-x=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x + y = v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y+x=4\,⟹\,v=4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2} \\ v=4\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 2 \\ v=4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2, 4).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -2 \leq u \leq 2, \, u^2 \leq v \leq 4\big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/0a/0a3d0211dfbe18e5737b62e8b61cf9308af2735ef827d14bae7b5dbfffaa4faa.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = (5)^{-1} = \dfrac 15.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[v]_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[4u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(8-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Image of a Point or Segment
questions.problem:
![](images/af/afc9e81f3294803794ba0d62773958913cf7475a0718e77052212a149050aecf.png)

Consider the segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ above, and the transformation $T$ defined as

$$
x=2u+2v-2,\,y=v-u+2.
$$

The image of $\overset{―}{PQ}$ under the action of $T$ is the segment $\overset{―}{{P}^{′}{Q}^{′}}$ in the $xy$-plane. Which of the following diagrams shows $\overset{―}{{P}^{′}{Q}^{′}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u+2v-2 \\ v-u+2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u+2v \\ -u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $T$ maps the endpoints of $\overset{―}{PQ}$ to the endpoints of $\overset{―}{{P}^{′}{Q}^{′}}.$ So, to find the image of $\overset{―}{PQ},$ we find the images of each endpoint.

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing the endpoints of our segment:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $b$ in each column:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The image of $u$ under $T$ is given by $Au+b.$ So, by applying $T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 10 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 8 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the endpoints of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(-6,2)$ and $(8,1).$

Drawing this segment in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](images/8e/8e57b4d47ef3c6ad1b1d70a97126aa865c4481ee67e16eaf4e79c09e3146b30d.png)

questions.problem:
Consider the transformation $T$ defined as

$$
x=3v+u,\,y=u-6v+3.
$$

Let $P(-2,3)$ be a point in the $uv$-plane. Suppose that the image of $P$ under the action of $T$ is the point ${P}^{′}$ in the $xy$-plane. What are the coordinates of ${P}^{′}?$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3v+u \\ u-6v+3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u+3v \\ u-6v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the image of $P$ under the action of $T,$ we first create a column vector $u$ containing the coordinates of $P:$

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Applying $T$ to $u,$ we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -17\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of ${P}^{′}$ are $(7,-17).$

questions.problem:
![](images/9b/9bfb4e21205db9550d88222e04449b9858137550b957ba652b3e6998dce8025c.png)

Consider the triangle $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-1\le v\le 1,\,0\le u\le \frac{1-v}{2}}.
$$

The transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the image of $Δ$ in the $xy$-plane under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation is already in matrix form 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $T$ maps the boundary of $Δ$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $Δ,$ we find the images of each side.

![](images/19/194428bede19351ba77866a9ca49f76b38c4327fd0a5e2c219afff9c14b12c28.png)

             

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our triangle:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $b$ in each column:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The image of $u$ under $T$ is given by $Au+b.$ So, by applying $T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertices of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(-2,0),(-1,-1),$ and $(0,2).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](images/02/02ab748669496bf50a8809cf822a969d731a18283d52272175fd5b615ef5b765.png)

          

Finally, since $det(A)=2>0,$ this transformation preserves orientation.

$$

$$

The transformation $T$ maps the boundary of $Δ$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $Δ,$ we find the images of each side.

$$

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $b$ in each column:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

![](images/14/146f9f36deeac0f3a7108a173485eb6d0d03138d18998a96dc9c3566bee21ca2.png)

questions.problem:
Consider the affine transformation $T$ defined as

$$
x=-2v+1,\,y=4u-v-5.
$$

Let $A$ be the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]$
- $det(A)=-4$
- The transformation $T$ is orientation-preserving
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

questions.problem:
Consider the affine transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

What is the area scale factor of the transformation?
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$

$$

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is

$$
|det(A)|=|-4|=4.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:

Consider the segment $\overline{PQ}$ above, and the transformation $\mathbf T$ defined as

$$
x = u - v + 7, \qquad y = u + v +1.
$$

The image of $\overline{PQ}$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ is the segment $\overline{P'Q'}$ in the $xy$-plane. Find $\overline{P'Q'}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v+7 \\ u+v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $\mathbf T$ maps the endpoints of $\overline{PQ}$ to the endpoints of $\overline{P'Q'}.$ So, to find the image of $\overline{PQ},$ we find the images of each endpoint.

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing the endpoints of our segment:
![](images/fa/faf8bd29c9813cf0f73fca4b58f5636d3eb3262eae64ac099bdcdc569096ab0c.png)

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $\mathbf b$ in each column:
![](images/07/074650a4370dd709462de2400991a1d7ec0e8279ea4e7e414bf956e511f7cace.png)

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $\mathbf T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 & 7 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -10 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 & 7 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the endpoints of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(0,-2)$ and $(-3,1).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](images/61/61508357c514f50b27498bee50dce36d22b7f55f0baf8c2d6a58ad2d53dc879d.png)

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$

$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v+1 \\ u+v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $\mathbf T$ maps the boundary of $\Delta$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $\Delta,$ we find the images of each side.

![](images/69/69d92e24d5b0c81e54d3878793efe7c07d16fc963222997fe4fec4ffb3f93bd5.png)

          

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our square:
![](images/04/047cd6bf2960418919b4a11ae6920d9fc589881062ddbb3eed918116a7e4c4fd.png)

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $\mathbf b$ in each column:
![](images/cf/cfc1c3e72dd7764d9835e35f1943ef96c6829703ca8f0b2bce67153df9df88e5.png)

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About the Stability of Other Methods
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true when testing the stability of the implicit Euler method on the test equation ${y}^{′}=-\lambda y$ with $y=y(x),y(0)=1,x\ge 0,\lambda =1,$ and step size $Δx?$  

- The stability function is $R(Δx)=\frac{1}{1+Δx}.$
- The stability region is $|\frac{1}{1+Δx}|<1.$
- The method is absolutely stable.
- The method is **unstable** for step size $Δx=0.50.$

*Hint:* The stability function $R$ is given by ${y}_{n+1}=R(\lambda Δx){y}_{n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
A numerical method 
${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$
is stable for a given step size $Δx$ if, when applied to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\lambda y,\,y(0)=1,\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda >0,
$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

When a method is applied to the test equation, the update takes the form

$$
{y}_{n+1}=R(\lambda Δx){y}_{n},
$$

where $R(\lambda Δx)$ is the stability function of the method. The set of values for which the method is stable, given by $|R(\lambda Δx)|<1,$ is called the stability region of the method.

A method that is stable for all possible values $\lambda Δx>0$ is called absolutely stable.

Now, let's check the stability of the implicit Euler method by applying it to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-y,\,y(0)=1.
$$

First, for an initial value problem ${y}^{′}=f(x,y),y({x}_{0})={y}_{0},$ the implicit Euler method is given by the update formula

$$
{y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+f({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n+1})\cdot Δx.
$$

We now examine our statements:

- Applying the implicit Euler method to the test equation, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{n+1} & ={y}_{n}+(-{y}_{n+1})\cdot Δx \\ {y}_{n+1}+{y}_{n+1}\cdot Δx & ={y}_{n} \\ {y}_{n+1}(1+Δx) & ={y}_{n} \\ {y}_{n+1} & =\frac{1}{1+Δx}\cdot {y}_{n}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the stability function is 

$$
R(Δx)=\frac{1}{1+Δx}.
$$

Hence, statement I is true.

- The method is stable when

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(Δx)| & <1 \\ |\frac{1}{1+Δx}| & <1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${y}_{n}$ converges to $0$ as $n\to \infty $ if and only if
$|\frac{1}{1+Δx}|<1.$
Hence, statement II is true.

- Now, since $1+Δx>1$ for any positive step size $Δx,$ we have

$$
|\frac{1}{1+Δx}|<1
$$

for all $Δx>0.$ So, the implicit Euler method is absolutely stable, and statement III is true.

- Finally, because the implicit Euler method is absolutely stable, it is stable for step size $Δx=0.50.$ Hence, statement IV is false.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only".

- $Δx=\frac{1.9}{\lambda }$

questions.worked_solution:

${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$

$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

For stability, we require that the following condition holds:

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(\lambda Δx)| & <1 \\ |1-\lambda Δx| & <1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this gives

$$
0<\lambda Δx<2.
$$

This means that Euler's method is stable when applied to the test equation for values in the region $0<\lambda Δx<2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & <\lambda Δx<2 \\ 0 & <0.6<2,\end{aligned}
$$

Euler's method must be stable for this step size.

- For $Δx=\frac{3}{\lambda },$ we have $\lambda Δx=3\ge 2.$ Since this value falls outside the given region, Euler's method is not stable (or unstable) for this step size.

- For $Δx=\frac{1.9}{\lambda },$ we have $\lambda Δx=1.9.$ Since this value falls within the given region,

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & <\lambda Δx<2 \\ 0 & <1.9<2,\end{aligned}
$$

Euler's method must be stable for this step size.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(0.3)| & =|1-0.3+\frac{(0.3)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(0.3)^{3}}{6}+\frac{(0.3)^{4}}{24}| \\  & =|\frac{59\,267}{80\,000}| \\  & =0.740…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}$  that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =-(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C}.
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)+C} \\ 1 & =-\frac{1}{\frac{\pi }{4}+C} \\ C & =-\frac{\pi }{4}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)-\frac{\pi }{4}-1}=\frac{4}{\pi +4-4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{xy}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}$ that satisfies $y(0)=e.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{xy}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y} \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-x \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\,\text{d}y & =-\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\text{d}y & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral in the left-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡y.$ Then,  we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=\frac{1}{y}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y.
$$

So we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{ln}⁡y(\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\int u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{ln}^{2}⁡y+{C}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{ln}^{2}⁡y+{C}_{2} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {ln}^{2}⁡y & =-{x}^{2}+2({C}_{1}-{C}_{2}) \\ {ln}^{2}⁡y & =C-{x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2({C}_{1}-{C}_{2})$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(0)=e$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{ln}^{2}⁡e & =C-{0}^{2} \\ {1}^{2} & =C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
{ln}^{2}⁡y=1-{x}^{2}.
$$

We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{e}^{-y} & =3{x}^{2}{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}{e}^{-y}-2x{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(3{x}^{2}-2x){e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}-2x \\ \int {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (3{x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & ={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+C)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3}-{1}^{2}+C) & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡C & =1 \\ C & =e\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{e}^{-y}=3{x}^{2}{e}^{-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+e).
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vectors

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ 2{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=8 \\ {x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-6 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & -14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=8 \\ {x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-6 \\ {x}_{3}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=5.$ Substituting this value in the second and first equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}_{2}-2(5)=-6\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=4 \\  & {x}_{1}+5=8\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=3$, ${x}_{2}=4$, and ${x}_{3}=5,$ which means 

$$
3{a}_{1}+4{a}_{2}+5{a}_{3}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=3+4+5=12.
$$

Consider the vectors

$$

$$

 

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the resulting equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

which we substitute into the second equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3(-5) & =1 \\ -2{x}_{1} & =-14 \\ {x}_{1} & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5$ into the third equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=-4 \\ 3(7)+5(-5) & =-4 \\ -4 & =-4,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5,$ which means

$$
7{a}_{1}-5{a}_{2}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=7+(-5)=2.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for Three Coefficients in a Linear Combination
questions.problem:
Consider the vectors

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -8 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 9 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -8 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 9 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 2{x}_{1} \\ -{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{2} \\ -8{x}_{2} \\ 5{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 9 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 9 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=1 \\ 2{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=9 \\ -{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=1\end{aligned}
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -8 & 2 & 9 \\ -1 & 5 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -8 & 2 & 9 \\ -1 & 5 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 & 7 \\ -1 & 5 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=1 \\ 2{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=7 \\ 0=2.\end{aligned}
$$

However, the final equation $0=2$  gives a false statement. So the system has no solution.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Distance Between Two Parallel Axes
questions.problem:
A circular plate of mass $1\,\text{kg}$ with uniform mass density occupies the region of a disk $D$ of radius $\sqrt{6}\,\text{m}$ and is centered at the origin.
Given that the moment of inertia of the plate about a line $l$ perpendicular to the plate is $4\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2},$ find the distance of the line $l$ from the center of mass of $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, notice that the region $D$ can be expressed in polar coordinates as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{6},\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

The area of the circular plate $D$ is $A=\pi \cdot (\sqrt{6})^{2}=6\pi \,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{1}{6\pi }\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid $(0,0).$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{6\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{6\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{6\pi }\cdot 9\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =3\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem and solving for $d,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\ 4 & =3+1{d}^{2} \\ {d}^{2} & =1 \\ d & =1\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Moment of Inertia of a Rectangular Plate About a Perpendicular Axis
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $6\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,-3\le y\le 3},$
where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=4\cdot 6=24\,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{6}{24}=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid:

$$
(\overset{¯}{x},\overset{¯}{y})=(\frac{-2+2}{2},\frac{-3+3}{2})=(0,0)
$$

Since the center of mass is at the origin, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{-3}^{3}\frac{1}{4}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{[{x}^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=-3}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-2}^{2}6{x}^{2}+18\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[2{x}^{3}+18x]_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(32+72) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(104) \\  & =26\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =26+(\sqrt{3})^{2}\cdot 6 \\  & =26+18 \\  & =44\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 6,\,0\le y\le 4}$
and has mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{1}{8}x,$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. The moment of inertia of the plate about a line $l$ perpendicular to the plate is $39\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$
Given that the center of mass of the plate is at $(4,2),$ find the distance of the line $l$ from the center of mass.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{8}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{6}x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{4}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{6}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 18\cdot 4 \\  & =9\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass $(4,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{―}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{―}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((x-4)^{2}+(y-2)^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{0}^{4}((x-4)^{2}+(y-2)^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{8}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{0}^{4}x(x-4)^{2}+x(y-2)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{6}{[x(x-4)^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}x(y-2)^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{6}4x(x-4)^{2}+\frac{16}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{6}4{x}^{3}-32{x}^{2}+\frac{208}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[{x}^{4}-\frac{32}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{104}{3}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(1\,296-2\,304+1\,248) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 240 \\  & =30\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem and solving for $d,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\ 39 & =30+9{d}^{2} \\ 9{d}^{2} & =9 \\ {d}^{2} & =1 \\ d & =1\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 3}$
and has mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=xy,$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters.
Given that the center of mass is at $(\frac{2}{3},2),$ find the moment of inertia about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $1\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass $(\frac{2}{3},2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{¯}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{¯}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+{(y-2)}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}({(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+{(y-2)}^{2})xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}x{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-4x{y}^{2}+4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}x{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}-\frac{4}{3}x{y}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{9}{2}x{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+\frac{81}{4}x-36x+18x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{9}{2}x{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+\frac{9}{4}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{9}{2}{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+\frac{17}{4}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{9}{8}{x}^{4}-2{x}^{3}+\frac{17}{8}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{9}{8}-2+\frac{17}{8}-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $1\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =\frac{5}{4}+{(1)}^{2}\cdot \frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}+\frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, notice that the region $D$ can be expressed in polar coordinates as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 4,\,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

Since the mass density is symmetric in $x$ and $y,$ the center of mass is at $(0,0).$ The mass density function, in polar coordinates, is given by 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{|r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |}{r}=\frac{1}{2}r|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|.
$$

Next, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{2}r|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}{|}_{1}^{4}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(64-1)\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =21\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =42\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{2}r|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{4}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1024-1)\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1023}{5}\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{2046}{5}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $1\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =\frac{2046}{5}+{1}^{2}\cdot 42 \\  & =\frac{2046}{5}+\frac{210}{5} \\  & =\frac{2256}{5}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $k(1-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{10})$ is the sum of the first $10$ terms of the geometric series $\frac{4}{3}+\frac{4}{9}+\frac{4}{27}+⋯,$ then $k=$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a geometric series, the sum of the first $N$ terms is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{N}={a}_{1}\frac{(1-{r}^{N})}{1-r},
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term of the series and $r$ is the common ratio.

In our case, ${a}_{1}=\frac{4}{3}.$ To find the value of $r,$ we find the ratio of the first two terms in the series:

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{(\frac{4}{9})}{(\frac{4}{3})}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

If we substitute ${a}_{1}=\frac{4}{3},N=10$ and $r=\frac{1}{3}$ into our formula, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{10} & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{(1-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{10})}{(1-\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{(1-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{10})}{(\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4}{3})}{(\frac{2}{3})}\cdot (1-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{10}) \\  & =2\cdot (1-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{10})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, comparing the expression above with $k(1-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{10}),$ we obtain $k=2.$

canonical_examples.problem: The second term of a geometric series is $20$ and the third term is $100.$ What is the sum of the first $6$ terms?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The sum of the first $N$ terms of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_N = a_1\dfrac{(1-r^N)}{1-r},
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term of the series, and $r$ is the common ratio.

To find $r,$ we find the ratio of the consecutive terms $a_2$ and $a_3 \mathbin{:}$

$$
r = \dfrac{a_3}{a_2} = \dfrac{100}{20} = 5
$$

Now we must determine the value of $a_1.$ To do this, we use the formula for the $n$th term, which states that

$$
a_n  = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}.
$$

For $n = 2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {5}^{2-1} \\ 20 & ={a}_{1}\cdot 5 \\ {a}_{1} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, if we substitute $a_1 = 4,$ $N = 6,$ and $r = 5$ into the formula for $S_N,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{6} & =4\cdot \frac{1-{5}^{6}}{1-5} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1-{5}^{6}}{-4} \\  & ={5}^{6}-1 \\  & =15\,624.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Solutions to First-Order Differential Equations
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2y\operatorname{cot}⁡2x.
$$

 Which of the following is a solution to this equation?

- $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$
- $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+1$
- $y=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a solution to a differential equation, it must satisfy the equation for all values of $x$ in the equation's domain.

We check each proposed solution by differentiating and substituting it into the original equation. 

- Differentiating $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x,$ we get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.$ Substituting into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2y\operatorname{cot}⁡2x \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & \overset{?}{=}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡2x \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This statement is *true*. Therefore, the function $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ *is* a solution to our differential equation.

- Differentiating $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+1,$ we get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.$ Substituting into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2y\operatorname{cot}⁡2x \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & \overset{?}{=}2(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+1)\operatorname{cot}⁡2x \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & \overset{?}{=}2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2\operatorname{cot}⁡2x \\ 0 & =2\operatorname{cot}⁡2x.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

This statement is *not true* for all $x.$ Therefore, the function $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+1$ is *not* a solution to our differential equation.

- Differentiating $y=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x,$ we get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.$ Substituting into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2y\operatorname{cot}⁡2x \\ -6\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & \overset{?}{=}2(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡2x \\ -6\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This statement is *true*. Therefore, the function $y=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ *is* a solution to our differential equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

This statement is *not true* for all $x.$ Therefore, the function $y=-2{e}^{x}$ is *not* a solution to our differential equation.
