questions.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 9\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}13 \\ -11\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](images/1b/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -10 & 13 \\ -3 & 1 & 9 & -11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -10 & 13 \\ 0 & 7 & -21 & 28\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -10 & 13 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -4 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-4)-(-3)\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}4 & -5 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Projection of the Intersection of a Surface and a Tilted Plane
questions.problem: Find the projection of the intersection between the sphere ${x}^{2}+(y+1)^{2}+{z}^{2}=4$ and the plane $x+z=2$ onto the $xy$-plane.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we want to find the projection onto the $xy$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $z.$ First, we solve for $z$ in the equation of the plane, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+z & =2\,⟹\,z=2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the expression for $z$ into the equation of the sphere, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y+1)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4 \\ {x}^{2}+(y+1)^{2}+(2-x)^{2} & =4 \\ {x}^{2}+(y+1)^{2}+(4-4x+{x}^{2}) & =4 \\ 2{x}^{2}-4x+4+(y+1)^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by completing the square for the variable $x$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-4x+4+(y+1)^{2} & =4 \\ 2{x}^{2}-4x+2+(y+1)^{2} & =2 \\ 2({x}^{2}-2x+1)+(y+1)^{2} & =2 \\ 2(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2} & =2 \\ (x-1)^{2}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the projection of the intersection is the ellipse $(x-1)^{2}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2}=1.$

First, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

$$
\frac{x-8}{4}=y=z=t\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=4t+8 \\ y=t \\ z=t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Substituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =3{z}^{2} \\ (4t+8)^{2}+3{t}^{2} & =3{t}^{2} \\ (4t+8)^{2} & =0 \\ 4t+8 & =0 \\ 4t & =-8 \\ t & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line. For $t=-2,$ we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4(-2)+8=0 \\ y=-2 \\ z=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(0,-2,-2).$

questions.problem: Given that $\,A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+6I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+6I) & =O \\ A-8I+6{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 6{A}^{-1} & =8I-A \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{4}{3}I-\frac{1}{6}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{4}{3},$ $q=-\frac{1}{6}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{4}{3}+(-\frac{1}{6})=\frac{7}{6}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(5-\lambda )+12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +22 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+22I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+22I) & =O \\ A-7I+22{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{22}I-\frac{1}{22}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{22},$ $q=-\frac{1}{22},$ and 

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{22}+(-\frac{1}{22})=\frac{3}{11}.
$$

questions.problem:
Given the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]$
and $\,f(x)={x}^{16}-4{x}^{14}+7x-3\,$, find $f(A).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,{x}^{14}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-4\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{16}$ | $-$ | $4{x}^{14}$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $7x$ | $-$ | $3$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\  & =7A-3I \\  & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A tank initially holds $500\,\text{L}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $12\,\text{kg}$ of salt.
A brine solution containing $0.02\,\text{kg}$ of salt per liter is poured into the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed brine leaves the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ Which differential equation best describes the amount of salt $Q,$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after the brine begins to be added?
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

First, note that a brine solution containing $0.02\,\text{kg/L}$ of salt enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.02\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.02\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.3\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $500\,\text{L}$ of brine.

- Brine enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $15t\,\text{L}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed brine leaves the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $20t\,\text{L}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of brine in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
500+15t-20t=(500-5t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the mass of salt in the tank, the *concentration* of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{500-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{500-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{500-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{500-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{4Q}{100-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}-\frac{4Q}{100-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{100-t}Q=\frac{3}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:

\frac{dQ}{dt}

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dissolved chemical enters the tank minus the rate at which dissolved chemical leaves the tank.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.14\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.14\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =2.52\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dissolved chemical exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which dissolved chemical leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $320\,\text{L}$ of solution.

- Chemical solution enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $18t\,\text{L}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $18t\,\text{L}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
320+18t-18t=320\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the mass of dissolved chemical in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{320}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min},$ *dissolved chemical* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(18\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{320}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{320}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{18Q}{320}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{9Q}{160}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =2.52-\frac{9Q}{160}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{9}{160}Q=2.52.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem:
A wastewater holding basin initially holds $480\,\text{gal}$ of water containing $12\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved contaminants.
Clean water is pumped into the basin at a rate of $24\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid leaves the basin at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of contaminants in the basin $10$ minutes after the clean water pumping begins.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of contaminants in the basin at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminants enter the basin minus the rate at which contaminants leave the basin.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminants enter the basin.

Note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of contaminants) enters the basin at a rate of $24\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminants* enter the basin is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (24\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (24\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminants exit the basin.

To find the rate at which contaminants leave the basin, we first determine the volume of wastewater in the basin at time $t.$

The basin initially contains $480\,\text{gal}$ of wastewater; water enters at $24\,\text{gal/min}$ and drains out at $18\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of wastewater in the basin after $t$ minutes is 

$$
480+24t-18t=(480+6t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminants in the basin, the *concentration* of the wastewater at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{480+6t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min},$ *contaminants* leave at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(18\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{480+6t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{480+6t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{18Q}{480+6t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{3Q}{80+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{3Q}{80+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{3}{80+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{3}{80+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{3}{80+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-3\int \frac{1}{80+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(80+t)^{3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the basin initially contains $12\,\text{lb}$ of contaminants. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=12,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =12 \\ \frac{A}{(80+0)^{3}} & =12 \\ A & =12\cdot {80}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=12{(\frac{80}{80+t})}^{3}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminants in the basin $10$ minutes after the clean water is first pumped in is

$$
Q(12)=12{(\frac{80}{90})}^{3}≈8.43\,\text{lb},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ A{e}^{-0/20} & =18 \\ A & =18\end{aligned}

A tank initially holds $600\,\text{L}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $25\,\text{kg}$ of salt.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a brine solution containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of salt) enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $600\,\text{L}$ of brine.

- Fresh water enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $18t\,\text{L}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed brine leaves the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $12t\,\text{L}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of brine in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
600+18t-12t=(600+6t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Then, since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the *concentration* of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{600+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{600+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{600+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{600+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{100+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =0-\frac{2Q}{100+t} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{100+t}\,Q.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{100+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{2}{100+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{100+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|100+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|100+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(100+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}

$$

questions.problem:
A wastewater holding basin initially holds $450\,\text{L}$ of water containing $9\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved contaminants.
Clean water is pumped into the basin at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid leaves the basin at a rate of $25\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of contaminants in the basin $12$ minutes after the clean water pumping begins.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of contaminants in the basin at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminants enter the basin minus the rate at which contaminants leave the basin.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminants enter the basin.

Note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of contaminants) enters the basin at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminants* enter the basin is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminants exit the basin.

To find the rate at which contaminants leave the basin, we first determine the volume of wastewater in the basin at time $t.$

The basin initially contains $450\,\text{L}$ of wastewater; water enters at $20\,\text{L/min}$ and drains out at $25\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of wastewater in the basin after $t$ minutes is 

$$
450+20t-25t=(450-5t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminants in the basin, the *concentration* of the wastewater at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{450-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $25\,\text{L/min},$ *contaminants* leave at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(25\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{450-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(25\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{450-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{25Q}{450-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{90-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{90-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{5}{90-t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{5}{90-t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{5}{90-t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-5\int \frac{1}{90-t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-5(-\operatorname{ln}⁡|90-t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(90-t)^{5}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(90-t)^{5}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =A(90-t)^{5},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the basin initially contains $9\,\text{kg}$ of contaminants. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=9,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =9 \\ A(90-0)^{5} & =9 \\ A & =\frac{9}{{90}^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{9}{{90}^{5}}(90-t)^{5} \\  & =9{(\frac{90-t}{90})}^{5} \\  & =9{(1-\frac{t}{90})}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminants in the basin $12$ minutes after the clean water is first pumped in is

$$
Q(12)=9{(1-\frac{12}{90})}^{5}≈4.40\,\text{kg},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

questions.problem: A $9\,500\,\text{mL}$-capacity vat initially holds $6\,500\,\text{mL}$ of a sugar-water solution containing $300\,\text{g}$ of sugar. Pure water begins to flow into the vat at a rate of $100\,\text{mL/s},$ while the completely mixed sugar-water flows out at a rate of $80\,\text{mL/s}.$ Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of sugar in the vat at the moment it begins to overflow.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of sugar in the vat at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in seconds. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the vat minus the rate at which sugar leaves the vat.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the vat.

First, note that pure water (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{g/mL}$ of sugar) enters the vat at a rate of $100\,\text{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the vat is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}})\cdot (100\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}})\cdot (100\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the vat.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the vat, we must first determine the volume of sugar-water in the vat at time $t.$

The vat initially contains $6\,500\,\text{mL}$ of solution; pure water enters at $100\,\text{mL/s},$ and mixed solution leaves at $80\,\text{mL/s}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the vat after $t$ seconds is 

$$
V(t)=6\,500+100t-80t=20(325+t)\,\text{mL}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the vat is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the vat, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{20(325+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $80\,\text{mL/s},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(80\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{20(325+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}) \\  & =(80\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{20(325+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}}) \\  & =\frac{4Q}{325+t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{4Q}{325+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{4}{325+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{4}{325+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{4}{325+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-4\int \frac{1}{325+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-4(\operatorname{ln}⁡|325+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(325+t)^{-4}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(325+t)^{-4}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(325+t)^{4}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the vat initially contains $300\,\text{g}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=300,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =300 \\ \frac{A}{(325+0)^{4}} & =300 \\ A & =300(325)^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{300(325)^{4}}{(325+t)^{4}} \\  & =300{(\frac{325}{325+t})}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Finally, the amount of sugar in the vat at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(150) & =300{(\frac{325}{325+150})}^{4} \\  & =300{(\frac{13}{19})}^{4} \\  & ≈65.75\,\text{g},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

questions.problem: A $240\,\text{gal}$-capacity tank initially holds $150\,\text{gal}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $32\,\text{lb}$ of salt. Fresh water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $3\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed brine flows out at a rate of $2\,\text{gal/min}.$ Find the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a brine solution containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt) enters the tank at a rate of $3\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (3\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (3\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $150\,\text{gal}$ of brine; fresh water enters at $3\,\text{gal/min},$ and mixed brine leaves at $2\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of brine in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=150+3t-2t=(150+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the concentration of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{150+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $2\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(2\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{150+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(2\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{150+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{2Q}{150+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{2Q}{150+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{2}{150+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{150+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{2}{150+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{150+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|150+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(150+t)^{-2}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(150+t)^{-2}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(150+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $32\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=32,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =32 \\ \frac{A}{(150+0)^{2}} & =32 \\ A & =32(150)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{32(150)^{2}}{(150+t)^{2}} \\  & =32{(\frac{150}{150+t})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $240\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=240$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =240 \\ 150+{t}_{o} & =240 \\ {t}_{o} & =90\,\text{min}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(90) & =32{(\frac{150}{150+90})}^{2} \\  & =32{(\frac{150}{240})}^{2} \\  & =32{(\frac{5}{8})}^{2} \\  & =12.5\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
A vat initially holds $360\,\textrm{L}$ of a sugar solution containing $18\,\textrm{kg}$ of sugar.
A sugar solution containing $0.30\,\textrm{kg}$ of sugar per liter is poured into the vat at a rate of $18\,\textrm{L/min},$ while the completely mixed solution leaves the vat at a rate of $30\,\textrm{L/min}.$ What differential equation describes the amount of sugar $Q,$ in kilograms, in the vat $t$ minutes after the inflow begins?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the vat at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the vat minus the rate at which sugar leaves the vat.

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}}
$$

Note that the units of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\textrm{out}}$ are $\textrm{kg}/\textrm{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the vat.

First, note that a sugar solution containing $0.30\,\textrm{kg/L}$ of sugar enters the vat at a rate of $18\,\textrm{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the vat is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.30\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.30\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =5.4\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the vat.

Now, to find the rate at which sugar leaves the vat, we must first determine the volume of solution in the vat at time $t.$

- The vat initially contains $360\,\textrm{L}$ of solution.

- Sugar solution enters the vat at a rate of $18\,\textrm{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $18t\,\textrm{L}$ have entered the vat.

- The completely mixed solution leaves the vat at a rate of $30\,\textrm{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $30t\,\textrm{L}$ have left the vat.

As a result, the volume of solution in the vat after $t$ minutes is 

$$
360 + 18t - 30t = (360-12t)\,\textrm{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the mass of sugar in the vat, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\dfrac{Q}{360 - 12t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $30\,\textrm{L/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(30\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{360-12t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(30\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{360-12t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{30Q}{360-12t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{60-2t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =5.4-\frac{5Q}{60-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{5}{60-2t}Q=5.4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which reactant exits the reactor.

To find the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor, we first determine the volume of solution in the reactor at time $t.$

$$
300 + 14t - 14t = 300\,\textrm{gal}.
$$

$$
\dfrac{Q}{300}\,\dfrac{\textrm{lb}}{\textrm{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed chemical solution leaves at a rate of $14\,\textrm{gal/min},$ *reactant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(14\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{300}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(14\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{300}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{14Q}{300}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{7Q}{150}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{7Q}{150}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\dfrac{7}{150}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{7}{150} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{7}{150})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-\frac{7}{150}\int 1\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{7t}{150}+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-\frac{7t}{150}+C} \\ Q(t) & =A{e}^{-7t/150},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A = \pm e^C$ is a constant of integration.

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ A{e}^{-7\cdot 0/150} & =18 \\ A & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$

$$
Q(t) = 18e^{-7t/150}
$$

$$
Q(25) = 18e^{-175/150} \approx 5.61\,\textrm{lb},

rounded to two decimal places.

$$

Note that the units of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\textrm{out}}$ are $\textrm{g}/\textrm{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\textrm{g/mL}$ of contaminant) enters the tank at a rate of $100\,\textrm{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}})\cdot (100\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}})\cdot (100\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $8\,000\,\textrm{mL}$ of water; clean water enters at $100\,\textrm{mL/s},$ and mixed water leaves at $60\,\textrm{mL/s}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ seconds is 

$$
V(t) = 8\,000 + 100t - 60t = 40(200+t)\,\textrm{mL}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the water at time $t$ is

$$
\dfrac{Q}{40(200 + t)}\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{mL}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $60\,\textrm{mL/s},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(60\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{40(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}) \\  & =(60\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{40(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}}) \\  & =\frac{3Q}{2(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{3Q}{2(200+t)}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\dfrac{3}{2(200 + t)}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{3}{2(200+t)} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{3}{2(200+t)})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{200+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{3}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|200+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(200+t)^{-3/2}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(200+t)^{-3/2}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(200+t)^{3/2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A = \pm e^C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $320\,\textrm{g}$ of contaminant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 320,$ and solve for $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =320 \\ \frac{A}{(200+0)^{3/2}} & =320 \\ A & =320(200)^{3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{320(200)^{3/2}}{(200+t)^{3/2}} \\  & =320{(\frac{200}{200+t})}^{3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $t_o$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $12\,000\,\textrm{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V(t_o) = 12\,000$ to solve for $t_o{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =12\,000 \\ 40(200+{t}_{o}) & =12\,000 \\ 200+{t}_{o} & =300 \\ {t}_{o} & =100\,\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(100) & =320{(\frac{200}{200+100})}^{3/2} \\  & =320{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3/2} \\  & ≈174.19\,\text{g}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Asymptotes of a Hyperbola Given Its Equation in Non-Standard Form
questions.problem: Calculate the asymptotes of the hyperbola $9{x}^{2}-25{y}^{2}=225.$
questions.worked_solution:
The standard equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

For a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin, the equations of the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{b}{a}x.
$$

To rewrite the given equation in standard form, we divide both sides of the equation by $225$ and then simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}-25{y}^{2} & =225 \\ \frac{9{x}^{2}}{225}-\frac{25{y}^{2}}{225} & =\frac{225}{225} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $a=\sqrt{25}=5,$ and $b=\sqrt{9}=3.$ 

Therefore, the asymptotes are $y=\pm \frac{3}{5}x.$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=3x-2y+1,\,y(1)=2
$$

We wish to approximate the solution using the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method. What entry should be placed in the cell indicated in the table below, where the first step has already been computed using the Runge-Kutta method, if the step size is $Δx=1?$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $3$ |  |  |  |  |  |
| $3$ | $\,?\,$ |  |  |  |  |  |

*Hint: The corrector equation of the two-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is defined as*

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx
$$

*where ${y}_{p}$ denotes the predictor at the current step, and ${y}_{-1}^{′}$ is the estimated slope at the previous point.*
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM2) method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

- ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

We're told that the first step is calculated using the Runge-Kutta Method, resulting in 

$$
y(2)≈3.
$$

Now, we'll continue from this point, using the ABM $2$-step method.

First, we compute the value of ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =3x-2y+1 \\  & =3\cdot 2-2\cdot 3+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $3$ | $1$ |  |  |  |  |

From the first row of the table, we see that the slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(1,2)$ is ${y}_{-1}^{′}=0.$

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot 1-0)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $3$ | $1$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |  |  |  |

So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=2+1=3, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=3+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{6}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $3$ | $1$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{9}{2}$ |  |  |

Hence, the slope at this predicted point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =3{x}_{\text{new}}-2{y}_{p}+1 \\  & =3\cdot 3-2\cdot \frac{9}{2}+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $3$ | $1$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{9}{2}$ | $1$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot 1+8\cdot 1-0)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot 13 \\  & =\frac{13}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $3$ | $1$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{9}{2}$ | $1$ | $\frac{13}{12}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=3.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =3+\frac{13}{12} \\  & =\frac{49}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $3$ | $1$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{9}{2}$ | $1$ | $\frac{13}{12}$ |
| $3$ | $\frac{49}{12}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(3)≈\frac{49}{12}.$

$$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point (${x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

We're told that the first step is calculated using the Runge-Kutta Method, resulting in 

$$
y(1)≈\frac{11}{12}.
$$

Now, we'll continue from this point, using the $2$-step ABM method.

First, we compute the value of ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-x(2y-x-1) \\  & =-1\cdot (2\cdot \frac{11}{12}-1-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\frac{1}{12}$ |
| $1$ | $\frac{11}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |  |  |  |  |

From the first row of the table, we see that the slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(0,1)$ is ${y}_{-1}^{′}=0.$

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot \frac{1}{6}-0)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\frac{1}{12}$ |
| $1$ | $\frac{11}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |  |  |  |

So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=\frac{11}{12}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| $1$ | $\frac{11}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{7}{6}$ |  |  |

$$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

$$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy=\frac{11}{12}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{19}{12}

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=4x-y-8,\,y(1)=2
$$

To approximate the solution, one step of the Runge-Kutta method has already been computed, resulting in the following estimate:

$$
y(2)≈-\frac{1}{4}
$$

Use the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method with one step to approximate $y(3).$

*Hint: The corrector equation of the two-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is defined as*

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx
$$

*where ${y}_{p}$ denotes the predictor at the current step, and ${y}_{-1}^{′}$ is the estimated slope at the previous point.*
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM $2$-step) Method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point (${x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

- ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

Before we start, let's add the initial condition data and Runge-Kutta step data to a table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ |  | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{1}{4}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Now, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=3,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=3-2=1.
$$

First, we compute the values of ${y}^{′}$ at each point according to the given rule:

- The slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(1,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{-1}^{′} & =4{x}_{-1}-{y}_{-1}-8 \\  & =4\cdot 1-2-8 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

- The slope at the current point $(x,y)=(2,-\frac{1}{4})$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4x-y-8 \\  & =4\cdot 2-(-\frac{1}{4})-8 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-6$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |  |  |  |  |

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot \frac{1}{4}-(-6))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{27}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-6$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{27}{8}$ |  |  |  |

So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=2+1=3, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{27}{8}=\frac{25}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-6$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{27}{8}$ | $\frac{25}{8}$ |  |  |

Hence, the slope at this predicted point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =4{x}_{\text{new}}-{y}_{p}-8 \\  & =4\cdot 3-\frac{25}{8}-8 \\  & =\frac{7}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-6$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{27}{8}$ | $\frac{25}{8}$ | $\frac{7}{8}$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot \frac{7}{8}+8\cdot \frac{1}{4}-(-6))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot (\frac{99}{8}) \\  & =\frac{33}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-6$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{27}{8}$ | $\frac{25}{8}$ | $\frac{7}{8}$ | $\frac{33}{32}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=3.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{33}{32} \\  & =\frac{25}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-6$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{27}{8}$ | $\frac{25}{8}$ | $\frac{7}{8}$ | $\frac{33}{32}$ |
| $3$ | $\frac{25}{32}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(3)≈\frac{25}{32}.$

questions.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ on the disk of radius $3$ centered at the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {3}^{2}=9\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2({(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}2{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\frac{81}{4}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{2}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{81}{2}(2\pi -0) \\  & =81\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{9\pi }\cdot 81\pi =9.
$$

questions.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=4{x}^{2}-2xy$ on the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3}.$

$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Amplitude for the Amplitude-Phase Form for Sine
questions.worked_solution:
The sum formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
6\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
6\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=6 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=8\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={6}^{2}+{8}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =36+64 \\ {R}^{2} & =100 \\ R & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

questions.problem: Given that the expression $4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ can be written as $R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ)$ with $R>0,$ what is the value of $R?$
questions.worked_solution:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=4 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=1\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={4}^{2}+{1}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =16+1 \\ {R}^{2} & =17 \\ R & =\sqrt{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

questions.problem: $\int \frac{2{log}_{4}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u={log}_{4}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,⟹\,\operatorname{ln}⁡4\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2{log}_{4}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =2\int {log}_{4}⁡x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =2\int u\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡4\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡4\int u\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡4\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4\cdot {u}^{2}+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4\cdot {log}_{4}^{2}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{3\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{x}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{1}^{e}\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{3/2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\cdot {u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2({1}^{3/2}-{0}^{3/2}) \\  & =2(1-0) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a VOP Equation by Substituting the Ansatz into the Original ODE
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}-3y=g(x).
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-3x}:$According to the method of variation of parameters, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={{field-1}}
$$

where ${u}_{1}={u}_{1}(x),{u}_{2}={u}_{2}(x),$ that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-2}}.
$$

Substituting the expressions $y={y}_{p}$ and ${y}^{′}={y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation yields the following relationship between ${u}_{1}^{′},{u}_{2}^{′},$ and $g(x):$

$$
{{field-3}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}={e}^{-3x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-3x})^{′}.
$$

Next, we substitute $y={y}_{p}$ and ${y}^{′}={y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}-3y & =g(x) \\ ({y}_{p}^{′})^{′}+2{y}_{p}^{′}-3{y}_{p} & =g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Using our expressions for ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-3x})^{′})}^{′}+2({u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-3x})^{′})-3({u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}) & =g(x) \\ {({u}_{1}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x})}^{′}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}-3{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x} & =g(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}+9{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}-3{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x} & =g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we group all terms proportional to ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}{{({e}^{x}+2{e}^{x}-3{e}^{x})}_{⏟}}_{0}+{u}_{2}{{(9{e}^{-3x}-6{e}^{-3x}-3{e}^{-3x})}_{⏟}}_{0}+{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}=g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the expressions in parentheses are both zero. Therefore, the equation reduces to

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}=g(x).
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-2y=x{e}^{4x}.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{2x}$ and ${y}_{2}={e}^{-x}.$ 

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

According to the method of variation of parameters, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={{field-1}}
$$

where ${u}_{1}={u}_{1}(x),{u}_{2}={u}_{2}(x),$ that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-2}}.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x,$ we obtain

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore, we have the following constraint equation relating ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}:$

$$
{{field-4}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{2x},\,{y}_{2}={e}^{-x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}({e}^{2x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-x})^{′}.
$$

We can form a constraint that relates ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}$ by differentiating ${y}_{p}$ and equating this expression to our constraint on ${y}_{p}^{′}.$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-x})}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}{e}^{2x})}^{′}+{({u}_{2}{e}^{-x})}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{1}({e}^{2x})^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-x})^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}-{u}_{2}{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}-{u}_{2}{e}^{-x} & ={u}_{1}({e}^{2x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-x})^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}-{u}_{2}{e}^{-x} & =2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}-{u}_{2}{e}^{-x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+\cancel{2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}-\cancel{{u}_{2}{e}^{-x}} & =\cancel{2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}}-\cancel{{u}_{2}{e}^{-x}}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}=0.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}.
$$

We can form a constraint that relates ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}$ by differentiating ${y}_{p}$ and equating this expression to our constraint on ${y}_{p}^{′}.$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}^{′}+{({u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\cancel{{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\cancel{{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x} & =\cancel{{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\cancel{{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0.
$$

questions.problem: Given the **orthonormal** basis $B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]}$  of ${R}^{2},$ find $[x]_{B}$ if $x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2}.$ 

Since $B$ is an orthonormal basis, we have that $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]$, where ${x}_{i}=x\cdot {q}_{i}.$ Computing the components of $x,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=-\frac{4}{\sqrt{13}}-\frac{21}{\sqrt{13}}=-\frac{25}{\sqrt{13}} \\ {x}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=-\frac{6}{\sqrt{13}}+\frac{14}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{8}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{25}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{8}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Given the orthogonal basis $B$ of ${R}^{3}$ and the vector $x$ below, find the value of $3{x}_{3}$, where ${x}_{3}$ is the third component of $[x]_{B}.$

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2},\,{q}_{3}.$ 

Since $B$ is an orthogonal basis, we have that $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]$, where ${x}_{i}=\frac{x\cdot {q}_{i}}{{q}_{i}\cdot {q}_{i}}.$ Computing ${x}_{3},$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} & =\frac{x\cdot {q}_{3}}{{q}_{3}\cdot {q}_{3}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 1+3\cdot 2+6\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4+6+6}{6} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
3{x}_{3}=3\cdot \frac{8}{3}=8.
$$

Given the **orthonormal** basis $B$ of ${R}^{3}$ and the vector $x$ below, find the value of $-2{x}_{2}$, where ${x}_{2}$ is the second component of $[x]_{B}.$

$$

$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2},\,{q}_{3}.$ 

Since $B$ is an orthonormal basis, we have that $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]$, where ${x}_{i}=x\cdot {q}_{i}.$ Computing ${x}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =x\cdot {q}_{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{2} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
-2{x}_{2}=-2\cdot (-1)=2.

Given the **orthonormal** basis $B$ of ${R}^{3}$ and the vector $x$ below, find the value of $-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}$, where ${x}_{3}$ is the third component of $[x]_{B}.$

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]},\,x=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} & =x\cdot {q}_{3} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\sqrt{5}+0+0 \\  & =\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \sqrt{5}=-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.

Given the orthogonal basis $B$ of ${R}^{3}$ and the vector $x$ below, find the value of $5{x}_{3}$, where ${x}_{3}$ is the third component of $[x]_{B}.$

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]},\,x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -7 \\ 6\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2},\,{q}_{3}.$ 

Since $B$ is an orthogonal basis, we have that $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]$, where ${x}_{i}=\frac{x\cdot {q}_{i}}{{q}_{i}\cdot {q}_{i}}.$ Computing ${x}_{3},$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} & =\frac{x\cdot {q}_{3}}{{q}_{3}\cdot {q}_{3}} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 2+(-7)\cdot 1+6\cdot 0}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10-7+0}{5} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
5{x}_{3}=5\cdot \frac{3}{5}=3.
$$

A type I region can be written as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,a\le x\le b,\,g(x)\le y\le f(x)},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type I region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $x:$

$$
x=\sqrt{3-y}+1\,⟹\,y=3-(x-1)^{2}
$$

The function $y=0$ is already written as a function of $x.$

Notice that the region lies between the vertical lines $x=1$ and $x=2.$ So, we have $0\le x\le 1.$

We draw a vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower function $g(x)$ and the upper function $f(x).$ A vertical line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type I region.

![](images/be/be799df2140d3a437bb311427dcae0e297cb6bd3844f88932157eb6ace6e7e59.png)

The vertical line enters the region through the lower function $y=0$ and leaves through the upper function $y=3-(x-1)^{2}.$ So, we have $0\le y\le 3-(x-1)^{2}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3-(x-1)^{2}}.
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the triangle bounded between the lines $y=1-x,$ $y=x-1,$ and $x=0?$

- It is a type I region
- It is a type II region
- It's neither a type I nor a type II region
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}y=1-x\, & ⟹\,x=1-y \\ y=x-1\, & ⟹\,x=y+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/27/27503f983e3e02fa748bb8ef32966a6cd3b5fff29082ffaf3c10d0521b630e93.png)

We have the following:

- Any vertical line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,x-1\le y\le 1-x}.
$$

So, this is a type I region.

- Any horizontal line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le 1-|y|}.
$$

So, this is a type II region.

Therefore, only statements I and II are true.

Which of the following statements are true regarding the finite region bounded between the ellipses $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ and $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1?$

- It is a type I region
- It is a type II region
- It's neither a type I nor a type II region
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](images/62/627e7e102a0f16cb0c4946e42b48ad122299d729c5bc419293e258a3f2e1701e.png)

We have the following:

- The vertical line $x=0.25$ intersects the region in two separate intervals, as shown below. So, this can't be a type I region.

![](images/d7/d7aa48c887d6fb1c3d0420867b7e74010fa93e16d7e24317e2cf214764e56113.png)

- The horizontal line $y=0.5$ intersects the region in two separate intervals, as shown below. So, this can't be a type II region.

![](images/ec/ec632fa5f86d8d9b34b9ccf661a3219e965f289c28bf69d7d80eeeb46093e7ae.png)

Therefore, only statement III is true.
