questions.problem:
Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0,$ given that

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,T(0)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨-1,-1,1⟩,\,N(0)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨0,-1,-1⟩.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point $P$, which is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$ The vectors $T(0)$ and $N(0)$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

$$
R(s,u)=r(0)+s\,T(0)+u\,N(0),\,s,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡0-\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡0+\operatorname{sin}⁡0⟩=⟨0,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $(0,1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(0)+s\,T(0)+u\,N(0) \\  & =⟨0,1,1⟩+s\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨-1,-1,1⟩+u\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨0,-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{3},\,1-\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{3}-\frac{u\sqrt{2}}{2},\,1+\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{3}-\frac{u\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0$, given that

$$
r(t)=⟨-2t,\,{t}^{2},\,-{t}^{2}⟩,\,T(0)=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩,\,N(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩
$$

where $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The position vector of the point where $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}p=r(0) & =⟨-2(0),\,{0}^{2},\,{0}^{2}⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(0)$ and the principal normal $N(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\times N(0) & =⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,\,-1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=-\sqrt{2}\cdot (T(0)\times N(0))=⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩ & =⟨0,0,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩ \\ 0\cdot x+1\cdot y+1\cdot z & =0 \\ y+z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for a curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,1,3)$ where $t=0,$ given that

$$
T(0)=i,\,N(0)=j.
$$

First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(0,1,3)$ is $p=⟨0,1,3⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\times N(0) & =i\times j \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our perpendicular vector $n$ is 

$$
n=T(0)\times N(0)=k=⟨0,0,1⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a general point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$

\begin{aligned}T(0)\times N(0) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,0,-1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,0,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨0,-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our perpendicular vector $n$ is 

$$
n=T(0)\times N(0)=⟨0,-1,0⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,-1,0⟩ & =⟨0,2,-1⟩\cdot ⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\ x(0)+y(-1)+z(0) & =0(0)+2(-1)+(-1)(0) \\ 0-y+0 & =0-2+0 \\ y-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=1,$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =6t\,i+2{t}^{3}\,j+3\sqrt{2}{t}^{2}\,k \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}(i+{t}^{2}\,j+\sqrt{2}tk) \\ N(t) & =\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}(-\sqrt{2}t\,i+\sqrt{2}t\,j+(1-{t}^{2})k)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=1$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =\frac{1}{1+1}(i+1\,j+\sqrt{2}k)=\frac{1}{2}(i+j+\sqrt{2}k) \\ N(1) & =\frac{1}{1+1}(-\sqrt{2}\,i+\sqrt{2}\,j+(1-1)k)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point  where $t=1$ is

$$
p=r(1)=6\,i+2\,j+3\sqrt{2}\,k.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(1)$ and the principal normal $N(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(1)\times N(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(i+j+\sqrt{2}k)k\times (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-i+j)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨-\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2},2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨-1,-1,\sqrt{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨6,2,3\sqrt{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{2}⟨-1,-1,\sqrt{2}⟩| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}|-6-2+6| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},-1⟩=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,-1,-1⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},-\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},0⟩=⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
p=r(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,-\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨2,0,-\frac{\pi }{2}⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and the principal normal $N(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2})\times N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,-1,-1⟩\times ⟨-1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(j-k) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨2,0,-\frac{\pi }{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,1,-1⟩| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|0+0+\frac{\pi }{2}| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem:
![](images/19/1990d7cb1625ca97f10debf834883f6e434473f154cf9683db60ee7c4a69c83e.png)

Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $\mathbf r(t)$ at the point where $t=1,$ given that

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle -2t , \: t^2 , \: \dfrac{1}{3}t^3 \right\rangle, \qquad
\mathbf T(1) = \dfrac{1}{3}\left\langle -2 , 2 , 1 \right\rangle, \qquad
\mathbf N(1) = \dfrac{1}{3}\left\langle 2 , 1 , 2\right\rangle.
$$

Note that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point $P,$ which is at the tip of the vector $\mathbf r(1).$ The vectors $\mathbf T(1)$ and $\mathbf N(1)$ are parallel to this plane and are not collinear, so a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

$$
\mathbf R(s,u) = \mathbf r(1) + s \, \mathbf T(1) + u \, \mathbf N(1), \qquad s,u \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

 

Computing $\mathbf r(1),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨-2(1),\,(1)^{2},\,\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}⟩=⟨-2,1,\frac{1}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $\left(-2,1,\dfrac 1 3 \right)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(1)+s\,T(1)+u\,N(1) \\  & =⟨-2,1,\frac{1}{3}⟩+s\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,2,1⟩+u\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,1,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-6-2s+2u,\,3+2s+u,\,1+s+2u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of an Osculating Plane
canonical_examples.problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ at the point where $t=0,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k \\ T(t) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k) \\ N(t) & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡tk).\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane, we need to compute the position vector $\mathbf p$ and a vector $\mathbf n$ that is perpendicular to the osculating plane. 

The position vector of the point where $t=0$ is

$$
\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}(0) = \cos{0}\,\mathbf i+\cos{0}\,\mathbf j+\sqrt{2}\sin{0}\, \mathbf k = \langle 1, 1, 0 \rangle.
$$

To compute the perpendicular vector, we first need to compute the unit tangent $\mathbf T(0)$ and the principal normal $\mathbf N(0)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,k)=k \\ N(0) & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡0k)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the cross product of these two vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =k\times (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the vector above, we can multiply it by a constant to yield a simpler vector that points in the same direction:

$$
\mathbf{n} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt 2}\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left(\mathbf i-\mathbf j\right) =\mathbf i-\mathbf j
$$

Finally, let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ denote the position vector of a general point in the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $\mathbf{p},$ its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,0⟩ & =⟨1,1,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,0⟩ \\ 1\cdot x+(-1)\cdot y+0\cdot z & =0 \\ x-y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/ad/ad22c676123844c2428febb34e0218cfcb05917154e8cff994f35fa4fbf68944.png)

**Note:** Because our curve is a plane curve, it has the same osculating plane at each point. As shown above, the osculating plane coincides with the plane of the curve. 

This result holds in general: any plane curve has the same osculating plane at each of its points (wherever the osculating plane is defined).

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane, we need to compute the position vector $\mathbf p$ and a vector $\mathbf n$ that is perpendicular to the osculating plane. 

The position vector of the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is

$$
\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \left\langle \sin{\left(6\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)} , \:  -\cos{\left(6\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)}, \: 8\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \right\rangle  = \left\langle -1, 0, 2\pi \right\rangle.
$$

To compute the perpendicular vector, we need to compute the unit tangent $\mathbf T \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)$ and the principal normal $\mathbf N \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right) \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,4⟩=\frac{1}{5}⟨0,-3,4⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,0⟩=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the cross product of these two vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(\frac{\pi }{4})\times N(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,-3,4⟩\times ⟨1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\,j+3\,k) \\  & =⟨0,\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the vector above, we can multiply it by a constant to yield a simpler vector that points in the same direction:

$$
\mathbf{n} = 5\cdot \left\langle 0 , \dfrac{4}{5} , \dfrac{3}{5} \right\rangle = \langle 0, 4, 3  \rangle
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖} \\  & =\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖} \\  & =\frac{|⟨-1,0,2\pi ⟩\cdot ⟨0,4,3⟩|}{‖⟨0,4,3⟩‖} \\  & =\frac{6\pi }{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{6\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The function ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is a particular solution of the Riccati differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,y+({cos}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Express this equation in the Bernoulli form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x){z}^{n}
$$

and state the functions $P(x)$ and $Q(x),$ and the value of $n.$

$P(x)=$
{{field-1}}
$,\,Q(x)=$
{{field-2}}
$,\,n=$
{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
A Riccati differential equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x).
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$, we have

$$
y=z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$
{z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x=(z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,(z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+({cos}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =({z}^{2}+2z\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,z-2{cos}^{2}⁡x+({cos}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ {z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={z}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {z}^{′} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This is a Bernoulli equation of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x){z}^{n}
$$

where

$$
P(x)=0,\,Q(x)=1,\,n=2.
$$

$$

find the general solution of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-x\,{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y+1-{x}^{3},
$$

is a Riccati differential equation of the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x),
$$

where

$$
a(x)=-x,\,b(x)=2{x}^{2},\,c(x)=1-{x}^{3}.
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=x.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=1$, we have

$$
y=z+x\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}+1.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$
{z}^{′}+1=-x\,(z+x)^{2}+2{x}^{2}(z+x)+1-{x}^{3}.
$$

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}+1 & =-x({z}^{2}+2xz+{x}^{2})+2{x}^{2}z+2{x}^{3}+1-{x}^{3} \\ {z}^{′}+1 & =-x{z}^{2}+1 \\ {z}^{′} & =-x{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve the obtained equation using separation of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-x{z}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-x \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int -x\,\text{d}x \\ \int {z}^{-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int -x\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{z} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ z & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Finally, let's substitute $z=y-x$ to recover the initial variable $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C} \\ y-x & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C} \\ y & =x+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Riccati Differential Equations
questions.problem:
Given that ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is a particular solution of the Riccati differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,y+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

 

find the general solution of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,y+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x,
$$

is a Riccati differential equation of the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x),
$$

where

$$
a(x)=1,\,b(x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,c(x)={sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$, we have

$$
y=z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$
{z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =({sin}^{2}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,z+{z}^{2})-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,z+2{sin}^{2}⁡x)+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x & ={z}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {z}^{′} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve the obtained equation using separation of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={z}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int {z}^{-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{z} & =x+C \\ z & =-\frac{1}{x+C}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Finally, let's substitute $z=y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ to recover the initial variable $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =-\frac{1}{x+C} \\ y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-\frac{1}{x+C} \\ y & =-\frac{1}{x+C}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{1}{x+C}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=3t-1\,⇒\,t=\frac{x+1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=\frac{x+1}{3}$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$

$$

Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$

$$

The Cartesian equation of this curve is

$y=$
{{field-1}}$,\,x\ge 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{\,t+1\,}\,⇒\,t={x}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t={x}^{2}-1$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =({x}^{2}-1)(4-({x}^{2}-1)) \\  & =({x}^{2}-1)(5-{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=({x}^{2}-1)(5-{x}^{2}).$

Finally, since $t\ge 0$ and $t={x}^{2}-1,$ we must have ${x}^{2}-1\ge 0,$ i.e., $x\ge 1.$

Therefore, the complete Cartesian equation is $y=({x}^{2}-1)(5-{x}^{2}),\,x\ge 1.$

$$
x=\frac{1}{t+1},\,\,\,y=\frac{1}{t-2},\,t\ne -1,\,2.

questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{t+1}\,⇒\,t=\frac{1}{x}-1\end{aligned}

$$

$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\frac{x}{1-3x}.$

Finally, since $t\ne -1,\,2$ and $x=\frac{1}{t+1},$ we must have $x\ne 0,\,\frac{1}{3}.$

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y=\frac{x}{1-3x},\,x\ne 0,\,\frac{1}{3}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Curve Defined Parametrically With Trigonometric Functions
questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\,\,y=\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,t\in (0,\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sec}⁡t=y\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the Pythagorean identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1$ by ${cos}^{2}⁡t$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{{cos}^{2}⁡t}+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t}{{cos}^{2}⁡t} & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\ {(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t})}^{2}+1 & ={(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t})}^{2} \\ {tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{tan}⁡t=\frac{x}{2}$ and $\operatorname{sec}⁡t=y$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}+1={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is ${y}^{2}={(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}+1.$

$$

Using the Pythagorean identity ${csc}^{2}⁡t=1+{cot}^{2}⁡t$, we get

$$

$$

We used here that $\operatorname{csc}⁡t>0$ and $\operatorname{cot}⁡t>0$ in the range $0<t<\frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, solving for $y$, we obtain

$$
y=2\sqrt{\,1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}\,}.
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the given curve is

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\,\,y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this curve is

$y=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t=-\frac{x}{4} \\ y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the double-angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡t=-\frac{x}{4}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{3} & =2{(-\frac{x}{4})}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\frac{2{x}^{2}}{16}-1 \\ y & =3(\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-1) \\ y & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{8}-3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\frac{3{x}^{2}}{8}-3.$

x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\,\,y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).

First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using double angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{3} & =1-2{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2} \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ y & =3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).$

$$
x=2t^2, \,\,\, y=t^2+1, \quad t \geq 0.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t^2\mathbin{:}$

$$
x=2t^2 \quad \Rightarrow\quad  t^2 = \dfrac{x}{2}
$$

Now substituting $t^2=\dfrac{x}{2}$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={t}^{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{x}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x+1.$

Finally, since $t \geq0$ and $x=2t^2,$ we must have $x \geq 0.$

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y=\dfrac{1}{2}x+1, \quad x \geq 0 .
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\csc{t},\,\,\, y=2\cot{t}, \quad 0 < t < \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{csc}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{csc}⁡t=x \\ y=2\operatorname{cot}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cot}⁡t=\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the Pythagorean identity $\sin^{2}{t}+\cos^{2}{t}=1$ by $\sin^{2}{t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t}+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t} & =\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\ 1+{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t})}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t})}^{2} \\ 1+{cot}^{2}⁡t & ={csc}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\csc{t} = x$ and $\cot t =\dfrac{y}{2}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{(\frac{y}{2})}^{2} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ {y}^{2} & =4({x}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y^2 = 4\left( x^2-1 \right).$

Finally, since $0 < t < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\csc t,$ the interval on the $x$-axis is $x \geq 1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Negating a Sentence Containing a Conjunction
questions.problem:
$\,$ $0\le 2$ and $4.3$ is not irrational

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law posits that the negation of a conjunction of two statements is equivalent to the disjunction of the negated individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows.

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(0\le 2\text{ and }4.3\text{ is not irrational}) & ≡¬((0\le 2)∧(4.3\text{ is not irrational})) \\  & ≡¬(0\le 2)∨¬(4.3\text{ is not irrational}) \\  & ≡(0>2)∨(4.3\text{ is irrational}) \\  & ≡(0>2)\text{ or }4.3\text{ is irrational}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
What is the negation of the following compound statement? 

$\qquad$ $6$ is composite and $5\!\not{|} \, 3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law posits that the negation of a conjunction of two statements is equivalent to the disjunction of the negated individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows.

$$
\neg ( A \land B) = \neg A \lor \neg B
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(6\text{ is composite}\text{ and }5\,\text{⧸}|\,3) & ≡¬((6\text{ is composite})∧(5\,\text{⧸}|\,3)) \\  & ≡¬(6\text{ is composite})∨¬(5\,\text{⧸}|\,3) \\  & ≡(6\text{ is not composite})∨(5\,|\,3) \\  & ≡6\text{ is not composite}\text{ or }5\,|\,3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
What is the negation of the following compound statement?

$\qquad$ $3$ is not prime or $\pi$ is not rational.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that the negation of a disjunction of two statements is equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of the individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows:

$$
\neg ( A \lor B) = \neg A \land \neg B.
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(3\text{ is not prime}\text{ or }\pi \text{ is not rational}) & ≡¬((3\text{ is not prime})∨(\pi \text{ is not rational})) \\  & ≡¬(3\text{ is not prime})∧¬(\pi \text{ is not rational}) \\  & ≡(3\text{ is prime})∧(\pi \text{ is rational}) \\  & ≡3\text{ is prime}\text{ and }\pi \text{ is rational}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature Given a General Parametrization
questions.problem: Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(t)=⟨t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $T(t)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the parameter $t.$ Since we are given the curve $r(t)$ parametrized by the parameter $t$ (not the arc length $s$), we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the corresponding unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖=‖{r}^{″}(s)‖
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3s+1}{5}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3-4s}{5})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{5},\,-\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3}{5}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\frac{4}{5})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature Given a General Parametrization
questions.problem:
Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(t)$ given that its derivative ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the corresponding unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t)$ are as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{e}^{t}},\,-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{e}^{t}}⟩,\,{T}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given both the derivative of the curve ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t)$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we find the magnitudes of ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${T}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =1 \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{e}^{t}})}^{2}+{(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{e}^{t}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}{{e}^{2t}}+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}{{e}^{2t}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\cdot \sqrt{2({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{{e}^{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{{e}^{t}})} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{2}⁡(x))(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})-\int (-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{{x}^{3}}\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})-\int (-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+(-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C) \\  & =-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}(2{ln}^{2}⁡(x)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.problem: Calculate the integral $\int (5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. 

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=5{x}^{2}+1\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 5{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(5{x}^{2}+1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(10x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate  $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10(x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D) \\  & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+10\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10D \\  & =(9-5{x}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=10D.$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(x)-\int (x)(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))(x)-\int (x)(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-\int \text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-x+D) \\  & =x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+2x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2D.$ 

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={(x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+2x)|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =(e{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-2e\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)+2e)-(1{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-2\cdot 1\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+2(1)) \\  & =e-2.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we define

\begin{aligned}u=4{x}^{2}+3\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=8x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+3)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8(x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D) \\  & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=8D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={[-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8\operatorname{cos}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(-(4{\pi }^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +8\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +8\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡0+8(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0+8\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =(4{\pi }^{2}+3-8)-(-3+8) \\  & =4{\pi }^{2}-5-5 \\  & =4{\pi }^{2}-10\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=12{x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 12{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=4{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}(4{x}^{3})-\int (4{x}^{3})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x) & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}+\frac{8{x}^{3}}{9}-8D \\  & ={x}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+\frac{8}{9})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-8D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\text{d}x & ={[{x}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+\frac{8}{9})]}_{1/2}^{e/2} \\  & =[{(\frac{e}{2})}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{e}{2}))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{e}{2})+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & \,-[{(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2}))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & =[\frac{{e}^{3}}{8}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\frac{8}{9})]-[\frac{1}{8}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & =[\frac{{e}^{3}}{8}(4-\frac{8}{3}+\frac{8}{9})]-\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{8}{9} \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{3}-2}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a One-Dimensional Subspace
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the orthogonal projection of $f(t)=12({t}^{2}-t)$ onto the subspace spanned by $g(t)=t-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $f(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{g(t)}$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t)=\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),g(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2}+12t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =[3{t}^{4}-8{t}^{3}+6{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(3-8+6)-0 \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),g(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}-2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+t]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1+1)-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the projection is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t) & =\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{3})}\cdot (t-1) \\  & =3(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t],$ the vector space of real polynomials of degree at most $2,$ and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1).
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=t,\,{p}_{2}(t)={t}^{2}-1,\,q(t)={t}^{2}+t
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{p}_{2}(t)}$ equals $0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,q(t)={\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t)=0,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{p}_{1}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)=\frac{⟨q(t),{p}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{p}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨q(t),{p}_{1}(t)⟩ & =q(-1){p}_{1}(-1)+q(0){p}_{1}(0)+q(1){p}_{1}(1) \\  & =({t}^{2}\,+\,t){|}_{-1}\,\,\cdot \,(t){|}_{-1}+({t}^{2}\,+\,t){|}_{0}\,\,\cdot \,(t){|}_{0}+({t}^{2}\,+\,t){|}_{1}\,\,\cdot \,(t){|}_{1} \\  & =0\cdot (-1)+0\cdot 0+2\cdot 1 \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={p}_{1}(-1){p}_{1}(-1)+{p}_{1}(0){p}_{1}(0)+{p}_{1}(1){p}_{1}(1) \\  & =(t)^{2}{|}_{-1}+(t)^{2}{|}_{0}+(t)^{2}{|}_{1} \\  & =(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t) & =\frac{2}{2}\cdot t=t.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally,  

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,q(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t) \\  & =t+0 \\  & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-1,1],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$ 

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=3t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={t}^{2}+1,\,g(t)=10{t}^{3}
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}$ equals $6t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=6t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}10{t}^{3}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}10{t}^{3}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $10{t}^{3}$ is an odd function, while ${t}^{2}+1$ is even. Hence, their product $10{t}^{3}({t}^{2}+1)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-1,1],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}10{t}^{3}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =6t+0 \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{1}[t],$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $1$ with real coefficients. Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1),
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=5t$ and $g(t)=7t-8$ with respect to the inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The distance between $f(t)=5t$ and $g(t)=7t-8$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\  & =‖5t-(7t-8)‖ \\  & =‖-2t+8‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨-2t+8,-2t+8⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-2t+8,-2t+8⟩ & =(-2t+8){|}_{0}\cdot (-2t+8){|}_{0}+(-2t+8){|}_{1}\cdot (-2t+8){|}_{1} \\  & =8\cdot 8+6\cdot 6 \\  & =100.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{100}=10.$

questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t],$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $2$ with real coefficients. Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1),
$$

find the distance between $p(t)=5{t}^{2}-5$ and the subspace spanned by $q(t)=t+1$ with respect to the inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $p(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{q(t)}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t) & =\frac{⟨p(t),q(t)⟩}{⟨q(t),q(t)⟩}\,q(t) \\  & =\frac{p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)}{q(-1)q(-1)+q(0)q(0)+q(1)q(1)}\cdot q(t) \\  & =\frac{{\sum }_{i\in {-1,0,1}}(5{t}^{2}-5){|}_{t=i}\cdot (t+1){|}_{t=i}}{{\sum }_{i\in {-1,0,1}}(t+1){|}_{t=i}\cdot (t+1){|}_{t=i}}\cdot (t+1) \\  & =\frac{0\cdot 0+(-5)\cdot 1+0\cdot 2}{0\cdot 0+1\cdot 1+2\cdot 2}\cdot (t+1) \\  & =\frac{-5}{5}\cdot (t+1) \\  & =-t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The distance between $p(t)=5{t}^{2}-5$ and the subspace spanned by $q(t)=t+1$ with respect to our inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖p(t)-{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t)‖ \\  & =‖5{t}^{2}-5-(-t-1)‖ \\  & =‖5{t}^{2}+t-4‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨5{t}^{2}+t-4,5{t}^{2}+t-4⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨5{t}^{2}+t-4,5{t}^{2}+t-4⟩ & ={\sum }_{i\in {-1,0,1}}(5{t}^{2}+t-4){|}_{t=i}\cdot (5{t}^{2}+t-4){|}_{t=i} \\  & =(0)\cdot (0)+(-4)\cdot (-4)+2\cdot 2 \\  & =0+16+4 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{20}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{1+xy}-1}=\frac{{0}^{2}-0}{\sqrt{1+0\cdot 1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{1+xy}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{({x}^{2}-x)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)}{(\sqrt{1+xy}-1)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{x(x-1)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)}{(\sqrt{1+xy})^{2}-{1}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{x(x-1)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)}{xy} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)}{y} & =\frac{(0-1)(\sqrt{1+0\cdot 1}+1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{-2}{1} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$

$$

$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,-3)}y & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}=\frac{{0}^{2}\cdot 0}{{0}^{3}+{0}^{3}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths. 

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the line $y=2x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=2x}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}+8{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}=\text{DNE}
$$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,-1)}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}-xy} & =\frac{0}{{0}^{2}-0(-1)} \\  & =\frac{0}{0+0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,-1)}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}-xy} & ={lim}_{x\to (0,-1)}\frac{x}{x(x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,-1)}\frac{\cancel{x}}{\cancel{x}(x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,-1)}\frac{1}{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,-1)}\frac{1}{x-y} & =\frac{1}{0-(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{0+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $1.$

$$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/8)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/8}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{8})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{8}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{8}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{8}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{8})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\sqrt{8}\,\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $3$ |

| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of a Given Rank Using Nullity
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -5)^{7},$ the nullity of $(A-5I)^{2}$ equals $1,$ and the nullity of $(A-5I)^{3}$ equals $2.$ If a basis of ${R}^{9}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =5,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(A-5I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-5I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{2}$ has dimension $1.$ This means that the solutions to $(A-5I)^{2}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $1.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{3}$ has dimension $2.$ This means that the solutions to $(A-5I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $2.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{2}$ is a subspace of dimension $1$ in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{3}$, which is a subspace of dimension $2,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{3}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{2}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{3}-\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{2}=2-1=1
$$

 generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5.$

$$
\text{nullity}(D-3I)^{4}=16-9=7.
$$

- Since the rank of $(D-3I)^{5}$ equals $8,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(D-3I)^{5}=16-8=8.
$$

So, the solutions to $(D-3I)^{5}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(D-3I)^{5}$ of dimension $8$ in ${R}^{16}.$

$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
questions.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & a \\ b & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & c & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-5.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
questions.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 11\end{aligned}]}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 11 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}11 & -2 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
questions.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
questions.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 4-2\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Laplace Transform of a Second-Order ODE With Step Function Forcing
questions.problem:
Find the Laplace transform of $y(t),$ if 

$$
{y}^{″}=-4{u}_{2}(t),\,y(0)=1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{2}(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the scalar multiplication property of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}} & =L{-4{u}_{2}(t)} \\ L{{y}^{″}} & =-4L{{u}_{2}(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce $L{y}=Y(s).$ 

To calculate $L{{y}^{″}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a second derivative:

$$
L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}L{y}-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)
$$

Taking into account the given initial conditions, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}Y(s)-s.\end{aligned}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{{u}_{2}(t)}=\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}} & =-4L{{u}_{2}(t)} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s)-s & =-\frac{4{e}^{-2s}}{s} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s) & =s-\frac{4{e}^{-2s}}{s} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-4{e}^{-2s}}{{s}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}L{y}-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)
$$

Taking into account the given initial conditions, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}Y(s)+3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{{u}_{1}(t)}=\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}} & =7L{{u}_{1}(t)} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s)+3 & =\frac{7{e}^{-s}}{s} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s) & =\frac{7{e}^{-s}}{s}-3 \\ Y(s) & =\frac{7{e}^{-s}-3s}{{s}^{3}}.\end{aligned}

Find the Laplace transform of $y(t),$ if 

$$
{y}^{″}+{y}^{′}-2y={u}_{2}(t),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=1,
$$

where ${u}_{2}(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}+{y}^{′}-2y} & =L{{u}_{2}(t)} \\ L{{y}^{″}}+L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =L{{u}_{2}(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce $L{y}=Y(s).$

$$
L{{u}_{3}(t)}=\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s}

questions.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ if

$$
{y}^{″}+9y=5{u}_{4}(t){e}^{3(t-4)},\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{4}(t)=u(t-4)$ is the unit step function.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}+9y} & =L{5{u}_{4}(t){e}^{3(t-4)}} \\ L{{y}^{″}}+9L{y} & =L{5{u}_{4}(t){e}^{3(t-4)}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L{{y}^{″}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a second derivative and the initial conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)
$$

For the right-hand side, we use the second shifting theorem:

$$
L{u(t-a)f(t-a)}={e}^{-as}F(s)
$$

Here, $a=4$ and $f(t-4)=5{e}^{3(t-4)}$, so $f(t)=5{e}^{3t}.$ The transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
F(s)=L{5{e}^{3t}}=\frac{5}{s-3}.
$$

Applying the shift, we get

$$
L{5{u}_{4}(t){e}^{3(t-4)}}={e}^{-4s}\cdot \frac{5}{s-3}=\frac{5{e}^{-4s}}{s-3}.
$$

Substituting these into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)+9Y(s) & =\frac{5{e}^{-4s}}{s-3} \\ ({s}^{2}+9)Y(s) & =\frac{5{e}^{-4s}}{s-3} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{5{e}^{-4s}}{(s-3)({s}^{2}+9)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}+9y} & =L{5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot (t-3)^{2}} \\ L{{y}^{″}}+9L{y} & =L{5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot (t-3)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=3$ and $f(t)=5(t-3)^{2}.$

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)}={e}^{-as}\cdot L{f(t+a)}.

$$
\begin{aligned}L{5u(t-3)\cdot (t-3)^{2}} & ={e}^{-3s}\cdot L{5((t+3)-3)^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{-3s}\cdot L{5{t}^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{-3s}\cdot 5\cdot \frac{2!}{{s}^{2+1}} \\  & =\frac{10{e}^{-3s}}{{s}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Using the transformed equation, we solve for $Y(s)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)+5sY(s)+4Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s} \\ ({s}^{2}+5s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s} \\ (s+1)(s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s} \\ Y(s) & ={e}^{-3s}\cdot \frac{1}{s(s+1)(s+4)}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the inverse transform, we first use partial fraction decomposition on the algebraic part:

$$
\frac{1}{s(s+1)(s+4)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{s+1}+\frac{C}{s+4}
$$

Solving for the constants, we find $A=\frac{1}{4}$, $B=-\frac{1}{3}$, and $C=\frac{1}{12}$, giving:

$$
\frac{1}{s(s+1)(s+4)}=\frac{1}{4s}-\frac{1}{3(s+1)}+\frac{1}{12(s+4)}
$$

 

Now, we apply the inverse Laplace transform. Let 

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{4s}-\frac{1}{3(s+1)}+\frac{1}{12(s+4)},
$$

then, we have 

$$
f(t)=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-t}+\frac{1}{12}{e}^{-4t}.

$$
{L}^{-1}{{e}^{-as}F(s)}={u}_{a}(t)f(t-a).

$$

The solution is $y(t)=u(t-2)\,\cdot \,($
{{field-1}}
$).$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the transformed equation, we solve for $Y(s)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}({s}^{2}+1)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s} \\ Y(s) & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot \frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the inverse transform, we first use partial fraction decomposition on the algebraic part:

$$
\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+1}
$$

Solving for the constants, we find $A=1$, $B=-1$, and $C=0$, giving:

$$
\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+1)}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}
$$

Now, we apply the inverse Laplace transform. Let 

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1},
$$

then, we have 

$$
f(t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

According to the second shifting theorem, 

$$
{L}^{-1}{{e}^{-as}F(s)}={u}_{a}(t)f(t-a).
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{e}^{-2s}(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1})} \\ y(t) & ={u}_{2}(t)(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-2)) \\ y(t) & =u(t-2)(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-2)).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Laplace transform of $y(t),$ if 

$$
y''+ y = u_1(t), \quad y(0)=0, \quad y'(0)=0,
$$

where $u_1(t)=u(t-1)$ is the unit step function.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition property of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}+y} & =L{{u}_{1}(t)} \\ L{{y}^{″}}+L{y} & =L{{u}_{1}(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce $\mathcal{L}\left\{ y \right\}=Y(s).$ 

To calculate $\mathcal L\left\{y''\right\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a second derivative:

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{y'' \right\}   = s^2 \mathcal{L}\{ y \}  - s y(0) - y'(0) =  s^2 Y(s) - s y(0) - y'(0)
$$

Taking into account the given initial conditions, we get

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{y''\right\}  =  s^2 Y(s).
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{ u_1(t) \right\}  = \dfrac{e^{-s}}{s}
$$

Therefore, we can solve for $Y(s)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}}+L{y} & =L{{u}_{1}(t)} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s)+Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s} \\ ({s}^{2}+1)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s({s}^{2}+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s) = \mathcal L\{y(t)\}$ if

$$
y'' + 25y = 6u_2(t)\sin(5(t-2)), \quad y(0)=0, \quad y'(0)=0,
$$

where $u_2(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}+25y} & =L{6{u}_{2}(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5(t-2))} \\ L{{y}^{″}}+25L{y} & =L{6{u}_{2}(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5(t-2))}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $\mathcal L\left\{y'' \right\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a second derivative and the initial conditions $y(0)=0$ and $y'(0)=0$:

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{y'' \right\} = s^2Y(s) - sy(0) - y'(0) = s^2Y(s)
$$

For the right-hand side, we use the second shifting theorem:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)f(t-a)\} = e^{-as}F(s)
$$

Here, $a=2$ and $f(t-2) = 6\sin(5(t-2))$, so $f(t) = 6\sin(5t).$ The transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
F(s) = \mathcal{L}\{6\sin(5t)\} = 6 \cdot \frac{5}{s^2+5^2} = \frac{30}{s^2+25}.
$$

Applying the shift, we get

$$
\mathcal{L}\{6u_2(t)\sin(5(t-2))\} = e^{-2s} \cdot \frac{30}{s^2+25} = \frac{30e^{-2s}}{s^2+25}.
$$

Substituting these into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)+25Y(s) & =\frac{30{e}^{-2s}}{{s}^{2}+25} \\ ({s}^{2}+25)Y(s) & =\frac{30{e}^{-2s}}{{s}^{2}+25} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{30{e}^{-2s}}{({s}^{2}+25)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $F(3)$ where $F(x)={\int }_{1}^{x}(4t-3)\,\text{d}t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Evaluating $F(x)$ at $x=3,$ we get the following definite integral:

$$
F\,(3)={\int }_{1}^{3}(4t-3)\,\text{d}t
$$

Then, computing the definite integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(3) & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(4t-3)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(2{t}^{2}-3t)\,{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =(2\cdot {3}^{2}-3\cdot 3)-(2\cdot {1}^{2}-3\cdot 1) \\  & =(18-9)-(2-3) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of a function $y=f(x)$ is shown above. It consists of two lines and the arc of a quarter-circle of radius $2.$ Given $g(t)={\int }_{-2}^{t}f(x)\,\text{d}x,$ determine the value of $g(3).$
questions.worked_solution:
Evaluating $g(t)$ at $t=3,$ we get the following definite integral:

$$
g(3)={\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral gives the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis shown below.

![](images/92/923b60ed63551bda207f7e3eeb09e62f8b8eb7465a488858bef54bc36ab20baa.png)

Note that the graph above consists of $2$ parts:

- $x\in [-2,1],$ for which the region between the curve and the $x$-axis is a rectangle. This corresponds to the area ${A}_{1}.$

- $x\in [1,3],$ for which the region between the curve and the $x$-axis is a quarter-circle. This corresponds to the area ${A}_{2}.$

Therefore, we can write the integral as follows:

$$
g(3)={\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}
$$

Now, let's compute these integrals:

- To find the first integral where $x\in [-2,1],$ we compute the area ${A}_{1}$ of the rectangle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =bh \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

- To find the second integral where $x\in [1,3],$ we compute the area ${A}_{2}$ of the quarter-circle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{4}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\pi \cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}g(3)={\int }_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=6+\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The total charge, in coulombs, stored in a device $t$ seconds after charging begins increases at a rate of $\frac{40}{(t+1)^{3}}.$ If, at $t=0$ seconds, the device already stored $7$ coulombs of charge, how much charge will the device store after $1$ second?

After $1$ second, the device stores
{{field-1}} coulombs of charge.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $a(t)=\frac{40}{(t+1)^{3}}$ be the rate at which the amount of charge stored is changing and let $A(T)$ be the amount of charge stored $T$ seconds after charging begins. 

Using our formula for the accumulation of change, we have

$$
A(T)=A(0)+{\int }_{0}^{T}a(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Substituting the known information and carrying out the necessary integration gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A(T) & =A(0)+{\int }_{0}^{T}a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =7+{\int }_{0}^{T}\frac{40}{(t+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =7+(-\frac{20}{(t+1)^{2}}){|}_{0}^{T} \\  & =7+(-\frac{20}{(T+1)^{2}})-(-\frac{20}{{1}^{2}}) \\  & =7-\frac{20}{(T+1)^{2}}+20 \\  & =27-\frac{20}{(T+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the amount of charge stored $T=1$ second after charging begins, we substitute in the above:

$$
A(1)=7-\frac{20}{(1+1)^{2}}+20=22.
$$

Thus, after $1$ second, the device stores $22$ coulombs of charge.

questions.problem:
A man starts a business, stocking a pond with $100$ catfish. After $t$ weeks, the birth and death rates of catfish in the pond are given by the functions $45+5t$ and $1+t,$ respectively.

Given that the rate at which catfish are sold is $30$ per week, identify the expression that gives the number $C(t)$ of catfish in the pond at any time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $c(t)$ be the rate at which the number of catfish in the pond is changing. Then according to the given information,

$$
c(t)={{45+5t}_{⏟}}_{\text{population increase}}-{{(1+t+30)}_{⏟}}_{\text{population decrease}}=4t+14.
$$

Let $C(T)$ be the population of the pond $T$ weeks after the man started the business.  Using our formula for the accumulation of change, we have

$$
C(T)=C(0)+{\int }_{0}^{T}c(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Substituting the known information and carrying out the necessary integration gives

$$
\begin{aligned}C(T) & =C(0)+{\int }_{0}^{T}c(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =100+{\int }_{0}^{T}(4t+14)\,\text{d}t \\  & =100+(2{t}^{2}+14t){|}_{0}^{T} \\  & =100+2{T}^{2}+14T.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's rewrite our final answer in terms of the original variable $t.$ We have

$$
C(t)=100+2{t}^{2}+14t.
$$

questions.problem: Cars are entering a traffic jam at a rate of $7t$ cars per minute. If at time $t=0$ there are $60$ cars in the traffic jam, write an expression for $A(t),$ the total number of cars caught up in the traffic jam at time $t,$ where $t$ is the time measured in minutes.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(t)=7t$ be the rate at which the cars enter the traffic jam, and let $A(T)$ be the total number of cars in the traffic jam after $T$ minutes.

Using our formula for the accumulation of change, we have

$$
A(T)=A(0)+{\int }_{0}^{T}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Substituting the known information and carrying out the necessary integration gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A(T) & =A(0)+{\int }_{0}^{T}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =60+{\int }_{0}^{T}7t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={60+(\frac{7{t}^{2}}{2})|}_{0}^{T} \\  & =60+\frac{7{T}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's rewrite our final answer in terms of the original variable $t.$ We have

$$
A(t)=60+\frac{7{t}^{2}}{2}.
$$
