$$
\begin{aligned}10({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+7\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (10{\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +7\lambda -1){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (10{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -1){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }. & \end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(10{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -1){a}_{0} & =0 \\ 10{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (2\lambda -1)(5\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-\frac{1}{5},\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Let $\displaystyle y = x^\lambda \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n$ be a Frobenius series solution about the regular singular point $x=0$ of the differential equation above.

$$

Now, we continue from this point.

**Step 1**: Consolidate all the series into a single series that is equal to $0.$

Collecting the terms for ${\color{blue}n=0},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+6\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-2{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (4{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +6\lambda -2){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ 2(2{\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -1){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }. & \end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, collecting terms for $n\geq 1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[4((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n))+3(\lambda +n-1){a}_{n-1}+6(\lambda +n){a}_{n}-2{a}_{n}]{x}^{\lambda +n} & = \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[4(\lambda +n)^{2}+2(\lambda +n){a}_{n}-2{a}_{n}+3(\lambda +n-1){a}_{n-1}]{x}^{\lambda +n} & = \\ 2{x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[(2(\lambda +n)^{2}+(\lambda +n)-1){a}_{n}+\frac{3}{2}(\lambda +n-1){a}_{n-1}]{x}^{n} & .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Similarly, setting the coefficients of $x^n$ for $n\geq1$ equal to $0,$ we obtain the following recurrence relation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2(\lambda +n)^{2}+(\lambda +n)-1){a}_{n}+\frac{3}{2}(\lambda +n-1){a}_{n-1} & =0 \\ ((\lambda +n)+1)(2(\lambda +n)-1){a}_{n} & =-\frac{3}{2}(\lambda +n-1){a}_{n-1}\end{aligned}

Substituting $\lambda=\dfrac12$ and solving for $a_n,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}((\frac{1}{2}+n)+1)(2(\frac{1}{2}+n)-1){a}_{n} & =-\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{2}+n-1){a}_{n-1} \\ (n+\frac{3}{2})(2n){a}_{n} & =-\frac{3}{2}(n-\frac{1}{2}){a}_{n-1} \\ n(2n+3){a}_{n} & =\frac{3}{4}(1-2n){a}_{n-1} \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{3(1-2n)}{4n(2n+3)}\,{a}_{n-1}.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Projection Matrix That Orthogonally Projects a Vector to the Subspace Spanned by an Eigenvector
questions.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{10}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(5\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(5\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}-40 & 30 \\ 30 & 40\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Proving Divisibility of Exponential Expressions
questions.problem: Use mathematical induction to prove that ${4}^{2n}-{10}^{n}$ is divisible by $6$ for all $n\in N.$
questions.worked_solution:
The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P(1),P(2),P(6),…,$ where

- $P(1)$ is true, and

- $P(k)⇒P(k+1)$ for every $k\in N.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every $n\in N.$

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

$P(n):\,6\,∣\,{4}^{2n}-{10}^{n}$ for all $n\in N$

We start by proving the base case, $P(1).$ To do this, we substitute $n=1$ into the expression and show it is divisible by $6:$

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove that our statement is true for the base case $n=1.$ Substituting $n=1$ into the expression ${4}^{2n}-{10}^{n},$ we have

$$
P(1):\,{4}^{2(1)}-{10}^{1}=6,\,\text{and}\,6\,∣\,6.
$$

Thus, our statement is true for $n=1.$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n=k\ge 1.$

Due to the base case, we already know that the statement is true for some value of $k,$ namely $k=1,$ so this assumption is valid.

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=k\ge 1,$ we have that

$$
P(k):\,6\,∣\,{4}^{2k}-{10}^{k}.
$$

We must show that $P(k)⇒P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the **inductive step**.

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
P(k+1):\,6\,∣\,{4}^{2(k+1)}-{10}^{k+1}.\,\,(∗)
$$

The idea is to rewrite the expression ${4}^{2(k+1)}-{10}^{k+1}$ as ${4}^{2k}-{10}^{k}$ (taken from the inductive hypothesis) plus a multiple of $6.$ We do this as follows:

We write

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{2(k+1)}-{10}^{k+1} & ={4}^{2k}\cdot {4}^{2}-{10}^{k}\cdot 10 \\  & =16({4}^{2k})-10({10}^{k}) \\  & =(6+10)({4}^{2k})-10({10}^{k}) \\  & =6({4}^{2k})+10({4}^{2k})-10({10}^{k}) \\  & =6({4}^{2k})+10({4}^{2k}-{10}^{k})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $6\,∣\,({4}^{2k}-{10}^{k})$ by the inductive hypothesis, and $6({4}^{2k})$ is clearly divisible by $6,$ their sum is also divisible by $6,$ as required.

Since we have shown that the expression in $(∗)$ is divisible by $6,$ our proof is complete. So, let's write down our conclusion.

Therefore, by the principle of induction, $6\,∣\,{4}^{2n}-{10}^{n}$ for all $n\in N.$

questions.knowledge_point: Arithmetic Modulo N
questions.problem:
Compute the result of the following operations on elements of ${Z}_{8}.$ Use the smallest nonnegative representative for the resulting class.

$[\,10\,]\cdot ([\,3\,]-[\,6\,])=[$
{{field-1}}
$]$
questions.worked_solution:
Addition, subtraction, and multiplication of integers in ${Z}_{n}$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,a\,]\pm [\,b\,] & =[\,a\pm b\,] \\ [\,a\,]\cdot [\,b\,] & =[\,a\cdot b\,]\end{aligned}
$$

Also, recall that we can pick any element of an equivalence class as its representative. 

In this case, all operations are carried out modulo $8.$

With that in mind, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,10\,]\cdot ([\,3\,]-[\,6\,]) & =[\,10\,]\cdot [\,3-6\,] \\  & =[\,10\,]\cdot [\,-3\,] \\  & =[\,10\,]\cdot [\,0-3\,] \\  & =[\,10\,]\cdot [\,8-3\,] \\  & =[\,10\,]\cdot [\,5\,] \\  & =[\,8+2\,]\cdot [\,5\,] \\  & =[\,0+2\,]\cdot [\,5\,] \\  & =[\,2\,]\cdot [\,5\,] \\  & =[\,2\cdot 5\,] \\  & =[\,10\,] \\  & =[\,8+2\,] \\  & =[\,2\,]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Proving the Parity of a Nonlinear Expression
questions.problem: Prove that ${n}^{2}-2$ is odd provided that $n$ is odd.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
n\text{ is odd}\,⇒\,{n}^{2}-2\text{ is odd}
$$

We start by using the fact that $n$ is odd.

Since $n$ is odd, it can be expressed as $n=2a+1$ for some integer $a.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a+1$ into our expression ${n}^{2}-2$ and show it is odd by writing it as a multiple of $2,$ plus $1.$

Now, writing ${n}^{2}-2$ in terms of $a,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}-2 & =(2a+1)^{2}-2 \\  & =(4{a}^{2}+4a+1)-2 \\  & =4{a}^{2}+4a-1 \\  & =(4{a}^{2}+4a-2)+1 \\  & =2{{(2{a}^{2}+2a-1)}_{⏟}}_{b}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we define another integer $b=2{a}^{2}+2a-1$ (highlighted above), we have that ${n}^{2}-2=2b+1,$ which shows that ${n}^{2}-2$ is indeed one more than a multiple of $2.$

Let $b=2{a}^{2}+2a-1.$ Since $a$ is an integer, we have that $b$ is an integer.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}-2 & =2{{(2{a}^{2}+2a-1)}_{⏟}}_{b}+1 \\  & =2b+1\end{aligned}
$$

which is  one more than  a multiple of $2.$ 

Finally, we write our conclusion.

Therefore, ${n}^{2}-2$ is odd.

questions.knowledge_point: Proving Parity Statements by Cases
questions.problem: Let $m$ and $n$ be integers. Prove that $g(m,n)=(m-1)(n+4)$ is odd only if $m$ is even and $n$ is odd.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
g(m,n)\text{ is odd}\,⇒\,m\text{ is even and }n\text{ is odd}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$

$$
¬(m\text{ is even and }n\text{ is odd})⇒¬(g(m,n)\text{ is odd})
$$

Negating the right-hand-side of our implication is straightforward:

$$
¬(m\text{ is even and }n\text{ is odd})⇒g(m,n)\text{ is even}
$$

To negate the statement "$m$ is even and $n$ is odd", we use De Morgan's law for conjunctions:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(m\text{ is even and}n\text{ is odd}) & =¬(m\text{ is even}∧n\text{ is odd}) \\  & =¬(m\text{ is even})∨¬(n\text{ is odd}) \\  & =m\text{ is odd}∨n\text{ is even} \\  & =m\text{ is odd or }n\text{ is even}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's write down the contrapositive of our statement.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:

$$
m\text{ is odd or }n\text{ is even}\,⇒\,g(m,n)\text{ is even}
$$

We'll prove this statement instead of the original one.

Now, we have two cases: $m$ is odd, or $n$ is even.

- First, we consider the case when $m$ is odd.

**Case 1**. If $m$ is odd, then $m=2a+1$ for some integer $a.$

As a result, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}g(m,n) & =(m-1)(n+4) \\  & =(2a+1-1)(n+4) \\  & =(2a)(n+4) \\  & =2{{a(n+4)}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $b=a(n+4).$ Since $a$ and $n$ are integers, we have that $b$ is an integer.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(m,n) & =2{{a(n+4)}_{⏟}}_{b} \\  & =2b,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a multiple of $2.$ Hence, $g(m,n)$ is even.

- Now, we consider the case when $n$ is odd.

**Case 2**. If $n$ is even, then $n=2a$ for some integer $a.$

As a result, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}g(m,n) & =(m-1)(n+4) \\  & =(m-1)(2a+4) \\  & =2{{(m-1)(a+2)}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $b=(m-1)(a+2).$ Since $a$ and $m$ are integers, we have that $b$ is an integer.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(m,n) & =2{{(m-1)(a+2)}_{⏟}}_{b} \\  & =2b,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a multiple of $2.$ Hence, $g(m,n)$ is even.

Finally, we write our conclusion.

Therefore, combining the cases above, we conclude that $g(m,n)$ is odd only if $m$ is even and $n$ is odd.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About the Chinese Remainder Theorem
questions.problem:
According to the Chinese remainder theorem, which of the following systems of congruences has a unique solution modulo $48?$ 

$$
\text{I.}\,{\begin{aligned}x≡4 & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x≡5 & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}\,\text{II.}\,{\begin{aligned}x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,3) \\ x≡14 & (\text{mod}\,16)\end{aligned}\,\text{III.}\,{\begin{aligned}x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,4) \\ x≡7 & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}\,
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The Chinese remainder theorem states that if the natural numbers ${n}_{1},{n}_{2},…,{n}_{k}$ are pairwise coprime, meaning that $\text{gcd}({n}_{i},{n}_{j})=1$ whenever $i\ne j,$ then for any integers ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},…,{a}_{k}$ the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}x≡{a}_{1} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{1}) \\ x≡{a}_{2} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{2}) \\ \,⋮ \\ x≡{a}_{k} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{k})\end{aligned}
$$

has a unique solution modulo ${n}_{1}{n}_{2}⋯{n}_{k}.$

Let's now inspect each of the given systems in turn.

- The theorem does *not* apply to system I since $6$ and $8$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(6,8)=2>1
$$

- The theorem applies to system II. The numbers $3,$ and $16$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $3\cdot 16=48.$

- The theorem does *not* apply to system III since $4$ and $12$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(4,12)=4>1
$$

So, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Given that $|R\times R|=c,$ complete the following reasoning about the cardinality of the set $R\times [-5,6):$

Since the function $f:(x,y)\to (x,y)$ (that maps any ordered pair to itself) is an injection from $R\times [-5,6)$ into $R\times R,$ and 

$$
g:(x,y)\to (x,{{field-1}}{{field-2}})
$$

is an injection from $R\times R$ onto $R\times (-5,5)⊆R\times [-5,6),$ according to Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem, we have that 
$|R\times [-5,6)|=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
According to the Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem, if $|A|\le |B|$ and $|B|\le |A|,$ then $|A|=|B|.$ 

In other words, if there exist injections $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to A,$ then there exists a bijection between $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, we note the following:

- The function $f:(x,y)\to (x,y)$ (that maps any ordered pair to itself) is an injection from $R\times [-5,6)$ into $R\times R.$ So, we have 

$$
|R\times [-5,6)|\le |R\times R|.
$$

- On the other hand, the function

$$
x\to x
$$

injectively maps $R\to R,$ and 

$$
y\to \frac{10}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(y)
$$

injectively maps $R$ onto $(-5,5)⊆[-5,6).$ Thus,

$$
g:(x,y)\to (x,\frac{10}{\pi }\,\operatorname{arctan}⁡(y))
$$

is an injection from $R\times R$ onto $R\times (-5,5)⊆R\times [-5,6),$ as shown below. 

![](images/af/af4472ba9056eaf9c62c7dca99de4904339aff6dbf0de8d1225bc41b0fde9c00.png)

So, we have

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Proving De Morgan's Law Using Biconditionals
questions.problem:
Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Prove that 

$$
\overset{―}{A\cup B}=\overset{―}{A}\cap \overset{―}{B}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To prove a set equality using biconditionals, we must show an element belongs to one set if and only if it belongs to the other.

In this case, we're required to prove De Morgan's Law for disjunctions:

$$
\overset{―}{A\cup B}=\overset{―}{A}\cap \overset{―}{B}
$$

Since we're proving this statement using a sequence of biconditionals, we begin our proof as follows:

For any element $x,$ the sequence of logical equivalences unfolds as follows:

First, we assume $x\in \overset{―}{A\cup B}$ and apply the definition of the set complement:

To belong to $\overset{―}{A\cup B}$ is synonymous with not belonging to $A\cup B:$

$$
x\in \overset{―}{A\cup B}\,⇔\,x\notin A\cup B
$$

Next, we apply the definition of negation and the definition of union:

Not being a member of the union $A\cup B$ is equivalent to not satisfying the conditions $x\in A$ or $x\in B$ individually: 

$$
x\notin A\cup B\,⇔\,¬(x\in A∨x\in B)
$$

Next, we apply De Morgan's law for disjunctions: $¬(P∨Q)≡¬P∧¬Q:$

The negation of the conditions individually is the same as the conjunction of their negations by De Morgan's Law for disjunction:

$$
¬(x\in A∨x\in B)\,⇔\,¬(x\in A)∧¬(x\in B)
$$

Applying the definition of negation gives:

The conjunction of the negations corresponds to not belonging to $A$ and not belonging to $B:$

$$
¬(x\in A)∧¬(x\in B)\,⇔\,(x\notin A)∧(x\notin B)
$$

Finally, applying the definition of the set complement and intersection gives:

Consequently, the combined condition is satisfied if and only if $x$ belongs to the intersections of the complements, sets:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x\notin A)∧(x\notin B)\, & ⇔\,(x\in \overset{―}{A})∧(x\in \overset{―}{B}) \\  & ⇔\,x\in \overset{―}{A}\cap \overset{―}{B}\end{aligned}
$$

Following the sequence of equivalent statements, we've shown that an element belongs to one set if and only if it belongs to the other. Thus, our proof is complete, and we write down our conclusion.

Thus, it follows that for any element $x,$ membership in $\overset{―}{A\cup B}$ is equivalent to membership in $\overset{―}{A}\cap \overset{―}{B},$ leading to the conclusion:

$$
\overset{―}{A\cup B}=\overset{―}{A}\cap \overset{―}{B}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Proving an Equivalence Involving Divisibility and Congruences
questions.problem:
Let $n$ be an integer. Prove that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,10)$ if and only if $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,2)$ and $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,5).$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:* 

$$
2\cdot (-2)+5\cdot 1=\text{gcd}(2,5)=1
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The connector "if and only if" means we must prove an equivalence. 

$$
P⇔Q
$$

However, instead of proving an equivalence directly, we can instead prove two conditional statements. 

$$
P⇔Q≡(P⇒Q)∧(Q⇒P)
$$

So, we start our proof as follows:

We need to show  the following:

$$
a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,10)\,⇔\,(a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,2)\,∧\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,5))
$$

This is the same as proving two implications.

First, we consider the "left to right" implication.

** Case $⇒:$** We need to show that 

$$
a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,10)\,⇒\,(a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,2)\,∧\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,5)).
$$

To do that, we first write the statement in terms of divisibility. 

Or, in terms of divisibility,

$$
10∣a-b\,⇒\,(2∣a-b\,∧\,5∣a-b).
$$

Then, we write $n=a-b$ to simplify the notation. 

Let's denote $n=a-b.$

So, we now need to prove that 

$$
10∣n\,⇒\,(2∣n\,∧\,5∣n).
$$

We proceed as follows:

If $10∣n,$ then $n=10k$ for some integer $k.$ We can rewrite this equation as

$$
n=2(5k),
$$

which means that $2∣n.$ Also, we can write

$$
n=5(2k),
$$

which means that $5∣n.$ Therefore, $2∣n$ and $5∣n.$

Next, we consider the "right to left" implication.

**Case $⇐:$** We need to show that

$$
(a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,2)\,∧\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,5))\,⇒\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,10).
$$

Or, in terms of divisibility,

$$
(2∣a-b\,∧\,5∣a-b)\,⇒\,10∣a-b.
$$

Again, we simplify the notation by introducing $n=a-b.$ 

Let's again denote $n=a-b.$

So now, we need to prove

$$
(2∣n\,∧\,5∣n)\,⇒\,10∣n.
$$

Next, we use the definition of divisibility.

Since $2∣n,$ then $n=2s$ for some integer $s,$ and since $5∣n,$ then $n=5t$ for some integer $t.$

Notice that the divisibility of $n$ by $2$ and $5$ are independent. So, in general, we should use different letters ($s$ and $t$) in the reasoning above. 

Next, we'll use the fact that our divisors are coprime.

The integers $2$ and $5$ are coprime and $2\cdot (-2)+5\cdot 1=1.$ So, multiplying this equation by $n,$ we get

$$
2\cdot (-2n)+5\cdot n=n.
$$

Now, substituting $n=5t$ into the first term on the left-hand side and $n=2s$ into the second term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot (-2(5t))+5\cdot (2s)=n \\ 10\cdot (-2t)+10\cdot (s)=n \\ 10\cdot (-2t+s)=n,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $10∣n.$ So, the second implication is proved.

Finally, we write down the conclusion:

Therefore, $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,10)$ if and only if $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,2)$ and $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,5).$

questions.knowledge_point: Proving a Function is Injective
questions.problem: Prove that the function $f:C\times C\to C\times C$ defined by $f(z,w)=(\overset{―}{z-w},z\text{i}+w)$ is injective.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the definition of an injection:

A function $f:X\to Y$ is an injection if every element $x\in X$ is mapped to a distinct element in $Y:$

$$
{x}_{1}\ne {x}_{2}\,⇒\,f({x}_{1})\ne f({x}_{2})
$$

In this case, it would be easier to prove the contrapositive statement. 

This implication is equivalent to its contrapositive:

$$
f({x}_{1})=f({x}_{2})\,⇒\,{x}_{1}={x}_{2}
$$

Now, we simply need to derive ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}$ by assuming that $f({x}_{1})=f({x}_{2}),$ where ${x}_{1}=({z}_{1},{w}_{1})$ and ${x}_{2}=({z}_{2},{w}_{2}):$

So, let $({z}_{1},{w}_{1}),({z}_{2},{w}_{2})\in C\times C,$ and suppose that $f({z}_{1},{w}_{1})=f({z}_{2},{w}_{2}).$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({z}_{1},{w}_{1}) & =f({z}_{2},{w}_{2}) \\ (\overset{―}{{z}_{1}-{w}_{1}},{z}_{1}\text{i}+{w}_{1}) & =(\overset{―}{{z}_{2}-{w}_{2}},{z}_{2}\text{i}+{w}_{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Since two pairs are equal if and only if their respective components are equal, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{{z}_{1}-{w}_{1}}=\overset{―}{{z}_{2}-{w}_{2}} \\ {z}_{1}\text{i}+{w}_{1}={z}_{2}\text{i}+{w}_{2}\end{aligned} & \,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}-{w}_{1}={z}_{2}-{w}_{2} \\ {z}_{1}\text{i}+{w}_{1}={z}_{2}\text{i}+{w}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & \,⇒\,{z}_{1}+{z}_{1}\text{i}={z}_{2}+{z}_{2}\text{i} \\  & \,⇒\,{z}_{1}(1+\text{i})={z}_{2}(1+\text{i}) \\  & \,⇒\,{z}_{1}={z}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}\text{i}+{w}_{1} & ={z}_{1}\text{i}+{w}_{2} \\ {w}_{1} & ={w}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we state the conclusion:

Hence, $({z}_{1},{w}_{1})=({z}_{2},{w}_{2}),$ as was to be shown. Therefore, $f$ is an injection.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Functional Relations
questions.problem:
Which of the following relations are functional?

- $x\,R\,y$ if and only if $x={y}^{2},$ defined on $R$

- $x\,S\,y$ if and only if $x{y}^{3}=1,$ defined on ${R}^{+}$

- $x\,T\,y$ if and only if $y∣2x,$ defined on $Z$
questions.worked_solution:
A binary relation $R$ defined over $A$ and $B$ is *functional* (or a *partial function*) if, for all $a\in A$ and ${b}_{1},{b}_{2}\in B,$ we have 

$$
(a,{b}_{1})\in R\,\text{and}\,(a,{b}_{2})\in R\,⇒\,{b}_{1}={b}_{2}.
$$

In other words, if the first components of two ordered pairs are equal, then the second components must also be equal.

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

- $R$ is *not* functional. Notice that $1={1}^{2}$ and $1=(-1)^{2}.$ So, $R$ contains pairs $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ with the same first component but different second components.

- $S$ is functional. Indeed, $a{b}_{1}^{3}=1$ and $a{b}_{2}^{3}=1$ is equivalent to ${b}_{1}={b}_{2}$ over ${R}^{+}.$ So, when the first components of two pairs are equal, then the second components are also equal.

- $T$ is *not* functional. Notice that $2∣2(3)$ and $3∣2(3).$ So, $T$ contains pairs $(3,2)$ and $(3,3)$ with the same first component but different second components.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$S$ only."

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Linear Diophantine Equation
questions.problem: Consider the Diophantine equation $7x+9y=11.$ The integer pair $(\overset{∼}{x},\overset{∼}{y})$ is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of $x.$ What is the value of $\overset{∼}{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We have the linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

where $a=7,$ $b=9,$ and $c=11.$ We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of $\text{gcd}(7,9)$ using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}9 & = & 7\cdot 1 & + & 2 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 7 & = & 2\cdot 3 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =9-7 \\ 1 & =7-2\cdot 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =7-2\cdot 3 \\  & =7-3(9-7) \\  & =7\cdot 4+(-3)\cdot 9.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that $d=\text{gcd}(a,b)=1$ and

$$
7\cdot 4+9\cdot (-3)=1.
$$

Multiplying this equation by $11,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}7\cdot 4+9\cdot (-3) & =1 \\ 7\cdot 4\cdot 11+9\cdot (-3)\cdot 11 & =11 \\ 7\cdot 44+9\cdot (-33) & =11,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $(x,y)=(44,-33)$ is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

$$
(44+\frac{b}{d}t,\,-33-\frac{a}{d}t)=(44+9t,\,-33-7t),
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$

The smallest possible positive value of $x=44+9t$ is attained when $t=-4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{∼}{x}=44+9\cdot (-4)=8.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Linear Diophantine Equation
questions.problem: Consider the Diophantine equation $7x+3y=5.$ The integer pair $(\overset{∼}{x},\overset{∼}{y})$ is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of $y.$ What is the value of $\overset{∼}{y}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We have the linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

where $a=7,$ $b=3,$ and $c=5.$ We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of $\text{gcd}(7,3)$ using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}7 & = & 3\cdot 2 & + & 1 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 3 & = & 1\cdot 3 & + & 0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =7-3\cdot 2.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that $d=\text{gcd}(a,b)=1$ and

$$
7+3\cdot (-2)=1.
$$

Multiplying this equation by $5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}7+3\cdot (-2) & =1 \\ 7\cdot 5+3\cdot (-2)\cdot 5 & =5 \\ 7\cdot 5+3\cdot (-10) & =5,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $(x,y)=(5,-10)$ is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

$$
(5+\frac{b}{d}t,\,-10-\frac{a}{d}t)=(5+3t,\,-10-7t),
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$

The smallest possible positive value of $y=-10-7t$ is attained when $t=-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{∼}{y}=-10-7\cdot (-2)=4.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Proving the Limit of a Sequence
questions.problem:
Using the formal definition of a limit, prove that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1-{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}-7}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1-{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}-7}=-\frac{1}{3}
$$

means that

$$
∀ε>0,\,∃N\in N,∀n\in N,\,n\ge N\,⇒\,|\frac{1-{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}-7}-(-\frac{1}{3})|<ε.
$$

Let's write this in words.

We need to show that for any real $ε>0,$ there exists a natural number $N$ such that, for every natural number $n\ge N,$ we have

$$
|\frac{1-{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}-7}-(-\frac{1}{3})|<ε.
$$

Before we start the proof, we would like to figure out how $N$ may depend on $ε.$

First, simplifying $|{a}_{n}-L|,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|{a}_{n}-L| & =|\frac{1-{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}-7}-(-\frac{1}{3})| \\  & =|\frac{1-{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}-7}+\frac{1}{3}| \\  & =|\frac{3(1-{n}^{2})}{3(3{n}^{2}-7)}+\frac{3{n}^{2}-7}{3(3{n}^{2}-7)}| \\  & =|\frac{3-3{n}^{2}+3{n}^{2}-7}{3(3{n}^{2}-7)}| \\  & =|-\frac{4}{9{n}^{2}-21}| \\  & =|\frac{4}{9{n}^{2}-21}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\frac{4}{9{n}^{2}-21}>0$ for any natural $n\ge 2.$ With that in mind, we have

$$
|{a}_{n}-L|=|\frac{4}{9{n}^{2}-21}|=\frac{4}{9{n}^{2}-21}.
$$

Now, we solve the inequality $|{a}_{n}-L|<ε$ for $n\ge 2:$

Solving this inequality for $n,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9{n}^{2}-21} & <ε \\ 4 & <ε(9{n}^{2}-21) \\ \frac{4}{ε} & <9{n}^{2}-21 \\ \frac{4}{ε}+21 & <9{n}^{2} \\ \frac{4}{9ε}+\frac{7}{3} & <{n}^{2} \\ n & >\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}+\frac{4}{9ε}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, if we want $|\frac{1-{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}-7}-(-\frac{1}{3})|<ε,$ it's sufficient to take all values of $n$ that are larger than $\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}+\frac{4}{9ε}}.$

We can now continue the proof:

Therefore, we choose $N>\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}+\frac{4}{9ε}}.$

Notice that, since $\frac{4}{9ε}>0,$ then $\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}+\frac{4}{9ε}}>\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}≈1.53$ and therefore $N\ge 2.$

With that in mind, we'll find the upper bound for the absolute value of the sequence's $n$th term:

Then, for any natural number $n\ge N,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\frac{1-{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}-7}-(-\frac{1}{3})| & =\frac{4}{9{n}^{2}-21} \\  & <\frac{4}{9{(\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}+\frac{4}{9ε}})}^{2}-21} \\  & =\frac{4}{(21+\frac{4}{ε}-21)} \\  & =ε.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make the conclusion:

Therefore, according to the definition, ${lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1-{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}-7}=-\frac{1}{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Prenex Normal Form When the Predicates Have Common Variables
questions.problem:
$\,$ $∃n\in N\,(\sqrt{n}\notin N)⇒∀n\in N\,(n∣2).$

Re-write the above statement by moving all the quantifiers to the front of the expression.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote:

- $P(n):\,\sqrt{n}\notin N$

- $Q(n):\,n∣2$

Then, our statement can be written as

$$
∃n\,P(n)⇒∀n\,Q(n).
$$

By eliminating implication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∃n\,P(n)⇒∀n\,Q(n) & ≡¬(∃n\,P(n))∨∀n\,Q(n) \\  & ≡∀n\,¬P(n)∨∀n\,Q(n)\end{aligned}
$$

We can't "factor out" the quantifier since, in general, 

$$
∀n\,P(n)∨∀n\,Q(n)≢∀n\,(P(n)∨Q(n)).
$$

However, we can change the variable in one of the predicates. For example, in the second one:

$$
∀n\,P(n)∨∀n\,Q(n)≡∀n\,P(n)∨∀m\,Q(m)
$$

Now, since $P(n)$ does not depend on $m$ and $Q(m)$ does not depend on $n,$ we can move the quantifiers to the front, as follows:

$$
∀n\,¬P(n)∨∀m\,Q(m)≡∀n\,∀m\,(¬P(n)∨Q(m))
$$

The final expression reads 

$\,$ $∀n,m\in N\,(\sqrt{n}\in N∨m∣2).$

questions.knowledge_point: Combining Inference Rules in Symbolic Form
questions.problem:
Complete the following proof: 

$$
\begin{aligned}¬Z \\ (X∨Y)⇒Z \\ ∴\,{{field-1}} \\ ¬(X∨Y)⇒¬W \\ ∴\,{{field-2}}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the logical inference rule of *denying the consequent* (also known as modus tollens), we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬Z \\ (X∨Y)⇒Z \\ ∴¬(X∨Y)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the logical inference rule of *implication elimination* (also known as *modus ponens*) with the conclusion from the previous step, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(X∨Y) \\ ¬(X∨Y)⇒¬W \\ ∴¬W\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Disjoint Union of Overlapping Sets
questions.problem: Find the disjoint union of the sets ${A}_{1}={3,a,7}$ and ${A}_{2}={a,b}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the sets are overlapping since

$$
{3,a,7}\cap {a,b}={a}\ne ∅.
$$

So, for each of our sets, we form the associated set, where each element is tagged with the corresponding index, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {A}_{1} &  & \,\to \, &  & {A}_{1}^{∗}={(3,1),(a,1),(7,1)} \\  & {A}_{2} &  & \,\to \, &  & {A}_{2}^{∗}={(a,2),(b,2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the disjoint union of our sets is simply the union of the associated tagged sets:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2} & ={3,a,7}⊔{a,b} \\  & ={A}_{1}^{∗}\cup {A}_{2}^{∗} \\  & ={(3,1),(a,1),(7,1)}\cup {(a,2),(b,2)} \\  & ={(3,1),(a,1),(7,1),(a,2),(b,2)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Properties of Indicator Functions
questions.problem:
$$
{1}_{A}(c)=0,\,{1}_{B}(c)=1
$$

Given the values of the indicator functions of the sets $A$ and $B,$ which of the following statements are true?

- ${1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(c)=1$
- ${1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(c)=0$
- $c\in A\cap B$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the indicator functions of $\overset{―}{A},$ $A\cap B,$ and $A\cup B$ have the following properties:

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}_{\overset{―}{A}}\,(x) & =1-{1}_{A}(x) \\ {1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(x) & =min{{1}_{A}(x),{1}_{B}(x)} \\ {1}_{A\,\cup \,B}\,(x) & =max{{1}_{A}(x),{1}_{B}(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false while statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(c) & =min{{1}_{A}(c),{1}_{B}(c)} \\  & =min{0,1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since ${1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(c)=0,$ we conclude that $c$ does not belong to $A\cap B.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Laplace Transform of a Second-Order ODE
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+2y} & =L{6{e}^{-t}} \\ L{{y}^{″}}-3L{{y}^{′}}+2L{y} & =6L{{e}^{-t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce $L{y}=Y(s).$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}}$ and $L{{y}^{″}},$  we use formulas for the Laplace transforms of the derivatives and apply the initial conditions:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}} & =sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s) \\ L{{y}^{″}} & ={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)-3\end{aligned}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{-t}}=\frac{1}{s+1}
$$

Therefore, we can solve for $Y(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}}-3L{{y}^{′}}+2L{y} & =6L{{e}^{-t}} \\ ({s}^{2}Y(s)-3)-3(sY(s))+2Y(s) & =6(\frac{1}{s+1}) \\ ({s}^{2}-3s+2)Y(s) & =3+\frac{6}{s+1} \\ (s-1)(s-2)Y(s) & =\frac{3s+9}{s+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3(s+3)}{(s+1)(s-1)(s-2)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3(s+3)}{({s}^{2}-1)(s-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Laplace Transform of a Second-Order ODE
questions.problem:
Find the Laplace transform of $y(t),$ if 

$$
{y}^{″}+2y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}+2y} & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\ L{{y}^{″}}+2L{y} & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce $L{y}=Y(s).$ 

To calculate $L{{y}^{″}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a second derivative:

$$
L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}L{y}-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)
$$

Taking into account the given initial conditions, we get

$$
L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}Y(s).
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}}+2L{y} & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s)+2Y(s) & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ ({s}^{2}+2)Y(s) & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{1}{({s}^{2}+1)({s}^{2}+2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Laplace transform of $y(t),$ if 

$$
{y}^{″}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(0)=1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the scalar multiplication property of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}} & =L{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\ L{{y}^{″}} & =2L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce $L{y}=Y(s).$ 

To calculate $L{{y}^{″}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a second derivative:

$$
L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}L{y}-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)
$$

Taking into account the given initial conditions, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}}={s}^{2}Y(s)-s.\end{aligned}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}} & =2L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s)-s & =\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s) & =\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}+1}+s \\ {s}^{2}Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{3}+3s}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{3}+3s}{{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+1)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+3}{s({s}^{2}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order Initial Value Problem Using Laplace Transforms
questions.problem:
Find $y(t)$ given that the Laplace transform of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}(t)-y(t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t-6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(0)=3,\,{y}^{′}(0)=2
$$

is given by

$$
{s}^{2}Y(s)-3s-2-Y(s)=-4(\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1})-6(\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}).
$$

The solution is $y(t)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Using the transformed equation, we can solve for $Y(s)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)-3s-2-Y(s) & =-4(\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1})-6(\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}) \\ ({s}^{2}-1)Y(s) & =3s+2-\frac{4}{{s}^{2}+1}-\frac{6s}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ ({s}^{2}-1)Y(s) & =\frac{(3s+2)({s}^{2}-1)}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3s+2}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3s}{{s}^{2}+1}+\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

which is valid for $s>1.$

Now, taking the inverse Laplace transform, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}(Y(s)) & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{3s}{{s}^{2}+1}+\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+1}} \\  & =3{L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}}+2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}} \\  \\ y(t) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Scalar Triple Product Using a Determinant
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the scalar triple product $r\cdot (q\times p)$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $r,$ $q,$ and $p.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot (q\times p) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 3 & -3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|-(-4)\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =((-3)\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot 2)+4(3\cdot 0-2\cdot 2)+(3\cdot (-1)-2\cdot (-3)) \\  & =2-16+3 \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we factor out the constants and get

$$
\begin{aligned}2a\cdot ((-3b)\times c) & =10 \\ 2\cdot (-3)\cdot [a\cdot (b\times c)] & =10 \\ a\cdot (b\times c) & =-\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $a$ and $c$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot (b\times a) & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the triple scalar product 

$$

$$

Then, we swap $a$ and $b$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}b\cdot (a\times c)=-8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Scalar Triple Product Using a Determinant
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the scalar triple product $a\cdot (b\times c)$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $a,$ $b,$ and $c.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =0\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}|\,-\,2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}|\,+\,1\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =0\,(0\cdot 5-3\cdot 4)\,-\,2\,(2\cdot 5-3\cdot 1)\,+\,1\,(2\cdot 4-0\cdot 1) \\  & =0(-12)\,-\,2\,(7)\,+\,1\,(8) \\  & =0-14+8 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Series Solution to a Second-Order Initial Value Problem About Zero
questions.problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=5y-2{x}^{2},\,y(0)=3,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0)$ and ${y}^{′}(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=3,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & =5y(0)-2(0)^{2} \\  & =5(3)+0 \\  & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}=5{y}^{′}-4x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & =5{y}^{′}(0)-4(0) \\  & =5(0)-0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\  & =3+x\cdot 0+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}\cdot 15+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}\cdot 0+⋯ \\  & =3+\frac{15{x}^{2}}{2}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=1$, in ascending powers of $(x-1)$ up to and including the term in $(x-1)^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=y\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2{y}^{′},\,y(1)=4,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=1$:

$$
y(x)=y(1)+(x-1){y}^{′}(1)+\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(1)+\frac{(x-1)^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(1)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(1)$ and ${y}^{′}(1),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{″}(1)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(1).$

We substitute $y(1)=4$ and ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ into the given equation to find ${y}^{″}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(1) & =y(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2{y}^{′}(1) \\  & =4\cdot 0+2\cdot 1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)={y}^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{y}{x}+2{y}^{″}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(1)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(1) & ={y}^{′}(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{y(1)}{1}+2{y}^{″}(1) \\  & =1\cdot 0+4+2\cdot 2 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Finaly, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(1)+(x-1){y}^{′}(1)+\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(1)+\frac{(x-1)^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(1)+⋯ \\  & =4+(x-1)\cdot 1+\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2}\cdot 2+\frac{(x-1)^{3}}{6}\cdot 8+… \\  & =4+(x-1)+(x-1)^{2}+\frac{4}{3}(x-1)^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Series Solution to a First-Order Initial Value Problem
questions.problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2{e}^{x},\,y(0)=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=0,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & ={y}^{2}(0)-2{e}^{0}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{″}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{″}(x)=2y{y}^{′}-2{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{″}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & =2y(0){y}^{′}(0)-2{e}^{0} \\  & =2(0)(-2)-2 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)=2{y}^{′}{y}^{′}+2y{y}^{″}-2{e}^{x}=2({y}^{′})^{2}+2y{y}^{″}-2{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & =2({y}^{′}(0))^{2}+2y(0){y}^{″}(0)-2{e}^{0} \\  & =2(-2)^{2}+2(0)(-2)-2{e}^{0} \\  & =8+0-2 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\  & =0+x\cdot (-2)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\cdot (-2)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\cdot 6+⋯ \\  & =-2x-{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Line Is a Subspace of Two-Dimensional Space
questions.problem:
Let $L$ be the line with equation $x=2y-1$ in ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $L$ contains the zero-vector
- $L$ is closed under vector addition
- $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- $L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2y-1 \\ y\end{aligned}],\,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The coordinates of the zero-vector do not satisfy the equation $x=2y-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2y-1 \\ (0) & =2(0)-1 \\ 0 & =-1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ from $L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1+1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 
However, $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\notin L$ since substituting the coordinates into the equation, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2y-1 \\ (0) & =2(1)-1 \\ 0 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $x=5y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5y \\ (0) & =5(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}5a \\ a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}5b \\ b\end{aligned}]\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}5a \\ a\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5b \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5a+5b \\ a+b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5(a+b) \\ a+b\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot [\begin{aligned}5a \\ a\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5ka \\ ka\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $x=5y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- $L$ is closed under vector addition

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

$$

$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $y=-3x:$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}a \\ -3a\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}b \\ -3b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a+b \\ (-3a)+(-3b)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a+b \\ -3(a+b)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}

which satisfies the condition $y=-3x.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot [\begin{aligned}a \\ -3a\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}ka \\ k(-3a)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}ka \\ -3(ka)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=-3x.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

\begin{aligned}2y & =3x \\ 2(0) & =3(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}a \\ \frac{3}{2}a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}b \\ \frac{3}{2}b\end{aligned}]\in L.$ Then,

$$

$$

which satisfies the condition $2y=3x.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}a \\ \frac{3}{2}a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot [\begin{aligned}a \\ \frac{3}{2}a\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}ka \\ k(\frac{3}{2}a)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}ka \\ \frac{3}{2}(ka)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $2y=3x.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

questions.problem:
Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(-2,2,-2)$ and $(3,-4,2).$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $L$ contains the zero-vector
- $L$ is closed under vector addition
- $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- $L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -6 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -6 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
\frac{x+2}{5}=\frac{y-2}{-6}=\frac{z+2}{4}.
$$

But this line does not pass through the origin since 

$$
\frac{(0)+2}{5}\ne \frac{(0)-2}{-6}\ne \frac{(0)+2}{4}.\,\times 
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider the vectors $[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ from $L$ (the position vectors of the given points). Then,

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

However, the point $(1,-2,0)$ does not belong to $L$ since

$$
\frac{(1)+2}{5}\ne \frac{(-2)-2}{-6}\ne \frac{(0)+2}{4}.\,\times 
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

questions.problem:
Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(0,0,0)$ and $(4,3,-2).$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $L$ contains the zero-vector
- $L$ is closed under vector addition
- $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 3t \\ -2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
\frac{x}{4}=\frac{y}{3}=-\frac{z}{2}.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, from the definition of $L$ we have that the point $(0,0,0)$ is in $L.$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}4a \\ 3a \\ -2a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}4b \\ 3b \\ -2b\end{aligned}]\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}4a \\ 3a \\ -2a\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4b \\ 3b \\ -2b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4a+4b \\ 3a+3b \\ (-2a)+(-2b)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4(a+b) \\ 3(a+b) \\ -2(a+b)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $\frac{x}{4}=\frac{y}{3}=-\frac{z}{2}.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}4a \\ 3a \\ -2a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot [\begin{aligned}4a \\ 3a \\ -2a\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}k(4a) \\ k(3a) \\ k(-2a)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4(ka) \\ 3(ka) \\ -2(ka)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $\frac{x}{4}=\frac{y}{3}=-\frac{z}{2}.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true."

Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,-1,1).$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $L$ contains the zero-vector
- $L$ is closed under vector addition
- $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- $L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}t \\ -t \\ t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
x=-y=z.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, from the definition of $L$ we have that the point $(0,0,0)$ is in $L.$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}a \\ -a \\ a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}b \\ -b \\ b\end{aligned}]\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}a \\ -a \\ a\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}b \\ -b \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a+b \\ -a+(-b) \\ a+b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a+b \\ -(a+b) \\ a+b\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $x=-y=z.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}a \\ -a \\ a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot [\begin{aligned}a \\ -a \\ a\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}ka \\ k(-a) \\ ka\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}ka \\ -(ka) \\ ka\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $x=-y=z.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."

- $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].

$$

$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$

$$

\frac{(4)-3}{2}\ne (-1)\ne \frac{(0)+1}{-2}.\,\times 
$$

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

questions.problem:
Let $Π$ be the plane with equation $3x+2y+z=1$ in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

- $Π$ contains the zero-vector
- $Π$ is closed under vector addition
- $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- $Π$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ 1-3x-2y\end{aligned}],\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The line does not pass through the origin since

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2y+z & =1 \\ 3(0)+2(0)+(0) & =1 \\ 0 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\in Π$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\in Π.$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0+1 \\ 0+(-1) \\ 1+0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

However, $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ does not belong to $Π$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2y+z & =1 \\ 3(1)+2(-1)+(1) & =1 \\ 2 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin Π,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

Let $Π$ be the plane with equation $z=x+y$ in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

- $Π$ contains the zero-vector
- $Π$ is closed under vector addition
- $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- $Π$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$

Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ x+y\end{aligned}],\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $z=x+y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x+y \\ (0) & =(0)+(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}+{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in Π$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in Π.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}+{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ ({a}_{1}+{a}_{2})+({b}_{1}+{b}_{2})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ ({a}_{1}+{b}_{1})+({a}_{2}+{b}_{2})\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=x+y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in Π.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}+{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in Π$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot [\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}+{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ k({a}_{1}+{a}_{2})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ k{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=x+y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in Π.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, the plane $Π$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true."

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ 2x-5y\end{aligned}],\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $z=2x-5y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2x-5y \\ (0) & =2(0)-5(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

which satisfies the condition $z=2x-5y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in Π.$

{(3)-1}\neq\dfrac{(3)-2}{-1}=\dfrac{(3)-2}{-1}. \quad {\color{red}\times}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\mathbf{0} \not\in L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Plane Is a Subspace of Three-Dimensional Space
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $\Pi$ be the plane with equation $x+4y-3z=2$ in $\mathbb{R}^3.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

- $\Pi$ contains the zero-vector

- $\Pi$ is closed under vector addition

- $\Pi$ is closed under scalar multiplication

- $\Pi$ is **not** a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0 \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for any vector $\mathbf{v}$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $\Pi$ contains vectors of the form 

![](images/d6/d64a36f48b3ad9b9c4fb1426260daa832254ec37abea4b1b33fafeb793aa1798.png)

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The plane does not pass through the origin since

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4y-3z & =2 \\ (0)+4(0)-3(0) & =2 \\ 0 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider ![](images/2e/2e5c2dab37c97d3f13e1ce3c981a31d51d46a64daa6f21e2102747afbc84d015.png) and ![](images/19/19be68b7d6cf1b05832601c75bb456ec66a9f15f56188c89bf9ba98ad83d937d.png) Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2+1 \\ 0+1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

However, $[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ does not belong to $\Pi$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4y-3z & =2 \\ (3)+4(1)-3(1) & =2 \\ 4 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\mathbf{0} \not\in \Pi,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $\Pi$ is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | $1$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{4}(1))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-3}} | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ $n=4,$ and $\lambda =1.$

Since $n=4,$ we need to compute the first $4-1=3$ derivatives of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{4}(1)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) & \frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(1) \\ 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{1} & -\frac{1}{{1}^{2}\cdot 2} & \frac{2}{{1}^{3}\cdot 6} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{1} & -\frac{1}{{1}^{2}\cdot 2} \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{1} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡([\begin{aligned}{J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(\pi )\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi ))\end{aligned}] \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi )).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & \frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{3}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{1}(\pi ),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(\pi )) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(\pi )) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi )) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t],$ the vector space of real polynomials of degree at most $2,$ and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1).
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{p}_{1}(t)={t}^{2}-t,\,{p}_{2}(t)={t}^{2}+t,\,q(t)=4{t}^{2}-t-1
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{p}_{1}(t)}$ equals $2{t}^{2}-2t.$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=1,\,{f}_{2}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,g(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}$ equals $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3)\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3)\,\text{d}t \\  & =[-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3t]_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =(2-0+3\pi )-(2-0-3\pi ) \\  & =6\pi \end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }1\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t) & =\frac{6\pi }{2\pi }\cdot 1=3.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =3-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace
questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t],$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $2$ with real coefficients. Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1),
$$

find the distance between $p(t)=5{t}^{2}-5$ and the subspace spanned by $q(t)=t+1$ with respect to the inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $p(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{q(t)}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t) & =\frac{⟨p(t),q(t)⟩}{⟨q(t),q(t)⟩}\,q(t) \\  & =\frac{p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)}{q(-1)q(-1)+q(0)q(0)+q(1)q(1)}\cdot q(t) \\  & =\frac{{\sum }_{i\in {-1,0,1}}(5{t}^{2}-5){|}_{t=i}\cdot (t+1){|}_{t=i}}{{\sum }_{i\in {-1,0,1}}(t+1){|}_{t=i}\cdot (t+1){|}_{t=i}}\cdot (t+1) \\  & =\frac{0\cdot 0+(-5)\cdot 1+0\cdot 2}{0\cdot 0+1\cdot 1+2\cdot 2}\cdot (t+1) \\  & =\frac{-5}{5}\cdot (t+1) \\  & =-t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The distance between $p(t)=5{t}^{2}-5$ and the subspace spanned by $q(t)=t+1$ with respect to our inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖p(t)-{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t)‖ \\  & =‖5{t}^{2}-5-(-t-1)‖ \\  & =‖5{t}^{2}+t-4‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨5{t}^{2}+t-4,5{t}^{2}+t-4⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨5{t}^{2}+t-4,5{t}^{2}+t-4⟩ & ={\sum }_{i\in {-1,0,1}}(5{t}^{2}+t-4){|}_{t=i}\cdot (5{t}^{2}+t-4){|}_{t=i} \\  & =(0)\cdot (0)+(-4)\cdot (-4)+2\cdot 2 \\  & =0+16+4 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{20}.$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=7t$ and the subspace spanned by $g(t)=t-2$ with respect to the inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $f(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{g(t)}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t) & =\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}7t\cdot (t-2)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{0}^{1}(t-2)^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot (t-2) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}(7{t}^{2}-14t)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}-4t+4)\,\text{d}t}\cdot (t-2) \\  & =\frac{[\frac{7}{3}{t}^{3}-7{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1}}{[\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}+4t]_{0}^{1}}\cdot (t-2) \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{14}{3})}{(\frac{7}{3})}\cdot (t-2) \\  & =-2t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

The distance between $f(t)=7t$ and the subspace spanned by $g(t)=t-2$ with respect to our inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t)‖ \\  & =‖7t-(-2t+4)‖ \\  & =‖9t-4‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨9t-4,9t-4⟩}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨9t-4,9t-4⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9t-4)\cdot (9t-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9t-4)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(81{t}^{2}-72t+16)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(27{t}^{3}-36{t}^{2}+16)\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{7}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $6{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/52/52fc197612dac35373ecebf771b8444505902b5c6e00c7c55d2b21dab4809136.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6{x}^{3}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=6{x}^{3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

$$

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $-4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/46/466c0aa389beb6d1a42092b73bae75508ef2c50f1f08cca5efaac20d25615f30.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4(1+2x).
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4(1+2x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int 4(1+2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=4(x+{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=-4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4(x+{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-4)^{2} & =4(1+{1}^{2})+C \\ 8 & =8+C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4(x+{x}^{2})+0 \\ {v}^{2} & =8(x+{x}^{2}) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{2(x+{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-2\sqrt{2(x+{x}^{2})}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $0\,m$ when its velocity is $-2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/ba/ba6a85da04d9ba03bcdba9b938dac208a770933310cd25c19bf0ec3e19ef17c7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (\frac{1}{16}x)\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=-2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}(0)^{2}+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}({x}^{2}+64) \\ v & =\pm \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.
$$
