questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/32/3278eca2ae91f59c7c20d91f9190611291924dcc0cd6ffe74456552ba8400335.png)

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(-\sqrt{\pi })^{2} & =-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+C \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =-2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+C \\ C & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x \\ {v}^{2} & =2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v=-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡3)} \\  & ≈-1.1\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${e}^{x-3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{x-3}.

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={e}^{x-3}.
$$

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int {e}^{x-3}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={e}^{x-3}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=3\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & ={e}^{3-3}+C \\ 2 & =1+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+1 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({e}^{x-3}+1) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/ec/ec4af1357e75dcee6d7d5412467c2ee2ea9e54fa38fb6e83817b0ae909c529aa.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2+3{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2x-3{e}^{-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2(0)-3{e}^{-0}+C \\ 2 & =-3+C \\ C & =2+3 \\ C & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2x-3{e}^{-x}+5 \\ {v}^{2} & =4x-6{e}^{-x}+10 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4(3)-6{e}^{-3}+10} \\ v & =\sqrt{22-6{e}^{-3}} \\ v & ≈4.7\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/ad/ad437638f22672a10a183f1521929637f8d43725f37a9736c569516232e7c468.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -2{e}^{-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2{e}^{0}+K \\ K & =2-2 \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ v & =\pm 2{e}^{-x/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2{e}^{-x/2} \\ {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{x/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{x/2} & =t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{x/2}=t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/2} & =t+1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x/2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}} \\ (1+x)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int (1+x)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int (1+x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{3}(1+x)^{3} & =t+K \\ (1+x)^{3} & =3t+C \\ 1+x & =\sqrt[3]{3t+C} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{3t+C}-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x(t)=\sqrt[3]{3t+1}-1.
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(0+2)^{4}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4} \\ {v}^{2} & =(x+2)^{4} \\ v & =\pm (x+2)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=(x+2)^{2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=(x+2)^{2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(x+2)^{2} \\ \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 1\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ -\frac{1}{x+2} & =t+C \\ \frac{1}{x+2} & =-t-C.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=-\frac{1}{2},$ and the particular solution is

$$
\frac{1}{x+2}=-t+\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+2} & =-t+\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{x+2} & =\frac{1-2t}{2} \\ x+2 & =\frac{2}{1-2t} \\ x & =\frac{2}{1-2t}-2 \\ x & =\frac{4t}{1-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, the velocity is given by $v(x)=3x\,m/s.$ If $x=2\,m$ when $t=0,$ find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/ef/efdb69673b4088d3c021d78282642ff7abc57158e23704cd3d5e7ff2559cbdbb.png)

We're given that the velocity function $v(x)$ is

$$
v(x)=3x.
$$

We know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3x.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =3x \\ \frac{1}{3x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{3x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x| & =t+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|x| & =3t+3K \\ x & ={e}^{3t+3K} \\ x & =C{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=2$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=2,$ and the particular solution is

$$
x(t)=2{e}^{3t}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0$. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\, \rm{ m/s}$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $\sin^2 x \,\rm{m/s}^2.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ what differential equation describes this motion?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](images/f1/f187eff194f136838b67ab12b44f8f6882eafb59885a5c3f440d41492def4a42.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\sin^2 x$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -\sin^2 x.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-{sin}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},$ we have

$$
v \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = -\sin^2 x.\qquad \qquad (\ast)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(v^2) = 2v\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac12v^2\right) = v\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(\ast)$ as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac12v^2\right) = -\sin^2 x.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x \,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s}$ and its acceleration is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \, \rm{m/s}^2.$ If $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x = 1 \, \textrm m.$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](images/4f/4fdd70a4ca80965c0adce9c60be36b0712852b662cff69f9733f50c739fd1b32.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{e}^{x-2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = x^2 + e^{x-2} + C.
$$

Now, since $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={2}^{2}+{e}^{2-2}+C \\ 8 & =4+1+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v = \sqrt{2\left(x^2 + e^{x-2} + 3\right)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x = 1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({1}^{2}+{e}^{1-2}+3)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(4+{e}^{-1})} \\  & ≈2.96\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\geq 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\textrm m,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](images/ec/eca36626e6a0cfb30d293e684483c37ddce6f18d4004c3f77258e9663565d8d7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =-\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=0\, \textrm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{2}{0+1}+K \\ 2 & =2+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{4}{x+1} \\ v & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x) > 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}} \\ \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{2}{3}(x+1)^{3/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = \dfrac{3C_1}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+1)^{3/2} =3t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+1 \\ x+1 & =(3t+1)^{2/3} \\ x & =(3t+1)^{2/3}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Are Attained on the Unit Sphere
questions.problem: The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-17{x}_{2}^{2}+7{x}_{3}^{2}-18{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -17 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-20)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -17 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 7\end{aligned}]+20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}19 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 27\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-20)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Is Attained Over an Ellipse
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & -4 \\ -6 & -12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -12 \\ -12 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}]+72[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
2{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x(2x-3){y}^{′}-3y=0
$$

The general solution near $x=0$ of the differential equation is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are arbitrary constants and ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent solutions. According to the Frobenius method, what is the best choice for the first solution ${y}_{1},$ where ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants determined by substitution?

*Hint: You may assume $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the ODE and the indicial equation of the ODE is $2{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -3=0.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution near a regular singular point $x=0$ of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation with indicial roots ${\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}$ is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{1}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1}){x}^{n}$ is the first Frobenius solution corresponding to the larger root of the indicial equation, and

- ${a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1})$ are the coefficients produced by the method when $\lambda ={\lambda }_{1}.$

We are given that the indicial equation is $2{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -3=0.$
Solving for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (2\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-\frac{1}{2},3\end{aligned}
$$

The larger solution is ${\lambda }_{1}=3.$ Therefore, the first Frobenius series solution we take is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{3}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}.
$$

where ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are arbitrary constants and ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent solutions. According to the Frobenius method, what is the missing coefficient in the first solution ${y}_{1}?$

*Hint: You may assume $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the ODE, the indicial equation of the ODE is $2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda =0,$ and the recurrence relation for the coefficients is

$$
{a}_{n}(\lambda )=\frac{5}{(\lambda +n)(2(\lambda +n)-1)}\,{a}_{n-1}.
$$

${y}_{1}(x)={a}_{0}({x}^{1/2}+\frac{5}{3}{x}^{3/2}\,+$ {{field-1}} ${x}^{5/2}+⋯).$
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution near a regular singular point $x=0$ of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation with indicial roots ${\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}$ is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{1}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1}){x}^{n}$ is the first Frobenius solution corresponding to the larger root of the indicial equation, and

- ${a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1})$ are the coefficients produced by the method when $\lambda ={\lambda }_{1}.$

We are given that the indicial equation is $2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda =0.$
Solving for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (2\lambda -1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The larger solution is ${\lambda }_{1}=\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore, the first Frobenius series solution we take is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{1/2}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}.
$$

With $\lambda =\frac{1}{2},$ the recurrence relation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{5}{(\frac{1}{2}+n)(2(\frac{1}{2}+n)-1)}\,{a}_{n-1} \\  & =\frac{5}{(n+\frac{1}{2})(2n)}\,{a}_{n-1} \\  & =\frac{5}{n(2n+1)}\,{a}_{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, with ${a}_{0}\ne 0$ arbitrary, we evaluate the first three coefficients using the given recurrence relation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & \ne 0, \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{5}{1(2\cdot 1+1)}\,{a}_{0}=\frac{5}{3}{a}_{0}, \\ {a}_{2} & =\frac{5}{2(2\cdot 2+1)}\,{a}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{5}{3}{a}_{0}=\frac{5}{6}{a}_{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first Frobenius solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & ={x}^{1/2}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n} \\  & ={x}^{1/2}({a}_{0}+\frac{5}{3}{a}_{0}x+\frac{5}{6}{a}_{0}{x}^{2}+⋯) \\  & ={a}_{0}({x}^{1/2}+\frac{5}{3}{x}^{3/2}+\frac{5}{6}{x}^{5/2}+⋯).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
2{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x(2x-3){y}^{′}-3y=0
$$

The general solution near $x=0$ of the differential equation above is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{3}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(3){x}^{n}+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are arbitrary constants and ${a}_{n}(\lambda )$ are coefficients dependent on $\lambda $ (solutions of the indicial equation) and determined by substitution.
Which of the following is the form of the second Frobenius solution ${y}_{2}?$

*Hint: You may assume $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the ODE and the indicial equation of the ODE is $2{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -3=0.$*

The general solution near a regular singular point $x=0$ of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation with indicial roots ${\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}$ is given by

$$

$$

where

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1}){x}^{n}
$$

is the first Frobenius solution, and the second Frobenius solution is determined as follows:

- **Case 1**: If ${\lambda }_{1}-{\lambda }_{2}\notin Z,$ then 
${y}_{2}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{2}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{2}){x}^{n}.$

- **Case 2**: If ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2},$ then
${y}_{2}(x)={y}_{1}(x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{b}_{n}{x}^{n}.$

- **Case 3**: If ${\lambda }_{1}-{\lambda }_{2}\in N,$ then
${y}_{2}(x)={b}_{-1}{y}_{1}(x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{{\lambda }_{2}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{b}_{n}{x}^{n}.$

We are given that the indicial equation is $2{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -3=0.$
Solving for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (2\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-\frac{1}{2},3\end{aligned}
$$

The larger solution is ${\lambda }_{1}=3\ge -\frac{1}{2}={\lambda }_{2}.$ Therefore, the first Frobenius series solution we take is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{3}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(3){x}^{n}.
$$

Now, since ${\lambda }_{1}-{\lambda }_{2}=3-(-\frac{1}{2})=\frac{7}{2}$ *is not* an integer, the other solution is the second Frobenius solution, given by

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{-1/2}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\,(-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{n}.

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
x^2y'' + x(x-4)y' - 4y = 0
$$

The general solution near $x=0$ of the differential equation is given by

$$

$$

where $c_1$ and $c_2$ are arbitrary constants and $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are linearly independent solutions. According to the Frobenius method, what is the best choice for the first solution $y_1,$ where $a_n$ for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$ are constants determined by substitution?

canonical_examples.worked_solution:

$$
y = c_1y_1(x) + c_2y_2(x),
$$

where

- $\displaystyle y_1(x) = x^{\lambda_1} \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(\lambda_1)x^n$ is the first Frobenius solution corresponding to the larger root of the indicial equation, and

- $a_n(\lambda_1)$ are the coefficients produced by the method when $\lambda = \lambda_1.$

$$

$$
y_1(x) = x^4\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n.

The general solution near $x=0$ of the differential equation is given by

$$
y = c_1y_1(x) + c_2y_2(x),
$$

where $c_1$ and $c_2$ are arbitrary constants and $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are linearly independent solutions. According to the Frobenius method, what is the first solution $y_1?$

*Hint: You may assume $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the ODE, the indicial equation of the ODE is $5\lambda^2-3\lambda=0,$ and the recurrence relation for the coefficients is

$$
a_n(\lambda) = \dfrac{6}{(\lambda+n)(5(\lambda+n)-3)}\,a_{n-1}.
$$

*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The general solution near a regular singular point $x=0$ of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation with indicial roots $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2$ is given by

$$
y = c_1y_1(x) + c_2y_2(x),
$$

where

- $\displaystyle y_1(x) = x^{\lambda_1} \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(\lambda_1)x^n$ is the first Frobenius solution corresponding to the larger root of the indicial equation, and

- $a_n(\lambda_1)$ are the coefficients produced by the method when $\lambda = \lambda_1.$

We are given that the indicial equation is $5\lambda^2-3\lambda=0.$
Solving for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (5\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

The larger solution is $\lambda_1 = \dfrac35.$ Therefore, the first Frobenius series solution we take is

$$
y_1(x) = x^{3/5}\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n.
$$

With $\lambda = \dfrac35,$ the recurrence relation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{6}{(\frac{3}{5}+n)(5(\frac{3}{5}+n)-3)}\,{a}_{n-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{5n(n+\frac{3}{5})}\,{a}_{n-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{n(5n+3)}\,{a}_{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, with $a_0\neq0$ arbitrary, we evaluate the first three coefficients using the given recurrence relation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & \ne 0, \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{6}{1(5\cdot 1+3)}\,{a}_{0}=\frac{6}{8}{a}_{0}=\frac{3}{4}{a}_{0}, \\ {a}_{2} & =\frac{6}{2(5\cdot 2+3)}\,{a}_{1}=\frac{6}{26}\cdot \frac{3}{4}{a}_{0}=\frac{9}{52}{a}_{0},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first Frobenius solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & ={x}^{3/5}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n} \\  & ={x}^{3/5}({a}_{0}+\frac{3}{4}{a}_{0}x+\frac{9}{52}{a}_{0}{x}^{2}+⋯) \\  & ={a}_{0}({x}^{3/5}+\frac{3}{4}{x}^{8/5}+\frac{9}{52}{x}^{13/5}+⋯).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
x^2y'' - 5xy' + (3x+9)y = 0
$$

The general solution near $x=0$ of the differential equation above is given by

$$
y = c_1x^3\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n + c_2y_2(x),
$$

where $c_1$ and $c_2$ are arbitrary constants and $a_n$ are constants.
What is the form of the second Frobenius solution $y_2,$ where $b_n$ for $n \geq 0$ are the constant coefficients of the $n$th term determined by substitution?

*Hint: You may assume $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the ODE and the indicial equation of the ODE is $\lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 9 = 0.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The general solution near a regular singular point $x=0$ of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation with indicial roots $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2$ is given by

$$
y = c_1y_1(x) + c_2y_2(x),
$$

where

$$
\displaystyle
y_1(x) = x^{\lambda_1} \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(\lambda_1)x^n
$$

is the first Frobenius solution, and the second Frobenius solution is determined as follows:

- **Case 1**: If $\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 \not\in \mathbb{Z},$ then 
$\displaystyle
  y_2(x) = x^{\lambda_2} \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(\lambda_2)x^n.$

- **Case 2**: If $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2,$ then
$\displaystyle
  y_2(x) = y_1(x)\ln x + x^{\lambda_1} \sum_{n=0}^\infty b_nx^n.$

- **Case 3**: If $\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 \in \mathbb{N},$ then
$\displaystyle
  y_2(x) = b_{-1}y_1(x)\ln x + x^{\lambda_2}\sum_{n=0}^\infty b_nx^n.$

We are given that the indicial equation is $\lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 9 = 0.$
Solving for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $\lambda=3$ is a double root. So, the indicial roots are equal $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = 3.$ Therefore, the first Frobenius series solution we take is

$$
y_1(x) = x^3\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n.
$$

Now, since the roots are equal, the second solution is given by

$$
y_2(x) = y_1(x)\ln x + x^3 \sum_{n=0}^\infty b_nx^n,
$$

where the constants $b_n$ are found by substitution.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Invertible Affine Transformations
questions.problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-2u-5v-9 \\ 4u+9v-9\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3u+3v+4 \\ 3u+3v-1\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3u+v \\ 8\end{aligned}]$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2u-5v-9 \\ 4u+9v-9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2u-5v \\ 4u+9v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}|=9\cdot (-2)-(-5)\cdot 4=2\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+3v+4 \\ 3u+3v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u+3v \\ 3u+3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 3-3\cdot 3=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+v \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u+v \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|=0\cdot 3-1\cdot 0=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ only."

questions.problem:
The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2u-3v-4,\,y=2u-4v-5.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=2x+ay+b,\,v=x-y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u-3v-4 \\ 2u-4v-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u-3v \\ 2u-4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-4\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x+4 \\ y+5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot (x+4)+(-\frac{3}{2})\cdot (y+5) \\ 1\cdot (x+4)+(-1)\cdot (y+5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x-\frac{3}{2}y+\frac{1}{2} \\ x-y-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
![](images/af/afee2a3c30384baa044088177550b0ac5ed2de228b14e48dd7f729e8a7493318.png)

Consider the affine transformation $T,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 
What would be the image of the pentagon shown above under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot (-4)-(-2)\cdot 6 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible, and the image of the pentagon under the action of $T$ is a line segment.

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ defined as

$$
x = u - v - 2, \qquad y = v - u + 5.
$$

Suppose that $A$ is the matrix representing the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ![](images/b3/b3d58dc3ce18b0f5c977b930088152bb7b9c4c821edb656bc478904b67ae8acf.png)

- $\det(A) = 0$

- The transformation is invertible
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v-2 \\ v-u+5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ -u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 
![](images/83/83207d393e930561d8d1f45fb0b21a61f0af7350bfc684f38e846a2cebd1493b.png)

- Statement II is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get
![](images/01/01afe0c9e10a71665dc2ea7d4bd076bb2b9ba63e8dff10d6fbd3264a88008c39.png)

- Statement III is false. Since $\det(A) = 0,$ the affine transformation is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

u = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{5}x - y + \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{(-1)}, \qquad v = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{4}x - y + 1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c = 5 + (-1) + 4 = 8.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Types of Images Formed by an Affine Transformation
canonical_examples.problem:
![](images/87/8797a50ddc0750a97190f96d8bc1cffe70c6ef9cc8e55a46f5a75d6b6702c81d.png)

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by
![](images/34/347a44c388bd81e78d4dcf5f40584ce76273ffe25513ebb1522568ba479ac4fc.png) 
Describe the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $\mathbf{T}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf{T}$ is 
![](images/94/94625329d7eba1da88a9dde36b6e64335a9801658a8c1fd054cea9db835ea4fa.png)

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 2-4\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $\mathbf{T}$ is non-invertible and the image of the triangle under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is a line segment.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding General Solutions to Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs With Variable Coefficients
questions.problem: Given that ${y}_{1}(x)={x}^{3}$ is a solution to the equation ${x}^{2}{y}^{″}-5x{y}^{′}+9y=0$ for $x>0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation, and write down the general solution.
questions.worked_solution:
According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){x}^{3}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{x}^{3}+3u{x}^{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{x}^{3}+6{u}^{′}{x}^{2}+6ux.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}({u}^{″}{x}^{3}+6{u}^{′}{x}^{2}+6ux)-5x({u}^{′}{x}^{3}+3u{x}^{2})+9(u{x}^{3}) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}({u}^{″}{x}^{2}+6{u}^{′}x+6u-5{u}^{′}x-15u+9u) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}({u}^{″}{x}^{2}+{u}^{′}x) & =0 \\ {x}^{4}({u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{4}\ne 0$ for $x>0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}x+w=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w=\frac{{c}_{1}}{x}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}=\frac{{c}_{1}}{x}\,⟹\,u={c}_{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{x}^{3}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{3}({c}_{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{c}_{2}).
$$

Setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Finally, because $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})={x}^{5}\ne 0,$ we know that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent (you should verify this calculation yourself).

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y=A{x}^{3}+B{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding General Solutions to Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs Using Reduction of Order
questions.problem: Given that ${y}_{1}(t)={e}^{2t}$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+4y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(t)$ to the equation, and write down the general solution.
questions.worked_solution:
According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(t){e}^{2t}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{2t}+2u{e}^{2t} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{2t}+4{u}^{′}{e}^{2t}+4u{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}{e}^{2t}+4{u}^{′}{e}^{2t}+4u{e}^{2t})-4({u}^{′}{e}^{2t}+2u{e}^{2t})+4(u{e}^{2t}) & =0 \\ {u}^{″}{e}^{2t}+4{u}^{′}{e}^{2t}+4u{e}^{2t}-4{u}^{′}{e}^{2t}-8u{e}^{2t}+4u{e}^{2t} & =0 \\ {u}^{″}{e}^{2t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{2t}\ne 0$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating the equation twice gives

$$
u={c}_{1}t+{c}_{2}.
$$

Thus, our expression for ${y}_{2}(t)=u{e}^{2t}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(t)={e}^{2t}({c}_{1}t+{c}_{2}).
$$

Setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(t)={e}^{2t}\cdot t=t{e}^{2t}.
$$

Finally, because $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})={e}^{4t}\ne 0,$ we know that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent (you should verify this calculation yourself).

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{2t}+Bt{e}^{2t}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding General Solutions to Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs Using Reduction of Order
questions.problem: Given that ${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}+y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation, and write down the general solution.
questions.worked_solution:
According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-u\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-u\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-u\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+u\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ {u}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ {u}^{″} & =2{u}^{′}\operatorname{tan}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}=2w\operatorname{tan}⁡x.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}{sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}{sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,u={c}_{1}\operatorname{tan}⁡x+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x({c}_{1}\operatorname{tan}⁡x+{c}_{2}).
$$

Setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Finally, because $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=1\ne 0,$ we know that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent (you should verify this calculation yourself).

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}-4y=5{e}^{x}
$$

Consider the differential equation above, for which the corresponding complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-4x},$ where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants. Select the correct options below.$\,$

{{field-5}} are arbitrary constants.
questions.worked_solution:
For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{c}(x)$ is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

- ${y}_{p}(x)$ is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

- For ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({e}^{x})^{′}={e}^{x}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =({e}^{x})^{′}={e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
({e}^{x})+3({e}^{x})-4({e}^{x})=5{e}^{x}.\,\,\times 
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{x}$ $\text{isn't}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

- For ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =(x{e}^{x})^{′}={e}^{x}+x{e}^{x}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =({e}^{x}+x{e}^{x})^{′}=2{e}^{x}+x{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
(2{e}^{x}+x{e}^{x})+3({e}^{x}+x{e}^{x})-4(x{e}^{x})=5{e}^{x}.\,\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{x}$ $\text{is}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-4x}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-4x}+x{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $A\text{ and }B$ are arbitrary constants.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying a Row Operation Given the Connection Between Two Determinants
questions.problem:
Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Multiplying a Matrix by a Scalar
questions.problem: Suppose $X$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $det(X)=10.$ What is the value of $det(6X)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot X)={k}^{n}\cdot det(X).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=6$ and $n=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(6X) & ={6}^{3}\cdot det(X) \\  & =216\cdot 10 \\  & =2160.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Suppose $C$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $det(C)=-2.$ What is the value of $det(-3C)?$

Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot C)={k}^{n}\cdot det(C).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=-3$ and $n=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(-3C) & =(-3)^{4}\cdot det(C) \\  & =81\cdot (-2) \\  & =-162.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Applying Several Elementary Operations
questions.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $det(A)=23.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}$ and ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+5{R}_{3}.$ What is the value of $det(B)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+5{R}_{3}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

Therefore, we only have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =-det(A) \\  & =-(23) \\  & =-23.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Regular and Irregular Singular Points
questions.problem:
$$
(x-1){y}^{″}+{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^{2}}y=0
$$

Consider the differential equation given above. Which of the following statements are true?

- The functions $P(x)=\frac{1}{x-1}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{1}{(x-1)^{3}}$ are analytic about $x=1.$
- The functions $(x-1)P(x)$ and $(x-1)^{2}Q(x)$ are analytic about $x=1.$
- The point $x=1$ is an **irregular** singular point of the differential equation.
questions.worked_solution:
A singular point $a$ of the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x)
$$

is regular if both $(x-a)P(x)$ and $(x-a)^{2}Q(x)$ are analytic about $x=a.$ Otherwise, the singular point is irregular.

First, we rewrite the differential equation in standard form by dividing by $(x-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1){y}^{″}+{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^{2}}y & =0 \\ {y}^{″}+\frac{1}{x-1}{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^{3}}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
P(x)=\frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{and}\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{(x-1)^{3}}.
$$

Let's now check each statement in turn.

- Since the denominators of both $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ vanish at $x=1,$ they are *not* analytic about $x=1.$ So, statement I is false.

- The function

$$
(x-1)P(x)=(x-1)\frac{1}{x-1}=1
$$

is analytic about $x=1,$ while the function

$$
(x-1)^{2}Q(x)=(x-1)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{(x-1)^{3}}=\frac{1}{x-1}
$$

is *not* analytic about $x=1$ since its denominator vanishes at $x=1.$ Therefore, statement II is false.

- Since statement I is false, $x=1$ is a singular point. Also, since statement II is false, it follows that $x=1$ is an **irregular** singular point. Thus, statement III is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Ordinary and Singular Points
questions.problem:
$$
x(x+3){y}^{″}+(x-2){y}^{′}+4y=0
$$

Which of the following is a **singular** point of the differential equation above?

- $x=-3$
- $x=0$
- $x=2$
questions.worked_solution:
The point $x=a$ is an ordinary point of the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x)
$$

if both coefficients $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are analytic about $x=a.$ Otherwise, $x=a$ is a singular point of the differential equation.

First, we rewrite the differential equation in standard form by dividing by $x(x+3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(x+3){y}^{″}+(x-2){y}^{′}+4y & =0 \\ {y}^{″}+\frac{x-2}{x(x+3)}{y}^{′}+\frac{4}{x(x+3)}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
P(x)=\frac{x-2}{x(x+3)}\,\text{and}\,Q(x)=\frac{4}{x(x+3)}.
$$

Let's now check the analyticity of these functions at the given points.

- *Neither* function is analytic about $x=-3,$ since both denominators at $x=-3$ equal zero. So, $x=-3$ is a singular point of the differential equation.

- *Neither* function is analytic about $x=0,$ since both denominators at $x=0$ equal zero. So, $x=0$ is a singular point of the differential equation.

- *Both* functions are analytic about $x=2.$ So, $x=2$ is an ordinary point of the differential equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

if both $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are analytic about $x=a.$ Otherwise, $x=a$ is a singular point of the differential equation.

A singular point $x=a$ is regular if both $(x-a)P(x)$ and $(x-a)^{2}Q(x)$ are analytic about $x=a.$ Otherwise, the singular point is irregular.

First, we rewrite the differential equation in standard form by dividing by $(x+1)(x-2)^{3}(x-4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)(x-2)^{3}(x-4){y}^{″}+(x-2){y}^{′}+(x+1)(x-4)y=0 \\ {y}^{″}+\frac{1}{(x+1)(x-2)^{2}(x-4)}{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
P(x)=\frac{1}{(x+1)(x-2)^{2}(x-4)}\,\text{and}\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}.
$$

The function $P(x)$ is *not* analytic about points where $(x+1)(x-2)^{2}(x-4)=0,$ which occurs at $x=-1,$ $x=2,$ and $x=4.$

The function $Q(x)$ is *not* analytic about points where $(x-2)^{2}=0,$ which occurs at $x=2.$

Therefore, $x=0$ is $\text{an ordinary}$ point of the differential equation, and the singular points are

$$
x=-1,\,x=2,\,x=4.
$$

Now, let's classify each singular point.

- For $x=-1,$ the function

$$
(x+1)P(x)=(x+1)\cdot \frac{1}{(x+1)(x-2)^{2}(x-4)}=\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}(x-4)},
$$

is analytic about $x=-1,$ and the function

$$
(x+1)^{2}Q(x)=(x+1)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}},
$$

is also analytic about $x=-1.$ Therefore, $x=-1$ is $\text{a regular singular}$ point of the differential equation.

- For $x=2,$ the function

$$
(x-2)P(x)=(x-2)\cdot \frac{1}{(x+1)(x-2)^{2}(x-4)}=\frac{1}{(x+1)(x-2)(x-4)},
$$

is *not* analytic about $x=2.$ So,  $x=2$ is an $\text{an irregular singular}$ point of the differential equation.

- For $x=4,$ the function

$$
(x-4)P(x)=(x-4)\cdot \frac{1}{(x+1)(x-2)^{2}(x-4)}=\frac{1}{(x+1)(x-2)^{2}},
$$

is analytic about $x=4,$ and the function

$$
(x-4)^{2}Q(x)=(x-4)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}},
$$

is also analytic about $x=4.$ Therefore, $x=4$ is $\text{a regular singular}$ point of the differential equation.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Maximum and Minimum Values of a Quadratic Form on the Unit Sphere
questions.problem: Find the maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}=3.
$$

questions.problem: Find the minimum value of $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${x}_{1}^{2}\ge 0.$ So, we have that

$$
3{x}_{1}^{2}\ge -2{x}_{1}^{2}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & \ge -2{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-2({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$ So,  

$$
\begin{aligned}-2({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2})=-2(1)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

and, in turn, $Q(x)\ge -2.$

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no smaller than $-2.$ But before we conclude that $-2$ is the minimum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=-2.$

Notice that when $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =3(0)^{2}-2(1)^{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the minimum value of $Q(x)$ is equal to $-2.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${x}_{1}^{2}\ge 0$ and ${x}_{3}^{2}\ge 0.$ So, we have that

$$
3{x}_{1}^{2}\le 6{x}_{1}^{2},\,4{x}_{3}^{2}\le 6{x}_{3}^{2}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & \le 6{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+6{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =6({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}=1.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}6({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2})=6(1)=6.\end{aligned}
$$

and, in turn, $Q(x)\le 6.$ 

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no greater than $6.$ But before we conclude that $6$ is the maximum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=6.$

Notice that when $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =3(0)^{2}+6(1)^{2}+4(0)^{2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the maximum value of  $Q(x)$ is equal to $6.$

questions.problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined by 

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y<1-x}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ contains all of its boundary points.
- $A$ contains none of its boundary points.
- $\text{int}\,A=A$
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

In this case, the set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](images/51/5151df3c5b84ffaca9aa16b401cd9364fea10a240d39c9c28d815b36e417b16d.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

Notice that, in this case, the set $A$ contains none of its boundary points. 

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. As we've seen, $A$ contains none of its boundary points.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ contains none of its boundary points, we must have $\text{int}\,A=A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

$$

$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.  

![](images/2a/2a93b912f0d7b3a84bf0ec9c3b3596d080a9e71a345ff436e2f591edf042d9db.png)

- Statement I is true. Since $\text{int}\,A$ contains all points in $A$ except the boundary points, we must have $\text{int}\,A\cap ∂A=∅,$ where $∅$ denotes the empty set.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ contains none of its boundary points, we must have $A=\text{int}\,A$ or, equivalently,  $A-\text{int}\,A=∅.$

- Statement III is true. In this case, the set $A$ contains none of its boundary points, so we must have $∂A⊂{R}^{2}-A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and  III only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following are logically equivalent to $G?$

- $(H∨G)∧G$
- $H∧(H∨G)$
- $(G∨H)∨G$

The law that conjunction absorbs disjunction is stated as

$$
G∧(G∨H)≡G.
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given statements.

- Statement I is logically equivalent to $G.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}(H∨G)∧G & ≡G∧(H∨G) \\  & ≡G∧(G∨H) \\  & ≡G.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is *not* logically equivalent to $G.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}H∧(H∨G) & ≡H≢G.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is *not* logically equivalent to $G.$ This statement cannot be simplified using the absorption laws.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Numerator is Greater
questions.problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)=\frac{3{x}^{3}-{x}^{5}}{2{x}^{4}+{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{4}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{4},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3{x}^{3}-{x}^{5}}{2{x}^{4}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{{x}^{4}})}{(\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{x}-x)}{(2+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{3}{x}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{3}{x}-x)}{(2+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ≈\frac{0-x}{2+0} \\  & =-\frac{x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Denominator is Greater
questions.problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{2{x}^{2}+3}{8{x}^{5}+x-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{5}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{5},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+3}{8{x}^{5}+x-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{5}})}{(\frac{8{x}^{5}}{{x}^{5}}+\frac{x}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{5}})}{(8+\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{5}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{2}{{x}^{3}},\frac{3}{{x}^{5}},\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{5}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{5}})}{(8+\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & \to \frac{0+0}{8+0-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$

questions.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3x+2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{x})}{(\frac{3x}{x}+\frac{2}{x})} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{(3+\frac{2}{x})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the term $\frac{2}{x}$ becomes very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$

$$

$$

$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. You're given that the system of equations given below connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$  

$$
{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{2}+2{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{6}{a}_{3}-4{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ as a linear combination of the vectors ${q}_{1},{q}_{2},{q}_{3}:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{2}+2{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{6}{a}_{3}-4{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=2{q}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}=-8{q}_{1}+4{q}_{2} \\ {a}_{3}=24{q}_{1}-6{q}_{2}+6{q}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, this system can be written in matrix form as follows:

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {q}_{1} & {q}_{2} & {q}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 & -8 & 24 \\ 0 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]}}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{r}_{12}+{r}_{22}+{r}_{23}=-8+4+(-6)=-10.
$$

$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ of $A$ are orthogonal, and that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained by normalizing the columns of $A,$ what is the value of ${q}_{32}\cdot {r}_{11}?$

Since the columns of $A$ are already orthogonal, to construct an orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we simply normalize ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{‖{a}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{‖{a}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by ${Q}^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 4 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 4 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the QR Factorization of a Matrix
questions.problem:
$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{q}_{11} & {q}_{12} \\ {q}_{21} & {q}_{22} \\ {q}_{31} & {q}_{32}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} \\ 0 & {r}_{22}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find the value of $\frac{{r}_{22}}{{q}_{12}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-(-\frac{1}{3})[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+(\frac{1}{3})[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ 0 & \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ 0 & \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{r}_{22}}{{q}_{12}}=\frac{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}})}{(\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}})}=2.$

$$

$P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]$, then ${P}^{6}=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${P}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{2} & =P\cdot P \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =P\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${P}^{2}=P,$ so $P$ is an idempotent matrix.

We can use this fact to compute ${P}^{6}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{6} & ={P}^{2}\cdot {P}^{2}\cdot {P}^{2} \\  & =P\cdot P\cdot P \\  & ={P}^{2}\cdot P \\  & =P\cdot P \\  & ={P}^{2} \\  & =P\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{P}^{6}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Constructing a Stochastic Matrix Given Some Data
questions.problem:
In a particular country, there are two groups of people: those who use trains to travel and those who use cars. A study has shown that, each year 

- $42%$ of people who used trains swap to cars, and

- $33%$ of people who used cars swap to trains.

Which of the following tables describes how these people change their preferences each year?
questions.worked_solution:
We are given the following situation for each year: 

- $42%$ of people who used trains swap to cars. This implies that $58%$ of them remain using trains.

- $33%$ of people who used cars swap to trains. This implies that $67%$ of them remain using cars.

Writing this information in tabular form, we obtain the following:

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Trains** | **Cars** |
| To: | **Trains** | $0.58$ | $0.33$ |
| **Cars** | $0.42$ | $0.67$ |  |

Note that we can write a corresponding stochastic matrix as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.58 & 0.33 \\ 0.42 & 0.67\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Constructing a Stochastic Matrix and Making a Prediction
questions.problem:
A certain company produces two types of footwear: casual and sports. The following table describes how the number of customers changes between both types of footwear each year:

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Casual** | **Sports** |
| To: | **Casual** | $0.55$ | $0.7$ |
| **Sports** | $0.45$ | $0.3$ |  |

That is, $45%$ of casual customers switch to sports each year, and $70%$ of sports customers change to casual.

Currently, $700\,000$ customers purchase casual footwear, while $300\,000$ customers purchase sports footwear. How many customers will purchase sports footwear in one year? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix: 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.55 & 0.7 \\ 0.45 & 0.3\end{aligned}]
$$

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of footwear is

$$
[\begin{aligned}700\,000 \\ 300\,000\end{aligned}].
$$

Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(1\,000\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

$$
{x}_{0}=\frac{1}{1\,000\,000}[\begin{aligned}700\,000 \\ 300\,000\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.7 \\ 0.3\end{aligned}]
$$

To find the state vector ${x}_{1}$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.55 & 0.7 \\ 0.45 & 0.3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.7 \\ 0.3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.595 \\ 0.405\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, after one year, $40.5%$ of customers will purchase sports footwear. Computing $40.5%$ of $1\,000\,000,$ we obtain

$$
1\,000\,000\cdot 0.405=405\,000.
$$

Therefore, $405\,000$ customers will purchase sports footwear in one year.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Stochastic Vectors and Stochastic Matrices
questions.problem:
Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 \\ 1.1 & 0.8\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.9 & 0.8\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.5\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$ A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

- Matrix $U$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (it contains negative entries): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 \\ 1.1 & 0.8\end{aligned}]
$$

- Matrix $V$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one): 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.9 & 0.8\end{aligned}]\,\begin{aligned}0.1+0.9=1 \\ 0.2+0.8=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- Matrix $W$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are non-negative and add up to one): 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.5\end{aligned}]\,\begin{aligned}0.5+0+0.5=1 \\ 0+1+0=1 \\ 0.5+0+0.5=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$V$ and $W$ only."
