questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function with $f(2)=3,{f}^{′}(2)=2,{f}^{″}(2)=-4$ and ${f}^{‴}(2)=6.$ Which of the following is the third-degree Taylor polynomial for $f$ about $x=2?$
questions.worked_solution:
The third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2)+\frac{{f}^{″}(2)}{2!}(x-2)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(2)}{3!}(x-2)^{3} \\  & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2)+\frac{{f}^{″}(2)}{2}(x-2)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(2)}{6}(x-2)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We have been given the following set of values: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & =3 \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =2 \\ {f}^{″}(2) & =-4 \\ {f}^{‴}(2) & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given values into our Taylor polynomial, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =3+2(x-2)+\frac{-4}{2}(x-2)^{2}+\frac{6}{6}(x-2)^{3} \\  & =3+2(x-2)-2(x-2)^{2}+(x-2)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ about $x=0$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the third-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!} \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to compute $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡0=-1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(0) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0)$ into our third-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =1+0\cdot x-1\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+0\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{6} \\  & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the coefficient of $(x-1)^{3}$ in the third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ about $x=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The coefficient of $(x-1)^{3}$ is $\frac{1}{3!}{f}^{(3)}(1).$ Let's compute the necessary derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt[3]{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{2}{9}{x}^{-5/3} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{10}{27}{x}^{-8/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate ${f}^{‴}(1),$ which gives

$$
{f}^{‴}(-1)=\frac{10}{27}\cdot {1}^{-8/3}=\frac{10}{27}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(1)=\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{10}{27}=\frac{5}{81}.
$$

So the coefficient of $(x-1)^{3}$ is $\frac{5}{81}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying a Quadratic Curve Type
questions.problem:
Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}-2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-26.
$$

 

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}+4\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}-2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-26
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}-2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2} & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{5}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2})-2\sqrt{5}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2}) & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{2} & =-26\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{2} & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+({y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{2}+25)-25 & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{({y}_{2}-5)}^{2}-25 & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{({y}_{2}-5)}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2}={y}_{2}-5,\end{aligned}
$$

 

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{z}_{1}^{2}+{z}_{2}^{2} & =-1 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}})^{2}}+{z}_{2}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

This defines an empty set, also called an imaginary ellipse. Notice that the left-hand side is non-negative for all ${z}_{1}$ and ${z}_{2},$ while the right-hand side is negative.

questions.problem:
Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,11{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}+12{x}_{1}+16{x}_{2}=20.
$$

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=11{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $20{y}_{2}^{2}-5{y}_{1}^{2}$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{11{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}+12{x}_{1}+16{x}_{2}=20
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{3}{5}{y}_{1}+\frac{4}{5}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}=\frac{4}{5}{y}_{1}-\frac{3}{5}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}11{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}+12{x}_{1}+16{x}_{2} & =20 \\ 20{y}_{2}^{2}-5{y}_{1}^{2}+12(\frac{3}{5}{y}_{1}+\frac{4}{5}{y}_{2})+16(\frac{4}{5}{y}_{1}-\frac{3}{5}{y}_{2}) & =20 \\ 20{y}_{2}^{2}-5{y}_{1}^{2}+20{y}_{1} & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{1}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}20{y}_{2}^{2}-5{y}_{1}^{2}+20{y}_{1} & =20 \\ 4{y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{1} & =4 \\ 4{y}_{2}^{2}-({y}_{1}^{2}-4{y}_{1}+4-4) & =4 \\ 4{y}_{2}^{2}-({y}_{1}-2)^{2}+4 & =4 \\ 4{y}_{2}^{2}-({y}_{1}-2)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}={y}_{1}-2, \\ {z}_{2}={y}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}_{2}^{2}-({y}_{1}-2)^{2} & =0 \\ 4{z}_{2}^{2}-{z}_{1}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

This represents the pair of intersecting lines ${z}_{1}=2{z}_{2}$ and ${z}_{1}=-2{z}_{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero
questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-5}^{5}2{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-4}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-1}^{1}3{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=2{x}^{4}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =2(-x)^{4} \\  & =2{x}^{4} \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6(-x)) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-6x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x) \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $f(x)=3{e}^{-x}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =3{e}^{-(-x)} \\  & =3{e}^{x} \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-5}^{5}\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{0}^{2}x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}}$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\frac{(-x)}{1+(-x)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}} \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $g(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $h(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}h(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem: Simplify the integral ${\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ using symmetry.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

questions.problem: Simplify the integral ${\int }_{-4}^{4}\sqrt[3]{x}\,\text{d}x$ using symmetry.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\sqrt[3]{x} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{(-x)} \\  & =-\sqrt[3]{x} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{4}\sqrt[3]{x}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{0}^{10}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x=A,$ what is the value of ${\int }_{-10}^{0}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=2\sqrt[5]{x}$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =2\sqrt[5]{(-x)} \\  & =-2\sqrt[5]{x} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=2\sqrt[5]{x}$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-10}^{10}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-10}^{10}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-10}^{0}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{10}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-10}^{0}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x+A & =0 \\ {\int }_{-10}^{0}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property
questions.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,e]\times [e,{e}^{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x})\text{ }(\frac{1}{y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{e}^{{e}^{2}}\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{1}^{e}\cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡y]_{e}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡e) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{\sqrt{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,{x}^{1/2}\,{y}^{1/2}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}})\text{ }(\sqrt{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral When the Integrand Contains Only One Variable
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(3{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2})\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}3{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}6{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{-1}^{0}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2({x}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{0}) \\  & =2({0}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}6{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{2}6{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{y}^{3}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\cdot {2}^{3}-0 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(3{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=2+16=18.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[1,2]\times [0,8].$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & =(8-0){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{0}^{8}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{8} \\  & =\frac{{8}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A=3+32=35.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[1,e]\times [0,\pi ].$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(\pi -0){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi \cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\pi (\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =(e-1)[-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(e-1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =2(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A=\pi +2(e-1)=2e+\pi -2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate ${∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[-3,0]\times [0,4].$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-0){\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]_{-3}^{0} \\  & =4(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-3)){\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =3(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot 4=12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A=36-24+12=24.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate ${∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[0,3]\times [0,2].$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A=2\,\text{Area}(R)=2\cdot (3\cdot 2)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot [{x}^{2}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =2({3}^{2}-(0)^{2}) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2y\,\text{d}A & =(3-0){\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3\cdot [{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3({2}^{3}-{0}^{3}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=12+18-24=6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Additivity of Double Integrals
questions.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
{∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=12,\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=-8,
$$

find the value of 

$$
{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =3({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =3(12-8) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A$, where

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\, & \text{if}\,-1<x<1,\,0<y<\pi , \\ x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\, & \text{if}\,1<x<2,\,0<y<\pi ,\end{aligned}
$$

and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have $R={R}_{1}\cup {R}_{2}$, where ${R}_{1}=(-1,1)\times (0,\pi )$ and ${R}_{2}=(1,2)\times (0,\pi ).$ So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A= & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & =(1-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y+({\int }_{1}^{2}x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2[\operatorname{sin}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi }+[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]_{1}^{2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(0)+(2-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (-(-1)+1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} xy\ \!e^{x+y}\ \textrm d A$ over the rectangle $R= [0,1] \times [1,2].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R}  xy\  e^{x+y}\: \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R} \Big( x\ \! e^x \Big)\Big( y\ \! e^{y} \Big) \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= \left(\int_0^1x\  e^{x}  \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_1^2 y \ \!e^{y} \ \textrm d y\right)\[5pt]
                                                                         &= \Big[x\ \!e^x-e^x\Big]_0^1 \cdot  \Big[y\ \!e^y-e^y\Big]_1^2\[5pt]
                                                                         &=  \Big(e^1-e^1 - \left(0-e^0\right)\Big) \cdot \Big(2e^2-e^2 - \left(e^1-e^1\right) \Big)\[5pt]
                                                                         &= 1\cdot e^2\[5pt]
                                                                         &= e^2
}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \left(x^2-y^2 +3\right)  \textrm d A,$  where $R= [-1,3] \times [2, 4].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\text{ }\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each of the three integrals.

- The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-2){\int }_{-1}^{3}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-1}^{3} \\  & =2(\frac{27}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{56}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-(-1)){\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{4}^{3}-\frac{4}{3}{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{224}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the third integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A=3\,\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot (2\cdot 4)=24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}A=\frac{56}{3}-\frac{224}{3}+24=-32.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
\iint\limits_{C}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = 8,
\qquad
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = -5,
$$

find the value of 

$$
\iint\limits_{C \cup D}  3f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =3({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =3(8+(-5)) \\  & =3\cdot 3 \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/fe/feda4016e31449244cf758fe239e49c6dd384a91b216763f72210b3c1b213827.png)
and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have $R = R_1 \cup R_2,$ where $R_1= (0,2) \times (-1,0)$ and $R_2= (0,2) \times (0,1).$ So, we can write

$$
\eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R_1} 2 \ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{R_2}    \dfrac{1}{xy+x+y+1} \ \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= 2\iint\limits_{R_1} \textrm d A
+ \iint\limits_{R_2}  \dfrac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)} \ \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= 2(2-0)(0-(-1)) + \Bigg( \int_0^2 \dfrac{1}{x+1} \ \textrm d x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int_0^1 \dfrac{1}{y+1}\ \textrm d y \Bigg) \[5pt]
&= 4 + \Big[\ln(x+1)\Big]_0^2  \cdot \Big[\ln(y+1)\Big]_0^1\[5pt] 
&= 4+ \ln 3\ln 2.
}
$$

questions.problem:
$\,$ $∀x\in R,{x}^{2}\in {R}^{+}$

Which of the following expresses the statement given above?
questions.worked_solution:
The universal quantifier "$∀$" means "for all." So, our quantified statement reads as follows:

$\,$ **For all** $x\in R,{x}^{2}\in {R}^{+}.$

This can be further simplified as follows:

$\,$ The square of any real number is positive.

**Note:** This statement is false.

questions.problem:
$\,$ $P(z):$ ${e}^{z}<0$ or ${z}^{4}\le -1.$

Given that the above predicate is defined over the universal set $R,$ which of the following statements are true?

- The truth set of $P(z)$ is $∅.$
- The truth set of $P(z)$ is $R.$
- $∀z\in R,\,P(z).$
questions.worked_solution:
The *universal quantification* of a predicate $P(x),$ defined over the universal set $U,$ transforms this predicate into a statement that we write as

$$
∀x\in U,\,P(x).
$$

This statement is true if the predicate $P(x)$ is true on the entire universal set $U,$ i.e. if the truth set ${T}_{P}$ of the predicate coincides with the universal set $U:$

$$
{T}_{P}=U
$$

First, notice that:

- the truth set of "${e}^{z}<0$" is $∅,$ and

- the truth set of "${z}^{4}\le -1$" is $∅.$

So, the truth set of our predicate is 

$$
{T}_{P}=∅\cup ∅=∅.
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given statements.

- Statement I is true. The truth set is empty.

- Statement II is false. Indeed, ${T}_{P}\ne R.$

- Statement III is false. Since ${T}_{P}$ does *not* coincide with the universal set, the statement $∀z\in R,\,P(z)$ is false.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

choices.value: None of the statements are true

- the truth set of "$|x|\ge 1$" is $(-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).$

$$
{T}_{P}=(-\infty ,1)\cap ((-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ))=(-\infty ,-1].
$$

- Statement I is false. The truth set is *not* empty.

- Statement II is false. Indeed, ${T}_{P}\ne R.$

- Statement III is true. Since ${T}_{P}$ is not empty, the statement $∃x\in R,\,P(x)$ is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

$$

$$
T_P = U
$$

First, notice that:

- the truth set of "$\dfrac{n}{3} \in \mathbb{Q}$" is $\mathbb{N},$ and

- the truth set of "$\sqrt{n}\in \mathbb{N}$" is $\{n=m^2 : m \in \mathbb{N} \} = \{1,4,9,16, 25, \ldots \}.$

So, the truth set of our predicate is 

$$
T_P = \mathbb{N} \cup  \{1,4,9,16, 25, \ldots \} =\mathbb N.
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given statements.

- Statement I is false. The truth set is *not* empty.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $T_P= \mathbb{N}.$

- Statement III is true. Since $T_P$ coincides with the universal set, the statement $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n)$ is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}} & =-2 \\ z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =-2{e}^{x-y} \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=-2$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}.$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,e)$ is the surface $z=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{xy}.$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}$ that passes through the point $P(1,0,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,-1) & =\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{z}^{2}} & =1 \\ {z}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,0,-1)$ is the cone ${z}^{2}={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{xy}$ that passes through the point $P(1,1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,2) & =\frac{(2)-(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}{(1)(1)}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{z-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{xy} & =2 \\ z-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2xy \\ z & ={x}^{2}+2xy-{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,2)$ is the surface $z={x}^{2}+2xy-{y}^{2}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface
canonical_examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z) = x^2+4y^2-z,$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c = 0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-z & =0 \\ z & ={x}^{2}+4{y}^{2} \\ z & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{1/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=0$ is the elliptic paraboloid $z = x^2+\dfrac{y^2}{{1/4}}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Describing a Level Surface of a Function
canonical_examples.problem: Find the family of surfaces that describe the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y, z) = \ln(x^2 + 2y^2 - z^2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & ={e}^{c} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}+\frac{2{y}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{{e}^{c}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of hyperboloids of one sheet:

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{e^c} + \dfrac{y^2}{e^c/2} - \dfrac{z^2}{e^c} =  1, \qquad c \in (-\infty,\infty)
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z) = \sin{xyz}$ that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
  f\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&= \sin \left(\pi\cdot 1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} = 1}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c = 1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡xyz & =1 \\ xyz & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2\pi k\end{aligned}
$$

where $k$ is any integer.

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is the surface $xyz= \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k,$ where $k$ is any integer.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Images of the Four Fundamental Subspaces of the Matrix Under Its Action
questions.problem: Let $A$ be a $m\times n$ matrix. What is the image of $\text{Col}(A)$ under the action of ${A}^{T}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First,  notice that ${A}^{T}$ is a $n\times m$ matrix.

Now, pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{m}$ by ${A}^{T}$ gives a linear combination of the columns of ${A}^{T}:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ {a}_{1}^{T} & {a}_{2}^{T} & ⋯ & {a}_{m}^{T} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{T}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{m}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{1}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{2}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]+⋯+{x}_{m}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{m}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{m}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}$ must be $\text{Col}({A}^{T}),$ the column space of ${A}^{T},$ or equivalently, the row space of $A.$

Furthermore, since $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$ is mapped to the zero vector $0$ by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement $\text{Col}(({A}^{T})^{T})=\text{Col}(A)$ must be $\text{Col}({A}^{T}).$

This can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8ca8508d05e28e4c91b5a7f3c65826ce68b5dacd382bfb1a76f09c09d1d004bf.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Orthogonal Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix
questions.problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Null}({B}^{T})$ for every matrix $B?$

- $\text{Null}(B)$
- $\text{Col}(B)$
- $\text{Col}({B}^{T})$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{Null}({B}^{T})$ is the left null space of $B.$ This consists of vectors that, when pre-multiplied by ${B}^{T},$ result in the zero-vector $0.$

When pre-multiplying a vector by ${B}^{T},$ we actually multiply each row of ${B}^{T}$, that is, each column of $B$, by that vector. So, $\text{Null}({B}^{T})$ must be orthogonal to the column space of $B,$ which is $\text{Col}(B).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

**Note:** In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $B$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvectors of a 3x3 Matrix
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is an upper triangular matrix, we have that its eigenvalues are the entries in the main diagonal, that is, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

Also, since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & -9 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ -9{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 0=0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the augmented matrix $M$ is already in its row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 7 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{2}{9}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{4}(7{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(7(\frac{2}{9}{x}_{3})+2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{32}{9}{x}_{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{9}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{2}{9}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=9,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2 \\ 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{8}{2}=4.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Eigenvector Corresponding to a Given Eigenvalue
questions.problem: Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $2$nd and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvectors of a 3x3 Matrix
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )[(3-\lambda )^{2}-1] & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-(2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System
questions.problem:
Find the least-squares solution to the system of linear equations given below. You're given that the columns of the corresponding coefficient matrix are linearly independent.

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=5 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2 \\ -3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=4\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}}\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}14 & 7 \\ 7 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{35}[\begin{aligned}6 & -7 \\ -7 & 14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Find the least-squares solution to the system of linear equations given below. You're given that the columns of the corresponding coefficient matrix are linearly independent.

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=8 \\ 4{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=2 \\ -4{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=2 \\ 4{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=-6\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 4 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ -6\end{aligned}]}}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 & 4 \\ -4 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 4 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}])}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 & 4 \\ -4 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}36 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 36 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 36\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -36 \\ 36\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{36}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -36 \\ 36\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Distance Between a Vector to a Subspace of Solutions of a Linear System
questions.problem:
Consider the system $Ax=b$, where the matrix $A$ and the vector $b$ are shown below. Given that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, find the minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖.$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 12 \\ 0 \\ 12 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 12 \\ 0 \\ 12 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ Ax & =b\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 12 \\ 0 \\ 12 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}16 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}16 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖$ is attained when $x=\overset{^}{x},$ which is the least-squares solution of the system $Ax=b.$ In this case, $A\overset{^}{x}$ represents the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A,$ and $‖A\overset{^}{x}-b‖$ is the distance between the vector $b$ and the column space. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}A\overset{^}{x}-b & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 \\ 8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 12 \\ 0 \\ 12 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -4 \\ -8 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
‖A\overset{^}{x}-b‖=\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-8)^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=2\sqrt{26}.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{0}^{x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region
questions.problem:
Calculate ${∬}_{D}x\,dA,\,$
where $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{3}\le y\le x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{3}\le y\le x}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{x}x\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{x}x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{x}x\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{x}dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x{[\,y\,]}_{{x}^{3}}^{x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(x-{x}^{3})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{4})dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{4})dx & ={[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region
questions.problem:
Calculate ${∬}_{D}(1-y)\,dA,\,$
where $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,x\le y\le \sqrt{x}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,x\le y\le \sqrt{x}}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-y)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{x}}(1-y)\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{x}}(1-y)\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{x}}(1-y)\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{x}^{\sqrt{x}}dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{x})^{2}-x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2\sqrt{x}-3x+{x}^{2})dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2\sqrt{x}-3x+{x}^{2})dx & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{1/2}-3x+{x}^{2})dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3/2}-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{4}{3}(1)^{3/2}-\frac{3}{2}(1)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{4}{3}-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](images/78/786dd06154d1bda5483ed992dce8922c9629f759b498a3f713c35612311c1ee6.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA,$
where $D$ is the finite region below the line $y=2$ enclosed by the lines $y=x$ and $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- We already know the intersection of the line $y=x$ with the line $y=2.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$0\le x\le 2.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/92/92b1eda4ccf9e62e1f7310b1ba9bef5cc6c434755e74196d1829a30f2c4a3c53.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,x\le y\le 2}
$$

So, we can express the integral, as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{8}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{8}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})\,dx & ={[\frac{8x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{12}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}-\frac{4}{3}-0 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Calculate ${∬}_{D}\frac{{e}^{2y}}{x}\,dA,$
where $D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 5,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\le y\le 3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 5,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\le y\le 3}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{e}^{2y}}{x}\,dA & ={\int }_{1}^{5}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}^{3}\frac{{e}^{2y}}{x}\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}^{3}\frac{{e}^{2y}}{x}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{x}[{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}^{3}{e}^{2y}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{x}{[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2y}]}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}^{3}dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{5}(\frac{{e}^{6}}{x}-\frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{x})dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{5}(\frac{{e}^{6}}{x}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{x})dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{5}(\frac{{e}^{6}}{x}-x)dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{5}(\frac{{e}^{6}}{x}-x)dx & =\frac{1}{2}{[{e}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(({e}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-\frac{25}{2})-({e}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{2}-6\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral When the Limits are Given
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $x=0,$ $y=0,$ and the curve $y=\sqrt{4 - x^2}.$ What is $\displaystyle \iint\limits_D (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}A$ expressed as a repeated integral?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region, as usual.

![](images/3d/3d67d73d3ede011d6c2fe4bc9e160aa3c2af522bff6cddfcc7c351c97418e764.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x  \leq 2, \quad 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt{4-x^2} \big\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(x+y)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}(x+y)\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral When the Limits are Not Given
canonical_examples.problem: If $D$ is the finite region in the first quadrant enclosed by the curves $y=3x$ and $y=x^3,$ then what is $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} f\left( {x,y} \right) \, \mathrm{d}A$ expressed as a repeated integral?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](images/f8/f8a5fd7fc3e98d7f08b5ea48636e5de4a1a45b7a94fbe9e968789afcfe3a582c.png)

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =3x \\ {x}^{3}-3x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are $0 \le x \le \sqrt{3}.$ Note that we disregarded the solution $x=-\sqrt 3$ since $x\geq 0$ in our region.

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region, as usual.

![](images/23/232f885d2230694bf62f81f5987cd2b3a12a49430d90d2cae4712c552587a48c.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x  \leq \sqrt{3}, \quad x^3 \leq y \leq 3x \right\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{3x}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}[{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{3x}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Repeated Integral Defined Over a Type I Region
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_0^x x^2y \,\textrm{d}y \,\textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{x}y\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-0)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{4}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{4}\,dx & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{5}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region
canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} xy\,\mathrm{d}A,\:$
where $D$ is the finite region below the $x$-axis enclosed by the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $y \leq 0,$ we obtain

$$
x^2 + y^2 = 4
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
y = -\sqrt{4-x^2}.
$$

Let's sketch our region.

![](images/31/31e7bb281a36a3676730de0883d7abd5445093713de1bbd41899cce50a7e0e48.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- We already know the intersection of the circle with the line $y=0.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$-2 \le x \le 2.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/2a/2a84d17b83fb1e2036c6edc0a71c5c10a58bf893c33bbf38662ebb417aab3164.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D = \Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq x \leq 2, \quad -\sqrt{4-x^2} \leq y \leq 0 \Big\}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\iint \limits_{D} xy\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{-2}^2 \int_{-\sqrt{4-x^2}}^{0} xy\,\mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}^{0}xy\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}x[{\int }_{-\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}^{0}y\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}x{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{-\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}^{0}\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}x(0-(-\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}})^{2})\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}x(-(4-{x}^{2}))\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}x({x}^{2}-4)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}({x}^{3}-4x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}({x}^{3}-4x)\,dx & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-2{x}^{2}]}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((4-8)-(4-8)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Translating Statements Involving Nested Quantifiers
questions.problem:
$\,$ $∃\,m,n\in N,\,m+n=10.$

Which of the following expresses the statement given above?
questions.worked_solution:
Our quantified statement reads as follows:

$\,$ There **exists** $m\in N$ and there **exists** $n\in N$ **such that** $m+n=10.$

This can be re-phrased as follows:

$\,$ There exist natural numbers $m$ and $n$ such that $m+n=10.$

choices.value: There exist natural numbers $m$ and $n$ such that $m+n=10.$
For any natural $n$ there exists a natural $m$ such that $m+n=10.$
There exists a natural $m$ such that for all natural $n,$ $m+n=10.$
For every natural $m$ there exists a natural $n$ such that $m+n=10.$

answer_fields.correct_value: There exist natural numbers $m$ and $n$ such that $m+n=10.$

questions.problem:
$\,$ $∃\,n\in N,\,∀\,m\in Z,\,nm$ is divisible by $2.$

questions.worked_solution:
Our quantified statement reads as follows:

$\,$ **There exists** $n\in N$ **such that**, **for all** $m\in Z,\,nm$ is divisible by $2.$

This can be re-phrased as follows:

$\,$ There exists a natural number $n$ such that the product of $n$ and any integer $m$ is divisible by $2.$

choices.value: There are natural numbers whose product with some integers is divisible by $2.$
There exists a natural number $n$ such that the product of $n$ and any integer $m$ is divisible by $2.$
There exists an integer $n$ such that the product of $n$ and any natural number $m$ is divisible by $2.$
Given an integer $n$ there is a natural number $m$ such that the product $nm$ is multiple of $2.$
Given a natural number $n,$ there is an integer $m$ such that the product $nm$ is even.

answer_fields.correct_value: There exists a natural number $n$ such that the product of $n$ and any integer $m$ is divisible by $2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Free and Bound Occurrences of Variables
questions.problem:
$$
(\,∀x\in N,\,x>{n}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{I}\end{aligned}}+1\,)⇒(\,∃z\in R,\,{{z}^{3}}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{II}\end{aligned}}-1={y}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{III}\end{aligned}}\,)
$$

Which occurrences of the variables in the expression above are free?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our expression and mark the occurrences of the variables as bound $(\text{b})$ or free $(\text{f}).$

- Occurrence I of the variable $n$ is *free* since it isn't placed right next to a quantifier and it doesn't lie within the scope of a quantifier that uses $n.$

- Occurrence II of the variable $z$ is *bound* since it lies within the scope of the quantifier $∃z$ that uses $z:$ 

$$
(\,∀x\in N,\,x>n+1\,)⇒(\,∃z\in R,\,\overset{\text{scope of }∃z}{\overset{⏞}{{z}^{3}-1={y}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{b}\end{aligned}}}}\,)
$$

- Occurrence III of the variable $y$ is *free* since it isn't placed right next to a quantifier and it doesn't lie within the scope of a quantifier that uses $y.$

The occurrences of variables in the expression are as follows:

$$
(\,∀{x}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{b}\end{aligned}}\in N,\,{x}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{b}\end{aligned}}>{n}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{f}\end{aligned}}+1\,)⇒(\,∃{z}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{b}\end{aligned}}\in R,\,{{z}^{3}}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{b}\end{aligned}}-1={y}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{f}\end{aligned}}\,)
$$

Therefore, the free occurrence is "I and III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Truth Value of a Statement Involving Nested Quantifiers
questions.problem:
Let $x\in R$ and $y\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $∀\,y\in R,\,2y=0.$
- The truth set of the predicate $(\,∀y\in R,\,xy=0\,)$ is $∅.$
- $∃\,x\in R,\,∀y\in R,\,xy=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the statement 

$$
∃\,x\in R,\,∀y\in R,\,xy=0
$$

from option III reads as follows:

$\,$ There exists a real $x$ such that, for every real $y,$ we have $xy=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false since $2y=0$ is not true for some real $y.$ Say, for $y=1.$

- Statement II is false.  The predicate

$$
P(x):\,∀\,y\in R,\,xy=0
$$

is true for some $x\in R.$ For example, 

$$
P(0):\,∀\,y\in R,\,0\cdot y=0
$$

is true. Therefore, its truth set is not empty.

- Statement III is true. The sentence 

$$
(\,∃\,x\in R,\,∀y\in R,\,xy=0\,)
$$

can be written as

$$
∃\,x\in R\,(\,{{∀y\in R,\,xy=0}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}\,)
$$

which is true whenever the inner predicate $P(x)$ has a nonempty truth set. And according to statement II, this is the case.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

choices.value: None of the statements are true

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Truth Value of a Statement Involving Nested Quantifiers
questions.problem:
Let $m\in N$ and $n\in N.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $∀\,n\in N,\,1\le n.$
- The truth set of the predicate $(\,∀\,n\in N,\,m\le n\,)$ is $N.$
- $∀\,m,n\in N,\,m\le n.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the statement 

$$
∀\,m,n\in N,\,m\le n
$$

from option III reads as follows:

$\,$ For all natural $m$ and $n,$ we have $m\le n.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true, since $1\le n$ for all natural numbers $n.$

- Statement II is false. For the predicate

$$
P(m):\,∀\,n\in N,\,m\le n
$$

we note that $P(m)$ is true for some $m\in N$ and false for others. For example,

is true. However, 

$$

$$

is false, since $2≰1.$

can be written as

$$
∀m\in N\,(\,{{∀n\in N,\,m\le n}_{⏟}}_{P(m)}\,)
$$

which is true whenever the inner predicate $P(m)$ is true over the universal set $N.$ But, according to statement II, this is not the case.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:

- $∃\,n\in N,\,5\le n.$
- The truth set of the predicate $(\,∃n\in N,\,m\le n\,)$ is $N.$
- $∀\,m\in N,\,∃n\in N,\,m\le n.$

$$

$$

from option III reads as follows:

$\,$ For every natural $m$ there exists natural $n$ such that $m\le n.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true since $5\le n$ for some natural number $n$ (e.g., for $n=6$).

- Statement II is true. The predicate

$$
P(m):\,∃\,n\in N,\,m\le n
$$

is true for any natural $m.$ For example,

$$
P(1):\,∃\,n\in N,\,1\le n
$$

is true since we can take $n=2.$ Similarly,

$$
P(2):\,∃\,n\in N,\,2\le n
$$

is true since we can take $n=3.$ And so on. In general, it's sufficient to take $n=m+1.$

- Statement III is true. The sentence 

$$
(\,∀\,m\in N,\,∃n\in N,\,m\le n\,)
$$

can be written as

$$
∀\,m\in N\,(\,{{∃n\in N,\,m\le n}_{⏟}}_{P(m)}\,)
$$

which is true whenever the inner predicate $P(m)$ is true over the universal set $N.$ And, according to statement II, this is the case.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem:
Let $x\in Z$ and $y\in Z.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $∀\,x\in Z,\,x+1=0.$
- The truth set of the predicate $(\,∀x\in Z,\,x+y=0\,)$ is $∅.$
- $∃\,y\in Z,\,∀x\in Z,\,x+y=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the statement 

$$
∃\,y\in Z,\,∀x\in Z,\,x+y=0
$$

from option III reads as follows:

$\,$ There exists a integer $y$ such that, for every integer $x,$ we have $x+y=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false since $x+1=0$ is not true for some integer $x.$ Say, for $x=1.$

- Statement II is true. The predicate

$$
P(y):\,∀x\in Z,\,x+y=0
$$

is false for every value of $y.$ For example,

$$
P(0):∀\,x\in Z,\,x=0
$$

is false for any $x\ne 0.$ In general, it's sufficient to take $x\ne -y$ for any $y\in Z.$ Therefore, its truth set is empty.

- Statement III is false. The sentence 

$$
(\,∃\,y\in Z,\,∀x\in Z,\,x+y=0\,)
$$

can be written as

$$
∃\,y\in Z\,(\,{{∀x\in Z,\,x+y=0}_{⏟}}_{P(y)}\,)
$$

which is true whenever the inner predicate $P(y)$ has a nonempty truth set. And according to statement II, this is not the case.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- $\exists \, y \in \mathbb{R}, \, 2+y=0.$

- The truth set of the predicate $\big( \, \exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y = 0 \, \big)$ is $\mathbb{R}.$

- $\forall\, x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y=0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that the statement 

$$
\forall\, x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y=0
$$

from option III reads as follows:

$\qquad$ For every real $x$ there exists real $y$ such that $x+y=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true since $2+y=0$ for some real number $y$ (e.g., for $y=-2$).

- Statement II is true. The predicate

$$
P(x): \quad \exists \, y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y=0
$$

is true for any real $x.$ For example,

$$
P(1): \quad \exists \, y \in \mathbb{R}, \, 1 + y=0
$$

is true since we can take $y=-1.$ Similarly,

$$
P(2): \quad \exists \, y \in \mathbb{R}, \, 2+ y=0
$$

is true since we can take $y=-2.$ And so on. In general, it's sufficient to take $y=-x.$

- Statement III is true. The sentence 

$$
\big( \, \forall\, x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y=0 \, \big)
$$

can be written as

$$
\forall\, x \in \mathbb{R} \, \big( \, \underbrace{\exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y=0}_{P(x)} \, \big)
$$

which is true whenever the inner predicate $P(x)$ is true over the universal set $\mathbb R.$ And, according to statement II, this is the case.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

The function $F$ can be expressed in terms of its components $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as

F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j,
$$

where

$$
P(x,y)=y\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-{x}^{2}),\,Q(x,y)=x\sqrt{1-|y|}.

We first find the domain of each component function. Then, we compute their intersection to find the domain of $F:$

$$
1-{x}^{2}>0\,⟹\,-1<x<1.
$$

This defines the region ${D}_{1},$ shown below:

![](images/89/89c78ec587826c15c90ef4ffdfc0fd9f8af3d7b4d3d1cc099ce24b883b9842c2.png)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Vector Fields on Two-Dimensions
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following are vector fields on $\mathbb R^2?$

- $\mathbf A(x,y) = \sqrt{x}\,\mathbf i + y^3\,\mathbf j$

- $\mathbf B(x,y,z) = \ln y\,\mathbf i - (x+y)\,\mathbf j  + z\,\mathbf k$

- $\mathbf C(t) = \sin{t}\,\mathbf i + (2-t^3)\,\mathbf j$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Suppose that $S$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^2.$ A vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ is a function $\mathbf F$ that maps every point $(x,y)$ in $S$ to a vector $\mathbf F(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2.$

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $\mathbf A(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2.$ It maps every point in the set $S,$ given by

$$
S = \big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \:|\: x \geq 0\big\}
$$

to a vector in $\mathbb R^2.$

- The function $\mathbf B(x,y,z)$ is *not* a vector field on $\mathbb R^2.$ It is a vector field on $\mathbb R^3.$

- The function $\mathbf C(t)$ is *not* a vector field on $\mathbb R^2.$  It assigns points in $\mathbb{R}$ (not $\mathbb{R^2}$) to vectors in $\mathbb{R^2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following are vector fields on $\mathbb R^3?$

- $\mathbf R(x,y,z) = 2\,\mathbf i - x\,\mathbf j + y\,\mathbf k$

- $\mathbf S(x,y) = 2x\,\mathbf i - y^3\,\mathbf j$

- $\mathbf T(x,y,z) = \dfrac{x}{z}\,\mathbf i - \dfrac{y}{z}\,\mathbf j + \dfrac{z}{2}\,\mathbf k$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Suppose that $S$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^3.$ A vector field on $\mathbb R^3$ is a function $\mathbf F$ that maps every point $(x,y,z)\in S$ to a vector $\mathbf F(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3.$

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $\mathbf R(x,y,z)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^3.$ It assigns every point $(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R^3}$ to a vector in $\mathbb{R^3}.$

- The function $\mathbf S(x,y)$ is *not* a vector field on $\mathbb R^3.$ It assigns points in $\mathbb R^2$ (not $\mathbb R^3$) to vectors in $\mathbb R^2$ (not $\mathbb R^3$).

- The function $\mathbf T(x,y,z)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^3.$ It assigns every point in the set $S,$ given by

$$
S = \big\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3\:|\: z \neq 0\big\}
$$

to a vector in $\mathbb R^3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the domain of the vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) =\dfrac{1}{x^2+y^2}\, \mathbf{i} + \sqrt{1+x-y} \, \mathbf{j}\,.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function $\mathbf F$ can be expressed in terms of its components $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j,
$$

where

$$
P(x,y) =\dfrac{1}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad Q(x,y) = \sqrt{1+x-y} .
$$

We first find the domain of each component function. Then, we compute their intersection to find the domain of $\mathbf F\mathbin{:}$

- The function $P(x,y)$ is defined everywhere other than when the denominator vanishes. To find where the denominator vanishes, we set it equal to zero and solve:

$$
x^2 + y^2 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow \quad x=y = 0
$$

Therefore, the domain of $P$ is given by

$$
D_1 = \big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\: | \: (x,y)\neq (0,0)\big\}.
$$

The region $D_1$ is the entire plane $\mathbb R^2$ with the origin removed, as shown below.

![](images/d4/d4a418bc0dbfc61c0e55c494db51ee0fa8125b6b7056ccbe4e32ddca82574dc2.png)

- The function $Q(x,y)$ is defined when the expression under the radical is positive or zero. To find the domain, we solve the following inequality:

$$
1+x - y \geq 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad y\leq 1 + x
$$

Therefore, the domain of $Q$ is given by

$$
D_2 = \big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\: | \: y \leq 1 + x\big\}.
$$

The region $D_2,$ shown below:

![](images/24/242903cc94103f8bb9cdc190a229fe7e86395f44600e8318d728fea3bc339385.png)

Finally, the domain $D$ of $\mathbf F$ is given by 

$$
D =  D_1\cap D_2 = \big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\: | \: (x,y)\neq 0,\, y \leq 1 + x\big\}.
$$

The region $D$ is shown below.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product
questions.problem:
Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨t,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )}{2}-(-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )}{2})+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{4}{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =0+(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )}{4}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )}{4}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}+{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-(-(-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})))+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =0+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =1-(-1) \\  & =2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

- ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ differentiating we have $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$ Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{2}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(1)q(1)+p(2)q(2),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
