questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)={x}^{2}+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & ={x}^{2}+y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =(-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2x)\,i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,0) & =(-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-2\cdot (-1))\,i+(-(-1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-1)\,j \\  & =2\,i-j \\  & =⟨2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,0)=⟨2,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x+1}{2} & =-y \\ x+1 & =-2y \\ x+2y+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Curve
canonical_examples.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 +x$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1, 1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,1).$  

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,j \\  & =(2x+0+1)\,i+(0+4y+0)\,j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i+4y\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(2(1)+1)\,i+4(1)\,j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we want a unit normal vector, we normalize $\nabla f(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,1)}{‖∇f(1,1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the plane curve $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0, 4).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16} - 1,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,4).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)j \\  & =\frac{2x}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{8}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{(4)}{8}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j \\  & =⟨0,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{x-{x}_{0}}=\frac{{v}_{y}}{{v}_{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{y}(x-{x}_{0}) & ={v}_{x}(y-{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(x-0) & =0(y-4) \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the equation of the normal line to the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1$ at the point $(0,4)$ is $x=0.$

canonical_examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z) = 2x^2 - xy - z^2,$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)$ can be found by computing 
$\nabla f(2, 3, \sqrt 2).$   

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j-2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,3,\sqrt{2}) & =(4\cdot 2-3)\text{ }i-2\text{ }j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k \\  & =5i-2j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $5 \mathbf i  - 2 \mathbf j - 2 \sqrt 2\ \mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z = \ln (x^2 - xy)$ at the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z) = \ln (x^2 - xy) - z,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2){:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)k \\  & =(\frac{2x-y}{{x}^{2}-xy})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{y-x})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =(\frac{2\cdot 2-1}{{2}^{2}-2\cdot 1})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{1-2})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{3}{2}i-\,j-k \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf v = \langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2)= \left\langle  \dfrac {3} {2}, -1, -1\right  \rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-1} \\ \frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Compute $\text{E}[(X-2)(X-3)]$ if $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=5$ and $\text{E}[X]=-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Expanding out the product inside the expected value, using the properties of the expected value, and substituting in the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[(X-2)(X-3)] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}-5X+6] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]+\text{E}[-5X]+\text{E}[6] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-5\text{E}[X]+6 \\  & =5-5(-2)+6 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Higher Moments of a Random Variable
questions.problem:
A random variable $X$ has the probability distribution given below.

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $0.15$ | $0.25$ | $0.4$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ |

Calculate $\text{E}[{X}^{4}].$
questions.worked_solution:
If $X$ is a discrete random variable with probability mass function $f(x)$ and sample space $S,$ the expected value of ${X}^{4}$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{4}]={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{4}\cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each squared value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{4}] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{4}\cdot f(x) \\  & ={0}^{4}\cdot 0.15+{1}^{4}\cdot 0.25+{2}^{4}\cdot 0.4+{3}^{4}\cdot 0.05+{4}^{4}\cdot 0.15 \\  & =0\cdot 0.15+1\cdot 0.25+16\cdot 0.4+81\cdot 0.05+256\cdot 0.15 \\  & =0+0.25+6.4+4.05+38.4 \\  & =49.1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\text{u}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$ and $\text{v}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we construct a matrix where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, we find the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot 3-2\cdot 4 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

The absolute value of $det(M)$ gives the area $A$ of the parallelogram:

$$
A=|\,1\,|=1
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Missing Constants in First-Order Partial Derivative Expressions
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =axy-{x}^{2}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =y-5b{x}^{2}-7, \\ {f}_{x}(1,2) & =19.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(axy-{x}^{2}) \\  & =ax-0 \\  & =ax \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-5b{x}^{2}-7) \\  & =0-10bx-0 \\  & =-10bx\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =-10bx.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we get $b=-\frac{a}{10}.$ 

Now, since ${f}_{x}(1,2)=21$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,2) & =19 \\ a\cdot 2\cdot 1-{1}^{2} & =19 \\ 2a & =20 \\ a & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
b=-\frac{a}{10}=-\frac{10}{10}=-1.
$$

$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}2a{x}^{2}y+6x=3b{x}^{2}y+6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of ${x}^{2}y$, we see that $a=\frac{3b}{2}.$ 

Now, since ${f}_{y}(-1,1)=3$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,1) & =3 \\ b(-1)^{3}(1)+3(-1)^{2}+2 & =3 \\ -b+3+2 & =3 \\ b & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
a=\frac{3b}{2}=3.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point
questions.problem:
Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}=(x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3},\,\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}=6x{z}^{2}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3}) \\  & =(x{y}^{2}+2y)\cdot x{e}^{xy}+(2xy+2)\cdot {e}^{xy}+0 \\  & =({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4xy+2){e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(6x{z}^{2}) \\  & =12xz.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =(0+0+2){e}^{0}=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =12(1)(1)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =2+12=14.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate ${f}_{xyy}(2,2,2)$ given that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{yx}(x,y,z)=2y\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyy}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{yxy}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{yx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}) \\  & =2\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{x}(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}}) \\  & =2\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}-\frac{3}{2}{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{{y}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point  $(2,2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyy}(2,2,2) & =2\sqrt{\frac{(2)^{3}}{(2)}}-\frac{3}{2}(2)^{3}\sqrt{\frac{(2)}{(2)^{3}}} \\  & =2\cdot 2-3\cdot 2 \\  & =4-6 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b,$ if 

$$
f_x(x,y) = 6xy+axy^3-5, \qquad
f_y(x,y) = 3x^2+bx^2y^2, \qquad
f_y(2,-1) = -24.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we compute the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy+ax{y}^{3}-5) \\  & =6x+3ax{y}^{2}-0 \\  & =6x+3ax{y}^{2} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+b{x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & =6x+2bx{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. So, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & ={f}_{yx}(x,y) \\ 6x+3ax{y}^{2} & =6x+2bx{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $xy^2,$ we see that $3a=2b.$ 

Now, since $f_y(2,-1)=-24,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,-1) & =-24 \\ 3(2)^{2}+b(2)^{2}(-1)^{2} & =-24 \\ 12+4b & =-24 \\ 4b & =-36 \\ b & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}3a & =2b \\ 3a & =2(-9) \\ 3a & =-18 \\ a & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=-6$ and $b=-9.$

Consider the function $f(x,y,z).$ Given that all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z\partial x} = -e^xy\sin{(yz)},
$$

 

evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,\pi,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial z\partial x\partial z}+ \dfrac{\partial^3 f }{\partial x \partial z \partial y}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂z∂x} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂z∂x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-{e}^{x}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)) \\  & =-{e}^{x}{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz).\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂z∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂z∂x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{e}^{x}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)-{e}^{x}yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz) \\  & =-{e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)+yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,\pi,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,\pi ,1)} & =-{e}^{(1)}(\pi )^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)=e{\pi }^{2} \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂z∂y}{|}_{(1,\pi ,1)} & =-{e}^{(1)}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)+(\pi )(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1))=e\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following functions are bijections?

- $f:{R}^{+}\to R$ defined by $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$
- $g:R\to R$ defined by $g(x)={x}^{3}$
- $h:Q\to Q$ defined by $h(x)=|x|$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a function $f:X\to Y$ is a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection.

- I is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. Remember that the range of $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ is $f(x)\in (0,\infty )$ for $x\in {R}^{+}.$ So, for example, there is no value $x\in R$ such that $f(x)=-1.$

- II is a bijection. First of all, it is a surjection because $∀\,y\in R,$ we can choose an $x\in R$ such that $g(x)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =y \\ {x}^{3} & =y \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{y}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

We verify that

$$
g(x)=g(\sqrt[3]{y})={(\sqrt[3]{y})}^{3}=y.
$$

Second, it is an injection:

$$
\begin{aligned}g({x}_{1}) & =g({x}_{2}) \\ {x}_{1}^{3} & ={x}_{2}^{3} \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Because $g$ is both surjective and injective, $g$ is bijective.

- III is *not* a bijection because it is not injective. Notice that $h(-1)=1=h(1),$ while $-1\ne 1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

$$
\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{8}}={({2}^{3/2})}^{1/3}={2}^{1/2}=\sqrt{2}.
$$

- Statement III is false because the function is not a surjection.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following functions are bijections?

- $f:R\to R$ defined by $f(x)=|x|$
- $g:Q\to Q$ defined by $g(x)=4(x-2)$
- $h:Q\to R$ defined by $h(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a function $f:X\to Y$ is a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection.

- I is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. For example, there is no value $x\in R$ such that $f(x)=-1.$

- II is a bijection. First of all, it is a surjection because $∀\,y\in Q,$ we can choose an $x\in Q$ such that $g(x)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =y \\ 4(x-2) & =y \\ x & =\frac{y}{4}+2\in Q\end{aligned}
$$

We verify that, 

$$
g(x)=g(\frac{y}{4}+2)=4([\frac{y}{4}+2]-2)=y.
$$

Second, it is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}g({x}_{1}) & =g({x}_{2}) \\ 4({x}_{1}-2) & =4({x}_{2}-2) \\ {x}_{1}-2 & ={x}_{2}-2 \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Because $g$ is both surjective and injective, $g$ is bijective.

- III is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. Remember that the range of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is $[-1,1].$ This means that 

$$
-1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x\le 1.
$$

So,  for example, there is no value $x\in Q$ such that $h(x)=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

So,  for example, there is no value $x\in R$ such that $f(x)=2.$

- III is a bijection. First of all, it is a surjection because $∀\,y\in Q,$ we can choose an $x\in Q$ such that $h(x)=y:$

$$

We verify that, 

$$
h(x)=h(\frac{y+3}{8})=8(\frac{y+3}{8})-3=y.
$$

Second, it is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}h({x}_{1}) & =h({x}_{2}) \\ 8{x}_{1}-3 & =8{x}_{2}-3 \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Because $h$ is both surjective and injective, $h$ is bijective.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

- an injection if $∀\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in X,$ whenever $f({x}_{1})=f({x}_{2}),$ we have ${x}_{1}={x}_{2},$

- a surjection if $∀\,y\in Y,$ $∃\,x\in X$ such that $f(x)=y,$

- a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection.

With this in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true. Indeed

$$
\begin{aligned}f({x}_{1}) & =f({x}_{2}) \\ {x}_{1}^{3} & ={x}_{2}^{3} \\ \sqrt[3]{{x}_{1}^{3}} & =\sqrt[3]{{x}_{2}^{3}} \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false because the function is not a surjection.

Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $f:X \to Y$ represented by the mapping diagram above?

- $f$ is an injection

- $f$ is a bijection
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that a function $f: X \to Y$ is 

- a surjection if $\forall\, y \in Y,$ $\exists\, x \in X$ such that $f(x)=y,$

- an injection if $\forall\, x_1,x_2 \in X,$ whenever $f(x_1)=f(x_2),$ we have $x_1=x_2,$

- a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection.

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. According to the diagram, for every element $y \in Y,$ we have an arrow from some element $x \in X$ to it, which means that $f(x)=y.$ So, $f$ is a surjection.

- Statement II is false. We have $f(4)=f(6)$ but $4 \neq 6.$ So, it's *not true* that for all $x_1$ and $x_2$ contained within the domain $X,$ if $f(x_1)$ and $f(x_2)$ are equal, then we must have $x_1=x_2.$ As a result, $f$ is *not* an injection.

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, $f$ is not a bijection.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following functions are bijections?

- $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x) = 1-x^2$

- $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $g(x) = \sin x$

- $h: \mathbb{R} \to (0, \infty)$ defined by $h(x) = 3^x$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that a function $f: X \to Y$ is a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection.

- I is *not* a bijection because it is not injective. Notice that $f(x)=1-x^2$ has two roots, $x=\pm 1.$ So, we have $f(-1)=0=f(1),$ while $-1 \neq 1.$

- II is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. Remember that the range of $\sin x$ is $[-1,1].$ This means that 

$$
-1 \leq \sin x \leq 1.
$$

So,  for example, there is no value $x \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $g(x) = 2.$

- III is a bijection. First of all, $h$ is a surjection because $\forall\, y \in (0, \infty),$ we can choose an $x \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $h(x)=y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}h(x) & =y \\ {3}^{x} & =y \\ {log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x}) & ={log}_{3}⁡(y) \\ x & ={log}_{3}⁡(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's verify the above formula:

$$
h(x) = h \left(\log_3\left(y\right) \right) = 3^{\log_3\left(y\right)}  = y
$$

Second, $h$ is an injection:

$$
\begin{aligned}h({x}_{1}) & =h({x}_{2}) \\ {3}^{{x}_{1}} & ={3}^{{x}_{2}} \\ {log}_{3}⁡({3}^{{x}_{1}}) & ={log}_{3}⁡({3}^{{x}_{2}}) \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Because $h$ is both surjective and injective, we conclude that $h$ is bijective.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}$ at the point $(1,2,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2xy \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}) \\  & =2xy+{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(1,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2) & =3(1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+2(1)(2)=11 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) & =2(1)(2)+{1}^{2}-3(2)^{2}=-7\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-(-1) & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) \\ z+1 & =11(x-1)-7(y-2) \\ z+1 & =11x-7y+3 \\ -11x+7y+z-2 & =0 \\ 11x-7y-z+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\sqrt{y}-y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\sqrt{y}-\frac{y}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\sqrt{y}-y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{x}{2\sqrt{y}}-\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,4) & =\sqrt{4}-\frac{4}{2\sqrt{1}}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}-\sqrt{1}=-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z-(-2) & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,4)+(y-4)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,4) \\ z+2 & =0(x-1)-\frac{3}{4}(y-4) \\ z+2 & =-\frac{3}{4}y+3 \\ \frac{3}{4}y+z-1 & =0 \\ 3y+4z-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) & =-4\cdot 1=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)+2(y-1)-4(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2+2y-2-4z+4 \\ -2x-2y+4z+w & =0 \\ 2x+2y-4z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz)$ at the point $(-1,1,1,-\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xz}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xy}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1) & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1\cdot 1)=\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-(-\pi ) & =(x-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi (x+1)-2(y-1)-2(z-1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi x-2y-2z+4+\pi  \\ \pi x-2y-2z-w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx}$ at the point $(2,2,2,6).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{\sqrt{z}}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{y}}+\frac{\sqrt{z}}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{z}}+\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,2,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-6 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,2)+(z-2)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,2) \\ w-6 & =(x-2)+(y-2)+(z-2) \\ w-6 & =x+y+z-6 \\ -x-y-z+w & =0 \\ x+y+z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
At which points on the surface $z=4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6$  is the tangent plane 
horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6) \\  & =8xy+{y}^{3} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6) \\  & =4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨8xy+{y}^{3},\,4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}8xy+{y}^{3}=0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $y=0$ or ${y}^{2}+8x=0.$ So, we have two cases.

- If $y=0$, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
4{x}^{2}+3x(0)^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

- If ${y}^{2}=-8x$, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
4{x}^{2}+3x(-8x)^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

Substituting $x=0$ back into ${y}^{2}=-8x$ gives

$$
{y}^{2}=-8(0)\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

So, in both cases, we have $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Finally, substituting these values into our function, we get

$$
z=4(0)^{2}(0)+(0)(0)^{3}-6=-6.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,-6).$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z={x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}+2y$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨-4,0,1⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2x+2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x+2,\,2y+2,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-4,0,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2x+2,\,2y+2,\,-1⟩=⟨-4,0,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}c(2x+2)=-4 \\ c(2y+2)=0 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-(2x+2)=-4\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-(2y+2)=0\,⟹\,y=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =(1)^{2}+2(1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(1,-1,2).$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2y \\  & =\frac{2y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{2y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=0 \\ \frac{2y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=0$ while the second equation gives $y=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2})=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z= x^2 + xy$ at the point $(1,2, 3).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2x+y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy) \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (1,2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2) & =2(1)+2=4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) \\ z-3 & =4(x-1)+1(y-2) \\ z-3 & =4x+y-6 \\ -4x-y+z+3 & =0 \\ 4x+y-z-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=x^2+y^2+z^2-2xyz$ at the point $(1,-1,1,5).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2x-2yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2y-2xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2z-2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (1,-1,1)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =2(1)-2(-1)(1)=4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =2(-1)-2(1)(1)=-4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =2(1)-2(1)(-1)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-5 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1)+(y+1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}w-5 & =4(x-1)-4(y+1)+4(z-1) \\ w-5 & =4x-4y+4z-12 \\ -4x+4y-4z+w+7 & =0 \\ 4x-4y+4z-w-7 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: At which points on the surface $z={y^2}+ {xy}$  is the tangent plane horizontal?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent plane to a surface is horizontal if and only if the normal vector to the tangent plane is vertical. So, let's first find the general expression of a normal vector to the surface.

Remember that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)
$$

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2y+x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, a normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
\left\langle y, \: 2y+x, \: -1 \right\rangle.
$$

We want to find where this normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0\mathbin{:}$

![](images/df/df6542baabd72b24ce115cb79c912c7b19fd3bd1b663467956445553b60a68c1.png) 

From the first equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
2(0) +x = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 0.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z = 0^2+(0)(0)= 0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$

questions.problem:
Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
f(3,2)=9,\,{f}_{x}(x,y)=-\frac{3x}{\sqrt{26-{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}}},\,{f}_{y}(x,y)=-\frac{6y}{\sqrt{26-{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}}}.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(3,2),$ estimate the value of $f(3.05,2.05).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(3,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(3,2)+∇f(3,2)\cdot ⟨x-3,y-2⟩ \\  & =f(3,2)+⟨{f}_{x}(3,2),{f}_{y}(3,2)⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-2⟩ \\  & =9+⟨{f}_{x}(3,2),{f}_{y}(3,2)⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(3,2)$ and ${f}_{y}(3,2)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(3,2) & =-\frac{3(3)}{\sqrt{26-(3)^{2}-2(2)^{2}}}=-3 \\ {f}_{y}(3,2) & =-\frac{6(2)}{\sqrt{26-(3)^{2}-2(2)^{2}}}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)≈9+⟨-3,-4⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-2⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(3.05,2.05)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=3.05$ and $y=2.05,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3.05,2.05) & ≈9+⟨-3,-4⟩\cdot ⟨3.05-3,2.05-2⟩ \\  & =9+⟨-3,-4⟩\cdot ⟨0.05,0.05⟩ \\  & =9-0.15-0.2 \\  & =8.65\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-y.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,-1).$

The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(0,-1)+∇f(0,-1)\cdot ⟨x,y+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(0,-1)=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =4x\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(0,-1)=0, \\ {f}_{y} & =-1 &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(0,-1)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(0,-1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(0,-1) & =⟨0,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(0,-1)+∇f(0,-1)\cdot ⟨x,y+1⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x,y+1⟩ \\  & ≈1+0-(y+1) \\  & ≈-y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
f(x,y) \approx 1 + \langle 2, 1 \rangle \cdot \langle x-1, y-1 \rangle.

\begin{aligned}f(1.01,2.02,4.95) & ≈2+⟨4,1,-2⟩\cdot ⟨1.01-1,2.02-2,4.95-5⟩ \\  & =2+⟨4,1,-2⟩\cdot ⟨0.01,0.02,-0.05⟩ \\  & =2+0.04+0.02+0.1 \\  & =2.16\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Best Linear Approximation of a Multivariable Function
canonical_examples.problem: Let $f(x,y, z)= xyz+y^2.$ Find the best linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(3, -1, 1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z) \approx f(a,b,c) + \nabla f(a,b,c)\cdot \langle x-a, y-b, z-c \rangle.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(3, -1, 1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(3,-1,1)+∇f(3,-1,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y+1,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(3, -1, 1)= -2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =yz\, &  & ⇒\, &  & {f}_{x}(3,-1,1)=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =xz+2y\, &  & ⇒\, &  & {f}_{y}(3,-1,1)=1 \\ {f}_{z} & =xy\, &  & ⇒\, &  & {f}_{z}(3,-1,1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(3, -1,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(3,-1,1) & =⟨-1,1,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(3,-1,1)+∇f(3,-1,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y+1,z-1⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨-1,1,-3⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y+1,z-1⟩ \\  & =-2-(x-3)+(y+1)-3(z-1) \\  & =-2-x+3+y+1-3z+3 \\  & =5-x+y-3z.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{(x,y)\in {{field-1}}\,:\,-x-3\,{{field-2}}\,y\,{{field-3}}\,x+4}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The points in our set include all those that lie *above* the line $y=-x-3$ and *below* the line $y=x+4.$

A point $P(x,y)$ lies *inside* the shaded region if the following conditions are satisfied:

$$
y>-x-3,\,y<x+4.
$$

 

Combining this into a single condition, we have

$$
-x-3<y<x+4.
$$

We must also include the lines $y=-x-3$ and $y=x+4$ since the boundaries are included in the set (the lines are solid). So, we change the corresponding inequality symbols above as follows:

$$
-x-3\le y\le x+4
$$

Moreover, since we're considering *every* real value in this region, $x\in R,y\in R,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in R\times R={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-x-3\le y\le x+4}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Describing Non-Rectangular Sets Using Set-Builder Notation
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the elliptical boundary of our region has horizontal radius $a=2$ and vertical radius $b=4.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which we can write as

$$
16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64.
$$

We're interested in describing all points that lie *outside* the ellipse. So, let's pick any point outside the region, say, $(0,5).$ Substituting its coordinates into the equation of the boundary, we obtain

$$
16(0)^{2}+4(5)^{2}\,>\,64.
$$

As a result, the points $P(x,y)$ in our region are any real numbers that satisfy the condition

$$
16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}>64.
$$

We must also include the curve $16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64$ since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}\ge 64.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}\ge 64}.
$$

questions.problem: Simplify the expression $[(P⇒¬Q)∧P]∧Q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operation

- First, we use the associative law:

$$
[(P⇒¬Q)∧P]∧Q≡(P⇒¬Q)∧(P∧Q)
$$

- Then, we use that $X⇒Y≡¬X∨Y:$

$$
(P⇒¬Q)∧(P∧Q)≡(¬P∨¬Q)∧(P∧Q)
$$

- Next, we use a De Morgan's law:

$$
(¬P∨¬Q)∧(P∧Q)≡¬(P∧Q)∧(P∧Q)
$$

- Finally, we use the fact that the conjunction of a statement and its negation is a contradiction:

$$
¬(P∧Q)∧(P∧Q)≡c
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
[(P⇒¬Q)∧P]∧Q≡c.
$$

$$

- Finally, we use the fact that the disjunction of a statement and its negation is a tautology:

$$

$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
[(X∧Y)∨¬X]∨¬Y≡t.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Simplify the expression $(A \land \neg B)\Rightarrow \neg B.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operation

- First, we use that $X \Rightarrow Y  \equiv \neg X \lor Y {:}$

$$
(A \land \neg B)\Rightarrow \neg B \equiv
	\neg (A \land \neg B) \lor \neg B
$$

- Next, we use a De Morgan's law:

$$
{\color{blue}\neg (A \land \neg B)} \lor \neg B \equiv
	{\color{blue}(\neg A \lor \neg  \neg B)} \lor \neg B
$$

- Then,  we simplify the double negation:

$$
(\neg A \lor {\color{blue}\neg \neg} B) \lor \neg B  \equiv
	(\neg A \lor B) \lor \neg B
$$

- Next, we use the associative law:

$$
(\neg A \lor B) \lor \neg B  \equiv 
	\neg A \lor (B \lor \neg B)
$$

- Then,  we use the fact that the disjunction of an expression and its negation is a tautology:

$$
\neg A \lor  {\color{blue} (B \lor \neg B)}   \equiv
	\neg A \lor {\color{blue} \textrm{t}}
$$

- Finally, we use the fact that the disjunction of an expression and a tautology gives  a tautology:

$$
\neg A \lor  \textrm{t}  \equiv   \textrm{t}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
(A \land \neg B) \Rightarrow \neg B  \equiv   \textrm{t}
$$

questions.problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\,$ For all $r\in Q,$ $r\ne \frac{1}{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
If we denote

$$
P(r):r=\frac{1}{2},
$$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀r\in Q,\,¬P(r).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀r\in Q,\,¬P(r)) & ≡∃r\in Q,\,¬¬P(r) \\  & ≡∃r\in Q,\,P(r).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $∃r\in Q,\,P(r)$ reads as follows:

$\,$ **There exists** $r\in Q$ such that $r=\frac{1}{2}.$

$$

which reads

To negate the universal statement $\forall y \in \overline{S}, \, \neg P(y),$ we flip the quantifier to existential and negate the predicate: 

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀y\in \overset{―}{S},\,¬P(y)) & ≡∃y\in \overset{―}{S},\,¬¬P(y) \\  & ≡∃y\in \overset{―}{S},\,P(y)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Negating Universal Statements
canonical_examples.problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ For all $n \in \mathbb{N},$ $n$ is a composite number.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we denote

![](images/b8/b8d152c4a9f69b2a6ea0657d9e66ca4adbc11bc480d25a28ea07eac28a646ac3.png)

our statement can be written as

$$
\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\neg \left( \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n)  \right) \equiv \exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg P(n).
$$

Finally, $\exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg P(n)$ reads as follows:

$\qquad$ **There exists** $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n$ is **not** a composite number.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Negating Existential Statements
canonical_examples.problem:
Negate the following statement: 

$\qquad$ Some quadrilaterals are squares.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $Q$ be the set of all quadrilaterals and $S$ the set of all squares. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $q \in Q$ such that $q \in S$

Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\exists q \in Q, \, q \in S.$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∃q\in Q,\,q\in S) & ≡∀q\in Q,\,¬(q\in S) \\  & ≡∀q\in Q,\,q\notin S\end{aligned}
$$

which reads 

$\qquad$ For all $q \in Q,$ $q \not\in S.$

or simply

$\qquad$ All quadrilaterals are not squares.

questions.problem: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T([\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x={e}^{u+v}$ and $y={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ \,\text{ }2u\, & \,\text{ }2v\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot 2v-{e}^{u+v}\cdot 2u \\  & =2{e}^{u+v}(v-u).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-{v}^{2} \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}.$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$

questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u-v} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(uv)\end{aligned}].
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u-v}$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(uv).$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v} \\ \frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u-v}\cdot (\frac{1}{v})-(-{e}^{u-v})\cdot \frac{1}{u} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{u-v}}{v}+\frac{{e}^{u-v}}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,1)}=\frac{{e}^{(1)-(1)}}{(1)}+\frac{{e}^{(1)-(1)}}{(1)}=2.
$$

questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v).$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & -\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v))-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is 

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=2.
$$

Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(2,4)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$

$$

Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{2u}{v} & -\frac{{u}^{2}}{{v}^{2}} \\ v & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{2u}{v}\cdot u-v\cdot (-\frac{{u}^{2}}{{v}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2{u}^{2}}{v}+\frac{{u}^{2}}{v} \\  & =\frac{3{u}^{2}}{v} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(2,4)} & =(\frac{3{u}^{2}}{v})\,{|}_{u=2\,v=4} \\  & =\frac{3(2)^{2}}{4} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|3|\cdot \delta A \\  & =3\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} \\ u-\frac{1}{3}v\end{aligned}],
$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} \\ u-\frac{1}{3}v\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & -v \\ 1 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}| \\  & =(3{u}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})-(1)\cdot (-v) \\  & =v-{u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}v-{u}^{2} & <0 \\ v & <{u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v={u}^{2}
$$

defines a parabola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

![](images/13/1368ee41963c1abcc320d2cd35449c08599582f37c7d68f750e137fcdcd2e57b.png)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=(u+v)^3$ and $y=(u-v)^2.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =3(u+v)^{2} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =3(u+v)^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3(u+v)^{2} & 3(u+v)^{2} \\ 2(u-v) & -2(u-v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(u+v)^{2}\cdot (-2(u-v))-3(u+v)^{2}\cdot 2(u-v) \\  & =-12(u+v)^{2}(u-v).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Rectangular Matrix
questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}0-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )((5-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Two Dimensions
questions.problem: Given that $F=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\,i+xy\,j,$ what is $\text{div}\,F?$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}+x \\  & =\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

questions.problem:
![](images/b3/b315be9ba524ab538388fdaad31161c280d7d6e5ab71261345063ac6ffe819d5.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

- $∇\cdot F=0$
- $∇\cdot F>0$
- $∇\cdot F<0$
- $F$ is solenoidal
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement II is true, whereas statements I and III are false. Notice that the lengths of the vectors increase as we move vertically and horizontally away from the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a source at every point.

- Statement IV is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=\ln(2x+y)\,\mathbf{i}+ x^2e^{3y}\,\mathbf{j}.$ 
Evaluate $\nabla \cdot\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,0).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y))+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{3y}) \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{3y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf {F}$ at the point $(1,0),$ and obtain

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Three Dimensions
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=(2x-y)^2\,\mathbf{i}+(3y-2z)^2\,\mathbf{j}+(x-2z)^2\,\mathbf{k}.$ Evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,2,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j} + R\,\mathbf k$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((2x-y)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((3y-2z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((x-2z)^{2}) \\  & =4(2x-y)+6(3y-2z)-4(x-2z) \\  & =4x+14y-4z.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf { F}$ at the point $(1,2,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F(1,2,1) & =4(1)+14(2)-4(1) \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Interpreting Divergence
canonical_examples.problem:
![](images/d3/d37f2a445986b2aae60603fed3bef1b480d8f049dfe17a0cf26325ac2eb167d8.png)

 

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $\mathbf F?$

- $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = 0$

- $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0$

- $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F <                    0$

- $\mathbf F$ is solenoidal
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that $\textrm{div}\, \mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $\mathbf F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $\mathbf F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $\mathbf F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P\mathbin{:}$

- If $\mathbf F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $\nabla \cdot  \mathbf F > 0$ at $P.$

- If $\mathbf F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $\nabla \cdot  \mathbf F <         0$ at $P.$

- If $\mathbf F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $\nabla \cdot  \mathbf F =0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = 0$ everywhere in the domain of $\mathbf F,$ we say that $\mathbf F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement I is true, whereas statements II and III are false. For any point $P,$ the sum of the inward-pointing vectors equals the sum of the outward-pointing vectors. Therefore, $\mathbf F$ acts neither like a source nor a sink.

- Statement IV is true. Since $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = 0$ everywhere, the vector field $\mathbf F$ is solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and IV only."

questions.knowledge_point: The Singular Value Decomposition of a 2x2 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that since ${A}^{T}\,A$ is diagonal, the singular values of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\sigma }_{1}={\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{5}.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$): Seeking non-zero solutions of $({A}^{T}\,A-5I)v=0,$ we obtain the unit eigenvectors 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $Σ,$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A{A}^{T}$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.
$$

 

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Curl of a Vector Field
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F={x}^{2}\,i+xz\,j+{z}^{2}\,k.$ Evaluate $∇\times F$ at the point  $(-2,-3,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned}|.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ {x}^{2} & xz & {z}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2})]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xz)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2})]k \\  & =(0-x)i-(0-0)j+(z-0)k \\  & =-x\,i+z\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\,F$ at the point $(-2,-3,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(-2,-3,1) & =-(-2)\,i+(1)\,k \\  & =2\,i+\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F=xy{e}^{z}\,j+yz{e}^{x}\,k.$ Evaluate $∇\times F$ at the point $(0,2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3},$ and the first partial derivatives exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field on ${R}^{3}$ defined by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned}|.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 0 & xy{e}^{z} & yz{e}^{x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz{e}^{x})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{e}^{z})]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz{e}^{x})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(0)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{z})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(0)]k \\  & =(z{e}^{x}-xy{e}^{z})i-(yz{e}^{x}-0)j+(y{e}^{z}-0)k \\  & =(z{e}^{x}-xy{e}^{z})\,i-yz{e}^{x}\,j+y{e}^{z}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\,F$ at the point $(0,2,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(0,2,1) & =(1\cdot {e}^{0}-0\cdot 2\cdot {e}^{1})\,i-2\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{0}\,j+2\cdot {e}^{1}\,k \\  & =i-2j+2e\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Scalar Curl of a Vector Field
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=(x+{y}^{2})\,i+y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\,j.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $F$ at the point $(0,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1))-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1}-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(0,-1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(0,-1)} & =\frac{2(0)(-1)}{{0}^{2}+1}-2(-1) \\  & =0+2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem:
![](images/56/5643e87bfb5dfb5c29750f48abffe2443bf656901d74a47a0aa39bddfd0c1590.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $\text{curl}\,F=0$
- $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$
- $\text{curl}\,F$ points in the positive $z$-direction.
- $F$ is irrotational
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has a curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

![](images/86/86aee33cdfa96ac0a61468cc9657e791e399f31c024cdbc3a932193dc897d534.png)

If $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement II is true, whereas statement I is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would rotate clockwise. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- Statement III is true. Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (counterclockwise), our thumb will point away from the screen. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F$ also points away from the screen, in the direction of increasing $z.$

- Statement IV is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not irrotational.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = y\,\mathbf{i} + x^2\,\mathbf{j} - 2z\,\mathbf{k}.$ Evaluate $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}$ at the point  $\left(-1,0,2\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j}+R\,\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the curl of $\mathbf F$ is the vector field given by

![](images/88/888b12c4f687dba1199a82d7e3a5e6897e7599ea812753423de5a23ffd756888.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ y & {x}^{2} & -2z\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2})]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(y)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)]k \\  & =(0-0)i-(0-0)j+(2x-1)k \\  & =(2x-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm {curl}\, \mathbf{F}$ at the point $\left(-1,0,2\right),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(-1,0,2) & =(2(-1)-1)\,k=-3\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Scalar Curl of a Vector Field
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = e^{x+y} \, \mathbf{i} + 3xy \, \mathbf{j}.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(-1,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3xy)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y}) \\  & =3y-{e}^{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(-1,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(-1,1)} & =3(1)-{e}^{-1+1} \\  & =3-{e}^{0} \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Interpreting the Curl of a Vector Field
canonical_examples.problem:
![](images/71/71c58bf1b0fe4259ac50633a457f6a76639c0a0c188b66cce5e0fc3c7e5b0329.png)

 

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \mathbf 0$

- $\textrm{curl}\, \mathbf F \neq \mathbf 0$

- $\mathbf F$ is irrotational

- $\textrm{curl}\, \mathbf F$ points in the positive $z$-direction.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $\mathbf F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \neq  \mathbf 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F =  \mathbf 0.$

![](images/86/86aee33cdfa96ac0a61468cc9657e791e399f31c024cdbc3a932193dc897d534.png)

If $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \mathbf 0$ everywhere in $\mathbb R^3$, we say that $\mathbf F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement I is false, whereas statement II is true. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would rotate counterclockwise. Therefore, $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \neq \mathbf 0.$

- Statements III is false. Since $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \neq \mathbf 0,$ the vector field $\mathbf F$ is not irrotational.

- Statement IV is true. Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (counterclockwise), our thumb will point upward. Therefore, $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ points upward, in the direction of increasing $z.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and IV only."

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=t+2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t+2)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+4t+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}+2{t}^{2}+4t)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+2+4 \\  & =\frac{19}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{\frac{19}{3}}.
$$

\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $p(t)=3-t+{t}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
p(-2)=9,\,p(0)=3,\,p(2)=5.
$$

Computing $‖p(t)‖$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{p(-2)p(-2)+p(0)p(0)+p(2)p(2)} \\  & =\sqrt{[p(-2)]^{2}+[p(0)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(9)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{81+9+25} \\  & =\sqrt{115}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[\pi ,2\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[\pi ,2\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1.$

The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,(4{cos}^{2}⁡t+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }((2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(3+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(3t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t){|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =(6\pi +0+0)-(3\pi +0+0) \\  & =3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity 

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡t=\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
