questions.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Normalize the vector $f(t)=2-3t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{(2-3t)}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,(4-12t+9{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(4t-6{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4-6+3 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
‖f(t)‖=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}=1.
$$

To normalize the vector $f(t),$ we divide $f(t)$ by its norm $‖f(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{f(t)}{‖f(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{2-3t}{1} \\  & =2-3t\end{aligned}
$$

An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+5{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector  $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.

The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =(-1)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 2+5\cdot (1\cdot 1) \\  & =1+4+5 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Inverting a Frobenius Matrix
questions.problem:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we're given a Frobenius matrix:

- all entries on the main diagonal are ones

- the matrix has only one column (the $2$nd column) where some entries below the main diagonal are not zeros

- all the other entries outside the main diagonal are zeros

To find the inverse of a Frobenius matrix, we simply take the non-zero entries outside the main diagonal with opposite signs. 

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The given matrix can be obtained from the identity matrix by permuting its columns. Therefore, $A$ is a permutation matrix.

The inverse of a permutation matrix can be found as follows: 

$$
{P}^{-1}={P}^{T}
$$

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $2\,m$ when its velocity is $8\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/01/017463f3ac8abac9c2b00c4d9a715a4109a5f4bc1b070e0a12c4d3a7bac64351.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=2\,\text{m}$ when $v=8\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =2(2)^{2}+C \\ C & =32-8 \\ C & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+24 \\ {v}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}+48 \\ {v}^{2} & =4({x}^{2}+12) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, the velocity is given by $v(x)=(4-2x)\,m/s.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/7b/7bd0200a651aec7283e5c96d3cdc1589d795531e179ca0eb7cc36ef5bad8de56.png)

We're given that the velocity function $v(x)$ is

$$
v(x)=4-2x.
$$

We know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4-2x.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4-2x \\ \frac{1}{4-2x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{4-2x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{4-2x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-x| & =t+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|2-x| & =-2t-2K \\ 2-x & =C{e}^{-2t} \\ x & =2-C{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=2,$ and the particular solution is

$$
x(t)=2-2{e}^{-2t}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
![](images/4e/4e0b8b816ca3b86fa90ea785df1308f53a4763baa2c2aa2192b9d7bfa0259855.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(4{x}^{3}+4x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4{x}^{3}+4x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4{x}^{3}+4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (4{x}^{3}+4x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & ={1}^{4}+2(1)^{2}+C \\ 3 & =3+C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2} \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2})}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=2$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({2}^{4}+2(2)^{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{48} \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2+\frac{x}{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (2+\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x\end{aligned}

$$

questions.worked_solution:
We need to express the summation $S(k+1)$ in terms of $S(k).$

Let ${a}_{i}$ for $i\ge 1$ be a sequence, and let $S(k)$ denote the sum of the first $k$ terms.

$$
S(k)={\sum }_{i=1}^{k}{a}_{i}
$$

We can always express $S(k+1)$ in terms of $S(k)$ by writing the last term on its own, as follows: 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}{a}_{i}=({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}{a}_{i})+{a}_{k+1}.
$$

In our case, we have ${a}_{i}=6i+1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{k+1}=6(k+1)+1=6k+7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}(6i+1)=({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}(6i+1))+(6k+7),
$$

which we can write as 

$$
S(k+1)=S(k)+6k+7.
$$

questions.problem: Prove that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{n}4(i-1)i(i+1)=(n-1)n(n+1)(n+2)$ using mathematical induction.
questions.worked_solution:
The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P(1),P(2),P(3),…,$ where

- $P(1)$ is true, and

- $P(k)⇒P(k+1)$ for every $k\in N.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every $n\in N.$

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}4(i-1)i(i+1)=(n-1)n(n+1)(n+2)
$$

We start by proving the so-called base case, $P(1).$ To do this, we substitute $n=1$ into both the left-hand side and right-hand side and show that they're equal:

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove our statement is true for the base case $n=1.$
For the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}4(i-1)i(i+1)=4(0)(1)(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and for the right-hand side,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(0)(1)(2)(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, our statement is true for $n=1.$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n=k\ge 1.$ 

Due to the base case, we already *know* that the statement is true for *some* value of $k,$ namely $k=1,$ so this assumption is valid.

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=k\ge 1,$ we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k}4(i-1)i(i+1)=(k-1)k(k+1)(k+2).
$$

We must show that $P(k)⇒P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the so-called **inductive step**, so let's write that, too.

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}4(i-1)i(i+1)=k(k+1)(k+2)(k+3).\,\,(∗)
$$

The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of $(∗)$ *using the inductive hypothesis* and apply algebraic techniques to show that this equals the right-hand side.

When proving sums of finite series using induction, the key to unlocking the proof is to write the last term on its own, as follows: 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}{a}_{i}=({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}{a}_{i})+{a}_{k+1}
$$

Let's apply this technique in this case:

We write

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}4(i-1)i(i+1)=({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}4(i-1)i(i+1))+4k(k+1)(k+2).
$$

By the inductive hypothesis, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}4(i-1)i(i+1))+4k(k+1)(k+2) \\  & =(k-1)k(k+1)(k+2)+4k(k+1)(k+2) \\  & =k(k+1)(k+2)((k-1)+4) \\  & =k(k+1)(k+2)(k+3),\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

Since we've shown that the left-hand side of $(∗)$ equals the right-hand side, our proof is complete. So let's write down our conclusion. 

Therefore, by the principle of induction, ${\sum }_{i=1}^{n}4(i-1)i(i+1)=(n-1)n(n+1)(n+2)$ is true for all $n\ge 1.$

questions.worked_solution:
A variant of the principle of induction states the following: Let ${n}_{0}$ be an integer. Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P({n}_{0}),P({n}_{0}+1),P({n}_{0}+2),…,$ where

- $P({n}_{0})$ is true, and

- $P(k)⇒P(k+1)$ for every natural number $k\ge {n}_{0}.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every natural number $n\ge {n}_{0}.$

$$
{\sum }_{i=2}^{n}{3}^{i}=\frac{1}{2}({3}^{n+1}-9)
$$

We start by proving the so-called base case, $P(2).$ To do this, we substitute $n=2$ into both the left-hand side and right-hand side and show that they're equal:

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove our statement is true for the base case $n=2.$
For the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=2}^{2}{3}^{i}={3}^{2}=9,\end{aligned}
$$

and for the right-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}({3}^{2+1}-9)=\frac{1}{2}(18)=9.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, our statement is true for $n=2.$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n=k\ge 2.$ 

Due to the base case, we already *know* that the statement is true for *some* value of $k,$ namely $k=2,$ so this assumption is valid.

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=k\ge 2,$ we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=2}^{k}{3}^{i}=\frac{1}{2}({3}^{k+1}-9).
$$

We must show that $P(k)⇒P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the so-called **inductive step**, so let's write that, too.

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
{\sum }_{i=2}^{k+1}{3}^{i}=\frac{1}{2}({3}^{k+2}-9).\,\,(∗)
$$

The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of $(∗)$ *using the inductive hypothesis* and apply algebraic techniques to show that this equals the right-hand side.

When proving sums of finite series using induction, the key to unlocking the proof is to write the last term on its own, as follows: 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}{a}_{i}=({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}{a}_{i})+{a}_{k+1}
$$

Let's apply this technique in this case:

We write

$$
{\sum }_{i=2}^{k+1}{3}^{i}=({\sum }_{i=2}^{k}{3}^{i})+{3}^{k+1}.
$$

By the inductive hypothesis, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({\sum }_{i=2}^{k}{3}^{i})+{3}^{k+1} & =\frac{1}{2}({3}^{k+1}-9)+{3}^{k+1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot {3}^{k+1}-\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {3}^{k+2}-\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({3}^{k+2}-9),\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

Since we've shown that the left-hand side of $(∗)$ equals the right-hand side, our proof is complete. So let's write down our conclusion. 

Therefore, by the principle of induction, ${\sum }_{i=2}^{n}{3}^{i}=\frac{1}{2}({3}^{n+1}-9)$ is true for all $n\ge 2.$

**Conclusion**: Therefore, $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n 3i(i+3) = n(n+1)(n+5)$ for all $n\geq 1.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing S(k+1) in Terms of S(k)
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $\displaystyle S(k) = \sum_{i=1}^k 2^i,$ express $S(k+1)$ in terms of $S(k).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to express the summation $S(k+1)$ in terms of $S(k).$

Let $a_i$ for $i\geq 1$ be a sequence, and let $S(k)$ denote the sum of the first $k$ terms.

$$
S(k) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i
$$

We can always express $S(k+1)$ in terms of $S(k)$ by writing the last term on its own, as follows: 

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k+1} a_i = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i\right) + a_{k+1}.
$$

In our case, we have $a_i = 2^i.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{k+1}={2}^{k+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k+1} 2^i = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k} 2^i \right) + 2^{k+1},
$$

which we can write as 

$$
S(k+1) = S(k) + 2^{k+1}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Proving Sums of Series Using Induction
canonical_examples.problem: Prove that $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} \dfrac{1}{4^i} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4^n}\right)$ using mathematical induction.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P(1), P(2), P(3),\ldots,$ where

- $P(1)$ is true, and

- $P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)$ for every $k\in\mathbb N.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every $n\in\mathbb N.$

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n \dfrac{1}{4^i} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4^n}\right)
$$

We start by proving the so-called base case, $P(1).$ To do this, we substitute $n=1$ into both the left-hand side and right-hand side and show that they're equal:

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove our statement is true for the base case $n=1.$
For the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}\frac{1}{{4}^{i}}=\frac{1}{{4}^{1}}=\frac{1}{4},\end{aligned}
$$

and for the right-hand side,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}(1-\frac{1}{{4}^{1}})=\frac{1}{3}(\frac{3}{4})=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, our statement is true for $n=1.$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n = k \geq 1.$ 

Due to the base case, we already *know* that the statement is true for *some* value of $k,$ namely $k = 1,$ so this assumption is valid.

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n = k \geq 1,$ we have

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k} \dfrac{1}{4^i} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4^k}\right).
$$

We must show that $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the so-called **inductive step**, so let's write that, too.

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} \dfrac{1}{4^i} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4^{k+1}}\right). \qquad\qquad (\ast)
$$

The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of $(\ast)$ *using the inductive hypothesis* and apply algebraic techniques to show that this equals the right-hand side.

When proving sums of finite series using induction, the key to unlocking the proof is to write the last term on its own, as follows: 

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k+1} a_i =  \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i\right) + a_{k+1}
$$

Let's apply this technique in this case:

We write

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}\frac{1}{{4}^{i}} & =({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{{4}^{i}})+(\frac{1}{{4}^{k+1}}).\end{aligned}
$$

By the inductive hypothesis, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{{4}^{i}})+(\frac{1}{{4}^{k+1}}) & =\frac{1}{3}(1-\frac{1}{{4}^{k}})+\frac{1}{{4}^{k+1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3\cdot {4}^{k}}+\frac{1}{{4}^{k+1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{{4}^{k}}(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{{4}^{k}}(\frac{1}{12}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{{4}^{k}}(\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3\cdot {4}^{k+1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(1-\frac{1}{{4}^{k+1}}),\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

Since we've shown that the left-hand side of $(\ast)$ equals the right-hand side, our proof is complete. So let's write down our conclusion. 

Therefore, by the principle of induction, $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} \dfrac{1}{4^i} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4^n}\right)$ is true for all $n\geq 1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=y+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,x=s$ and $y=2s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/7e/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)={e}^{x+2y},x={s}^{2},$ and $y=s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/7e/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+2y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 2s+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 1 \\  & =2s{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s} \\  & =2(s+1){e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)={e}^{2y-x},x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/f0/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-{e}^{2y-x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{2y-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =-{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t){e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y},x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2s$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/7e/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s)+(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s} \\  & =-2-2{cot}^{2}⁡2s \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=y{e}^{x},$ $x=\sqrt{s}$ and $y=s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}$ for $s>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/7e/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =s{e}^{\sqrt{s}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =s{e}^{\sqrt{s}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}}+{e}^{\sqrt{s}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}{e}^{\sqrt{s}}+{e}^{\sqrt{s}} \\  & =(1+\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}){e}^{\sqrt{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)$ and $y={x}^{2},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})\cdot 2x \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$ and $y={x}^{2},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x+2{x}^{2}}{x+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x(1+2x)}{x(1+x)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{1+2x}{1+x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x+1}$ and $y={x}^{3},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(1+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2},$ where $x=s\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(2s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡s)(t\operatorname{cos}⁡s) \\  & =2s{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s\operatorname{cos}⁡s \\  & =2s{sin}^{2}⁡t-2{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{st})^{2}}=-{e}^{-2st}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{-st})^{2}}=-{e}^{2st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t{e}^{st}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =-t{e}^{-st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(-{e}^{-2st})(t{e}^{st})+(-{e}^{2st})(-t{e}^{-st}) \\  & =t{e}^{st}-t{e}^{-st} \\  & =t({e}^{st}-{e}^{-st}).\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)=y{x}^{2},$ where $x=ts$ and $y=s-t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂t}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(ts)(s-t)=2t{s}^{2}-2s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(ts)^{2}={t}^{2}{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2t{s}^{2}-2s{t}^{2})(s)+({t}^{2}{s}^{2})(-1) \\  & =2t{s}^{3}-2{s}^{2}{t}^{2}-{t}^{2}{s}^{2} \\  & =2t{s}^{3}-3{t}^{2}{s}^{2} \\  & =t{s}^{2}(2s-3t).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(st))(s\operatorname{cos}⁡(st))+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(st))(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡(st)) \\  & =s{cos}^{2}⁡(st)-s{sin}^{2}⁡(st) \\  & =s({cos}^{2}⁡(st)-{sin}^{2}⁡(st)) \\  & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡(2st).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=1.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(-1)\cdot {e}^{s}+(-1)\cdot 1+(1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-{e}^{s}-2.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z},$ where $x=s-t,$ $y={t}^{2}$ and $z=s+t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂t}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/b5/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={e}^{x+y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot (-1)+({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot 2t+({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot 1 \\  & =-{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}+2t{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}+{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}} \\  & =2t{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{2}z,$ where $x=3t,$ $y=t-s$ and $z=2st.$ Given that

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+{c}_{1}s{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}{s}^{2}t+{c}_{3}{s}^{3},
$$

find the value of ${c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/b5/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(t-s)(2st)=4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =(t-s)^{2}={t}^{2}-2st+{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =3, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)\cdot 3+(4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t)\cdot 1+({t}^{2}-2st+{s}^{2})\cdot 2s \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t+2s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t+2{s}^{3} \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+6s{t}^{2}-8{s}^{2}t+2{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=6,$ ${c}_{2}=-8$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=6+(-8)+2=0.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2z.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem: If $f(x,y)=\cos(xy), x=t,$ and $y=e^t,$ compute $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](images/f0/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x = x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} 
= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =[-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})]\cdot 1+[-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})]\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})-t{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}) \\  & =-(1+t){e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
canonical_examples.problem: If $f(x,y) = 2\sqrt{x+y}$ and $y=\cos x,$ compute $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables
canonical_examples.problem: Let $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2,$ where $x = s\cos{t}$ and $y = t\sin{s}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y = y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2s\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2t\operatorname{sin}⁡s)(\operatorname{sin}⁡s) \\  & =-2{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t{sin}^{2}⁡s \\  & =2t{sin}^{2}⁡s-2{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2t{sin}^{2}⁡s-{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used the identity $\sin 2t = 2\sin t\cos t$ in the above simplification.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables
canonical_examples.problem: Let $f(x,y,z) = e^{xy + z},$ where $x = s + t,$ $y = s-t$ and $z = -s^2.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](images/b5/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t), y = y(s,t)$ and $z = z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x, y$ and $z\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={e}^{xy+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(s-t){e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}=(s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(s+t){e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}=(s+t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}={e}^{-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot 1+(s+t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot (-1)+{e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot 0 \\  & =(s-t-s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}} \\  & =-2t{e}^{-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

- $P({a,∅})={∅,{a},{a,∅}}$
- $P({∅})={∅,{∅}}$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement II is false. Notice that we are given the set ${a,∅}.$ So, its power set must be ${∅,{a},{∅},{a,∅}}.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the power set of the set ${∅}$ is ${∅,{∅}}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Sum of a Geometric Series by Determining the Common Ratio
questions.problem: Determine the value of the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{4}\frac{1}{{6}^{n}}$  rounded to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we can rewrite the series as follows:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{4}\frac{1}{{6}^{n}}={\sum }_{n=1}^{4}{(\frac{1}{6})}^{n}
$$

Since the above series is in the form ${\sum }_{n=1}^{N}a{r}^{n},$ it is a geometric series. 

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum ${S}_{N}$ of a geometric series.

$$
{S}_{N}={a}_{1}\frac{(1-{r}^{N})}{1-r}
$$

In this case, $r=\frac{1}{6}$ and $N=4.$ We need to figure out ${a}_{1}.$

The formula for the $n$th term of the series is

$$
{a}_{n}={(\frac{1}{6})}^{n},
$$

and therefore the first term of the series is

$$
{a}_{1}={(\frac{1}{6})}^{1}=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

If we substitute ${a}_{1}=\frac{1}{6},r=\frac{1}{6}$ and $N=4$ into the formula for ${S}_{N}$, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{4}{(\frac{1}{6})}^{n} & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{[1-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{4}]}{(1-\frac{1}{6})} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot [1-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{4}] \\  & ≈0.200\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the final answer has been rounded to three decimal places.

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 9 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}13 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A,$ $Σ,$ and $V$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the first column of $U?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ and ${\sigma }_{i}\ne 0,$ then the $i$th column of $U$ can be found as

$$
{u}_{i}=\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{i}}A{v}_{i},
$$

 

where ${v}_{i}$ is the $i$th column of the matrix $V.$

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=13$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$ Therefore, the first column of $U$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}4 & 9 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{13}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{A}^{T}\,A=[\begin{aligned}9 & -24 \\ -24 & 73\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{11} & {v}_{12} \\ {v}_{21} & {v}_{22}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{12}|+|{v}_{22}|?$
questions.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$ So, the second column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1.$ Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-I=[\begin{aligned}9 & -24 \\ -24 & 73\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 & -24 \\ -24 & 72\end{aligned}]
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-I)v=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we get 

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore,

$$
|{v}_{12}|+|{v}_{22}|=|\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}|=\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}}.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-100I & =[\begin{aligned}180 & -60 \\ -60 & 145\end{aligned}]-100[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}80 & -60 \\ -60 & 45\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-100I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$

$$

$$

questions.problem:
Let $Y$ be the set of all ordered pairs $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$  such that $x+y\le 3.$ Complete the following sentence:

*$Y$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to the usual component-wise addition and scalar multiplication in ${R}^{2}$) because $\text{_________}\,.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The correct answer is as follows:

*$Y$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to the usual component-wise addition and scalar multiplication in ${R}^{2}$) because **multiplication of $(x,y)\in Y$ by a scalar is not closed.** *  

For example, $(1,1)\in Y$ because $1+1=2\le 3.$ However, if we add the components of $2\cdot (1,1)=(2,2),$ we get $2+2=4>3.$ So, $2\cdot (1,1)\notin Y.$

On the other hand:

- Addition in $Y$ is associative. $\,✓$

- The zero element in $Y$ is $(0,0).$ $✓$

- Addition and scalar multiplication in $Y$ satisfy the distributive laws. $\,✓$

- Addition in $Y$ is commutative. $\,✓$

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Let $V$ be the set of all real polynomials of degree exactly $3$, equipped with the usual addition and scalar multiplication operations. Complete the following sentence:

*$V$ is **not** a vector space because $\textrm{_________}\,.$*

- the sum of two polynomials of degree $3$ may not be a polynomial of degree $3$

- $V$ does not contain the polynomial $-p(x)$ for every $p(x) \in V$

- addition of polynomials is not commutative
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The correct answer  is as follows:

*$V$ is **not** a vector space because **the sum of two polynomials of degree $3$ may not be a polynomial of degree $3$.** *

For instance, if $p(x) = 1 +x^3$ and $q(x) = 1-x^3$, then $p(x)$ and $q(x)$ are in $V.$ However  

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x)+q(x) & =(1+{x}^{3})+(1-{x}^{3}) \\  & =2\notin V.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand:

- Addition of polynomials is commutative.

- For any polynomial $p(x)$ of degree $3$, the corresponding negative polynomial $-p(x)$ also has degree $3.$

questions.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y).$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y) \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y) \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y,z)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\,j+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The joint probability distribution $f(x,y)$ of the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below. 

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.05$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.15$ | $0.6$ |

Which of the following statements are true?

- $P(X=1,Y=1)=P(X=1)\cdot P(Y=1)$
- $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$
- $X$ and $Y$ are independent
questions.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Computing the marginal probability mass functions for  $X$ and $Y,$ we obtain the following:

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.05$ | $0.2$ | $0.25$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.15$ | $0.6$ | $0.75$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.2$ | $0.8$ | $1$ |

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=1,Y=1)=f(1,1)=0.6.$ On the other hand, 

$$
P(X=1)\cdot P(Y=1)={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1)=0.75\cdot 0.8=0.6.\,✓
$$

- Statement II is true. Checking all other possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =0.05=0.25\cdot 0.2={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0) & ✓ \\ f(1,0) & =0.15=0.75\cdot 0.2={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0) & ✓ \\ f(0,1) & =0.20=0.25\cdot 0.8={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1) & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ must be independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem: Use mathematical induction to prove that ${n}^{3}-7n+9$ is divisible by $3$ for all $n\in N.$
questions.worked_solution:
The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P(1),P(2),P(3),…,$ where

- $P(1)$ is true, and

- $P(k)⇒P(k+1)$ for every $k\in N.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every $n\in N.$

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

$P(n):\,3\,∣\,{n}^{3}-7n+9$ for all $n\in N$

We start by proving the base case, $P(1).$ To do this, we substitute $n=1$ into the expression and show it is divisible by $3:$

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove that our statement is true for the base case $n=1.$ Substituting $n=1$ into the expression ${n}^{3}-7n+9,$ we have

$$
P(1):\,{1}^{3}-7(1)+9=3,\,\text{and}\,3\,∣\,3
$$

Thus, our statement is true for $n=1.$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n=k\ge 1.$

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=k\ge 1,$ we have that

$$
P(k):\,3\,∣\,{k}^{3}-7k+9.
$$

We must show that $P(k)⇒P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the **inductive step**.

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
P(k+1):\,3\,∣\,(k+1)^{3}-7(k+1)+9.\,\,(∗)
$$

The idea is to rewrite the expression $(k+1)^{3}-7(k+1)+9$ as ${k}^{3}-7k+9$ (from the inductive hypothesis) plus a multiple of $3.$ We do this as follows:

We write

$$
\begin{aligned}(k+1)^{3}-7(k+1)+9 & ={k}^{3}+3{k}^{2}+3k+1-7k-7+9 \\  & ={k}^{3}+3{k}^{2}-4k+3 \\  & =({k}^{3}-7k+9)+3({k}^{2}+k-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $3\,∣\,({k}^{3}-7k+9)$ by the inductive hypothesis, and $3({k}^{2}+k-2)$ is clearly divisible by $3,$ their sum is also divisible by $3,$ as required.

Since we have shown that the expression in $(∗)$ is divisible by $3,$ our proof is complete. So, let's write down our conclusion.

Therefore, by the principle of induction, $3\,∣\,{n}^{3}-7n+9$ for all $n\in N.$

questions.worked_solution:
The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P(1),P(3),P(7),…,$ where

- $P(1)$ is true, and

- $P(k)⇒P(k+1)$ for every $k\in N.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every $n\in N.$

$P(n):\,7\,∣\,{2}^{3n}+{15}^{n}-2$ for all $n\in N$

We start by proving the base case, $P(1).$ To do this, we substitute $n=1$ into the expression and show it is divisible by $7:$

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove that our statement is true for the base case $n=1.$ Substituting $n=1$ into the expression ${2}^{3n}+{15}^{n}-2,$ we have

$$
P(1):\,{2}^{3(1)}+{15}^{1}-2=7,\,\text{and}\,7\,∣\,7
$$

Thus, our statement is true for $n=1.$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n=k\ge 1.$

Due to the base case, we already know that the statement is true for some value of $k,$ namely $k=1,$ so this assumption is valid.

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=k\ge 1,$ we have that

$$
P(k):\,7\,∣\,{2}^{3k}+{15}^{k}-2.
$$

We must show that $P(k)⇒P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the **inductive step**.

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
P(k+1):\,7\,∣\,{2}^{3(k+1)}+{15}^{k+1}-2.\,\,(∗)
$$

The idea is to rewrite the expression ${2}^{3(k+1)}+{15}^{k+1}-2$ as ${2}^{3k}+{15}^{k}-2$ (taken from the inductive hypothesis) plus a multiple of $7.$ We do this as follows:

We write

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{3(k+1)}+{15}^{k+1}-2 & ={2}^{3k}\cdot {2}^{3}+{15}^{k}\cdot 15-2 \\  & =8({2}^{3k})+15({15}^{k})-2 \\  & =7({2}^{3k})+14({15}^{k})+{2}^{3k}+{15}^{k}-2 \\  & =7({2}^{3k})+14({15}^{k})+({2}^{3k}+{15}^{k}-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $7\,∣\,({2}^{3k}+{15}^{k}-2)$ by the inductive hypothesis, and $7({2}^{3k})$ and $14({15}^{k})=7\cdot 2({15}^{k})$ are both clearly divisible by $7,$ their sum is also divisible by $7,$ as required.

Since we have shown that the expression in $(∗)$ is divisible by $7,$ our proof is complete. So, let's write down our conclusion.

Therefore, by the principle of induction, $7\,∣\,{2}^{3n}+{15}^{n}-2$ for all $n\in N.$

A vector field $F$ is conservative if it is the gradient of a scalar function $f.$ That is, there exists a function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ The function $f$ is called a potential function for $F.$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F=({y}^{3}-ay)\,i+(3x{y}^{2}-2x)\,j$ on ${R}^{2}$, where $a$ is a constant. Given that $F$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $F,$ the domain $D={R}^{2},$ and we have 

$$
P={y}^{3}-ay,\,Q=3x{y}^{2}-2x.
$$

 

Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}-a,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{y}^{2}-2.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${R}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}-a & =3{y}^{2}-2 \\ -a & =-2 \\ a & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=2.$

$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i+ Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j$ be a vector field with domain $D = \mathbb R^2,$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$\mathbf F$ *is conservative if and only if $\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $\mathbf F,$ the domain $D = \mathbb R^2,$ and we have

$$
P = \dfrac{2ay}{1+9x^2}, \qquad Q = \arctan{3x}.
$$

 
Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \dfrac{2a}{1 + 9x^2}, 
\qquad 
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = \dfrac{3}{1 + 9x^2}.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on $\mathbb R^2.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2a}{1+9{x}^{2}} & =\frac{3}{1+9{x}^{2}} \\ 2a & =3 \\ a & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a = \dfrac{3}{2}.$

$\mathbf F$ *is conservative if and only if $\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

Note that for each of our functions, $D = \mathbb R^2.$ With this in mind, let's check each of the vector fields. 

- For the vector field $\mathbf F,$ we have $P = e^{y^2} - 2xy$ and $Q = 2xye^{y^2} - y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 2ye^{y^2} - 2x, \qquad  \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 2ye^{y^2}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $\mathbf F$ is not conservative on $\mathbb R^2.$

- For the vector field $\mathbf G,$ we have $P = 3x^2 - y^2$ and $Q = 4 - 2xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = -2y, \qquad  \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = -2y.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on $\mathbb R^2,$ we conclude that $\mathbf{G}$ is conservative on $\mathbb R^2.$

- For the vector field $\mathbf H,$ we have $P = xy^2 + 1$ and $Q = 2xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 2xy, \qquad \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 2y.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $\mathbf{H}$ is not conservative on $\mathbb R^2.$

questions.problem:
Let $f:U\to R$ be continuously differentiable on an open set $U⊆R$ such that $f(a)=b$ and ${f}^{′}(a)\ne 0$ for $a\in U.$ Which of the following statements **must** be true?

- The function $f$ is invertible on $U.$
- The inverse ${f}^{-1}$ is continuously differentiable on $U.$
- The derivative of ${f}^{-1}$ is given by ${({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The inverse function theorem for single-variable functions states the following:

*If $f:U\to R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U⊆R,$ $f(a)=b$ and ${f}^{′}(a)\ne 0$ for $a\in U,$ then*

- *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$*

- *${f}^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and*

- *the derivative of ${f}^{-1}$ is given by* 

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(b))}\,.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the theorem, the function $f$ must be invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$ which could be smaller than $U.$ 

For example, the function $f(x)=2{x}^{4}$ satisfies the conditions of the inverse function theorem for $U=(-2,2)$ and $a=-1.$ However, $f(x)$ is not invertible on the entire set $U,$ only on a subset of $U.$

- Statement II is false. According to the theorem, the function${f}^{-1}$ must be continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ which could be smaller than $U.$

- Statement III is true. According to the theorem, we must have ${({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u{v}^{2} \\ {u}^{2}+2v\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=u{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}+2v.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2uv \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & 2uv \\ 2u & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & ={v}^{2}\cdot 2-2uv\cdot 2u \\  & =2{v}^{2}-4{u}^{2}v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2{v}^{2}-4{u}^{2}v & =0 \\ v(2v-4{u}^{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $v(2v-4{u}^{2})=0$ defines the line $v=0,$ i.e., the $u$-axis, and the parabola $v=2{u}^{2}$ in the $uv$-plane.

choices.value: The critical points lie on the lines $u=-2v$ and $u=v.$
The critical points lie on the line $v=0$ and on the parabola $v=2{u}^{2}.$
The critical points lie on the parabola $u={v}^{2}.$
The critical points lie on the line $v=0$ and on the hyperbola ${v}^{2}-{u}^{2}.$
The critical points lie on the line $u=2v.$

answer_fields.correct_value: The critical points lie on the line $v=0$ and on the parabola $v=2{u}^{2}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-6y \\ x+3y\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=2x+-y$ and $v(x,y)=x+3y.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-6 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -6 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 3-(-6)\cdot 1 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

$$

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=2x-y$ and $v(x,y)=x+2y.$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-1 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=-x+7y$ and $v(x,y)=3x-y.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Inverse Function Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
![](images/6e/6e97c59a7c736ec70142bc402566385fc2cd9c6aa78e304d70cefab1027078c1.png)

The function $f(x),$ whose graph is shown above, has a stationary point at $x=0$ and is continuously differentiable everywhere except at $x=-3.$ Which of the following statements **must** be true according to the inverse function theorem?

- $f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $x=-3$

- $f^{-1}(y)$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $y=0$

- The derivative of $f^{-1}(y)$ at $y=-1.1$ equals $\dfrac{1}{f'(2)}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The inverse function theorem for single-variable functions states the following:

*If $f: U \to \Bbb R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R,$ $f(a) = b$ and $f'(a)\neq 0$ for $a\in U,$ then*

- *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$*

- *$f^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and*

- *the derivative of $f^{-1}$ is given by* 

$$
\left(f^{-1}\right)'(b) = \dfrac{1}{f'(a)} =\dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(b))}\,.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that $f$ is not continuous at $x = -3.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.

- Statement II is also false. Notice that $y = 0 = f(0).$  However, the function $f$ does *not* satisfy the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x = 0$ since $f'(0) = 0.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.

- Statement III is true. Notice that $y = -1.1 = f(2),$ and the function $f$ satisfies the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x = 2.$ Indeed,

- $f$ is continuously differentiable on an open set containing $x=2,$ for example, $(0,4),$ and

- the derivative of $f$ is nonzero at $x = 2,$ i.e., $f'(2) \neq 0.$

Therefore, by the inverse function theorem, the derivative of $f^{-1}(y)$ at $y = -1.1$ equals $\dfrac{1}{f'(2)}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ where $\mathbf T$ is defined as 

![](images/4a/4a20bc6cf78708f70fb1a696b9dc5971feef974df6429fa4169f82881c6d22e0.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

![](images/66/665b1e0592a0b9d1528b4dedd05eb0410f5b08e70c7b7e1dbd9089b11bf797e6.png)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $\mathbf T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}  = 0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v) = u^2-v^2$ and $y(u,v) = u+v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & -2v \\ \,\,1\, & \,\,\,\,1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(u+v).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} =0.$ So, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2(u+v) & =0 \\ u & =-v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the critical points of $T$ consist of those points that lie on the line $u=-v$  in the $uv$-plane.

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}(x,y)\to(u(x,y), v(x,y))$ is given by

![](images/26/2614cbd879ea1014caf69d1239b69e81ebefcc76b8946962092cb83cc96dc987.png)

Find the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

![](images/9b/9b0ee6271962e3ede406351f05d805ae60f4b37ce5a45489b117ab3786ed3c23.png)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given $\mathbf T^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ using the relation

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y) = e^{x+y}$ and $v(x,y) = e^{x-y}.$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & ={e}^{x-y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+y} & {e}^{x+y} \\ {e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x+y}\cdot (-{e}^{x-y})-{e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x-y} \\  & =-{e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x-y}-{e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x-y} \\  & =-2\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x-y} \\  & =-2uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2uv}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Switching Two Rows
questions.problem: Suppose $C$ is a $9\times 9$ matrix and $det(C)=-69.$ The matrix $D$ is obtained from $C$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{5}↔{R}_{8}$ (switching the fifth and the eighth rows). What is the value of $det(D)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since swapping any two rows changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite sign, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D) & =-det(C) \\  & =-(-69) \\  & =69.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot C)={k}^{n}\cdot det(C).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=-3$ and $n=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(3C) & =(-3)^{4}\cdot det(C) \\  & =81\cdot 5 \\  & =405.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+5{R}_{3}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

Therefore, we only have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =-det(A) \\  & =-(23) \\  & =-23.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 1 & 8 & -1 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 1 & 8 & -1 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Multiplying a Matrix by a Scalar
canonical_examples.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $4\times4$ matrix and $\det(A)=5.$ What is the value of $\det(2A)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A)={k}^{n}\cdot det(A).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=2$ and $n=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(2A) & ={2}^{4}\cdot det(A) \\  & =16\cdot 5 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation $R_4 \leftrightarrow R_5$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation $R_6:= 4 R_6$ involves multiplying a row by $4,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $4$ as well.

- The operation $R_8:= R_8 - \dfrac{1}{2} R_7$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by $4$ as well. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =4\cdot (-det(A)) \\  & =-4det(A) \\  & =-4\cdot 5 \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$
